->**Decorative Marbled Paper**<-

This page features a hand-marbled design, a technique frequently used in historical bookbinding for endpapers—the sheets glued to the inside of the covers—or for the outer covers themselves. 

The pattern shown here is known as a **snail** or **curl** pattern. It was created by floating mineral pigments on a bath of thickened water (usually treated with carrageenan or gum tragacanth) and using a stylus or comb to swirl the colors into these distinct circular shapes. Once the pattern was set on the liquid, a sheet of paper was carefully laid on top to "pick up" the design.

The palette consists of:
*   **Blue-gray** tones
*   **Ochre-yellow** accents
*   **Terracotta-orange** swirls

<note>Marbling was both a decorative and practical choice; the complex patterns helped mask the glue stains and wear that naturally occur at the hinges and edges of a book over centuries of use.</note>

<summary>This page consists of a decorative hand-marbled paper featuring a "snail" pattern in blue, yellow, and orange, used as a traditional bookbinding element.</summary>

# Jordanus Brunus.

This couplet reflects Bruno's belief in the "divine spark" within human reason and his pursuit of the infinite mysteries of the universe. # INTRODUCTION.

**T**o see, summoned from the abyss of centuries—from the stench and mold of libraries, and indeed from the pyre, like a phoenix from its ashes—a deep and subtle intellect reborn into the divine light, rich and daring, a harbinger and prophet of truly <term>speculative knowledge</term> <note>In this context, "speculative" refers to high metaphysical philosophy that seeks to understand the fundamental nature of reality through reason rather than just observation.</note> (at least that which is steeped and impregnated with the consciousness of eternity and necessity), cannot fail to delight anyone who, in the diligent and rigorous studies of our own century, recognizes and greets the dawn of a new age. This remains true even if our age sometimes strays into precipitous extremes, seems to stiffen, or expires in pure formulas, and regardless of how much the stubborn defenders and praisers of the fading past may slander or despise it. For the living remembrance of the <term>Nolan philosopher</term> <note>original: "Nolano filosofo." This refers to Giordano Bruno, who was born in Nola, Italy.</note> still transports us back to a century where—thanks to the labors of strong and frank intellects, of profound and tranquil seekers, among whom it suffices to name Luther, Melanchthon, Hutten, Erasmus, Pomponazzi, Cesalpino, and Pico <note>The author lists major figures of the Reformation and Renaissance humanism who challenged medieval dogma.</note>—the mists of ignorance and of a blind, superstitious surrender to the spells of tradition were beginning to disperse. It was a time stimulated by the desire to return home, after a long and ignominious exile, to the ancestral fields and lands of the human mind, and by the necessity to reconcile the results of philosophical inquiries with those of revelation. Meanwhile, as the "ups and downs" of this blossoming world would have it, ignorance, fanaticism, and cunning labored to delay or oppress those noble efforts of <term>emancipation</term> <note>The author views the Renaissance and Bruno's philosophy as a movement to free the human mind from intellectual and religious constraints.</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the intellectual rediscovery of Giordano Bruno, framing him as a prophetic figure whose "rebirth" from historical obscurity mirrors the dawn of a new philosophical era. The author places Bruno alongside key Renaissance and Reformation thinkers who sought to liberate human reason from superstition and tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Giordano Bruno, Nolan philosopher, Renaissance philosophy, Reformation, intellectual emancipation, metaphysics, humanism</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal introduction to Giordano Bruno's works. The previous page established the historical context of the Renaissance and Reformation, positioning Bruno among the great thinkers of that era who fought against ignorance. This page focuses on the specific justification for this new edition of his rare Italian writings.</meta>

We hope, therefore, that our labor in collecting these few very rare Italian works of Giordano Bruno *) will be all the more welcomed by impartial and unprejudiced observers, especially since he has always been judged, even by his own adversaries, as a man endowed with a great and singular genius. He has been admired by sincere seekers of truth and was frequently and usefully accepted—and put to profit—by <term>Gassendi</term>, <term>Cartesio</term> <note>René Descartes</note>, and <term>Leibnizio</term> <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz</note>; **) moreover, our own age, having frankly overcome the obstacles to free inquiry, is better suited than any other to justly appreciate the endurance of the human mind in its search for a resting place and harbor against the storms of this ever-shifting and unstable sensible world, and perhaps even more against the quicksands and rocks within our own hearts. Indeed, it seems a duty owed to every martyr of truth to retrial their case <note>The author uses the legal metaphor "ritrattar la sua lite" to suggest a modern reassessment of the charges and condemnation Bruno faced.</note>, so that the world may be awakened and reinvigorated, and not allow ignorance and cowardice to steal away what privileged and strong intellects have won for it—that divine heritage, that <term>palladium</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the Palladium was a statue that protected Troy; here it refers to a fundamental safeguard of knowledge or liberty.</note>, which is never lost except through guilty neglect and wicked weakness.

Now, although—especially since <term>Jacobi</term> and <term>Scelling</term> <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, a central figure in German Idealism. The author uses an Italianized spelling.</note> have refreshed the memory of this rare genius among us Germans—everything that could serve to exalt and defend him against his adversaries (who, by burning him, defamed themselves rather than him) has been diligently searched for, nevertheless, the authentic documents themselves—namely, his works—have been lacking until now; both because of their great rarity...

only two manuscript ones, although important—those I mean, **On the Cause, Principle, and Unity**, and **On the Infinite Universe and Worlds**—were in very few hands, both because even the most fortunate men of letters were not always accurate and scrupulous, or perhaps calm and impartial enough to value them properly. Since, therefore, with this work we offer his writings to the public without entangling ourselves in uselessly long extracts—which are otherwise common in compendiums of the history of philosophy—we shall provide only a sketch of his external and internal life; that is, of his vicissitudes and fates, and of his manner of being and thinking. In this undertaking, where it might happen that in such an abundance of literary reports one or another might slip by, we will console ourselves with this: that since subsequent writers have for the most part, as is customary, only copied their predecessors without really advancing the understanding of the whole (except perhaps by adding one more title), such merit is not to be too greatly exaggerated or sought after. Meanwhile, so as not to fail entirely in what is required in such works, and lest it be thought that we wish to disguise some negligence or lack of practice on our part, here is appended in a note all the literary apparatus concerning Bruno. *)

<page-num>VI</page-num>

**Philotheus Giordano Bruno**, or **Bruno**, shares this common trait with the majority of extraordinary men: just as the roots of a tree spread out hidden in the ground while its flowers and fruits bloom cheerfully in the air and light, so too are his origins and birth as unknown as the beginnings of his education and culture. Consequently, we know nothing of them, except that he was born in **Nola**, in the kingdom of **Naples**, in the second half of the sixteenth century. For what *Lessmann* <note>Friedrich Lebrecht Lessmann, a writer who published a somewhat satirical account of Bruno.</note> tells us—though seemingly as a joke, referring to a certain "sterile and disorganized Giordano"—concerning his youth and precocious talent, his caustic responses, and his defense of a certain **Brother Joachim** <note>original: "Fra Giachimo"; likely a reference to the mystic Joachim of Fiore, whose ideas influenced Bruno.</note> and his beloved, the daughter of a contractor, at the expense of

<page-num>VII</page-num>
<meta>Catchword: ciò</meta>

N. D. <note>Likely an abbreviation for "Nostro Domenico" (Our Dominican) or "Nolano," referring to Bruno.</note>, of his patroness Silvia Gandini, a Roman woman, etc. is at most a story that is not too poorly invented, or rather a poetic construction of this figure. Setting aside **that** <note>original: "ciò"; this refers to the catchword from the previous page.</note>, and considering that Bruno's literary labors lasted thirteen years at most, and his imprisonment seven, which makes twenty, and that he must have been twenty years old or thereabouts when he wrote his ***Candlemaker*** <note>original: "Candelajo"; a comedic play written by Bruno and published in 1582.</note>; considering furthermore the youthful ardor that almost all his works breathe, I am led to believe that his birth falls roughly in the first decade of the second half of the sixteenth century <note>approximately 1550–1560</note>, and that he therefore lived forty to fifty years; which his portrait, appearing quite youthful, seems to confirm, although for that very reason it might have been painted during his youth.

His early studies, according to what he himself says in the book ***Of the Heroic Frenzies***, were from the beginning poetic, wavering between **Thalia** <note>The Muse of Comedy.</note> and **Melpomene** <note>The Muse of Tragedy.</note>, and thereafter, both by inclination and love, they became philosophical; certainly accurate, broad, and profound, as his writings attest. Until, having become a **Dominican**, and being annoyed and angered by the vile hypocrisy of this and other monastic orders, he turned from time to time back to the neglected, more serene worship of the Muses. Here then is the character of a generous spirit who, having turned and gathered within himself, ecstatic in the intuition of the original beauty and truth, seeks to fix its image; and while he pours it out from his breast, he is compelled to defend it strenuously and save it both from the adversary ever-awake in his own heart, and from the impure breath of the external world. Now, the fact that he was a Dominican fits both the spirit of his century and his philosophical studies, as the clergy were the primary custodians of knowledge in that age; and his later apostasy <note>The formal abandonment of a religious belief or order.</note> so well suits the frankness and breadth of his genius, that even if **Échard** <note>original: "Eccardo"; referring to Jacques Échard, a Dominican historian.</note> (*On the Writers of the Order of Preachers*, Vol. II. p. 188) denies it by saying:
> “If he had been of us, he certainly would have remained with us both in lifestyle and in sentiments” <note>original Latin: "si fuisset ex nobis, utique nobiscum permansisset et convictu et sensibus"</note>

VIII

It seems, in fact, to be a hierarchical consequence which—having strayed from intellectual sovereignty into secular usurpation—made a show of repudiating and refusing to recognize apostates by its own right, rather than out of factual truth. Indeed, it is very probable, following a hint from Schioppius <note>Kaspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a scholar who reported on Bruno’s trial and execution.</note>, who accuses him of heresy regarding transubstantiation and the virginity of Our Lady <note>original: "N. D." for "Nostra Donna" (The Virgin Mary).</note>, that this was precisely the reason for his abandoning the order and his homeland at the same time in 1580. He went to Geneva where, being no less frank and vehement—even a bitter critic of <term>Calvinism</term> <note>The Protestant theological system of John Calvin, which dominated Geneva at the time.</note> and other dogmas and concepts—he remained for only two years. From there, he passed to Lyon, Toulouse, and Paris. There, because the authority, authenticity, and truth of the <term>Aristotelian system</term> <note>The traditional philosophical framework based on Aristotle's works, which served as the foundation for university education in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> *) had already been modified, challenged, and shaken by others—a system in which, though misunderstood, a pedantic and servile "philosophical salvation" was still sought—Bruno, a profound scholar and philosopher, did not merely approve of that trend. Rather, he waged war against it in his own frank, courageous, and original way. He was less concerned with the authenticity or potential forgery of the majority of the Aristotelian books than he was with their internal inconsistency and the inconveniences that arose from wandering reflection and the confusion of logical truth with physical truth.

A genius so sovereign, lively, and noble could not help but despise and hate the stupid ignorance and pedantry, the cowardice, the coarseness, and the viciousness of his century, which it seems he quickly came to know. Truly, no sharper or more caustic lye could be prepared for the clumsiness and arrogance, the baseness and superstition, than that which is contained in

<margin>1582.</margin>
***The Candlemaker*** <note>original: "Il Candelajo".</note>. A comedy by Bruno the Nolan, Academician of no academy, known as "The Annoyed One." Paris, by Guillaume Julien, 1582. Reprinted in 1589. Translated into French under the title: *Boniface and the Pedant*.

Here, lustful women, sailors, soldiers, and cunning adventurers deceive greedy, superstitious, and lecherous old men. This comedy possesses the temper and tone of that age; while still a follower of the style of **Plautus** and **Terence** <note>Classical Roman playwrights whose works defined the structure of Western comedy.</note>, it draws general characters suited to various social classes and professions. In Italy, these characters gradually changed into those <term>fixed masks</term> <note>Known as "maschere," these were stock characters like Harlequin or Pantaloon who appeared in different plays with consistent traits.</note> that we see in the works of **Goldoni**, **Gozzi**, and others. The characters—as well as the humor and the language—are unrestrained and brazen. They reflect, on one hand, the national customs and manners of that time, and on the other, a powerful intellect that is not submerged in the dregs of society but, by virtue of a frank, sublime, and detached perspective, lashes out at them and annihilates them. The situations are quite ridiculous. Here, foulness and obscenity are indeed peddled as pastimes, jests, and witticisms. However, for those who would sooner blame a foul and low soul than a misguided taste, we would ask them to remember that, as the poet says, the world provides the chapters of the book. The comic force and virtue, while it allows fools to thrash and destroy one another, has not for that reason lost the key to the purer and more sublime world of the Idea. In the face of that higher sphere, the lower world sinks away—or rather, the higher sphere merely holds back and ignores the lower. Finally, in such privileged high intellects, the elements are always greatly contested and strongly strained; the hidden mastery of their nature is more vigorous, for without it, the process and labor of development would be weak, and the product would be meager, commonplace, and null.

In this context, the **mnemonic art** <note>A system of techniques used to improve and assist the memory, often involving mental "places" and "images."</note> of **Raimondo Lullio** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher and mystic who developed a complex system of logic known as the "Great Art" (Ars Magna) to unify all knowledge.</note> offered itself conveniently to him. While wanting to provide a table of categories or fundamental notions of human knowledge, it actually succeeded in being an artificial concatenation—a conscious and deliberate association of logical ideas for <term>heuristic</term> <note>The process of discovery or problem-solving.</note> and <term>eristic</term> <note>The art of philosophical debate or argument, particularly for the sake of victory in discussion.</note> use, consistent with the chivalrous character of the sciences of that time. Embracing this art with his characteristic fervor, turning and re-turning it in his spirit, **Bruno** treated and represented it in such varied ways, and transformed it into such diverse images and figures, that although his kindred and connected metaphysical ideas would flash through, it nonetheless frequently smothered and obscured them, so that his work is not always clear or simple. Moreover, with these various mnemonic essays, he almost always announced his lectures given at various academies, which he frequented during his continuous travels.

By **Shadows of Ideas**, he means the copies or figures of truth and goodness reflected in the senses or in reason. These are called "shadows" because they are not, and cannot be, absolute knowledge—since the first and supreme substance is not knowable, though the **soul of the universe** <note>Also known as the *Anima Mundi*, a concept suggesting that the entire universe is a living, spiritual entity.</note> is—but are merely traces and footprints of light, or intelligibility. Now, having distinguished between physical and ideal shadows—the former referring to sensual things, the latter to being in the universe—he argues that the series of things begins from that which exists in and for itself, most truly, and loses itself in that which is almost nothing: the same, the eternal, outside of which everything is infinite number (matter). The art of thinking is to depict within oneself, through **internal writing**, that which nature represents externally with **external writing**; it is to welcome the writing of nature into oneself, copying it and making the internal writing effective in the external world. Therefore, the principle of the universe and the principle of the human mind are one and the same. How often he brushes against the truth! By <term>seals</term> <note>In Bruno's system, "seals" (sigilli) are complex mnemonic devices—mental images or diagrams—used to organize knowledge and trigger memory.</note> he means symbolic mnemonic notes for certain combinations and strings of ideas, such as a field, sky, chain, tree, forest, etc. The *Seal of Seals* classifies elementary concepts, provides cautions for their use, and methods for weaning the mind away from material things; it reveals four internal governors of intellectual acts: love, art, magic, and mathematics. It also identifies four primary objects: light, color, figure, and form, to be considered metaphysically, physically, logically, and morally. He then develops the form of the physical and intellectual world from the primary "super-essential" form—all of it quite arbitrarily!

Far more interesting documents of his deep mind and penetrating spirit, however, are the three subsequent writings where he laid out his metaphysical system. All three breathe a generous and noble ardor and enthusiasm for divine things, a firm contempt for the ignorant and malicious rabble, a very clear awareness of his divine mission and his sincere will, and an accurate, sincere respect for every generous and pure effort to promote the knowledge of truth—and finally, a joy at having tracked it down. XV

Without detracting in any way from the extract of Jacobi <note>Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi (1743–1819), a philosopher who helped rediscover Bruno's work in the 18th century.</note> copied by Buhle, or from that of Rixner, we will provide a summary overview of his thought; if this overview lacks completeness, let the original works themselves supply it.

The great problem of all philosophy—that is, the reconciliation or composition of the apparent contrast between the infinite and finite, the ideal and real, freedom and necessity, or however this general gap is expressed from various points of reflection—was also the one whose solution occupied the Nolan <note>Giordano Bruno was often called "the Nolan" because he was born in Nola, near Naples.</note>. He also felt very clearly the danger to which the untamed flame of freedom on one hand, and the strength of a fresh and healthy conception or intuition on the other, exposed him perhaps more than any other: namely, either to thin out, weaken, and volatilize matter, destroying it and transforming it into a logical monochrome, or to plunge, harden, and stiffen the spirit.

Wherefore he, knowing well that playing with geometry is one thing and verifying with nature is another, understood that one must not divide with reason that which is undivided according to nature and truth; \*) that the most absolute act and the most absolute power cannot be understood by the intellect except by way of negation <note>original: "modo di negazione"; a philosophical approach where the ultimate reality is described by what it is not, rather than what it is.</note>, and that to know the deepest mysteries of nature, one must investigate the maximum and the minimum, the oppositions and the repugnanze <term>repugnances: the natural resistance or opposition between forces or elements</term> in all things, \*\*) since where there is difference, it arises from unity and returns to it.

To keep this unity whole and intact—this intimate and tenacious bond of nature and the mind—he carefully separated what was finite within the intuition or concept of the infinite and the One, to which neither time, space, motion, nor rest apply, except insofar as all these categories are identified and resolved within the infinite and one universe. The universe is one, infinite, immobile; because there is only...

\*) *On Cause, Principle, and Unity*, preface at fol. 243.
\*\*) Cf. *On the Heroic Frenzies* at fol. 382 ff.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical summary of Giordano Bruno's metaphysics, specifically focusing on the nature of the One/the Universe and the distinction between principles and causes.</meta>

XVI

...an absolute power and only one absolute act, only one soul of the world, only one matter or body, only one thing and one substance—that is, the highest and best, incomprehensible, undeterminable, without end and without limits, unbegotten, and indestructible. It is not matter, because it has no determined form; it is not form, because it does not form a particular substance; being the "all" and the "one," it is not composed of parts. In the universe, everything is a center; the center is everywhere and the circumference is nowhere <note>A famous philosophical paradox used to describe infinity: if the universe is infinite, any point can be considered its center, and it can have no outer boundary or circumference.</note>, and vice versa. 

Since the first and supreme substance is not knowable, we instead know the "soul of the world." This soul was called the "mover" or "stirrer of the universe" by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers and harmony were the basis of reality.</note>, the "smith of the world" by the Platonists, and the <term>internal craftsman</term> <note>original: "artefice interno"; Bruno's term for the divine force that shapes nature from the inside out, rather than as an external creator.</note> by Bruno. It is the constitutive formal principle of the universe and of everything contained within it; its first and primary, real and proper faculty is the universal intellect. The soul of the universe, insofar as it animates and gives form, is an intrinsic and formal part of the universe; but insofar as it directs and governs, it is not a "part," and is considered a cause rather than a principle. 

*Principle* <note>original: "Principio"</note> is that which intrinsically contributes to the constitution of things and remains within the result, such as matter and form, which remain in the finished compound, or the elements from which a thing is composed and into which it eventually dissolves. 

*Cause* <note>original: "Causa"</note> is that which contributes to the production of things from the outside and exists apart from the composition—such as the "efficient cause" <note>The agent that brings something about.</note> and the "end" <note>The purpose or goal for which a thing is made.</note> toward which the produced thing is directed. 

An *extrinsic cause*, acting as an efficient cause, is not part of the compounds or the things produced. An *intrinsic cause* exists insofar as it does not work upon matter from the outside, but within the very act of its operation. The *formal cause* is the "ideal reason." 

There are three kinds of intellect: the divine, which *is* everything; this worldly intellect, which *makes* everything; and the other particular intellects <note>Individual human or animal minds.</note>, which *become* everything. It is necessary that between these extremes we find this middle ground, which is the true efficient cause—not only extrinsic, but also intrinsic. — It [is]

<meta>catchword: It [is]</meta>

<summary>This page defines Bruno's concept of a singular, infinite substance and distinguishes between "principles" (internal components) and "causes" (external or governing forces). It introduces the "soul of the world" as the internal craftsman that shapes all existence.</summary>
<keywords>soul of the world, universal intellect, principle vs cause, efficient cause, formal cause, internal craftsman, infinity, Giordano Bruno, Pythagoreanism, Platonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the summary of Giordano Bruno's ontological system. After discussing the "Internal Craftsman" and the Soul of the World on the previous page, the text now transitions into a detailed breakdown of the relationship between Form and Matter as the two essential "geniuses" or types of substance.</meta>

->XVII<-

...it is necessary to recognize two kinds of substance in nature: one which is **form**, the other which is **matter**; because it is necessary that there be a <term>most substantial act</term> <note>In this context, "act" (atto) refers to the state of being "actual" or fully realized, as opposed to just being potential.</note>, in which resides the active power of everything; and also a power and a subject, in which there is no less <term>passive power</term> <note>The capacity to be acted upon or to receive form.</note> of everything. In the former lies the power to act; in the latter, the power to be acted upon. It is a kind of subject from which, with which, and in which nature carries out its operation, its work, and which is formed by nature into so many forms, presenting to the eye of contemplation such a variety of species. *Matter has no natural form of its own, but can receive all forms through the operation of the active agent, the principle of nature; it has no absolute form. Nature works from the center, so to speak, of its subject or matter, which is entirely formless.* That same relationship and regard that the form of art has toward its own material, according to the proper proportion, the form of nature has toward its matter. In nature, while forms vary infinitely and succeed one another, the matter remains always the same. Thus do seed, grass, ear of grain, bread, <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "chilo"; a milky fluid of lymph and fats formed in the small intestine during digestion, used here to show the constant transformation of matter.</note>, blood, seed, earth, stone, etc., follow one another. Only the outward forms change and are even annihilated, because they are not the things themselves, but *of* the things; they are not substances, but <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color or size) that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist, unlike its "substance."</note> and circumstances of substances. All things are animated; every thing is in every thing, because—since the spirit, or the soul, or the universal form is in all things—from everything, everything can be produced. According to substance, the whole is one. Matter, in order to be actually everything that it can be, possesses all measures, all kinds of figures and dimensions; and because it possesses them all, it possesses none of them: because that which is so many different things cannot be any one of those particular things. It is fitting for that which is "all" to exclude every particular being. Nothing is constant, firm, eternal, and worthy of being considered a principle, except for matter. It alone is the substantial principle, that...

<summary>This page explores the relationship between eternal matter and changing forms, arguing that while specific objects (accidents) perish, the underlying matter is the only eternal, substantial principle that contains all possibilities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of matter and form. On the previous page, Bruno established that matter is a permanent substance that underlies all change. Here, he elevates the concept of matter from a mere physical building block to a metaphysical principle that is "pregnant" with all possible forms, eventually leading to his core thesis: the unity of all things in the "Soul of the World."</meta>

->XVIII<-

...which always is and always remains. Theologians take the meaning of matter according to how it is the subject of natural things, and they do not consider that matter is understood by others as being common to both the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought, ideas, or spirit, as opposed to the physical world.</note> and the <term>sensible world</term> <note>The physical world that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, as they say, taking the meaning according to an analogous equivocation. The principle which is called matter can be considered in two ways: first as a <term>potency</term> <note>The capacity or potential to become something else.</note>, and second as a subject. Insofar as it is potency, there is no thing in which it cannot be found, in some way and according to its own nature. Common potency is divided into active and passive. Passive potency can be considered absolutely—that which *is*, *can be*—and this corresponds to active potency in such a way that one cannot exist without the other in any way; the one implies the other, and by positing one, you posit the other. Everyone attributes this to the first natural principle, which is everything that can be; and it would not be "everything" if it could not *be* everything; in this principle, therefore, <term>act</term> <note>Actualization or reality; the state of being fully realized.</note> and potency are the same thing. The universe is all that can be, by virtue of the same species and principal members and the containment of all matter, to which nothing is added and from which nothing of its total and unique form is lacking. But the universe is not already everything it can be in terms of the specific differences, modes, properties, and individuals; therefore, it is nothing other than a shadow of the first act and first potency; and for this reason, in the universe, potency and act are not absolutely the same thing. Absolute matter is act and form; it is both the power to be and being itself. If she is formless, she is so like a pregnant woman who carries the living seed within her. In the <term>soul of the world</term> <note>A vitalist concept where the entire universe is viewed as a single living organism with a governing spirit.</note>, which is the form and power of the whole, all things are one. This unity is the premise and the goal of all philosophy. True science is the knowledge of the one in the all, and of the all in the one.

The infinite is not an object of the senses. Truth is in the sensible object as if in a mirror; in reason, by way of argument and discourse; in the intellect, by way of prin- <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing "principles."</note>

<summary>Bruno defines matter as a divine potentiality that is "pregnant" with all forms, arguing that in the First Principle (God/Nature), what can be and what is are identical. He concludes that the ultimate goal of philosophy is to recognize the unity of all things—the "One in the All."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s metaphysical argument regarding the nature of the universe. While the previous page discussed matter as a "potency" or potential that is identical with "act" in the first principle (God), this page applies that logic to the physical cosmos. Bruno argues that if God is infinite power, His creation must be an infinite effect, leading to the conclusion that the universe is boundless and contains an infinite number of worlds.</meta>

->XIX<-

...beginning or conclusion; in the mind in its own living form. 

If the world is finite, and outside the world there is nothing, where is the world? It would be something that cannot be found. God, being without dimension, cannot be the location of a thing that has dimension. If beyond the surface [of the world] there is nothing, this is a <term>vacuum</term> <note>In Bruno's time, the existence of a "void" or "vacuum" was a major point of debate; he argues here that a finite world surrounded by "nothing" is logically impossible.</note> and empty, without mode or limit; which is more difficult to imagine than an infinite and immense universe. Just as the vacuum has no fitness to receive, it should have even less fitness to push the world away. If it is good that this world exists, it is good that that vacuum be filled; therefore, that space in which a body can exist and which can contain something, and in whose bosom are the <term>atoms</term> <note>Tiny, indivisible particles that Bruno believed were the building blocks of all matter.</note>. Therefore, the universe will be of infinite dimension, and the worlds will be innumerable. By the logic of the innumerable degrees of perfection, which must express the incorporeal divine excellence in a corporeal way, there must be innumerable individuals—which are these <term>great animals</term> <note>Bruno famously viewed planets and stars not as dead rocks, but as living, ensouled beings or "great animals" moving through space.</note>, of which one is this earth. For the containment of these innumerable [worlds], an infinite space is required. 

The divine goodness and efficacy cannot be idle. **The universe is all infinite, because it has no margin, limit, nor surface; it is not totally infinite, because each part of it is finite, and of the innumerable worlds, each is finite. God is all infinite, because he excludes every limit from himself, and every one of his attributes is one and infinite; but he is totally infinite, because he is entirely in the whole world and in each of its parts infinitely and totally.** One who denies the infinite effect denies the infinite power. Since the universe is infinite and immobile, there is no need to seek its <term>motor</term> <note>The "Prime Mover" in Aristotelian physics; Bruno argues that because the universe is everything, there is nothing outside of it to move it.</note>. Since the worlds contained within it are infinite, they all move by an internal principle, which is their own soul, and therefore it is vain to go investigating their extrinsic motor. These worldly bodies move in the <term>ethereal region</term> <note>The vast space beyond the Earth's atmosphere, thought by Bruno to be filled with a fluid-like substance called "ether" rather than being a vacuum.</note>, not fixed or nailed down. There are two active principles of motion: one finite, according to the logic of the finite subject, and this moves in time; the other infinite, according to...

<summary>Bruno argues for an infinite universe with innumerable worlds, asserting that a finite creation would contradict God's infinite power. He distinguishes between the universe's infinity (boundless but made of finite parts) and God's infinity (totally present in every part).</summary>

<page-num>XX</page-num>
<warning>Staining and foxing visible on the left side of the page.</warning>

...according to the principle of the soul of the world, or of the divinity, which is like the soul of the soul, which is entirely in everything and makes the soul be entirely in everything; and this moves in an instant. The infinite is immobile. Infinite motion and infinite rest coincide as one. <note>Bruno argues that for an infinite being or system, the fastest possible motion would appear as stillness because it would occupy all points simultaneously.</note> The earth is not absolutely in the center of the universe, but only in relation to this, our own region. Specific bodies do not have infinite motion, but a finite and determined motion around their own boundaries (just as, for example, our earth has four motions: namely, the <term>animal motion</term> <note>Bruno believed celestial bodies were living "animals" with internal souls that guided their movement.</note> of the center, the diurnal, the hemispheric, and the polar, or <term>colural</term> <note>original: "colurale"; referring to the colures, the two principal circles of the celestial sphere.</note>); but of the indeterminate and infinite there is neither finite nor infinite motion, and there is no difference of place or time. Of infinite bodies, none is heavy or light, because these qualities occur to the parts in so far as they tend toward their whole and the place of their conservation. <note>Bruno is suggesting that "weight" is not an absolute property, but a relative attraction between parts of a system—a precursor to the concept of gravity.</note> In infinite duration, which is eternity, hours are no longer than centuries. One is the heaven, the immense space, the womb, the universal container, the ethereal region through which everything moves and courses. There, innumerable stars, heavenly bodies, globes, suns, and earths are visibly seen, and infinite ones are reasonably argued to exist. Everything is one field, a general refuge. The order of the elements and worldly bodies is a dream and a most vain fantasy. —

This outline of the <term>Nolana metaphysics</term> <note>original: "metafisica Nolana"; referring to the philosophy of Giordano Bruno, who was known as "The Nolan" after his birthplace, Nola.</note> made here mostly with the philosopher's own expressed words—without, however, mixing in ethical or logical notions and maxims, and without altering or shadowing it with images such as those provided by his fertile and exuberant imagination (which he not infrequently pursued with abandon and loose reins)—will, we hope, spare us from the useless pain of defending it from the stain of atheism cast upon it by those who are both weak and malicious fanatics; instead, it will reveal to every unbiased person who chooses to follow the course of his thoughts, with what zeal and vigor he has excavated and severed from the dross of <term>scholastic sophistries</term> <note>The complex, logic-heavy academic style of the medieval universities which Bruno despised.</note> the idea of the universe as one...

<meta>This page transitions from the physical mechanics of Bruno’s infinite universe to the philosophical and psychological temperament of the man himself. It explores how his "infallible instinct" guided him toward a unified theory of existence, even when his methods seemed chaotic to his contemporaries.</meta>

<page-num>XXI</page-num>

...with what infallible instinct he mostly strikes, or skims close to the truth. The fact remains that he never ceases to draw upon the untainted, native brilliance, the sovereign power, and the eternal life of the idea and the mind, immersing and identifying himself within the innermost sanctuary of being. Thus, if he did not succeed in developing and expanding his entire system with that certain, analogous, or kindred method inherent to the vital process of the idea itself, perhaps his indomitable fervor and contentiousness are less to blame than the limits and measures prescribed to the human mind. For the mind does not approach the truth all at once; rather, as nature requires and the history of culture teaches, it identifies with it step by step—even though the foresight and anticipation of privileged geniuses, such as Bruno, surprises and dismays contemporaries as much as it cheers and blesses the prophets themselves. 

For if Bruno—within the Art of Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a philosopher who created a "logical machine" of rotating discs to combine concepts. Bruno was obsessed with this "Art," seeing it as a way to map the mind of God.</note>, which he cultivated so extensively and reproduced in so many forms—inserted or attached his own axiom (which was <term>Eleatic-Plotinian</term> <note>A fusion of the Eleatic school’s belief that "All is One" and Plotinus’s Neoplatonic theories of the soul's ascent to the divine.</note> all at once) regarding the universe and the One, the mind and the soul of the universe—*the One, Being, the Good, the Intellect, and the Soul of all things, or of the whole* <note>original Greek: "το ἐν, ὄν, ἀγαθον, ὁ νῦς, e ἡ ψυχη τῶν ὅλων, ossia τοῦ παντος"</note>—who would ever wish to deny that he, sensing the identity of the logical method and its object and content already took hold of it? Who could deny that he imagined and shaped it precisely within this "Art," though it was conceived in a broader and deeper sense? 

In this way, there already dawned in his mind the idea of an *organon* <note>In philosophy, an "organon" is a system of investigating the truth or a "tool" for knowledge, famously associated with Aristotle’s logic.</note> and of a truly speculative dialectic: one that, proceeding by its own motion, captures the unity of opposites, or fixes opposition and contrast within its own unity. If he, full of vital heat and still touched by the Hellenic breath, boldly lowered himself into the eternal, certain of being reborn there *) to a fresh new life, he strove to communicate and infuse this heat, to give pulse and breath to these noble notions...

---

*) See the first sonnet prefixed to the book *On the Infinite Universe and Worlds*. <note>original: "De l' infinito universo e mondi." This 1584 work is one of Bruno's most famous Italian dialogues.</note>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giordano Bruno’s philosophical temperament. ## XXII

...and pale fantasies of Aristotelian claims, who would not want to recognize in him that very person who was necessarily required by an age in which the torrent of life was freezing into traditional concepts, even though that age was destined to run vigorously toward the new goal of culture set by providence? And so his philosophy has been, is, and shall ever be a stimulus and spur to all those who do not allow themselves to be deceived or discouraged by an "obscurity" attributed to it—an obscurity that often seems to reside in the heads of his accusers rather than in his own writings, which are often not even read by them. 

For, should anyone perhaps wish to cite the abstract and negative nature of this Nolan philosophy <note>Giordano Bruno was often called "the Nolan" because he was born in Nola, Italy. His "Nolan philosophy" refers to his specific brand of Hermetic and Neoplatonic thought.</note> as proof of this opinion, let them first reflect that the flower of the human mind is never gathered without effort. Second—and this is more important—that, according to the laws of a doctrinal or scientific organism, the general abstract is always the base and the sprout from which concrete determinations and notions spring forth. Third, that every true speculation necessarily has a negative element, which is simultaneously skeptical and sometimes even polemical. 

And finally, consider the idea of the soul of the universe as a forming, vivifying, and internal artisan <note>Bruno viewed the "World Soul" (*anima mundi*) not as something outside of nature, but as an internal force that shapes matter from within, like an artist living inside their work.</note>, which shapes matter and form from within, just as the trunk pushes out branches from within. This is precisely a merit of this Nolan philosophy, a harbinger of Spinozism <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), which, like Bruno's, identified God with Nature, though in a more mathematical and "colder" way.</note>. However, in the cold abstraction of Spinozism, the liquefied gold of matter coagulates and congeals, so to speak, and individuality turns to stone—or rather, is entirely lost in the <term>absolute substance</term> <note>In Spinoza’s system, "Substance" is the fundamental reality (God/Nature); individual things are merely temporary "modes" or expressions of that one substance.</note>, outside of which the whole has no truth at all. 

In contrast, the Nolan philosophy provokes the mind to be active and free in itself. While remaining just and intimate with the achievements of the human mind in every age, and being an enemy of every perverse tendency, it presupposes and requires that same wisdom, that same effort from anyone who wishes to understand it—that is, to reproduce it and experience it from within. For the rest, let the attentive reader observe how our author never loses sight of the dyna- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("dinamica" or "dynamic"), likely continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page defends Bruno against charges of being "obscure" and "abstract," arguing that his philosophy of an internal, life-giving World Soul is a more vibrant precursor to Spinoza’s later monism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giordano Bruno’s philosophy against his critics. It then establishes the link between Bruno’s thought and the later philosophy of Baruch Spinoza.</meta>

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>

...the very substance of nature; what a living and profound combinatorial knowledge of ancient and contemporary philosophy he displays; and how, to such a healthy and solid contemplation, Peripatetic <note>Peripateticism refers to the followers of Aristotle, whose school in Athens featured a covered walkway (peripatos) where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note> idolatry could only be a negative and contemptible moment—an idolatry that, building on mere reputation, already presumed to know and grasp the truth. Therefore, however vehement and rude his polemic against Aristotle and his often stupid and stubborn followers may seem, it will nonetheless be recognized as excusable by anyone who reflects that he was attempting to rescue the rights of life from pure, dry abstractions and from the delusions and fantasies of sickly minds. 

With this, however, let readers be warned not to detract too much from the speculative merit of the <term>master of those who know</term> <note>original: *maestro di color che sanno*; a famous reference to Aristotle from Dante Alighieri's *Divine Comedy*.</note>, who among us Germans is beginning to be appreciated as a pillar of philosophy and the bridge from the Greeks to the moderns. He is valued for immersing the idea into the concrete and the particular, and for reconciling the whole and the parts, the positive and the negative; through motion and progress within opposites, he attempts to conquer the infinite within the realm of the finite. 

In this regard, if Aristotle’s speculation moves step-by-step, starting from empirical observations and pursuing them through their oppositions, and if, by contrast, Bruno fixes his gaze and holds firm to the primary principle, both nonetheless agree in taking account of the opposition of the minimum and the maximum. Thus, if the former concentrates himself less, the latter does not expand enough—or at least, in expanding, he sometimes loses himself indistinguishably in the "Whole." For this very reason, he is the precursor to Spinoza, though he is just as little an atheist as Spinoza was; rather, he is a <term>monotheist</term> <note>The author uses *monoteo* here to describe a "Monist" view—the belief that all of reality is one single substance—rather than traditional monotheism.</note> for whom the world vanishes and goes up in smoke before the unity of thought and extension.

But since we are certain that these few remarks given here regarding the relationship of <term>Brunism</term> with <term>Peripateticism</term> and <term>Spinozism</term> will suffice for every reader of sense and judgment well-versed in philosophy—and that, indeed, a further discussion, which does not even fit within this introduction, would not benefit the desi—

# XXVII

...frequented other academies in order to propagate his philosophy, which was opposed to the peripatetic <term>peripatetic: refers to the followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy dominated universities at the time; the name comes from the Greek word for "walking," as Aristotle often walked while teaching</term>. Indeed, his zeal—standing in opposition to the fanaticism of his adversaries, who were numerous everywhere—was enough to shorten his stays, so that there is no need to invent slanderous particular causes for his departures. He moved, then, to Marburg, where on July 25, 1586, he was matriculated as a student, though without obtaining permission to give lectures. *See Tennemann’s History of Philosophy, Vol. IX, p. 382.*

The authentic passage from the *Academic Annals of Marburg, Part II*, communicated to me by a friend from that place, is as follows:

->In the year of Christ our Savior 1586, on the Calends of July <note>July 1st</note>, by the unanimous consent of all the professors, Petrus Nigidius, Doctor of Laws and ordinary professor of moral philosophy, was elected Rector of the Academy of Marburg, under whose magistracy the following names of students were recorded in the matricula of the Academy.<-

Then follows, under number 8:

->Giordano the Nolan, a Neapolitan, Doctor of Roman Theology, July 25, year 86. Furthermore, when the power to publicly teach philosophy was denied to the same by me, with the consent of the philosophical faculty for grave reasons, he became so incensed that he insolently insulted me in my own house, as if I were acting in this matter against the law of nations, the custom of all German universities, and against all humanistic studies; and for that reason, he no longer wished to be considered a member of the Academy. Whereupon, his wish being easily granted, he was removed from the University roll by me.<-
<note>original Latin: "Anno Christi Salvatoris nostri MDLXXXVI... Jordanus Nolanus Neapolitanus... ex albo Universitatis per me exauctoratus est."</note>

Because of this, his name and rank were struck out, as were the words: *with the consent of the philosophical faculty*, though in such a way that the former were restored later, while the <unclear>aforementioned</unclear> words remained struck out. It appears, therefore, that at a later date, the academy chose to make a show of such a celebrated name.

# XXX

...whose principle is the concept of the minimum <term>minimum: the smallest possible unit of reality, which Bruno identified as both a physical atom and a spiritual monad.</term> combined with the maximum—the "one and all"—since, as the substance of things, it is of infinite magnitude; and within it rests the monad, the atom, and the soul of the universe, which is the base of everything: divinity, mother nature, and art. *On the Monad, Number, and Figure, a book following the five books on the minimum, the great, and measure. Item de innumerabilibus, immenso et infigurabili..."</note>

In that work, "*On the Innumerable,*" <note>original: "De innumerabilibus"</note> he begins with the primary intellectual goal of man; he proves the immeasurability of the world and that the center of the universe is everywhere, because space and the world are one—the heavens are an infinite ethereal space, and the planets are "earths." They all maintain themselves by their own gravity and are composed of the same elements: water and fire. The air is a spiritual substance, different from the ether, which is one with the vacuum, or absolute space, the heavens. The cause of the motion of the stars in the ethereal space and the vital principle is the soul. Everything tends toward the circle, and it all reduces to this: All is infinite and one.

From Frankfurt, he immediately went to Padua—no one knows for what reason. **Acidalius** <note>Valens Acidalius (1567–1595), a German scholar and critic.</note> rightly wonders at such an ill-considered step in a letter written to **Michael Forgatz**, page 10: "What is this man thinking, who dares to return to Italy, from which, as he once admitted, he fled as an exile? I am astonished, and I do not trust the rumor, even if I heard it from the most trustworthy sources." <note>original: "Ecquid hoc hominis, qui in Italiam audet redire, ex qua, ut ipse olim fatebatur, exul abiit? Miror, nec rumori fidem habeo, etiamsi ipsum a fide dignissimis habeam."</note> Consequently, discovered by the perpetual spies of the Inquisition, he was arrested in Venice, perhaps in the year 1595, and transported to Rome in 1598, where...

<meta>This page continues the account of Giordano Bruno’s life following his return to Italy. While the previous page focused on his revolutionary cosmological theories—such as the infinite universe and the plurality of worlds—this page details his final confrontation with the Roman Inquisition and his subsequent execution.</meta>

XXXI

For two years in the prisons of the Inquisition, he dragged out his recantation and mocked the authorities; because of this, on February 9, 1600, they published the sentence by which he was condemned. He then passed into the power of the ministers of justice under the Governor of Rome. There, after his biography was read aloud and his errors were noted along with the attempts to return him to the true faith, he was excommunicated and handed over to the secular authority, with the addition: "that he should be punished as mercifully as possible and without the shedding of blood!" <note>original: "ut quam clementissime et citra sanguinis effusionem puniretur!" This was a standard legal formula used by the Church; since the Church was forbidden from shedding blood, "mercy without blood" was a euphemism for execution by burning at the stake.</note> Bruno replied: *Perhaps you pronounce this sentence against me with greater fear than I receive it.* <note>original: "Maiori forsitan cum timore sententiam in me dicitis, quam ego accipiam." This famous retort highlights Bruno’s defiance in the face of death.</note> After another eight days as a prisoner in the secular jails, he was led to Campo de' Fiori <note>The "Field of Flowers," a square in Rome that served as a site for public executions.</note> opposite the Theater of Pompey and burned alive on February 17, 1600, although this is denied by Haym in *Notes on Rare Books, fol. 184* and Quadrio in *History and Reason of Every Poetry.* It is denied because Scioppio <note>Gaspar Scioppio was a scholar and convert to Catholicism who witnessed Bruno's execution and described it in a famous letter.</note> relates that when a crucifix was presented to him, Bruno gave it a fierce look, spitefully turned his gaze away, and died in his hardness and obstinacy; Scioppio ends his narrative quite sarcastically: *Thus, burned, he perished miserably, to report back, I believe, in those other worlds he imagined, how blasphemous and impious men are usually treated by the Romans. This, then, is the way in Rome that we usually proceed against impious men and monsters of this sort.* <note>original: "Sic ustulatus misere periit, renunciaturus, credo, in reliquis illis, quos finxit, mundis, quonam pacto homines blasphemi et impii a Romanis tractari solent. Hic itaque modus in Roma est, quo contra homines impios et monstra huiusmodi procedi a nobis solet."</note>

Among so many cited causes for this horrendous and cruel punishment—an eternal reproach and ignominy of a wolfish, or rather tiger-like, hierarchical tyranny—alleged by Zedler in his *Universal Lexicon*, Bayle, La Croze in *Interviews p. 284*, and Cromaziano p. 255, such as <term>atheism: the denial of the existence of God.</term>, <term>heresy: holding a belief at odds with established religious dogma.</term>, and <term>apostasy: the formal abandonment of one's religious faith.</term>, I believe one will not err in choosing above all that of stupid hierarchical fanaticism. This was directed not so much at holy religion itself, but rather at the authority of the Dominican order (of which, as we saw, he was a member) and of the papacy, which he always mocked, being a frank enemy of lies and a strenuous defender of the truth.

->XXXII<-

After his death, the following two books were also published:

> *Summary of the Metaphysical Terms of Giordano Bruno of Nola. To which is added his Practice of Descent, or Explanation of Being, from a manuscript by Raphael Eglinus Iconius of Turin. Marburg. From the workshop of Rudolph Hudtwelker, 1609. Octavo.* <note>original: "Summa terminorum metaphysicorum... Marpurgi Cattor." The term "8." refers to "Octavo," a standard book size of the period.</note>
>
> *The Art of Oratory, shared by Heinrich Alsted. Frankfurt, 1612. Octavo.* <note>original: "Artificium perorandi..." Heinrich Alsted was a famous German encyclopedist who preserved several of Bruno's works on logic and rhetoric.</note>

Other books of his, mentioned by himself—sometimes perhaps less accurately, so that they seem different from those we possess—are either unpublished manuscripts, or burned, or perhaps still hidden in the Roman archives. Here are the titles: *The Book of the Great Key*, which is perhaps one and the same as the book on the *Combinatoric Lamp*. — *The Book of Thirty Statues.* — *The Temple of Mnemosyne* (cited in the book *On the Composition of Images, Signs, and Ideas*) — *On the Soul.* — *On the Manifold Life of the World.* — *On the Acts of Nature.* — *On the Principles of Truth* — *On Astrology* — *On Physical Magic.* — *On the Sphere.* — Two others I do not find cited by any other man of letters, and they are: *Noah's Ark*, dedicated to Pope Pius V, cited in *The Ash Wednesday Supper* on page 149. — *The Purgatory of Hell* (cited in the same work on page 198).

It remains to give an account of our own labors spent on this edition. Having therefore had the texts copied—which were most courteously shared with us by the very learned Dresden librarian, Dr. **Ebert**, in whom literary Europe takes pride—and having cross-referenced them in cases of need with those of the Göttingen and Vienna libraries, we have first of all arranged them in chronological order, as indicated to us both by the course of the author's life and the hints given here and there by the author himself. In then providing a text that is as correct as possible, and of a style not entirely foreign to that century, the poor state of the original texts caused us no small amount of trouble. <note>Friedrich Adolf Ebert (1791–1834) was a pioneering German librarian and bibliographer known for his meticulous catalogs.</note>

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, detailing the linguistic and technical challenges of preparing Giordano Bruno’s works for a modern audience. It follows the previous page’s mention of the "labors spent on this edition."</meta>

XXXIII

...same <note>Referring to the manuscripts mentioned on the previous page.</note> [manuscripts] and their copies, the inconsistent **orthography** <term>orthography</term><note>The conventional spelling system of a language.</note> between ancient and modern, French and Italian, the very faulty or even absurd **punctuation**—or total lack thereof—in long, rambling sentences, the negligence of style, and the difference in the language of that age from that of today. It was therefore necessary to establish some principle regarding the spelling, which was so inconstant and variable. We chose to remove, for the sake of form, the useless and superfluous *h*—often kept due to ambiguity—in words like "man," "humor," "any," "to have," <note>original: "huomo", "humore", "alchuno", "havere"</note> and other words mostly of Latin origin. We also removed the *n* in "constant" <note>original: "constante"</note> and similar Latinate words, and the *y* and *x* in Latin and Greek terms, while changing *ph* to *f*.

Nonetheless, we have kept certain elements separate as a sign of their closer connection to their Latin source—which had not yet been altered by euphony—or for the sake of local custom and propriety. This includes the articles "of the" and "to the" <note>original: "de la", "a la"</note>, and conjunctions composed of prepositions and pronouns, such as "because," "since," "although," <note>original: "per che", "poi che", "ben che"</note> and others, as well as occasional adverbs. At the same time, we have removed a second consonant in certain words where it was introduced later and is not consistently preserved today; for it is a common observation that we write "on top," "near," "meanwhile," "on the," <note>original: "addosso", "appresso", "frattanto", "sulla"</note> etc., but not "outside," "suddenly," "above," "at a race," <note>original: "diffuori", "dibbotto", "dissu", "aggara"</note> etc. In such cases, if "tyrannical usage" <note>A reference to the linguistic idea that common custom (usage) often overrules logic or rules.</note> prevails, it should at least be recognized as an abuse, precisely because it is tyrannical. 

Therefore, if any inconsistency is still found here, the kind reader should excuse it, attributing it partly to the inconsistent usage itself and partly to the habits of the editor, who is more accustomed to modern spelling. This is especially true since in writings like these—where the subject matter, the argument, and the substance of the thoughts are what matter—a "diplomatically exact" <note>A transcription that reproduces every original character and error exactly as it appears in the source.</note> reprint is not required. We need not include all the errors, archaisms, and blunders which, though they may occasionally be of critical importance to scholars, would hinder the general reader. It is enough that the general character and a certain *patina of antiquity* remind the reader that they are reading an ancient book. Furthermore, great diligence was required for the **punctuation**, which is so necessary for understanding the meaning and the thoughts, and 

->***<-

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface concerning the linguistic and stylistic challenges of editing Giordano Bruno’s works, specifically focusing on the author's complex sentence structure, stylistic inconsistencies, and the use of archaic or technical terminology derived from classical languages.</meta>

XXXIV

...even more difficult still, where a rich, prompt, and exuberant intellect profusely scatters, weaves, and intertwines thoughts in an original way, though not always in a right and balanced order and measure; from this then arise those **prolix periods** <note>Long, complex sentences made of many subordinate clauses.</note> that are not at all preposterous or absurd, but in need of strenuous attention—though they are otherwise loathed by the lazy, thoughtless rabble of fashionable readers and writers, who are fond of sentences chopped up in the manner of **minced morsels** <note>original: "ammorsellati"; refers to a dish of small pieces of meat, used here as a metaphor for short, fragmented sentences.</note>, lacking in dignity and serious composure.

Regarding the negligence of style, which is so excusable in a soul full of fire, the reader will find evidence of it in **anacolutha** <term>anacoluthon</term><note>A grammatical interruption or lack of consistency in a sentence's structure.</note>, confusion of person and gender, and especially in **affixed pronouns** <term>affixed pronouns</term><note>In Italian, these are pronouns attached directly to the end of a verb, such as "tell-me" or "see-him."</note>, which we corrected at times without always providing notice.

The difference, finally, of this style from that of today consists especially in a great many Latin and Greek words now fallen out of use, although they are not unsuitable in themselves—indeed, they are perhaps necessary for an extremely subtle doctrinal and scientific style—as well as in **local vocabulary** <note>original: "vocaboli municipali"; words specific to a particular town or region rather than standard Italian.</note>, the meaning of which is hardly common. Now, in such cases, we were sometimes aided solely by combination and a certain etymological intuition, however much it may be mocked with a lordly air of pity (ridiculous even to experts) and despised today by so many of those withered philological recorders. These men, inept and disgusted by the idea of penetrating more deeply into the organism of languages, are content merely to know by heart the vocabulary and passages of authors—perhaps from the **Golden Age** <note>The peak period of classical literature.</note>—who used them. At most, they hyper-critically and pedantically twist and dislocate the limbs of good ancient authors, whether poets or prose writers, in such a way that it will take generations to reset them. They call it a rugged, fantastic, and hypothetical thing to want to trace the origin and structure or "fabric" of language; whereas, since the time of **Vossius, Hemsterhuis, and Lennep** <note>Gerardus Vossius, Tiberius Hemsterhuis, and Jan Daniel van Lennep: 17th and 18th-century scholars famous for their work in Greek and Latin philology and etymology.</note>, right in the faces of these unwary men and to their rotten spite, this sphere of philology expands and clears day by day, so that it is increasingly confirmed...

<summary>The editor discusses the difficulty of Bruno's complex, "exuberant" prose and justifies the correction of minor grammatical errors while defending the use of archaic Latinate and Greek terminology against the criticisms of narrow-minded philologists.</summary>
<keywords>Giordano Bruno, prose style, anacoluthon, philology, etymology, linguistics, Vossius, Hemsterhuis, Lennep, editing principles</keywords>

--- Page 41 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor’s justification for his editorial method. Having discussed Bruno's linguistic idiosyncrasies on the previous page, he now addresses the relationship between thought and style, defending his decision to avoid over-editing the text.</meta>

->XXXV<-

the equality, the intimate bond, and the identity of languages. We, therefore, far from any abuse or pedantry truly deserving of the name—which was rightly mocked by our author himself—have only sparingly, and only in urgent cases, sprinkled in some **small conjecture** <note>original: "conghietturina"; a modest editorial amendment to a difficult passage.</note> of our own, which anyone may mock if they wish. For a long time now, having observed the practices of sordid authors and editors in the **Republic of Letters** <note>The international community of intellectuals and scholars spanning the 17th to 18th centuries.</note>, we have heartily despised certain paltry masters and cheats who, to hide the shameful nakedness of their own self-interest from the common people, do not blush to cover it with a fog of slanders and vituperation. Instead of admitting their own stupidity and inability to understand, they blame the other's style as being strange, unintelligible, barbarous, bizarre, and I know not what else. Therefore, knowing that—as one of our truly original classic authors says—everyone has their own style just as they have their own nose <note>A common proverb suggesting that style is an inherent, personal characteristic that cannot be easily changed or judged by others' standards.</note>, and that, moreover, the German intuition of the universe and their style of thinking in science, art, and religion is at least different from that of the Italians or French of merit and honor (and therefore not to be summarily condemned as such), we have always found most true what was said by the incomparable **Perticari** <note>Giulio Perticari (1779–1822), an Italian scholar and writer involved in the debates over the Italian language.</note>, who was snatched away by a truly premature death:

> "Regarding as poor that style whose elegance rests only on beautiful phrases stolen here and there, but which are lacking in feeling and so poorly stitched together that I believe, if they were endowed with senses, they themselves would be amazed to find themselves huddle together; I have always studied how to draw not thoughts from a forest of borrowed words, but from thoughts the **fitting expressions** <term>dizioni</term><note>The specific choice of words or phrasing to express an idea.</note> for them. These, being nothing other than **masks** <note>original: "larve"; used here in the sense of an outward form or representation of an internal idea.</note> of our knowledge, must not be the tyrants of the mind, but its servants.

Creating phrases thus for the sake of the concepts, and not concepts for the sake of phrases, and adorning the maxims dictated by **philosophy** with a speech removed from the talk of the common people and from all **frivolous Tuscanisms** <note>original: "toscanerie"; a reference to the "Language Question" in Italy, where some insisted on using only 14th-century Florentine vocabulary, often at the expense of clarity or modern scientific thought.</note>, I have tried with all my power to avoid the all-too-common defect of feeding **eloquence**...

<summary>The editor defends his minimal use of editorial conjectures and argues that a writer's unique style should be respected as an extension of their thought, quoting the scholar Giulio Perticari to emphasize that language must serve philosophy rather than mere ornamental elegance.</summary>
<keywords>philology, editorial method, Giulio Perticari, Republic of Letters, style vs. thought, Tuscanisms, philosophy of language</keywords>

# THE CANDLEBEARER.

## A COMEDY BY THE NOLAN BRUNO, <note>Giordano Bruno (1548–1600) frequently called himself "the Nolan" (Il Nolano) to signify his birthplace of Nola, near Naples.</note>

# THE BOOK

## TO THOSE WHO HAVE DRUNK FROM THE HORSE’S FOUNTAIN.
<note>The "Horse’s Fountain" refers to the Hippocrene on Mount Helicon, which Greek myth says was created by the strike of the winged horse Pegasus’s hoof. It is a traditional symbol of poetic inspiration.</note>

You, who suckle at the Muses’ breast,
And who swim in their fatty broth
Face-first—let your excellencies hear me,
If faith and charity set your hearts on fire!

I weep, I ask, I beg for an epigram,
A sonnet, a panegyric, a hymn, or an ode,
To be placed upon my stern or my prow,
So I may go happily home to daddy and mommy.
<note>The book is personified here as a naked child or a bare ship, begging for introductory poems from famous authors to serve as "clothing" or decoration.</note>

Alas, for in vain do I long to go clothed!
Alas, for I go about naked, like a beggar;
And worse, I, wretched soul, shall perhaps be forced

To show uncovered to my Lady
The zero and the prick, like Father Adam,
<note>original: "Il zero e minchia." Bruno uses "zero" to refer to the anus and "minchia" as a vulgar term for the penis. This crude humor is typical of his defiance of academic "purity."</note>
When he was well-off inside his abbey.
<note>A sarcastic reference to the Garden of Eden as a "badia" (abbey).</note>

A beggarly scrap
Of <term>breeches</term> <note>Short trousers covering the hips and thighs.</note> while I seek, from the valleys
I see a great fury of horses ascending.

### HER BLESSED LADYSHIP S. O.
<note>The abbreviations "B. SUA SIG. S. O." likely stand for "Beata Sua Signoria, Signora Onorata"—Her Blessed Ladyship, Honored Lady. Morgana is often identified as a woman Bruno knew in Naples, perhaps representing a lost love or a personification of wisdom.</note>

**And** to whom shall I dedicate my **Candlebearer**? To whom, O great destiny, does it please you that I entitle my beautiful <term>groomsman</term> <note>original: "paraninfo"; one who introduces a bride to a groom, here used as a metaphor for the play's introduction</note>, my good <term>leader of the chorus</term> <note>original: "corifeo"</note>? Those wandering fireflies of the firmament have sifted down upon me, the dean of the twelve signs <note>The sun, as the leader of the Zodiac.</note> has shot like an arrow into my head, and the <term>seven wandering lights</term> <note>The seven planets of the ancient geocentric system: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> have breathed into my inner ears. To whom has it turned? I say; whom does it regard? At whom does it take aim? At his Holiness? No. At his Imperial Majesty? No. At his Serenity? By my faith, there is no prince or cardinal, king, emperor, or pope who shall take this candle from my hand in this most solemn offering. 

It falls to you, it is given to you—and you shall either hang it in your cabinet or fix it in your candlestick—my superlatively learned, wise, beautiful, and generous **Lady Morgana**! To you, the tiller of the field of my soul, who—after crushing the clods of its hardness and refining its style, so that the dusty mist raised by the wind of levity might not offend the eyes of this person or that—watered my intellect with divine water deriving from the fountain of your spirit. Therefore, at the time when we could touch hands, I first directed my cheerful thoughts to you near the <term>trough</term> <note>original: "truogo"</note> of living water. Now, between you—who enjoy <term>Abraham’s bosom</term> <note>A biblical reference to Paradise (Luke 16:22). This suggests Morgana is deceased or otherwise in a state of grace far removed from the author.</note>—and me—who, without waiting for that help of yours which used to cool my tongue, burn and spark desperately—there lies a great chaos, far too envious of my well-being; to show you that it cannot...

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to Lady Morgana. ...to prevent that same chaos, and so that my love—with some specific hostage and material gift—does not pass away to its own rotten spite, here is the candle offered to you <note>original: "porgiuta"; an archaic form</note> by this **Candlebearer** who departs from me. In the meantime, let him live, and manage himself, and attend to making himself fatter than he already is; because, on the other hand, I hope to recover the lard where I lost the grass <note>A proverbial expression meaning to recover one's losses or status.</note>—if not under one cloak, then under another; if not in one life, then in another.

Remember <note>The original text uses "ricordarvi" instead of "ricordatevi".</note>, my Lady, what I believe you do not need to be taught: **time takes everything and gives everything; everything changes, nothing is annihilated; there is only One who cannot change, only One is eternal, and can persevere eternally as one, similar, and the same.** With this philosophy my soul expands, and my intellect is magnified. Therefore, whatever the point of this evening I await may be, if change is true, I, who am in the night, await the day; and those who are in the day await the night. All that is, is either here or there, near or far, now or later, sooner or later. Rejoice, therefore, and if you can, stay healthy, and love those who love you!

<meta>This page transitions from the personal dedication to Lady Morgana to the structural outline of the play itself. # ARGUMENT
## AND ORDER OF THE COMEDY.

**T**here are three main subjects woven together in the present comedy: the love of Bonifacio, the alchemy of Bartolomeo, and the pedantry of Manfurio. However, for a distinct understanding of the subjects, the logic of the order, and the clarity of the ingenious structure, let us first report individually on the insipid lover; second, the sordid miser; and third, the clumsy pedant. Of these, the insipid one is not without clumsiness and sordidness; the sordid one is likewise insipid and clumsy; and the clumsy one is no less sordid and insipid than he is clumsy.

### *Bonifacio*

Thus, in *Act 1, scene 1*, being in love with Lady Vittoria and realizing that his love cannot be reciprocated (the reason being that she was a friend, as they say, of "flowers of beards and fruits of purses" <note>This is a colorful way of saying she prefers young men and rich men; Bonifacio is neither.</note>, and he was neither young nor generous), he places his hope in the vanity of magical superstitions to achieve his amorous goals. For this reason, he sends his servant to find Scaramure, who had been described to him as an effective magician. Scene II: Having sent Ascanio, he discourses with himself, calling to mind the power of that art. Scene III: Bartolomeo happens upon him and, with a certain clever method, makes him vomit up his secret <note>original: "vomitare il suo secreto"; a metaphor for tricking someone into revealing a confidence</note>, and shows the difference in the object of his own love. Scene IV: Sanguino, father and shepherd of rogues, and a student who studied under Manfurio—who had overheard these conversations from the side—discuss that event; Sanguino in particular begins to take the field to weave some plot against Bonifacio. Scene VI: Lucia, the procuress, appears with a small gift that Bonifacio was sending; she performs an anatomy <note>original: "notomia"; here meaning a thorough inspection or dissection</note> of it and prepares to take her "tithe" from it, and he very nearly caught her in the act. Scene VII: Bonifacio comes along all glorious because of a certain poem of his, written in a new style in honor and glory of his lady; during this celebration, Scene VIII: he was found by Gio. Bernardo, the painter, to whom he would have disclosed his new poetic fury; but he was distracted by the thought of his portrait, and by a thought regarding a doubt that Gio. Bernardo left in his mind. Scene IX: He remains perplexed by the enigma, because he more or less understands the term <term>Candlebearer</term> <note>original: "Candelajo"; the title of the play, referring here to a person who holds a candle, often used as a metaphor for a cuckold or a witness to others' deeds</note>, but he cannot quite grasp what the word <term>Goldsmith</term> <note>original: "Orefice"; likely a pun on "ore" (hours) or "oro" (gold), or a specific slang term used in the play's riddles</note> is meant to signify. While he dwells on this thought, behold Scene X: Ascanio returns with the magician: who after...
