They consider how his falling in love with Lady Vittoria inclined him toward being a "cuckold," <note>To be "horned" or a cuckold meant a man's wife was unfaithful; here the irony is that he was trying to cheat with a woman who turned out to be his own wife in disguise</note> and when he thought he was enjoying her, he became a cuckold in fact. He is truly represented by Actaeon, who, while going hunting, searched for his horns <note>In Greek mythology, Actaeon was a hunter who saw the goddess Diana bathing; she transformed him into a stag—with horns—and he was torn apart by his own hounds</note>, and just when he thought he would enjoy his Diana, he became a stag. Therefore, it is no wonder if this man is mangled and torn apart by these roguish "dogs."

## Bartolomeo
<note>Bartolomeo is the play's second protagonist, representing the vice of greed through his obsession with alchemy</note>

In **Act I, scene III**, where he mocks Bonifacio's love, he concludes that a love for gold and silver, and the pursuit of two other "ladies" <note>Likely referring to the chemical processes or the metals themselves</note>, is more appropriate. It is likely that, having departed from there, he went to perform alchemy, which he was studying under the teaching of Cencio. This Cencio is revealed to be a fraud in **scene II**, according to the judgment of Giovanni Bernardo, and then in **scene XII** he shows himself to be a complete swindler. Marta, his wife, appears in **scene XIII** and is overtaken by Sanguino, who was making fun of both her and her husband.

In **Act II, scene VI**, while Barra is talking with Lucia, he reveals part of the "profit" Bartolomeo was making: namely, that while he was attending to alchemy, his wife Marta was doing the laundry and soaping the linens <note>This suggests that while the husband wastes money on fake science, the wife is forced to do menial labor, or perhaps uses the laundry as a cover for her own affairs</note>.

In **Act III, scene I**, Bartolomeo discourses on the nobility of his new profession and demonstrates with his reasoning that there is no better study or doctrine than that *concerning minerals* <note>original Latin: "de mineralibus"</note>, and with this, reminded of his work, he departs.

In **Act IV, scene III**, Bartolomeo goes about waiting for the servant he had sent for the *powder of Christ* <note>original Latin: "pulvis Christi," a term used in alchemy for a transformative substance</note>, and in **scene IV** he discourses on that saying: *A light burden* <note>original Latin: "Onus leve"</note>, comparing gold to feathers. In **scene VIII**, his wife demonstrates what a "virtuous matron" she was in the conversation she has with Master Bonifacio. She shows how much more expert she was in the art of...

### *Manfurio*

In **Act One, scene V**, he begins to <term>thunder on high</term> <note>original: "altitonare." Meanwhile, in **Scene XVI**, Sanguino, Marca, and others arrive disguised as guards <note>Italian: "birri," the local police or bailiffs, often portrayed as corrupt in Renaissance comedy</note>. In **Act Five, in the penultimate scene**, he is offered a choice of one of three things to avoid going to prison: either pay a handsome bribe <note>original: "strena," literally a New Year's gift or gratuity</note> to the guards and the captain, receive ten slaps on the palm <note>Italian: "spalmate," a common disciplinary punishment</note>, or fifty lashes with his breeches lowered. He would have accepted almost anything rather than go to prison in such a state. Therefore, out of the three, he chooses the ten slaps; but when he reached the third one, he cried out: "Better fifty lashes on the buttocks!" In the end, because the count was confused for one reason or another, it happened that he received the slaps, the lashes, and paid whatever coins he had left in his surcoat <term>giornea</term> <note>A short, sleeveless tunic worn over other clothing</note>; he even left behind a cloak that was not his own. Having done all this, dressed in the gear of Don Paulino, he delivers the final call to **"Applaud"** <note>original: "Plaudite," the traditional Latin command for the audience to clap at the end of a Roman play</note> in the **last scene**.

# ANTI-PROLOGUE

**S**ir, yes; well-considered, well-noted, well-ordered—did I not perhaps prophesy that this comedy would not be performed tonight? That slut <note>original: "bagassa"</note> who was assigned to play the roles of Vittoria and Carubina has some sort of "womb-ache" <note>original: "mal di madre"; a common Renaissance term for hysteria or various female ailments</note>. The fellow who is supposed to play Bonifacio is so drunk that he hasn't been able to tell heaven from earth since noon; and as if he had nothing to do, he won't get out of bed. He says: "Leave me be! For in three and a half days and seven evenings, with four or two oarsmen, I shall be among the moths <note>original: "parpaglioni"</note> and bats; so be it, row; let the rowing be!" 

As for me, I was entrusted with the prologue, and I swear to you it is so intricate and devilish that I’ve been sweating over it for four days, day and night. Not even all the trumpets and drums of those whore Muses of Helicon <note>Mount Helicon was the mythological home of the Muses; the speaker is being intentionally irreverent toward classical inspiration</note> would be enough to shove a single straw of it into my memory. 

Now I want to perform <note>The original text says "fa" (does) instead of "far" (to do/perform).</note> the prologue—or rather, the lifeboat of this great old wreck of a ship, which is dismantled, smashed, broken, and so poorly patched with tar that it looks like it was dragged up from the deep abyss by force with hooks, grapples, and harpoons <term>arpagini</term> <note>Specialized iron hooks used in naval warfare or salvage</note>. Water is leaking into it from many sides, and it isn't caulked at all. And yet it wants to go out? It wants to head into the high seas? To leave this secure harbor of the Mandracchio <note>The inner harbor of the Port of Naples</note>? To set sail from the Pier of Silence? 

The author—if you knew him—you would say he has a bewildered countenance. He always looks as if he is contemplating the pains of hell. He looks like he’s been through a press, like a felt cap. He is a man who laughs only to do as others do. For the most part, you will see him annoyed, restless, and eccentric; he is satisfied by nothing, as stubborn as an eighty-year-old man, and as temperamental as a dog that has been beaten a thousand times and fed on nothing but onions. By the blood—I won't say whose!—for him and all these other philosophers, poets, and pedants, the greatest enemy they have is wealth and possessions. While they perform an anatomy <term>notomia</term> <note>An archaic term for a detailed dissection or critical analysis</note> on such riches with their brains, they flee from them like a hundred thousand devils, for fear of being truly torn apart, quartered, and squandered by them; instead, they go off to find those who...

## PRO-PROLOGUE

<margin>*) The text says Nilo.</margin>
Where did that scoundrel go—that back-ripe-for-beatings—who was supposed to perform the prologue? Gentlemen, the comedy will be without a prologue. Eh! It doesn't matter; for it is not necessary that there be one. The material, the subject, the method and order, and the circumstances of the play, I tell you, will present themselves to you in order, and will be placed before your eyes in order: which is much better than if they were narrated to you in order. This is a kind of fabric that has the warp and the weaving combined. Whoever can grasp it, let them grasp it! Whoever wants to understand it, let them understand it! But I will not fail to warn you that you must imagine yourselves to be in the most royal city of Naples, near the Seat of Nola <note>original: "seggio di Nola"; a "seggio" or "sedile" was a formal administrative district or council building in Naples where the nobility met. The margin note indicates a variant reading of "Nilo," another famous Neapolitan district</note>. *) This thing that you see shaped here, for tonight, will serve for certain cheats, rogues, and swindlers—watch yourselves, lest they make you "widows" of something you are carrying on your persons! Here these men will spread their nets, and <term>zara</term> <note>a game of chance played with dice; here used to mean "hazard" or "bad luck to whoever it hits"</note> to whom it touches! On this side, one goes to the room of the Candlemaker, that is <note>original: "id est"</note> Master Bonifacio, and Carubina, the wife of Master Bartolomeo. On this other side, one goes to the room of Lady Vittoria and of Giovanni Bernardo the painter, and Scaramure, who acts as a necromancer <note>a magician who claims to communicate with the dead</note>. Around these parts, for reasons I know not, a most solemn pedant named Manfurio is often seen wandering about. I assure you that you will see them all. And the procuress <note>original: "ruffiana"</note> Lucia, because of her many errands, must come and go more than a few times. You will see Pollula, mostly with his *teacher* <gloss>master</gloss>; this is a scholar of black and white ink. You will see Bonifacio’s page, Ascanio, a servant for sun and candle. Mochio, Bartolomeo’s apprentice, is neither hot nor cold; he neither smells sweet nor stinks. In Sanguino, Barra, Marca, and Corcovizzo, you will contemplate in part the dexterity of the swindler’s discipline. You will recognize the form of alchemical frauds in Cencio. And for a pastime, there will be presented to you Consalvo the apothecary, Marta, wife of Bartolomeo, and the most witty Lord Ottaviano. Consider

Fame is obligated to make his voice heard at one pole and the other, and to deafen with cries, noise, and rackets the North wind and the South wind, the Indian and the Moorish sea. How well it stands out—I seem to see so many pearls and margarites on a field of gold—when a Latin discourse is placed in the middle of the Italian! Or a Greek discourse in the middle of the Latin! He does not let a single sheet of paper pass without at least one little foreign word, a short verse, or a concept in a strange character and idiom appearing on it. 

Oh, it gives me life when, either by force or by choice, in speaking or in writing, they manage to bring in a verse of Homer, of Hesiod, or a little scrap of Plato or the Greek Demosthenes! How well they demonstrate that they are the only ones whose heads Saturn has pissed judgment into; the nine handmaidens of Pallas <note>The Muses</note> have unloaded a cornucopia of vocabulary between their <term>pia and dura mater</term> <note>the inner and outer membranes of the brain</note>. And so it is very fitting that they go about with that mask of theirs...

<meta>This page continues the "Pro-prologue" of the *Candelaio*. Having previously mocked the affectations of pedants and poets, the speaker now describes the physical and intellectual posturing of the stereotypical academic before the character of the Beadle (Bidello) steps forward to address the audience directly, introducing the play's titular "Candlemaker."</meta>

...with that slow-stepping gait, an upright torso, a steady head, and eyes held in an act of modest yet haughty circumspection. You will see one of these types, who chews on doctrine, sniffs out opinions, spits maxims, urinates authorities <note>The author uses "minge" (to urinate) to crudely satirize how pedants regurgitate the works of ancient authors</note>, belches mysteries, sweats clear and lunatic inks, and sows the ambrosia and nectar of his judgments—enough to fill the pantry of Ganymede <note>The cupbearer to the gods in Greek mythology</note> and then offer a toast to thundering Jove. 

You will see a man-child—a synonym-seeking, epithet-hurling, appositive, and <term>suppository</term> <note>A pun on the grammatical term "apposition" and the medical "suppository"</note> beadle of Minerva, a lieutenant of Pallas, a trumpet of Mercury, a patriarch of the Muses, and a prince of the Apollonian kingdom—I was nearly tempted to say a "coltish" <note>The original contains a pun on "Apollinesco" (Apollonian) and "polledresco" (resembling a young colt or foal), implying the scholar is more of a beast of burden than a god</note> kingdom. You will also see a confused jumble of rogue’s tricks, the stratagems of swindlers, and the enterprises of knaves; furthermore, sweet disgusts, bitter pleasures, foolish determinations, broken faiths, limping hopes, and meager charities; great and grave judgments regarding the affairs of others, but little sense regarding one's own; manly women, effeminate men, many voices coming from the head and not from the heart—he who believes most of all is the most deceived—and a universal love for coins. 

From this proceed quartan fevers <note>A type of malaria where fever recurs every four days</note>, spiritual cancers, thoughts lacking weight, overflowing nonsense, the stumbles of university graduates, masterful blunders, and slips enough to break one's neck; besides the Will that drives, the Knowledge that approaches, the Action that bears fruit, and Diligence, the mother of results. In conclusion, you will see that in all this, there is nothing certain; but plenty of business, enough defects, little of beauty, and nothing of good. But I seem to hear the characters. Farewell!

## B E A D L E .

Before I speak, I must excuse myself. I believe that if not all, at least the majority of you will say to me: "May cancer eat your nose! Where did you ever see a comedy presented by a beadle?" And I answer you: "The misfortune that God gives you! Before there were comedies, where were comedies ever seen? And where were you ever seen before you existed?" 

And does it seem to you that a subject such as this, which presents itself to you tonight, should not come forth and appear with some privileged peculiarity? An irregular baboon, a natural-born idiot, a moral simpleton, a <term>tropological</term> <note>Referring to the "moral" sense of interpreting scripture</note> beast, an <term>anagogical</term> <note>Referring to the "mystical" or "heavenly" sense of interpreting scripture; Bruno is mocking medieval scholarship</note> donkey like this one—I will make him worthy of a high constable, if you do not find him worthy of a beadle. Do you want me to tell you who he is? Do you want to know? Do you wish for me to make you understand? This fellow is (I will tell you softly) the **Candlemaker**. Do you want me to show him to you? Do you desire to see him? 

Here he is! Clear the way! Make room! Pull back to the sides, unless you want those horns to hurt you—horns that make people flee beyond the mountains.

# ACT ONE.

---

## SCENE ONE.

->Bonifacio. Ascanio.<-

**Bonifacio.** Go, find him, right now, and force him to come here! Go, do it, and come back soon!
**Ascanio.** I will strive to do it quickly and well. Better a little late than a little badly: *quickly enough, if well enough* <note>original: "sat cito, si sat bene." A Latin proverb often attributed to Cato or Augustus, used here to show Ascanio’s fondness for pedantic cliches.</note>.
**Bonifacio.** Praised be God! I thought I had only a servant, and instead I have a servant, a house-steward, a <term>satrap</term> <note>A term for a provincial governor in the ancient Persian Empire, used here sarcastically to mean a self-important official</note>, a doctor, and a counselor. And then they say I am a poor gentleman! I tell you in the name of the blessed donkey's tail that the Genoese worship at Castello <note>A mocking reference to a legend about a relic—the tail of the donkey that carried Jesus—supposedly kept in Genoa; Bruno frequently mocked such superstitions</note>, do it quickly, you wretch, and with a will, and beware of entering the house! Do you understand? Call him, have him come to the window; and you will tell him what I told you. Do you understand?
**Ascanio.** Yes, sir; I’m going.

## SCENE II.

->Bonifacio alone.<-

Art supplies what nature lacks, Bonifacio. Now, since by some ill hour I cannot make this traitress love me—or at least look at me with a feigned, loving glance—who knows? Perhaps she who has not been moved by Bonifacio's words, by Bonifacio's love, or by seeing Bonifacio suffer, might be forced by this occult philosophy <note>Occult philosophy refers to magic and the Hermetic arts, which Bonifacio hopes will win him the heart of the beautiful Carubina</note>. It is said that the magic art is of such importance that, against nature, it makes rivers flow backward, fixes the sea in place, makes mountains roar, makes the abyss resonate, forbids the sun from shining, plucks down the moon, uproots the stars, takes away the day, and makes the night stand still. Therefore, the **Academic of No Academy** <note>This is Bruno’s own pseudonym, signaling his rejection of the rigid, formal academic institutions of his time</note> in that hateful title and lost poem said:
> *It gives to rapid rivers their return,*
> *Moves from the high heavens the golden stars,*
> *Makes night be day, and makes the day be night,*
> *And plucks the moon from its own sphere,*

<summary>Bonifacio sends his servant Ascanio to fetch a practitioner of the magic arts, then soliloquizes on his plan to use "occult philosophy" to force a woman to love him, citing the supernatural powers of magic.</summary>
<keywords>magic, occult philosophy, Bonifacio, Ascanio, Academic of No Academy, nature vs art, Naples, satire</keywords>

*And he changes the right horn to the left,* <margin>A plebeian confusion of gender in the original! <note>The original Italian uses "gli" (him) instead of "le" (them), which the author notes as a commoner's grammatical error.</note></margin>
*And swells the waves of the sea, and fixes them,*
*Earth, water, fire, and air he strips of feathers,*
*And makes human will change its plumage.*

One could doubt everything: but concerning what he just said regarding the effect of love, we see the evidence of it every day. Not to mention that I hear truly marvelous things about the mastery of this Scaramuré <note>Scaramuré is a local sorcerer or "cunning man" Bonifacio is planning to hire to cast a love spell.</note>. Look, I see one of those who "steal the cow and then donate the horns for the love of God" <note>An Italian proverb describing hypocrites or those who try to make amends for a large theft with a small, pious gesture.</note>. Let's see what news he brings!

### SCENE III.

->**Mister Bonifacio. Mister Bartolomeo** (*conversing*). **Pollula** and **Sanguino** (*listening in secret*).<-

**Bartolomeo.** Cruel love, since your kingdom is so unjust and so violent, what does it mean that it lasts so long? Why do you make her flee from me, she whom I prize and adore? Why is she not bound to me as I am so tightly bound to her? Can this even be imagined? And yet it is true. What kind of snare is this? Of two people, it makes one chained to the other, while the other remains freer and looser than the wind.
**Bonifacio.** Am I perhaps alone? *Sob, sob, sob!*
**Bartolomeo.** What is the matter, my **Mister Bonifacio**? Are you weeping for my pain?
**Bonifacio.** And for my own martyrdom as well. I see well that you are struck; I see you have changed color; I just heard you lamenting. I understand your illness as one who shares the same passion—and perhaps worse—and I pity you. For many days now I have seen you walking pensive and distracted, astonished, lost (just as I believe others see me), deep sighs bursting from your chest, your eyes moist. "The Devil!" I said to myself, "No close relative or benefactor of his has died, he has no lawsuit in court, he has all he needs, no evil threatens him, everything goes well for him, and I know he doesn't care too much about his sins; and yet here he is, weeping and wailing, his brain seems to be like **clanging cymbals that sound poorly** <note>original: "cymbalis male sonantibus." A Latin phrase likely referencing the biblical "tinkling cymbals" from 1 Corinthians 13, here used to describe a mind that has lost its harmony or reason.</note>." Therefore, he is in love; therefore some <term>humor</term>—be it phlegmatic, choleric, sanguine, or melancholic <note>In ancient medicine, the "four humors" were bodily fluids thought to determine a person's temperament and health. Love was often seen as a physical imbalance of these fluids.</note> (I know not which "desirous" humor it is)—has gone to his head. Now that I hear you utter these sweet words, I conclude even more firmly that your stomach is full of that poisonous honey.
**Bartolomeo.** Alas, for I am too cruelly seized by her...

<summary>Bonifacio observes Bartolomeo wandering in a daze of unrequited love and realizes they share the same affliction. He uses the medical language of the "four humors" to diagnose Bartolomeo's lovesickness.</summary>
<keywords>humors, unrequited love, Scaramuré, Neapolitan comedy, melancholy, Bonifacio, Bartolomeo</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Bartolomeo and Bonifacio. Bonifacio is expressing his romantic distress, while Bartolomeo offers a more cynical, earthly perspective on human desire compared to animal instinct.</meta>

...looks! **But I marvel at you, Mister Bonifacio,** not at myself; for I am two or three years younger, and I have for a wife a hunchbacked <note>original: "scrignuta"; an insulting term for someone with a hunched back or physical deformity</note> old woman who is more than eight years my senior. You have a most beautiful wife, a young woman of twenty-five years, than whom it is not easy to find a more beautiful one in all of Naples: and yet you are in love!

**Bon.** By the words you have just spoken, I believe you understand how tangled and absurd the kingdom of Love is. If you wish to know the order—or rather the disorder—of my loves, listen to me, I pray.

**Bart.** Speak, **Mister Bonifacio**, for we are not like the beasts, who engage in slavish mating <note>original: "coito servile"; referring to mating driven purely by instinct rather than choice or romance</note> solely for the act of procreation, and therefore have a fixed law of time and place. Consider the donkeys, whose backs are warmed by the specific sun, or chiefly by the month of May; they reproduce in warm and temperate climates, and not in cold ones, such as in the seventh zone <margin>The ancients divided the Earth's surface into circles parallel to the equator, and called the areas between those circles "climates" <note>original: "climata"</note>; thus, from the equator to each polar circle, they counted twenty-four climates.</margin> and other parts closer to the pole. We humans, however, do so in every time and place.

**Bon.** I have lived in the world for forty-two years in such a way that I was not defiled by women <note>original: "mulieribus non sum coinquinato"; Bonifacio is boasting of his previous chastity or late-blooming libido using a Latin ecclesiastical phrasing</note>. Once I reached this age, in which we begin to have some white hairs on our head, and in which love usually begins to cool and fade away—

**Bart.** In some it ceases, in others it merely changes—

**Bon.** It usually begins to fade, like the heat in the time of autumn—it was then that I was seized by the love of *Carubina*. She seemed to me the most beautiful among all other beauties; she warmed me, she set me into such a flame that I was burned in a way that I have now become tinder <note>original: "esca"; material used to start a fire. Bonifacio means he is now highly flammable and easily "ignited" by new loves.</note>. Now, through habit and constant use between her and me, that first flame having been extinguished, my heart has remained easily ignited by new fires.

**Bart.** If the fire had been of a better quality, it would not have turned you into tinder, but into ash; and if I had been in your wife's place, I would have made it so—

**Bon.** Let me finish my speech, and then say what you like!

**Bart.** Continue with that beautiful metaphor!

**Bon.** Now, that flame having ceased in my heart—the one that tempered it into tinder—I was easily ignited this *April* by another flame.

**Bart.** It was at this same time of year that *Petrarch* <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet whose sonnets defined the "courtly love" tradition. He famously first saw his muse, Laura, in April.</note> fell in love, and the donkeys also begin to lift their tails.

**Bon.** What did you say?

**Bart.** I said, it was at this time that Pe—

<summary>Bonifacio explains that after forty years of chastity, his passion for his wife Carubina has turned him into "tinder," making him susceptible to a new, wandering infatuation. Bartolomeo mocks him by comparing this human "romance" to the seasonal mating habits of donkeys and the poetic tropes of Petrarch.</summary>

--- Page 62 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Bartolomeo and Bonifacio. Having discussed the biological and climatic influences on desire, the conversation shifts from philosophical theories to Bonifacio’s personal romantic obsession and Bartolomeo’s mocking response.</meta>

[Pe]trarch <note>original: "trarca"; the text begins mid-word, referring to the famous Italian poet Francesco Petrarca</note>, and even the donkeys rouse themselves to contemplation, because in winter the spirits are contracted by the cold, and in summer they are dispersed by the heat; in spring, they are in a moderate and quiet temperament. Thus, the mind is more fit for contemplation because of the tranquility of the body's disposition, which leaves it free for its own operations.

**Bon.** Let’s leave these nursery rhymes <note>original: "filastroccole"; refers to nonsense or tedious, repetitive talk</note> aside and get to the point! So, having gone for a walk at Posillipo <note>a scenic coastal district in Naples</note>, I was so deeply pierced by the glances of Lady Victoria, and so burned by her eyes <note>original: "lumi"; literally "lights," a poetic term for eyes</note>, and so bound by her chains, that, alas— —

**Bart.** This animal they call "love" usually attacks those who have little to think about and even less to do. Weren't you out for a stroll?

**Bon.** Now, let me understand the target of your love, since you have given me the occasion to reveal mine. I think you too should take no small comfort in conversing with those who suffer from the same malady—if love can indeed be called a malady.

**Bart.** **Nominative case:** Lady Argenteria <note>original: "Argenteria"; a name evoking "argento" or silver</note> afflicts me; Lady Orelia <note>original: "Orelia"; a name evoking "oro" or gold</note> breaks my heart.

**Bon.** A plague <note>original: "malan"; literally "malanno," an ill-fortune or sickness</note> upon you and her!

**Bart.** **Genitive case:** Of Lady Argenteria I have care; for Lady Orelia I hold a thought.

**Bon.** May a cancer consume Bartolomeo, Aurelia, and Argentina!

**Bart.** **Dative case:** To Lady Argenteria I bring love; for Lady Orelia I sigh. To Lady Argenteria and Orelia together, I commend myself.

**Bon.** I'd like to know what devil has possessed this man.

**Bart.** **Vocative case:** O Lady Argenteria, why do you leave me? O Lady Orelia, why do you flee from me?

**Bon.** May they flee from you so far that you never find joy! Go to the devil! You have come to make a fool of me.

**Bart.** And you stay with that god <note>referring to Cupid or Love</note> who has taken your brain—if it’s even true that you ever had one. I'm going to do business for my mistresses.

**Bon.** Look, look with what a trick and with what ease this scoundrel has made me say what would have been better told to fifty others. I fear that with this love, I have so far only gathered the first fruits of madness. Now, to the devil, I must go home to deal with Lucia <note>Bonifacio's wife</note>. I see certain rascals laughing. I suspect they too have heard this devilish dialogue. Love and anger cannot be hidden.

<summary>Bonifacio confesses his infatuation with Lady Victoria, only to be mocked by Bartolomeo, who parodies romantic devotion using the grammatical cases of a Latin lesson. The scene ends with Bonifacio realizing he has been made a fool of while onlookers laugh at his public display of "madness."</summary>

# SCENE IV.

## Sanguino. Pollula.

**San.** Ha, ha, ha, ha! May he be fed bread from a crossbow <note>an idiom meaning to treat someone harshly or to keep them at a distance</note>, that Indian buffalo, that donkey from the land of Otranto, that nitwit from Avella, that sheep of Arpaia! Did it really take much to make him confess everything without the rope <note>referring to the "corda" or strappado, a common method of judicial torture; Sanguino is boasting that Bonifacio yielded without physical force</note>? Ha, ha, ha! And that other blowhard, you saw with what a fine preamble he knew how to draw him out to say he’s in love; and who his goddess is—may God give him a foul plague—and when, how, and where!

**Pol.** I promise you, that when this fellow says the Office of Our Lady, he has no need to pray to God by saying: *Lord, you shall open my lips!* <note>original: "Domine, labia mea aperies"; the opening line of the Matins service</note>

**San.** What does that mean: *The Lord’s lamp is perishing*? <note>original: "Domino lampia mem periens"; Sanguino’s ignorant, phonetic garbling of the Latin prayer</note>

**Pol.** "Lord, open my mouth, so that I may speak!" And I say, that this prayer is not for those who are all too ready to tell their business to anyone who wants to know it.

**San.** Yes; but don't you see that in the end he repented having spoken? However, no harm can come to him from it, because the scripture says in a certain place: *He who sins and makes amends, let him be saved!* <note>original: "Chi pecca et emenda, salvo esto"; a mock-legal or pseudo-scriptural maxim</note>

**Pol.** Now here comes the Master! We shall linger here all day in the name of the devil, may he break his neck!

---

# SCENE V.

## Manfurio. Pollula. Sanguino.

**Manf.** *May you be found well, O youth of a good, better, and best disposition! How goes it with you? How is your health?* <note>original: "Bene reperiaris, bonae, melioris optimaeque indolis adolescentule! Quomodo tecum agitur? ut vales?"</note>

**Pol.** Well.

**Manf.** *I am truly joyful, and I congratulate you enough. If you are well, it is well; I indeed am well.* <note>original: "Gaudeo sane, gratulorque satis. Si vales, bene est; ego quidem valeo"; Manfurio is using a standard, overly formal Ciceronian greeting</note> Mark-Tullian <note>original: "Marcitulliana"; referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman standard for perfect Latin style</note> elegance observed in almost all his familiar missives <term>missorie: letters or formal correspondence</term>!

**Pol.** Do you command anything else, *Lord Master*? I am going ahead to finish some business with Sanguino, and I cannot delay with you.

**Manf.** Oh, my dictates <term>dictati: lessons or exercises dictated by a teacher to students</term> thrown away in vain! Those which, in my nurturing gymnasium of Minerva <note>a flowery way of saying "my school"</note>—extracting them from the sharp edge of my Mars <note>referring to his intellectual prowess</note>—I had you engrave upon snowy pages with a pen dipped in black ink <term>atramento: a formal term for ink</term>. Thrown away, I say, in vain, since it happens that at the right time and place, *having preserved their logic*, you do not know how to make use of them. While your preceptor inquires of you in that Latin idiom <note>original: "idioma lazio"</note> most celebrated *among all nations, even the barbarian ones*, you—*still persisting* in the *beast-like* commerce of the ignorant commoners—abdicate yourself from the *theater of letters*, giving me a response composed of...

<summary>Sanguino and Pollula mock Bonifacio for his foolish and easy confession of love, only to be interrupted by the pedantic schoolmaster Manfurio, who berates Pollula for using common speech instead of formal Latin.</summary>
<keywords>mockery, Latin puns, pedantry, Manfurio, Sanguino, Bonifacio, Ciceronian style, education satire</keywords>

--- Page 64 ---
<meta>This page continues the encounter between Sanguino, Pollula, and the pedantic schoolmaster Manfurio. Sanguino has been mocking Manfurio's overly complicated way of speaking, leading to a comedic clash between the rogue's street slang and the master's stiff, Latin-heavy academic jargon.</meta>

...words, such as you received from the nurse and midwife in **the cradle** <note>original: "incunabulis"; literally "swaddling clothes," referring here to the very beginnings of speech</note>, or, to put it better, received. **Tell me, you fool, when do you intend to stop acting like a child?** <note>original: "Dimmi, sciocco, quando vuoi dispuerascere?"</note>

**San.** Master, with this devilish way of speaking in **gibberish** <note>original: "gramuffa"; a slang term for pedantic or encoded speech</note>, or **crypt-talk**, or elegant and **latrine-like** \*) you sicken the heavens, and the whole world mocks you.

**Manf.** Indeed, if this **great world** <note>original: "megalocosmo"</note> and **world-machine**, O wicked and uncouth man, were stuffed and crammed with people like you.

**San.** What are you saying about Cosmo, Celesto, and Urbano? <note>Sanguino hilariously mistakes Manfurio’s high-flown terms for the world and the heavens for common Italian names</note> Speak to me so I can understand you; then I will answer you.

**Manf.** **Go then to the unlucky and accursed cross, and with a left-handed Hercules!** <note>original: "Vade ergo in infaustam nefastamque crucem, sinistroque Hercule!"; a Roman-style curse wishing bad luck upon the recipient</note> The Muses disdain to endure the pigsty of your companionship; **they are sickened by the gall of your conversation.** <note>original: "fele aran colloquii vestri"</note> What judgment do you make of this scoundrel, O Pollula? Pollula, **repository of the fruits of my learning**, **receptacle** of my doctrinal seed, **do not let the things just said by us move you!** <note>original: "appositorie fructus eruditionum mearum... ne te moveant modo a nobis dicta!"</note> for the reason that, **because, for, since (causal particles of response)** <note>original: "quia, namque, quandoquidem (particulae causae redditivae)"; Manfurio is literally listing Latin synonyms for "because" mid-sentence</note> I wanted to make you a participant in that phrase with which we **most charmingly and eloquently** perform rebukes, which you **hereafter, subsequently**, if the **heaven-dwellers** <note>original: "celicoli"; the gods</note> grant you that which they have granted us, may be able to imitate in reverse toward your students-to-be.

**Pol.** Good! but it must be done with purpose and on the right occasion.

**Manf.** The cause of my **outburst of anger** <note>original: "excandescentia"</note> was your saying: "I cannot delay with you." **You should have said, even more elegantly, with the infinitive preceding the subjunctive; or you should have said: your excellence, your erudition, leisure with your sweetest muses is not given, is not granted to me.** <note>original: "Debuisses dicere vel elegantius... non datur, non conceditur mihi cum tuis dulcissimis musis otium"</note> Furthermore, that saying "with you," **whether in the Tuscan style "with you-all"**, is neither well-said in Latin regarding a single person, nor civilly in the manner of **scholars and school-masters.** <note>original: "togati e ginnasiarchi"; literally "those wearing the toga and leaders of the gymnasium"</note>

**San.** See, see how the world goes! You two are in agreement, and I am left outside, like a door-bolt. Please, **lord master**, let us be friends again! Because, although I am not fit to be subject to your rod—**that is**, to be your disciple—perhaps I can serve you in some other way.

**Manf.** **I have nothing to do with you.** <note>original: "Nil mihi vobiscum"</note>

**San.** **And with your spirit.** <note>original: "Et con spiritu to"; Sanguino’s mangled version of the liturgical "Et cum spiritu tuo," used here as a flippant retort</note>

**Manf.** Ha, ha, ha! Pollula, how have you been joined by such a brute as a companion?

**San.** Ugly or beautiful, at the service of your majesty, my most honorable lord!

<meta>This page continues the comedic dialogue between the pedantic schoolmaster Manfredo and the rogues Sanguino and Polidoro. Sanguino has just finished insulting Manfredo’s convoluted style of speech, but Manfredo, in his vanity, has misinterpreted the interaction as a sign of respect.</meta>

**Manf.** This one seems very teachable to me, and not as unruly as he appeared at first, because he addresses me with very polite and appropriate titles.

**Pol.** **But at the beginning he seemed to you a worthless man.** <note>original: "Sed a principio videbatur tibi homo nequam."</note>

**Manf.** Away with that word **worthless** <note>original: "nequam"</note>! Although it is used in the Holy Scriptures, it is not, however, a **Ciceronian expression** <note>Manfredo is a "Ciceronian," a scholar who believed only Latin words used by the Roman orator Cicero were proper to use</note>. **"In living, follow the good; in writing, follow the experts!"** <note>original: "Tu vivendo bonos, scribendo sequare peritos!"</note> so said the Ninivite Johannes Despauterius <note>A famous Flemish grammarian (c. 1460–1520) whose Latin textbooks were used throughout Europe</note>, followed by my preceptor Aloisio Antonio of Sidicino, a branch of the Salani, successor to Lucio Giovanni Scoppa, **by the will of the heir** <note>original: "ex voluntate heredis"</note>. You should say instead: **"Unfair"** <note>original: "Non aequum"</note>, with the first letter of the word as a diphthong <note>meaning spelled with 'ae'</note>, to distinguish it from the **four-legged living sentient substance** <note>original: "quadrupede substantia animata sensitiva"; a horse (equum)</note>, which does not admit a diphthong at the beginning.

**San.** Most learned master, we must take our leave, for we need to be with Master Giovanni Bernardo, the painter, as soon as possible. Farewell!

**Manf.** **Go then with favorable omens!** <note>original: "Itene dunque coi fausti volatili!"; literally "go with the lucky birds," referring to the Roman practice of augury</note> — But who is this woman coming toward me with that **basket** <note>original: "calatho"</note> in her **arms** <note>original: "brachiis"</note>? She is a **little woman** <note>original: "muliercula"</note>, **which by etymology is "soft Hercules"** <note>original: "quod est per etymologiam mollis Hercules"</note>, defined by **contrast** <note>original: "iuxta se posita"</note>: the soft, mobile, fragile, and inconstant sex, the opposite of Hercules. Oh, what a beautiful etymology, drawn just now from my own **wit** <note>original: "Marte"; literally "Mars," often used to mean one's own efforts or skill</note>! Now, therefore, **I move my step nearly toward her** <note>original: "prope iam versus movo il gresso"</note>, because I want to record her **in larger letters** <note>original: "maioribus literis"</note> in my book of **personal night-studies** <note>original: "propriarum elucubrationum"</note>. **Not a day without a line!** <note>original: "Nulla dies sine linea!"; a famous maxim attributed to the painter Apelles, meaning one should practice one's craft every day</note>

### SCENA VI.

->Lucia, alone.<-

Oh my! I am tired. I want to rest here. This whole night—I don’t want to curse it—I’ve been standing guard on my feet, feeding on smoke, roast meat, and the smell of a fat cooking pot; and I am like a **kidney** <note>original: "rognone"</note> \*) —misery me—thin in the middle of the fat. Now let’s think of something else, Lucia! Since I am in a place where no one sees me, I want to see what these things are that Master Bonifacio is sending to Lady Vittoria. Here are **gravioli** \*\*), **sugar shields** <note>original: "targhe di zuccaro"; almond-paste or sugar wafers shaped like small shields</note>, and **Saint Sebastian’s spice cakes** \*\*). There are—

---

\*) Kidney <note>original: "Rene, arnione"</note>.
\*\*) **Sugar-plums** <note>original: "Treggee"</note>, marzipans, sweets—who knows? **Gravioli**, or **raviuoli**, are a species of small pastries made of candied grapes, almonds, pine nuts, minced meat, breadcrumbs, and Lodigiano or Parmesan cheese, then enclosed in a pastry crust and put in a pot to cook; then they are extracted with a slotted spoon and sprinkled with Parmesan cheese and melted butter. They are similar to those called **pancakes** <note>original: "Pfannekuchen"</note> in Germany, although the ingredients are different. — **Mastaccio**: sunflower seed or heliotrope.

<meta>This page continues from the previous scene where the servant Sanguino, having left the pedantic Manfredo, is inspecting a basket of gifts intended for a lady. He has discovered a hidden note among the sweets.</meta>

Further down are more kinds of sweets; there is a note at the bottom, and by my faith, they are verses! By my word, this man has become a poet. Now let’s read!

> *You have wounded, O gentle lady, my heart,*
> *And you have impressed upon my soul great pain;*
> *And if you do not believe me, look at my color!* <note>In Renaissance poetry, a pale complexion ("color") was a standard physical sign of being lovesick.</note>
> *For if it were not that I bear you so much love,*
> *As much as any other lovers, who are honorable,*
> *Have ever borne for their beloved ladies,*
> *I would do things quite out of my senses.*
> *Therefore I wished to be the author of this present gift,*
> *Exhausted by the great splendor of your beauties,*
> *So that you may understand by the tenor of this letter,*
> *That, if you do not help your Bonifacio, he dies.*
> *In sleeping, eating, drinking, he finds no flavor,*
> *Thinking of nothing else but you at all hours,*
> *Forgetful of father, mother, brothers, and sisters.*

Oh, what a fine conclusion! Fine intentions, exactly as futile as he is! For my part, I don’t understand rhyme; yet, if I can judge them, I’ll say two things: one, that the verses are longer than the ordinary ones; the other, that they are made with the sound of a bell and a donkey’s braying, which always hit the same rhyme. But I want to leave here and find a more convenient place where I can take the "tithe" <note>Sanguino intends to steal a portion of the sweets for himself.</note> of this gift; for in the end, it is necessary that I too be a sharer in the fruits of this man’s madness.

### S C E N A VII.

->Bonifacio, alone.<-

Great is the power of love. From where, O Muses, has such a vein and efficacy in making verses flowed into me, without any teacher having taught me? Where has a similar sonnet <note>Bonifacio calls his poem a "sonnet," but it is actually a clumsy string of fourteen lines all ending in the same rhyme (-ore), which was considered the "easiest" and most overused rhyme in Italian.</note> ever been composed? All the verses from the first to the last finish with the ending of the same sound. Read all of Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the definitive master of the Italian sonnet.</note>, look through all of Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), author of the epic *Orlando Furioso*.</note>, and you will not find the like. Traitress, traitress, my sweet enemy, I believe that by this hour you have read and been pierced by it; and if your soul is not more rugged than a tiger's, I am certain that you will no longer think little of your Bonifacio. Oh, here is Master Bernardo!

### S C E N A VIII.

->Giovanni Bernardo. Bonifacio.<-

**Gio. B.** Good day and a good year to you, Master Bonifacio! Have you performed any good deed today?

**Bonifacio.** What do you say? Today I have done something that I have never done in all the time of my life.

**Giovan Bernardo.** Oh! <note>The original transcription notes "ubi," likely a printer's error for the Italian exclamation "oibò," meaning "oh!" or "nonsense!"</note> You speak of great things. Is it possible that what you did today, you could have done yesterday, or some other day—either you, or anyone else? Or that you could do what is done once for all the rest of your life? Just as you will never again do what you did yesterday, I never before made the portrait that I made today; nor is it even possible that I could ever make it again. I could, certainly, make another one.

**Bonifacio.** Let us leave aside these sophistries <term>sofisticarie: overly clever, pedantic, or deceptive arguments intended to confuse</term> of yours! You have reminded me of the portrait. Have you seen the one I had made of myself?

**Giovan Bernardo.** I have seen it, and seen it again.

**Bonifacio.** What do you judge of it?

**Giovan Bernardo.** It is good; it resembles you far more than it resembles me. <note>A sarcastic remark implying the portrait is as ugly or foolish as Bonifacio himself.</note>

**Bonifacio.** Let it be as it may, I want another from your own hand.

**Giovan Bernardo.** Do you wish to give it to some lady as a souvenir of yourself?

**Bonifacio.** Enough! There are other things moving through my mind.

**Giovan Bernardo.** It is a good sign when things move through the mind. Take care, however, that the mind itself does not go wandering after those things! For it might remain stuck to one of them, and your brain would wait in vain for it at dinner this evening; then you would have to act like the mistress of a house who went searching for her intellect with a lantern. As for the portrait, I shall do it as soon as possible.

**Bonifacio.** Yes; but on your life, make me handsome!

**Giovan Bernardo.** Do not give so many orders if you wish to be well served. If you desire that I make you handsome, that is one thing; that I portray you <note>Meaning to paint a true and realistic likeness.</note> is quite another.

**Bonifacio.** I beg of you, leave off the jests! See that you do a good job! For I shall come to find you at your house for this purpose.

**Giovan Bernardo.** Come whenever you please, and do not doubt a good result on my part! You, for your part, see that you act well; because—

**Bonifacio.** What does "because" mean?

**Giovan Bernardo.** Leave behind the old craft.

**Bonifacio.** What? The devil himself would not understand you.

**Giovan Bernardo.** You wish to turn from a candle-maker <note>Original: *candelajo*. This is a central pun on the play's title. In this context, it suggests Bonifacio is trying to abandon his common, perhaps sordid, past to become something more refined.</note> into a goldsmith.

**Bonifacio.** How a goldsmith? How a candle-maker?

**Giovan Bernardo.** Enough, I commend myself to you.

**Bonifacio.** May God give you what you desire!

**Giovan Bernardo.** And to you, what you lack!

# S C E N A IX.

->Bonifacio alone.<-

From a candlemaker, do you wish to become a goldsmith? <note>A callback to the play's title and the painter's wordplay; Bonifacio is a "candlemaker" (candelajo), a term used here to imply a fool or someone of low status trying to refine himself into a "goldsmith" through love.</note> My situation is truly a serious thing. # S C E N A X.

->Scaramure. Bonifacio. Ascanio.<-

**Scar.** Well met, Master Bonifacio!
**Bon.** You are very welcome, Signor Scaramure, hope of my impassioned life!
**Scar.** A sign of an affected soul! <note>original: "Signum affecti animi!"</note>
**Bon.** If your lordship does not find a remedy for my ill, I am a dead man.
**Scar.** As I can see, you are in love.
**Bon.** It is so; I need say no more to you.
**Scar.** As your <term>physiognomy</term><note>The pseudo-scientific practice of judging character or predicting the future from facial features.</note> makes known to me—along with the calculation of your name, your relatives, and your ancestors—the lady of your birth was Venus retrograde in a masculine sign, and this perhaps in the twenty-seventh degree of Gemini, <note>original: "Venus retrograda in signo masculino, et hoc fortasse in geminibus vigesimo septimo gradu"</note> which signifies a certain mutation and conversion at the age of 45 years, in which you currently find yourself.
**Bon.** I don't exactly remember when I was born; but from what I have heard others say, I find myself to be around 45 years old.
**Scar.** I shall calculate the months, days, and hours more distinctly when, with the compass, I have taken the proportions from the width of the largest fingernail to the <term>life line</term>, and the distance from the top of the ring finger to that point at the center of the hand where the <term>Space of Mars</term> is designated. <note>Scaramure is using Chiromancy (palm reading) terms to impress Bonifacio with jargon.</note> But it is enough for now to have made such a universal and general judgment. Tell me, when you were struck by the love of that woman by looking at her, in what position was she? To the right or to the left?
**Bon.** To the left.
**Scar.** She is to be obtained by arduous effort! <note>original: "Arduo opere nanciscenda!"</note> Was it toward the south or north, east or west, or other places in between?
**Bon.** Toward the south.
**Scar.** It is necessary to summon the northern powers. <note>original: "Oportet advocare septentrionales"</note> Enough, enough! Nothing else is needed here. I want to carry out your business with natural magic— <note>Natural magic was considered a legitimate branch of science in the Renaissance, dealing with the hidden properties of herbs, stones, and stars, as opposed to "black magic" involving demons.</note>

...moral, leaving the superstitions of deeper arts for a better opportunity.
**Bon.** Make it so that I clinch the deal, and let it be as it will!
**Scar.** Do not trouble yourself! Leave the care to me! Was the matter already caused by <term>fascination</term>? <note>In the 16th century, "fascination" was not just attraction, but a quasi-physical process where one person's gaze could literally infect or alter another person's spirit.</note>
**Bon.** How "by fascination"? I do not understand.
**Scar.** That is to say <note>original: "Id est"</note>, by having looked at her, while she was looking at you too.
**Bon.** Yes, sir, yes, by fascination.
**Scar.** Fascination occurs by the power of a <term>lucid spirit</term> <note>These "spirits" were thought to be subtle vapors in the blood that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> and subtle, generated by the heat of the heart from the purest blood; this spirit, in the manner of rays, is sent out through open eyes. Looking with a strong imagination, these rays strike the thing being watched, touch the heart, and go on to *affect* <note>original: "afficere"</note> the other's body and spirit, whether with the passion of love, or hate, or envy, or <term>melancholy</term>, or other similar kinds of passive qualities. Being fascinated by love happens when, with a very frequent or even instantaneous, intense look, one eye meets the other, and reciprocally one visual ray meets the other, and light is coupled with light. Then spirit joins with spirit, and the superior light, by impressing itself upon the inferior, comes to sparkle through the eyes, running and penetrating to the internal spirit that is rooted in the heart; and thus they stir up an amorous fire. Therefore, he who does not wish to be fascinated must stay extremely cautious and keep a good guard over the eyes, which in the act of love are principally the windows of the soul: hence that saying: *Turn away, turn away your eyes!* <note>original: "Averte, averte oculos tuos!" — likely a reference to Song of Solomon 6:5.</note> This shall suffice for the present! We shall see each other again at better leisure, providing for the necessary things.

**Scar.** Master Bonifacio, I will give you to understand this: I wish first to be grateful to you, and then I am certain that if you are not grateful to me, you will have to be.
**Bon.** Give me your orders, for I am most devoted to you, and I have great hope in your prudence.
**Asc.** Come then, goodbye to all!
**Bon.** Let us go, for I see coming the most bothersome man to me that nature could have produced. I do not want to have an occasion to speak with him. I will come to you, Signor Scaramure.
**Scar.** Come, for I await you. Goodbye!

### SCENE XI.

->**Cencio. Giovanni Bernardo.**<-

**Cen.** Thus must this work be guided, according to the teachings of **Hermes** and **Geber**. <note>Hermes Trismegistus and Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) were the legendary founding fathers of alchemy; citing them was a way to claim ultimate authority.</note> The matter of all metals is Mercury; to Saturn belongs lead; to Jupiter, tin; to Mars, iron; to the Sun, gold; to Venus, bronze <note>or copper</note>; to the Moon, silver. Quicksilver is attributed to Mercury particularly, and it is found in the substance of all other metals. Therefore, he is called the messenger of the gods, male with males, and female with females. <note>In alchemy, Mercury was considered "hermaphroditic" or dual-natured because it could bond with almost any other metal.</note> Of these metals, Mercury Trismegistus called the heaven the father and the earth the mother, and said that this mother is sometimes impregnated in the mountains, sometimes in the valleys, sometimes in the fields, sometimes in the sea, sometimes in the abysses and caverns—an enigma I have already explained the meaning of to you. In the womb of the earth, the most learned Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher whose works were central to medieval science.</note> affirms in his letter written to Hazez that the matter of all metals is this [Mercury] together with sulfur; <note>original: "solphro," an archaic spelling of "zolfo"</note> to which opinion I prefer that of Hermes, who maintains the matter of metals to be all the elements; and together with Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his work in the natural sciences.</note> I call ridiculous the sentence attributed to Democritus by the alchemists: that lime and lye—by which they mean <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Literally "strong water," a highly corrosive nitric acid used to dissolve metals.</note>—are the matter of all metals. Nor can I approve the opinion of Gilgile in his book of secrets, where he maintains that **the matter of metals is infused ash** <note>original Latin: "metallorum materiam esse cinerem infusum"</note>; because he saw that **ash melts into glass and is solidified by the cold** <note>original Latin: "cinis liquatur in vitrum et congelatur frigido"</note>; an error which Prince Albert subtly goes about refuting.

**Gio. Ber.** These devilish arguments do not touch my intellect one bit. I would rather see the gold made, and you better dressed than you currently go about. I think quite rightly that if you knew how to make gold, you would not sell the recipe for making gold, but you would make it with that recipe; and while you make gold for someone else to show them the experiment, you would make it for yourself, so as not to have any need to sell the secret.

**Cen.** You have interrupted my discourse. Do you think you alone have good judgment, and that you have brought forth a great argument through the precautions you have used with me? Master Bartolomeo shows himself to be much more cautious than you consider yourself to be, and he knows that I was robbed and assaulted in the woods of Cancello while coming from Airola.

**Gio. Ber.** I believe he knows it more from your telling than from my own.

**Cen.** And therefore I, not having the means to buy the <term>simples</term> <note>Basic medicinal or chemical ingredients, usually derived from single plants or minerals.</note> and minerals required for such a work, have done as you know.

**Gio. Bern.** You should have put yourself up as collateral and security, and said: "Sir, I will produce gold for myself and for you"; for certainly he, as much as anyone else, would have helped you no less, and that gold, which you seek from other men's purses, you would have pulled from your own furnace with a better reputation and honor.

**Gio. Ber.** I suspect that silver and tin will soon be worth more than gold <note>Giovanni Bernardo is being sarcastic, implying that if Cencio’s "secret" makes gold common, it will lose its value.</note>.

So that in the end, with great joy, he found the purest and most proven gold at the bottom of the glass **vessel** <term>concurbita</term> <note>original: "concurbita" (cucurbit), a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note>, heated with the **seal of wisdom** <term>luto sapientiae</term> <note>original: "luto sapientiae," a chemical paste or "philosopher's clay" used to airtightly seal laboratory vessels to prevent the escape of vapors.</note>.

**Gio. **Cen.** Oh, you are always joking.

**Gio. Ber.** Yes, yes, I’m joking. But the first time I see you together, I will say: "Here is your cape, Cencio; here is your cape, Bartolomeo." But tell me as an honest man—let’s speak seriously!—didn't you pull one over on him just as Gigio did to Perrotino?

**Cen.** And what did he do?

**Gio. Ber.** You don't know what he did? I can tell you. That fellow took a piece of wood, hollowed it out and put gold inside, then charred it on the outside so it looked like any other piece of coal. At the right moment, with great dexterity, he took it from his pocket; then, while handling two other coals that were near the furnace, he found the opportunity to place that **pregnant coal** <note>A "pregnant coal" (carbone pregnante) was a classic trick used by fraudulent alchemists; it contained hidden gold that would "appear" once the coal burned away.</note> into the fire, where it was soon consumed by the heat and dripped the powdered gold through the holes into the bottom.

**Cen.** Oh, God help me! I never could have imagined—

### Cencio alone.

In truth, if Bartolomeo had this man’s brain, and if everyone were so poorly advised, I would have spread my net in this land in vain. Now, let us act with good grace, since the bird is in the trap! I don't want her to see me all bundled up <note>original: "imbottato," suggesting Cencio is disguised or wearing heavy traveling clothes to hide his identity while fleeing.</note> like this.

### Marta alone.

I believe that Satan, Barsabucco <note>A folk name for a demon, often associated with fire or soot.</note>, and all those who melt and dissolve metals will take him as a companion, because he certainly knows how to stir the fires of hell to sauté and roast damned souls. # ACT SECOND.

## SCENE FIRST.

### Master Ottaviano. Manfurio. Pollula.

Ottaviano: Master, what is your name?
Manfurio: **Manfurius** <note>original: "Manfurius"</note>.
Ottaviano: What is your profession?
Manfurio: **Master of arts** <note>original: "Magister artium"</note>, **governor** <note>original: "moderator"</note> of **little boys** <note>original: "pueruli"</note>, of **tender little fingernails**, **smooth cheeks**, **youths**, **adolescents**, **those who, like a young rod, are still able to be raised up, bent, and led in every direction**, **of the first voice** <note>original: "primae vocis"</note>, fit for the soprano, **of ungnawed little teeth, of plump little flesh, of fresh nature, of no wrinkles, of milky breath, of rosy little lips, of a sweet little tongue, of honeyed simplicity, living in the flower and not yet in the seed, having bright little eyes, and indistinguishable from girls**. <note>Manfurio uses a string of Latin diminutives to describe his pupils, highlighting his pedantic and perhaps unsettling obsession with their youth.</note>
Ottaviano: Oh gentle master, trim, most eloquent, most gallant **chief steward** <term>arcitriclino: the master of a feast or head of a dining room</term> and **cupbearer** <term>pincerna: a servant who pours wine</term> of the Muses!
Manfurio: Oh, what a beautiful apposition <note>A grammatical term for a descriptive phrase placed next to a noun.</note>!
Ottaviano: Patriarch of the **Apollonian** choir!
Manfurio: **It would be better said: Apolline.** <note>original: "Melius diceretur: apollineo." Manfurio cannot help but correct Ottaviano's Latinate grammar.</note>
Ottaviano: Trumpet of **Phoebus** <note>An epithet for Apollo, god of music and poetry.</note>, let me give you a kiss on the left cheek! For I do not repute myself worthy to kiss that sweetest mouth.
Manfurio: For which I do not envy **Jupiter** his ambrosia and nectar.
Ottaviano: That mouth, I say, which breathes forth such varied and beautiful maxims and unheard-of phrases.
Manfurio: **I shall add even more: on the very threshold of age, in the very beginnings of life, in the very rudiments of the business of this mundane, or cosmic, architecture, from the very entrance, in the very spring of age, as those who are ready for marriage, not even as far as the parsley.** <note>original: "Addam et plura... ne in apiis quidem." The phrase "not even as far as the parsley" refers to an ancient Greek and Latin proverb for something that has barely begun, as parsley was planted at the very edge of gardens.</note>
Ottaviano: Oh master, **horse-fountain** <note>original: "fonte cavallino." A reference to Hippocrene, the fountain on Mount Helicon created by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus; drinking from it brought poetic inspiration.</note>, please, do not make me die of sweetness before I confess my fault! Speak no more, I pray you, because you make me swoon.

**Manf.** *I shall be silent then, for one is overwhelmed by the glory of majesty;* <note>original: "Silebo igitur, quia opprimitur a gloria maiestatis"</note> just as happened to that wretched woman whom Ovid mentions in his *Metamorphoses*, whose thread of life the greedy Fates cut short when she beheld the lightning-bolt of Jove in all his majesty. <note>Manfurio refers to Semele, who was consumed by fire when Jupiter revealed his true form to her.</note>

**Ott.** I beg you, by that god Mercury who has flooded you with eloquence—

**Manf.** *I am compelled to comply.* <note>original: "Cogor morem gerere"</note>

**Ott.** Have pity on me, and do not hurl any more of those darts at me, for they make me lose my mind!

**Manf.** *Admiration draws him into a profound ecstasy. I shall be silent then—enough of these things for now, I shall add nothing—mute as fish—having spoken thus, his voice stuck in his throat.* <note>original: "In ecstasin profundam trahit ipsum admiratio. Taceo igitur — de iis hactenus, nil addam — muti pisces — tantum effatus, vox faucibus haesit." Manfurio strings together several Latin clichés and a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid to show off.</note>

**Ott.** Master Manfurio, most pleasant river of eloquence, most serene sea of doctrine!

**Manf.** *Tranquility of the sea, serenity of the air!* <note>original: "Tranquillitas maris, serenitas aëris!"</note>

**Ott.** Do you have any fine compositions of yours? For I have a great desire to have a copy of your most learned papers.

**Manf.** I believe, sir, that *in the whole course of my life* <note>original: "in toto vitae curriculo"</note> and across the discourse of many and various pages, you have never encountered verses of such symmetry, nor so well adapted, as these which I am presently about to show you, *written* <note>original: "exarati"</note> here.

**Ott.** What is the subject matter of your verses?

**Manf.** *Letters, syllables, diction, and speech; parts near and remote.* <note>original: "Litterae, syllabae, dictio, et oratio, partes propinquae et remotae." Manfurio lists the technical components of grammar rather than the actual topic.</note>

**Ott.** I mean, what is the subject and the purpose?

**Manf.** You mean to ask, *what is it about, the matter concerning which, or around which?* <note>original: "de quo agitur, materia, de qua, circa quam?"</note> It is the gluttony, greed, and belly-madness of that filth-hound Sanguino—a living image of Philoxenus, *who wished for the neck of a crane* <note>Philoxenus of Cythera was a legendary glutton who wished for a long neck so he could enjoy the taste of food for a longer time.</note>—along with others of his ilk: his partners, followers, peers, and associates.

**Ott.** Please, let me hear them!

**Manf.** *Most willingly. Secrets should not be hidden from the learned.* <note>original: "Lubentissime. Eruditis non sunt operienda arcana."</note> Here, I unfold the paper prepared and ruled by my own fingers. But first, I want you to note that Ovid of Sulmo (*Sulmo is my homeland* <note>original: "Sulmo mihi patria est," a quote from Ovid's Tristia.</note>) described the Calydonian boar with many epithets in the eighth book of his *Metamorphoses*; in imitation of which, I am sketching this domestic pig.

**Ott.** Please, read it quickly!

**Manf.** *So be it! He who gives quickly, gives twice. I shall begin with the emotion of one who marvels.* <note>original: "Fiat! Qui cito dat, bis dat. Exordium ab admirantis affectu."</note>

> O filthy pig, vile, useless life,
> Who has nothing else but that foolish snout,
> With which you think to acquire your food!
> Throat quadrupled by the grease <note><term>axungia</term>: animal fat or lard, used here to mock Sanguino's obesity.</note>
> Absorbed by the aforementioned slop-licker, <note><term>brodolario</term>: a Made-up Latinate word for one who licks the broth or slops.</note>
> Which the foul scullion prepares for you: <note><term>coquinario</term>: relating to the kitchen or a cook.</note>

*Through the drainage canal,*
*To fatten yourself further, vessel of gluttony,* <note>original: "vase d' ingluvie." *Ingluvie* refers to the crop of a bird or the gullet, used here to signify insatiable greed.</note>
*Into this pigsty you thrust yourself,*
*Where you look toward no other object but the pasture,*
*And, deprived of exercise,*
*For lack and penury*
*Of a better bed and a better chamber,* <note>original: "cubiculo." A private bedroom or sleeping chamber.</note>
*You do nothing else but wallow in dung and mud.*
->*After these things.*<- <note>original: "Post haec."</note>
*Unfit for no filthy wallow,* <note>original: "volutabro." A place where swine roll in the mud; a slough.</note>
*Incurable infirmity of throat and luxury,*
*Belly, which seems like the pit of the Pleiades,* <note>original: "Pleiade il puteo." Likely a mock-learned reference to a deep cosmic abyss or a "well" of stars.</note>
*Dweller of mud, muddy inhabitant,* <note>original: "incola luteo."</note>
*Tireless maw, with a most devouring throat,* <note>original: "gutture."</note>
*Greediest Harpy, vulture of Tityos,* <note>In Greek mythology, the giant Tityos was punished in the underworld by having two vultures eternally devour his liver.</note>
*Earth never satisfied, fire and greedy womb,*
*Extended orifice, putrid nostril,*
*Enemy of heaven, earthly observer,*
*Weak hand and foot, iron mouth and tooth,*
*Your soul was given to you only as salt,*
*So that you would not rot. Do I speak ill?* <note>This refers to a common classical and Renaissance trope—attributed to various philosophers like Chrysippus—that a pig has a soul only to serve as salt to keep its meat from spoiling.</note>

What do you think of these verses? What? Do you understand their meter with your wit?
**Ott.** Certainly, for being the work of one of your profession, they are not without fine consideration.
**Manf.** Without condition, and absolutely <note>original: "Sine conditione, et absolute"</note> they must be judged worthy of profound scrutiny—these fruits gathered from the best plants that the Heliconian mount ever produced, watered further by the Parnassian fount, tempered by fair Apollo, and cultivated by the sacred Muses. <note>Manfurio invokes the standard geography of Greek myth: Mount Helicon and Mount Parnassus were the homes of the Muses and Apollo, the patrons of poetry.</note> Eh, what do you think of this fine discourse? Do you not marvel now, as you did before?
**Ott.** A most beautiful and subtle concept! But tell me, I pray you, did you spend much time in ordering these verses?
**Manf.** No.
**Ott.** Did you fatigue yourself in making them?
**Manf.** Not at all. <note>original: "Minime"</note>
**Ott.** Did you spend great care and thought on them?
**Manf.** By no means. <note>original: "Nequaquam"</note>
**Ott.** Did you do and redo them?
**Manf.** Not at all. <note>original: "Haud quaquam"</note>
**Ott.** Did you correct them?
**Manf.** Not in the least: there was no need. <note>original: "Minime gentium: non opus erat"</note>
**Ott.** Did you cleverly take them, not to say pilfered them, from some author?
**Manf.** Not at all! Far be it from me to be envied! May the gods avert it! May the gods above not allow such a thing! <note>original: "Neutiquam! Absit verbo invidia! dii avertant! ne faxint ista superi!" Manfurio uses a string of dramatic Latin denials to defend his originality.</note> You wish to see too much of my erudi-

<term>Ingluvie</term>: Gluttony or the physical gullet of an animal.
<term>Volutabro</term>: A wallow or slough, specifically for swine.
<term>Puteo</term>: A well or pit.
<term>Mariolati</term>: To have cheated or pilfered (from *mariolo*, a rogue or cheat).
<term>Heliconian mount</term>: Mount Helicon, sacred to the Muses.
<term>Apollo</term>: The god of light and poetry.
<term>Muses</term>: The nine deities of artistic inspiration.
<term>Invidia</term>: Envy or ill-will.

--- Page 77 ---
<meta>The dialogue continues from the previous page where Master Manfurio, a pedantic schoolmaster, has just finished reciting a poem he composed to insult a gluttonous rival. He now shifts to boasting about his linguistic mastery and his command of rhetorical flourishes.</meta>

Believe me, I have drunk no small amount from the horse-fountain <note>original: "fonte cavallino." This refers to the Hippocrene fountain on Mount Helicon, which was said to have been created by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus and was the source of poetic inspiration.</note>, nor has the one **born from the brain of Jove** <note>original: "de cerebro nata Jovis." Refers to Minerva (Athena), the goddess of wisdom, who was born fully formed from Jupiter’s forehead.</note> infused me with little liquid: I mean the chaste Minerva, to whom wisdom is attributed. Believe me, I would not be **less fortunately resolved** if I had been challenged **to explain the markers of affirmation or assertion**. My memory has not failed me. **Yes, so, also, indeed, truly, openly, truly, certainly, without a doubt, especially, who could doubt it? Certainly, why not? By Hercules! By Pollux! By the God of Faith! and so forth.** <note>Manfurio recites a string of Latin affirmative particles: "Sic, ita, etiam, sane, profecto, palam, verum, certe, procul dubio, maxime, cui du-bium? utique, quidni? Mehercle, Aedepol, Mediusfidius." These demonstrate his status as a "pedant"—someone obsessed with showing off minor grammatical knowledge.</note>

**Ottaviano.** Pray, in place of that "and so forth," tell me another negation.

**Manfurio.** I will not commit this bad-sounding speech, **that is, poor elocution**, because **once an enumeration is finished, a single unit must not be added to the clause.** <note>original: "factae enumerationis clausulae non est adponenda unitas." This is a mock-logical rule Manfurio uses to avoid having to think of another word.</note>

**Ottaviano.** Of all these affirmative particles, which one pleases you more than the others?

**Manfurio.** That **certainly** <note>original: "utique."</note> matters quite a bit to me; it is an elegance in the Etruscan language, **or Tuscan, and it sticks in my mind**: an elegance of a deeper idiom.

**Ottaviano.** Of the negatives, which pleases you most?

**Manfurio.** That **by no means** <note>original: "nequaquam."</note> **is close to my heart**; it satisfies me.

**Ottaviano.** Now, you ask me something!

**Manfurio.** Tell me, Signor Ottaviano, do our verses please you?

**Ottaviano.** **By no means**.

**Manfurio.** How, **by no means**? Are they not **the best**?

**Ottaviano.** **By no means**.

**Manfurio.** **Two negatives make an affirmative**. <note>original: "Duae negationes affirmant." A standard rule of logic and grammar where two "nos" equal a "yes."</note> You mean to say, then, that they are good.

**Ottaviano.** **By no means**.

**Manfurio.** You are joking.

**Ottaviano.** **By no means**.

**Manfurio.** So you speak in earnest?

**Ottaviano.** **Certainly**. <note>original: "Utique."</note>

**Manfurio.** You are my enemy and you bear me envy. At first you were filled with wonder at our **abundance of speech** <note>original: "dicendi copia." A technical term in rhetoric for the ability to speak at length with a variety of vocabulary.</note>; now, **in the very progress of the reading**, has that wonder morphed into envy?

**Ottaviano.** **By no means**. Why envy? Why an enemy? Did you not tell me that these words please you?

**Manfurio.** You are joking then, saying this **for the sake of exercise**? <note>original: "exercitationis gratia."</note>

**Ottaviano.** **By no means**.

**Manfurio.** **Speak then without simulation or pretense!** <note>original: "Dicas igitur sine simulatione et fuco!" Literally "without paint or rouge," meaning to speak plainly.</note> Do my verses possess enormity, coarseness, and rudeness?

**Ottaviano.** **Certainly**.

**Manfurio.** You believe exactly that?

<summary>Master Manfurio boasts of his command over Latin rhetorical particles, only for Ottaviano to use Manfurio's own favorite words ("by no means" and "certainly") to mockingly insult the quality of Manfurio's poetry.</summary>
<keywords>Manfurio, Ottaviano, rhetoric, Latin particles, irony, pedantry, Minerva, poetic inspiration, linguistic humor</keywords>

**Ott.** Truly, surely, certainly, indeed, truly, truly. <note>original Latin: "Utique, sane, certe, equidem, utique, utique." Ottaviano is mocking Manfurio by repeating his list of affirmations.</note>
**Manf.** I no longer wish to speak with you.
**Ott.** If you cannot bear to hear what you say pleases you, what would happen if I told you something that displeases you? **Farewell!**
**Manf.** Go, go! *Come here, Pollula!* <note>original Latin: "Adesdum."</note> Have you considered the nature of this man, who has just taken his leave of us?
**Pol.** At first, he was mocking you in one way; by the end, he was making a fool of you in another.
**Ma.** Do you not think all this is due to the envy that the unskilled bear toward us (*it would be better said "to others," the difference making it something else*) <note>original Latin: "melius diceretur alii, differentia faciente aliud." Manfurio is pedantically correcting his own grammar mid-sentence, debating whether "us" or "others" is the more precise term.</note> learned men?
**Pol.** I believe everything you say, since you are my master, and to please you.
**Ma.** *Enough of these things! Let us let them go!* <note>original Latin: "De iis hactenus! missa faciamus haec!"</note> Right now I want to go and dispatch the Muses against this Ottaviano; and just as I made him hear, regarding another matter, those swinish epithets, *from now on regarding him* <note>original Latin: "posthac in suo proposito"</note> I want him to hear the epithets belonging to an incompetent judge of another's learning. Here, I hand you a love letter written at the request of **Master Bonifacio**, who, to please his *mistress* <note>term: "amasia" — a Latinate term for a lover or mistress.</note>, asked me to compose this "incendiary" letter for him. Go, and deliver it secretly into his hand on my behalf, telling him that I am entangled in other business concerning my <term>literary school</term> <note>original: "ludo literario." Refers to his grammar school or place of teaching.</note>. *I too shall take my leave from here* <note>original Latin: "Ego quoque hinc pedem referam."</note>, because I see two women approaching, *about whom the saying goes: Keep them far from me!* <note>original Latin: "de quibus illud: Longe fac a me!"</note>
**Pol.** *Greetings, Lord Teacher!* <note>original Latin: "Salve, domine praeceptor!"</note>
**Manf.** *A fortunate journey is what "Farewell" means.* <note>original Latin: "Faustum iter dicitur Vale." Manfurio defines the word "Vale" even as he uses it to end the conversation.</note>

### SCENA III.

->**S. Vittoria. Lucia.**<-

**S. Vitt.** The great <term>sheepishness</term> <note>original: "pecoraggine." Derived from "pecora" (sheep), implying both stupidity and a submissive nature.</note> that I perceive in him makes me fall in love with this man; his stupidity leads me to argue that we will lose nothing by having him as a lover, and being a **Bonifacio**, as you see, he can do nothing but good. <note>There is a pun here on the name "Bonifacio," which translates roughly to "well-doer" or "good fate."</note>
**Luc.** This man is not one of those madmen whose brains are too dry, but one of those whose brains are too damp. <note>This refers to the "humoral theory" of medicine. A "damp" brain was thought to make a person slow, foolish, and easily manipulated, whereas "dry" brains were associated with sharp, irritable, or "choleric" personalities.</note> Therefore, he must necessarily lean toward a thick and sweet temperament, rather than toward one that is too subtle, annoying, choleric, and erratic.
**S. Vitt.** Now go and thank him on my behalf, and tell him that I cannot see myself satisfied with reading his paper, and that in the short time you were with me, ten times me...

...you saw her pull it out and put it back in her breast. Tell him as many **tall tales** <note>original: "panzanate." This refers to ridiculous lies or nonsense stories intended to deceive.</note> as you can, to make him understand that I bear him great love.
