### SCENE IV.

->**Santa Vittoria alone.**<-

Love is painted as a young boy for two reasons: one, because it seems it does not suit the **old**; the other, because it makes a man of light and less serious sentiment, like children. Neither by the one way nor the other has love entered into this man. I do not say because it would suit him—since such **jousts** <note>A metaphor for romantic or sexual pursuits.</note> do not seem good for him—nor because it would have to take away his intellect; for no one can be deprived of what he does not have.
—But I must not look at him as much as I must think of my own affairs. I consider that, just as among virgins some are called foolish and others **prudent** <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25:1-13).</note>, so also among us others, who taste the best fruits the world produces, those are mad who love only for the sake of that pleasure which passes, and do not think of **old age**, which approaches quickly, without one seeing or feeling it, while at the same time making friends draw away. While the former wrinkles the face, the latter close their purses; the former consumes the humor within, and love without; the former strikes from nearby, and the latter salute from afar. Therefore, it is necessary to resolve oneself in time. He who waits for time, loses time. If I wait for time, time will not wait for me. We must make use of the affairs of others, while it seems they have need of us. Catch the prey while it follows you, and do not wait for it to flee! He will poorly catch the bird that flies, who does not know how to keep the one he has in the cage. Although this man has little brain and a weak back, he has, however, a **good purse**. For his first loss and his second misfortune I do not care; but of the third, one must take account. The wise live for the fools, and the fools for the wise. If all were lords, they would not be wise; and if all were fools, they would not be fools. The world is fine as it is. Now let us return to the point, **Porzia** <note>Santa Vittoria refers to herself as Porzia here, likely her "professional" name or the identity she is using for this specific deception.</note>! It is fitting for one who is beautiful in her youth to be wise for her old age. We have nothing else in the winter than what we gathered in the **summer**. Now let us act in such a way that this bird does not pass by with his feathers. Here comes Sanguino!

<summary>Santa Vittoria delivers a pragmatic monologue on the necessity of exploiting foolish, wealthy men like Bonifacio to secure her future before old age withers her beauty and leaves her destitute. She justifies her deception by arguing that the world is naturally balanced between the wise who profit and the fools who provide.</summary>

# SCENE V.

->Sanguino. Santa Vittoria.<-

**San.** I kiss those most beautiful knees and feet, my sweetest Lady Porzia, more flavorful than sugar, cinnamon, and true essence. <gloss>The original text reads: "and true sense" (*e senze verata*); a manifest error that requires a more likely emendation, perhaps "true essence" (*essenza verace*).</gloss> Oh, my dear, if we were not in the public square, even the **chains of Saint Leonard** <note>Saint Leonard of Noblac is the patron saint of prisoners; Sanguino means that even the strongest restraints could not hold him back.</note> would not stop me from planting a kiss on those lips that make me die of longing.
**S. Vitt.** What news do you bring, Sanguino?
**San.** Master Bonifacio commends himself to you just as good fathers commend their children to their teachers; **that is** <note>original: "i. e." (id est)</note> to say, if he is not wise, you should punish him well; and if you want someone who knows how and is able to **keep him on his horse** <note>A double entendre: it refers both to controlling a person and to a sexual position.</note>, make use of me!
**S. Vitt.** Ha, ha, ha! What do you mean by that?
**San.** You don’t understand? You don’t know what I mean? Are you really so simple?
**S. Vitt.** I do not have the same malicious thoughts that you have.
**San.** If you don’t have those particular malicious thoughts, you have these, and those, and those others besides. And if you are not as clever as I can be, you are as clever as anyone else could be. Now, let’s leave these words to the wind and get to our business! Once upon a time, the lion and the donkey were companions, and traveling together on a pilgrimage, they agreed that when crossing rivers they would carry each other in turn—which is to say, one time the donkey would carry the lion, and another time the lion would carry the donkey. Thus, having to go to Rome, and there being neither a ferry nor a bridge at their service, they arrived at the **Garigliano River** <note>A river in central Italy, south of Rome, often mentioned in historical and literary accounts of travel.</note>. The donkey took the lion upon his back; as he swam toward the other bank, the lion, for fear of falling, dug his claws deeper and deeper into the skin, so that they pierced that poor animal right to the bone. And the poor wretch, being a professional of patience, crossed as best he could without saying a word. Except that, once they reached safety out of the water, he shook his back a little and rolled around on the warm sand three or four times, and they went on their way. Eight days later, on their return journey, it was the lion's duty to carry the donkey. The donkey, being on top of him, grabbed the lion’s neck with his teeth so as not to fall into the water; and as that was not enough to hold him up, he thrust his "instrument"—or what shall we call it, you understand me, to speak **honestly** <note>A sarcastic euphemism for Sanguino's crude anatomical reference.</note>—into the empty space under the tail, where the skin is missing, in such a way that the lion felt greater agony than could be felt...

Who was that great bell-wether of a beast <note>The lead animal of a flock, usually wearing a bell, who the others follow blindly.</note> who drags such a large herd behind him? ...that without them, none of those things can be grasped or possessed. **Manf.** Come here a moment, I want a few words with you, Master Scaramure! <note>original Latin: "Adesdum, paucis te volo, domine Scaramure!"</note>
**Scar.** Consider it said <note>original Latin: "Dictum puta"</note>; I shall see you another time, when I have fewer chores.
**Manf.** Oh, what a fine response! Now, my Pollula, so that the discourse may return to the point from which it began <note>original Latin: "ut eo redeat, unde egressa est oratio"</note>, you will be amazed—oh!

**Pol.** Do you want me to read them?

## SCENE VI.

->**Manfurio. Gio. Bernardo. Pollula.**<-

**Manf.** Welcome to the one <note>original: "Bene veniat ille"</note> for whom the naming of resounding fame from the trumpet is no less fitting than it was for Zeuxis, Apelles, Phidias, Timagoras, and Polygnotus. <note>Manfurio lists famous artists of Greek antiquity to flatter Gio. Bernardo, though his speech is intentionally overblown.</note>
**Gio. Ber.** Of everything you have uttered, I understand nothing except that "cooking pot" <note>original: "pignatto" - likely a misunderstanding of a Latin word Manfurio used</note> you mentioned at the end. I believe that this, together with your drinking mug, makes you speak in various tongues. If I had already dined, I would answer you.
**Manf.** Wine gladdens and bread strengthens. <note>original: "Il vino exhilara et il pane confirma"</note>
> *Bacchus and nourishing Ceres, if by your gift the earth*
> *Exchanged Chaonian acorns for the rich ear of grain,* <note>original: "Bacchus et alma Ceres, vestro si munere tellus / Chaoniam pingui glandem mutavit arista"</note>
said Publius Virgilius Maro, the Mantuan poet, in his first book of the *Georgics*, near the beginning, making his invocation in the poetic manner <note>original: "more poetico"</note> wherein he imitates Hesiod, the Attic poet and seer.
**Gio. Ber.** Do you know, Lord Master <note>original: "domine magister"</note>—?
**Manf.** That is: "More, three times." <note>original: "Hoc est magis, ter" - Manfurio makes a pun on "magister," breaking it into the Latin words for "more" and "thrice."</note> *A few, whom impartial Jupiter loved, or whose burning virtue carried them to the heavens.* <note>original: "Pauci, quos aequus amavit Iupiter, aut ardens evexit in aethera virtus" - a quote from Virgil's Aeneid.</note>
**Gio. Ber.** What I want to say is this: I would like to know from you what the word "pedant" means.
**Manf.** Most gladly <note>original: "Lubentissime"</note> I wish to tell it to you, teach it to you, declare it to you, expose it to you, publish it to you, make it manifest <note>original: "palam"</note> to you, insinuate it into you, and—adding a conjunctive particle to the last word <note>original: "particula coniunctiva in ultima dictione apposita"</note>—shell it for you <note>original: "enuclearvelo," from "enucleare," to remove the kernel from a nut, used here to mean "explaining the core meaning"</note>; just as, like, as if, even as, in the manner that <note>original: "sicut, ut, velut, veluti, quemadmodum"</note> I shelled the Ovidian nut <note>original: "nucem Ovidianam"</note> before my students, so that they might better eat its kernel. "Pedant" means, as it were, *foot before* <note>original: "pede ante"</note>, seeing as <note>original: "utpote quia"</note> he has an orderly gait <note>original: "incesso prosequutivo"</note> by which he makes the youths to be educated go forward; or, by a tighter and more restricted etymology: *pe*, perfect; *dan*, giving; *te*, treasures. Now, what do you say to both of these?
**Gio. Ber.** They are good; but I like neither one nor the other, nor do they seem to the point.
**Manf.** You are permitted to say that, provided another better one is brought forth into the midst <note>original: "alia meliore in medium prolata"</note>; that is, when you have brought one much more worthy.
**Gio. Ber.** Here it is: *pe*, big sheep <note>original: "pecorone" - a term for a fool or a blockhead</note>; *dan*, good-for-nothing <note>original: "da nulla"</note>; *te*, donkey-head <note>original: "testa d’ asino"</note>.
**Manf.** As Cato the Elder said: *Tell no lies, and believe nothing rashly.* <note>original: "Nil mentiri, et nihil temere credideris"</note>
**Gio. Ber.** That is, that is <note>original: "Hoc est, id est"</note>, whoever says the contrary lies through his throat.

## SCENE X.

### Corcovizzo. Manfurio.

**Cor.** You know well enough that he is in love?
**Manf.** Oh, very well. His love passes through my hands; I have composed a love letter <note>original: "epistola amatoria"</note> for him, which he is to use as his own, so that he may be admired and more highly esteemed by his sweetheart <note>original: "amasia"</note>.
**Cor.** Now, yesterday—as if he were a young man of twenty-five—he went to suggest to Master **Luca** that he should have a pair of boots made for him out of Spanish leather <note>original: "marocchino di Spagna". This was a high-quality, soft goatskin leather prized for luxury footwear.</note> by today, suitable for walking about the city. Having heard this, that scoundrel was on the lookout today when **Master Bonifacio** came to try them on. Now, seeing him appear from the direction of Nola toward the shop, he slowly approached him without a cloak, until he followed him right inside the shop. Because he arrived at the same time as **Master Bonifacio**, the master of the shop took him for Bonifacio's servant; and because he was without a cloak and had his sleeves half-rolled up, **Master Bonifacio** took him for a shop hand. For this reason, while that poor gentleman was occupied with putting on his boots, he allowed his velvet-lined cloak, embroidered with gold, to be taken by the fellow. The rogue laid it over his two arms, either acting like a good valet or like one of the apprentices entitled to a tip <note>original: "strena"</note>; and while Master **Luca** was busy adjusting his handiwork, and **Master Bonifacio** was bent over his legs to be well-served, the thief—with a fine steady face—looked now at the shop's rafters, now at those passing by, now at those coming and going. Then he took a turn and spun around, until, seeing his chance, he set a foot outside the door. In conclusion: A cloak, of what case? The ablative! <note>original: "Cappa, cuius generis? Ablativi." A grammatical joke: in Latin, the ablative case is often associated with "taking away" or "removal."</note>
**Manf.** Ah, ah, ah! The dative is for giving, the ablative is for taking away! <note>original: "dativus a dando, ablativus ab auferendo". Manfurio, the pedant, can only communicate through schoolbook Latin rules.</note> If you had studied, and were not an unlettered man, you would have <note>The original text notes that Corcovizzo uses "plebeian" or vulgar verb forms like *avessivo* and *arestivo* instead of proper Italian.</note> a fine wit. I believe you had Minerva in the ascendant at your birth. <note>original: "Minerva in ascendente". In astrology, having the goddess of wisdom "rising" would indicate great intelligence.</note>
**Cor.** To return to the matter: once **Master Bonifacio** was fitted, and Master **Luca** had run the small brush over his back, shaking his hands, the gentleman asked for his cloak. Master **Luca** replied: "Your servant is holding it." "Hey! Where are you?" He stepped outside to look. "I have no need for such honors and flatteries," <note>original: "onori e castella". Literally "honors and castles," meaning empty formalities.</note> said **Master Bonifacio**. "Just tell me, which one is your shop hand?"

**Manf.** Oh *thief* <note>original: "fure"</note>, worthy food for vultures!

For my peers, that adage is fitting (*if it may properly be called an adage*): *Hurry slowly!* <note>original: "Festina lente!"</note> *Likewise also this: Step by step, little by little, cautiously.* <note>original: "Gradatim, paulatim, pedetentim."</note>

**Bar.** You are right, Master Doctor, to always have regard for your honor, and for the majesty of your gait.

**Manf.** Oh *thief* <note>original: "fure"</note>, whose bones I would like to see crushed upon a wheel! Alas! Perhaps he has not stolen them all from me! **Bar.** I believe he will be satisfied with that.

**Manf.** Oh, unjust moderators of justice! If you did your duty, there would not be such a wealth of evildoers. Perhaps he has not taken them all? Oh, most wicked man!

### SCENE XII.

->Sanguino. Barra. Manfurio. Marca.<-

**San.** Hey there, good men, why has that fellow fled? What has he done, that rogue?

**Bar.** Welcome, my Master! We are in the greatest distress in the world. We had that thief—or whatever the master <term>magister: teacher or master, usually implying a schoolmaster</term> wants him to be called—right in our hands; but because we don't know our letters, he escaped to the devil.

**San.** I don't know what kind of excuses these are. I am asking you, why did he flee?

**Manf.** He has stolen <note>original: "involati"</note> ten scudi from me.

**San.** How the devil did ten scudi fly away? <note>Sanguino makes a pun on "involare" (to steal) and "volare" (to fly).</note>

**Mar.** It is easy to see that you never went to school.

**San.** As soon as I had learned my **A-B-Cs** <note>original: "B. A. BA"</note>, my father gave me as a boy to Captain Mancino.

**Manf.** *Let us come to the point:* <note>original: "Veniamus ad rem"</note> he has robbed me of ten scudi.

**San.** Robbed? Robbed? From you, master? From you, master teacher? I kiss your hands; don't you recognize me?

**Manf.** I saw you a few hours ago, when you were with my pupil Pollula.

**San.** I am that one, sir, master teacher. Know that I am your servant and have a great desire to please you; and for now, know that your scudi are recovered.

**Manf.** *May the gods will it! May the powers above make it so! Oh, if only!* <note>original: "Dii velint! faxint ista superi! o utinam!"</note>

**Bar.** Oh, if you do such a good thing for this gentleman, you never did a better or more worthy work, and he will not be ungrateful to you; and for my part, I will give you a scudo <term>scudo: a gold or silver coin used in Renaissance Italy</term>.

**San.** They are recovered, I say.

**Mar.** Do you have them?

**San.** No, but it is just as if the master teacher had them in his hands.

**Bar.** Do you know that man?

**San.** I know him.

**Bar.** Do you know where he lives?

**San.** I know.

**Manf.** *O powers above, O inhabitants of heaven, O all gods and goddesses!* <note>original: "O superi, o celicoli, diique deaeque omnes!"</note>

**Mar.** We are in the saddle <note>an idiomatic expression meaning "we are in a good position" or "we've got it made"</note>.

**Bar.** We must help with the business of this gentleman <term>monsignore: a title of respect, here used somewhat mockingly or loosely for the schoolmaster</term> out of the love and obligation we have for letters and learned men.

**Manf.** *I commend myself to you;* <note>original: "Me vobis commendo"</note> I entrust myself to your courtesies.

**Mar.** Have no doubt, sir!

**San.** Let us all go together! For we shall find him. I know exactly the place where he goes to nest himself <note>original: "annidarsi"</note>. There is no doubt about catching him; he will not be able to deny the theft; for, although he [Manfurio] didn't see it, I saw him fleeing.

# ACT FOUR.

## SCENE I.

->Signora Vittoria alone.<-

To wait and have no one come is a thing to die of. If it gets too late, nothing can be done this time; and I do not know if such an opportunity will present itself again—as it does tonight—to make this **vile sheep** <note>original: "pecoraccia," a derogatory term for a foolish or easily led person</note> reap the fruits worthy of his "love." When I thought I would gain a dowry through his love, I hear instead that he seeks to bewitch me by having a wax image of me made. And could the combined force of deep hell, joined with the power found in the spirits of the air and water, ever make me love someone who is not a lovable subject? Even if he were the god of love himself, as handsome as you like, if he were poor—or (what amounts to the same thing) stingy—there he would be, dead of cold, and the whole world frozen for him. Certainly, to call someone poor or stingy is a wretched and most shameful label, which makes the beautiful look ugly, the noble look ignoble, the wise look ignorant, and the strong look impotent. Among us, what more can be said than kings, monarchs, and emperors? Yet even these, if they do not have **the wherewithal** <note>original: "de quibus," a Latin legalistic shorthand used here as slang for money</note>, if they do not make **the wherewithal** flow, they will be like old statues from stripped altars, to which no one shows any reverence. We cannot help but distinguish between divine worship and that of mortals. We adore sculptures and images, and we honor the written divine name, directing our intention to that which lives; we adore and honor these other gods, who piss and shit, directing our intention and suppliant devotion to their images and sculptures <note>Vittoria is using "images and sculptures" as a cynical metaphor for coins bearing the ruler's likeness</note>, so that through these they might reward the virtuous, exalt the worthy, defend the oppressed, expand their borders, preserve their own, and make themselves feared by opposing forces. A king or emperor of flesh and bone, therefore, is worth nothing if his image does not circulate in coin. Now, what will become of Bonifacio who—as if there were no other men in the world—thinks he is loved for his "beautiful eyes"? See what madness can do! Tonight he will understand what cash can achieve; tonight I hope he will see the effect of his incantation. But this witch-face, what is she doing that she doesn't come? Oh, I see her at last.

## SCENA II.

->Lucia. Signora Vittoria.<-

**Luc.** Are you here, My Lady?
**S. Vitt.** I could not bear to stay inside while waiting so long for you.

See, won’t the opportunity we have tonight with these men pass us by? Have you spoken to Bonifacio’s wife?

**Lucia.** I told her the whole truth, and even added a few extra sharp points, so that she is now entirely inflamed and burning to catch her husband in the act. In fact, she has thought of something else that pleases me greatly: she wants you to lend her your gown and cloak for two reasons. First, so she won't be recognized coming and going from your house; and second, so that when he embraces her—which we will have them do in the dark—he will take her for Signora Vittoria in every respect except for the face. She will keep her face covered while traveling, according to your **custom** <note>In 16th-century Naples, noblewomen and courtesans often wore veils or cloaks called "manti" to remain anonymous in public</note>, and then once inside the room, we will make them wait a while for a light, just long enough for them to "do it" once.

**Lucia.** Oh, providing for that is the easiest thing in the world. I will tell her to speak softly and in a whisper, because the walls are so thin and the neighbors so close that they hear everything said inside.

**Signora Vittoria.** You speak very well; she will pretend to fear being heard by others in the house or by the neighbors. Who is that coming?

**Lucia.** Master Bartolomeo.

### S C E N E  III.

**Bartolomeo.** I’m going to the devil.
**Lucia.** You’ll find him much sooner than you’ll find the Angel Gabriel.

**Signora Vittoria.** Perhaps you go there too often, which is why your <term>mustard</term> <note>original: "senapo" – mustard. To have the "mustard rise to the nose" is a common Italian idiom for losing one's temper</note> is rising. Hanging around the fire so much has dried you out so much that rage easily gets the better of you, and you burst into insults without being provoked.
**Bartolomeo.** I am not speaking to you, Signora Vittoria; for I hold you in every respect and honor.
**Signora Vittoria.** What? You aren't speaking to me? Do you think this insult you offer her does not reflect criminally upon my own person? Let us go, Lucia!
**Bartolomeo.** Don't be in such a fury, Signora! I am only joking with Lucia, who tempts me more the more she sees me annoyed.
**Lucia.** Yes, yes, <term>Messer</term> <note>a title of respect, here used sarcastically</note>, yes; in all of Naples there is no worse tongue than yours—may it be cut out!—a tongue fit only for brawls and discord!

## S C E N E  IV.

->Bartolomeo alone.<-

May a cancer rot all the procuresses and whores in the world! Their parts <note>original: *potte*, a vulgar term for female genitalia</note> would be left high and dry if they had to wait for our income—that is <note>original: *id est*</note>, our earnings; as for me, spiders could surely spin their webs there. They say that of all metals, gold is the heaviest: and yet nothing makes a man more free, light, and nimble than this. Not every weight or every thing added to a man weighs him down; rather, one is found that is so light that the greater it is, the more ready and dexterous it makes him. A man without silver and gold is like a bird without feathers: whoever wants to catch him, catches him; whoever wants to eat him, eats him. But if he has them, he flies, and the more he has, the more he flies, and the higher he perches. Messer Bonifacio, once he has shaken out his purse and his back, will feel heavier <note>A pun: he will be "heavy" with sorrow and poverty, despite having no "weighty" gold left in his pockets.</note> to spite all his enemies. <lang>English</lang>

Everyone knows how to find a reason for good outcomes, even when none existed: even if I manage my affairs with the fury of a wild boar and they turn out well, everyone will say: "This man is a fine speaker; he knew how to seize the heart of the business thus and so, and he did well." On the contrary, after I have measured my business with all the philosophies that those bearded rascals of Greece and Egypt <note>A dismissive reference to ancient philosophers like Plato, Aristotle, or the legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</note> ever possessed, if by misfortune the matter does not turn out right, everyone will call me a fool. If the matter goes well, who did it? The "Great Parisian Council." If it goes badly, who did it, who did it? "French fury." <note>Bonifacio is mocking how people use national stereotypes to explain success or failure: the French are seen as either wise in council or impulsively "furious."</note> Furthermore, why this? Because of "Spanish advice." Why? Why? Because of the "tall and long Spanish way." <note>Referring to the reputation of Spaniards for being haughty and slow to act.</note> Who won and maintains so many beautiful lands in Istria, Dalmatia, Greece, the Adriatic Sea, and Cisalpine Gaul? Who adorns Italy, Europe, and the whole world with such a Republic—one that is at no time and in no way a slave? The "mature Venetian counsel." <note>Venice was famous for its perceived political stability and "wisdom."</note> Who lost Cyprus? Who lost it? The "ball-less stupidity" <note>original: *coglioneria*</note> of those "Magnificoes," the greed of those **Master Pantaloons**. <note>"Pantalone" is the stock character of the elderly, stingy Venetian merchant in the Commedia dell'Arte.</note> Therefore, judgment is only taken into account and praised when luck and success are good.

**Bart.** So much so that you want to say regarding our situation: "God give me luck, for a little wit is enough." I see Lucia coming; I leave you to her. I have sent my boy to Consalvo’s shop for a certain powder and *I can’t wait to get there*: I must go.

**Bon.** Go then, for I have to speak with this woman about other matters than those you believe.

## S C E N A  IX.

->Marta alone.<-

*A cut-off nose has no need for glasses* <note>original French: *Nez coupé n' ha faute de lunettes*</note>, that good companion John of Brittany used to say—bless his soul, for he put the French tongue in my mouth before I was even twelve and a half years old! He meant to imply, appropriately, that as much as he was poorer than the King of France, so much more is the King of France in need than he. He who has more, thinks more, demands more, and enjoys less. The Prince of Conca <note>Conca was a small fiefdom; the "Prince" here is likely a local figure of modest means compared to a monarch</note> maintains his princedom by receiving a crown and a half a day: the King of France can hardly maintain his kingdom by spending ten thousand a day at times. Consider then, which of these two is richer, and who ought to be more content! He who has a little to receive, or he who has much to give? When the defeat at Pavia occurred <note>The Battle of Pavia (1525), where King Francis I of France was captured</note>, I heard it said the King of France needed more than eight hundred gold crowns. The Prince of Conca, when did he ever need more than twenty, or twenty-five crowns? When will it ever be possible for him to need more? Now see which of these two princes is less in need! Wretched me! I say it, I know it, I experience it. I was more content when this **Zarrabuino** <gloss>Cinciglione</gloss> <note>These are likely nicknames for her husband; *Cinciglione* often refers to a drunkard or a person of low status</note> of my husband did not have so much to spend as he has today. In the Erasmian adages <note>original: "adagiani erasmi... erasmiani adagii" — Manfurio is a pedantic schoolmaster referencing the *Adagia*, a famous collection of proverbs by the humanist scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam.</note>, I say in the Erasmian adages—I am hallucinating—I mean in the Erasmian adages, there is one among the others which says: *From the toga to the cloak* <note>original: "A toga ad pallium" — a proverb meaning to descend from a position of dignity (the toga) to a common or lower state (the cloak).</note>. This being fulfilled in my own self, makes this day for me one that must be marked with a black pebble <note>original: "nigro signandus lapillo" — an ancient Roman expression for an unlucky or disastrous day.</note>. *O heaven, o earth, o seas of Neptune!* After my money was taken from my hand by a most vile thief, under the pretext of wishing to be helpful to me, three others offered and presented themselves. These men, *not, I say, with dexterity, but with a certain "sinisterity"* <note>A pun on "dexterity" (right-handedness/skill) and "sinisterity" (left-handedness/malice).</note>, leaving upon my back a threadbare little cloak, and in place of a head covering <note>original: "proque capitis operculo"</note> an ancient little hood, which towards the center and in the middle, because of the excessive thickness of sweat <note>original: "versus centrum, et in medio prae nimii sudoris densitudine"</note>, appears waxed, or pitched, or leathery, or made of skin, have taken from me my hat and my magisterial gown. *By the faith of gods and men* <note>original: "Proh deûm atque hominum fidem"</note>, here I am fallen *from the frying pan into the coals* <note>original: "a patella ad prunas" — the Latin equivalent of the English idiom "out of the frying pan into the fire."</note>. They persuaded me by saying: "Come with us, for we will help you find the thief." I went with them in good faith <note>original: "bona fide"</note>, until we arrived at the home of certain—as I might easily believe—little harlots <note>original: "meretricule"</note>; having entered there, they made me remain in the lower hall, saying to me: "It is well that we enter first to warn him, so that it does not seem that we wish to confound him abruptly <note>original: "ex abrupto"</note> with your presence; therefore, wait here! For soon you will be called by one of us to decide with as little heat <note>original: "excandescentia" — meaning anger or outburst.</note> as possible regarding what pertains to the restitution <note>original: "quod ad restitutionem attinet"</note>." Now, having waited a great interval of time walking about, thinking of the arguments with which I was to confound that fellow, at last <note>original: "tandem"</note>, there being no one to call me, I ascended to the upper floor by certain stairs and knocked on the door of the first chamber...

### S C E N A XIII.

#### Lucia alone.

The proverb says it well: he who wants <term>Lent</term><note>original: "quadragesima"</note> to seem short should go into debt, to be paid at Easter. All day today has not seemed like an hour because of the thought I've had of making these eggs hatch this evening. One must hammer in rhythm when more than one are striking an iron. By the faith of <note>A humorous, likely invented saint's name related to "time" or "timing"</note> Saint Temporina, I think this is him.

### S C E N A XIV.

#### Lucia. Master Giovanni Bernardo.

**Luc.** You have arrived exactly at the right moment.
**Gio. Ber.** What have you done, my Lucia?
**Luc.** Everything; Messer Bonifacio has gone to disguise himself and fit a beard similar to yours. His wife, now in the dress of Lady Victoria, has entered; Sanguino, dressed as Captain Palma with a long, white beard; Marca, Flora, Barra, Corcovizzo are all ready as <term>guards</term><note>original: "birri," the local constabulary or police force</note>.
**Gio. Ber.** I have seen them just now; I spoke with them. I left them nearby in a shearer's shop. I'll keep my wits about me, so that I don't let this morsel escape my mouth. Have you spoken of my matter to Lady Carubina?
**Luc.** Let us drink to the Lord! <note>original: "Libemus domino!" a mock-liturgical phrase parodying church Latin</note> Do you think I am so little clever?
**Gio. Ber.** You have done wisely. I want to give you a kiss as a <term>tip</term><note>original: "beveraggio," literally money for a drink, here used for a small reward</note>. Here!
**Luc.** Many thanks! I have need of something other than that.
**Gio. Ber.** This is only a pledge. My Lucia, it is impossible to find a woman for such dealings equal to you.

**San.** Quick, quick! Lock him up in this room! We will take him to the Vicaria <note>The Vicaria was the main court and prison in Naples during the 16th century.</note> later. He wants to show himself off as a doctor of learning, but he makes us understand he belongs to the craft of skinning goats. <note>original: "spelazzar capretti." This is slang suggesting either a low-class butcher or, more likely in this context, someone who engages in lewd or sodomitic behavior.</note>

**Manf.** *O wretched me! Words are of no use. O unlucky and atrocious day!* <note>original: "O me miserum! verba nihil prosunt. O diem infaustum atque atrocem!"</note>

## SCENE XI.

### Giovan Bernardo. Carubina.

**Gio. Ber.** Do you see, my love, what a great wrong this great fool <note>original: "pazzerone"</note> does to your divine beauty? Does it not seem just to you that he be paid back in the same coin <note>original: "moneta"</note>?
**Car.** If he does not do what is proper, I ought not to do the same.

**Gio. Ber.** You will do, my heart, what is proper, when you do nothing other than what any person of judgment and feeling living on this earth would do. **Gio. Ber.** My life, I am such a man that for your service I would throw myself into a thousand precipices. I am the one who loves you; I am the one who adores you. For if the heavens had granted to me what they granted to that boorish and foolish man <note>original: "sconcante e sciocco," referring to her husband Bonifacio</note>, who does not prize your admirable beauty, never would a spark of any other love have found a place in my breast, just as it finds no place now.

**Car.** Alas! What things am I seeing and hearing? To what state have I been reduced?

**Gio. Ber.** I pray you, my sweet goddess, if you ever felt the flame of love—which usually finds a greater place in more noble, generous, and human breasts—do not take what I say the wrong way. Do not believe, nor let it ever enter your mind, that I seek what I seek from you because I hold your honor in low esteem; for that honor I would shed all my blood a thousand times over. I seek it only to satisfy the intense heat that consumes me, which I cannot believe could ever be diminished, even by death itself.

**Car.** Alas! Master Giovan Bernardo, I have a very tender heart; I easily believe what you say, even though the flatteries of lovers are a proverb. Therefore, I desire your every consolation. But on my part, it is not possible without prejudice to my honor.

**Gio. Ber.** Life of my life, I truly believe you know what honor is, and also what dishonor is. Honor is nothing other than an estimation, a reputation; therefore, honor always remains intact as long as that estimation and reputation remain the same. Honor is the good opinion that others have of us; as long as this persists, honor persists. And it is not what we... <note>Giovan Bernardo begins a philosophical argument that "honor" is merely public perception, a common theme in Renaissance literature used to justify secret affairs</note>

**Car.** I beg of you, let us go to a more remote place, and let us not speak of these things here!

**Gio. Ber.** Let us go, my sweetness! For people are coming.

### S C E N E XIX.

->Master Gio. Bernardo. Ascanio.<-

**Gio. Ber.** So that, my son, returning to our subject, it is a common opinion that things are so ordered that nature does not fail in what is necessary and does not abound in the superfluous. Oysters, which have no feet, because in whatever part of the sea they find themselves, they have everything sufficient for their sustenance; for they maintain themselves by water alone and the heat of the sun, whose power penetrates even to the depths of the sea. Moles, too, have no eyes, because their life is spent underground, and they live on nothing but earth, and cannot lose it. To those who have no art, tools are not given.
**Asc.** This is most certain. I have heard it said that a certain censor of Jove’s works, who is called Momus <note>In Greek mythology, Momus is the personification of mockery and unfair criticism.</note>—for such as speak freely are necessary everywhere, first so that princes and judges realize the errors they make and do not recognize, thanks to the lazy and most vile flatterers; second, so that they fear doing one thing more than another; third, so that goodness and virtue, when they have an opposite, become more beautiful, manifest, and clear, and are confirmed and strengthened—this censor of Jove, then—

## SCENE XXIII.

->**Carubina. Sanguino. Scaramure. Master Giovanni Bernardo. Bonifacio. Barra. Corcovizzo. Ascanio. Marca.**<-

**Car.** Is this <term>concubinary</term> <note>original: *concubinaro*; a man who keeps a mistress. The irony here is that Bonifacio was trying to commit adultery but ended up with his own wife by mistake.</note> of his own wife still here?

**San.** This is a great novelty; I believe that those who make a profession of "cases of conscience" <note>Moral theologians who specialized in judging specific sins.</note> have not yet imagined how one can be a fornicator or a "concubinary" by laying with his own and legitimate wife.

**Scar.** Come now, let us leave these ironies and this anger! We must resolve this matter here among us, since Captain Palma does us the great favor of letting us consult on your honor, Lady Carubina; seeing that the shame of your husband cannot result in your honor, nor in any benefit to you, Master Giovanni Bernardo.

**Bon.** That is most certain. Mercy, pity, compassion, charity, for the love of God! My dear Master Giovanni Bernardo, and my wife, forgive me, I pray you, for this first time!

**Bar.** The world is a strange thing: some always commit errors and never do penance, from what we see; others do it after many errors; others are caught in the first; others have not even sinned yet and already bear the punishment; others suffer without sin; others carry the burden for the sins of others. In this man, if one considers well, all these types are joined together.

**Bon.** I beg you for mercy and grace; I supplicate you to grant it to me, just as Our Lord Jesus Christ granted it to the <term>good thief</term> <note>Dismas, the penitent thief crucified alongside Jesus.</note> and to Mary Magdalene.

**Bar.** Good God, what a "good thief" this one is! When you become a good thief like that one—who "stole" paradise—how then will mercy be shown to you by Our Lord? You are a thief who takes what belongs to your wife and gives it to others: her milk, her liquor, her manna, her substance, and her well-being.

**Gio. Ber.** And my person, and my beard, and my <term>hood</term> <note>original: *biscappa*; a professional or academic hood/cloak that Bonifacio stole to use as a disguise.</note>, and perhaps my honor, for what he might have done in my name.

**Bar.** Therefore he should not be forgiven like a "good thief," but rather like the Magdalene.

**Cor.** Look, what a noble Magdalene! May the cancer take...

**Car.** That does not matter; peace is already made between us.

**Mar.** <note>Likely Barra or another member of the group.</note> At home, treat your wife well, **Master Bonifacio**; otherwise she will punish you, along with **Master Giovanni Bernardo**. <note>A biting irony, as Carubina and Giovanni Bernardo are actually plotting to be together.</note>

**San.** Now then, go with God, all of you! Pass through this room, for you will exit through that other door; and you, **Master Bonifacio**, will leave that offering you promised to these companions for the trouble we have gone through on your account.

**Bon.** Very willingly, my lord.

**Scar.** Let us go, and let God be praised, who has brought about this peace and union of **Master Bonifacio**, **Lady Carubina**, and **Master Giovanni Bernardo**: three in one! <note>A blasphemous parody of the Holy Trinity, mocking Bonifacio’s foolishness as he is joined with his wife and her lover.</note>

**Bon.** Amen! Amen!

**Car.** After you, **Master Giovanni Bernardo**!

**Gio. Ber.** I would never do so, madam; **Your Ladyship** must go first.

**Car.** It must be so.

**Gio. Ber.** It is your turn, my lady.

**Car.** I go then, to do you service and obey you.

**Gio. Ber.** Follow me, **Master Bonifacio**! Hold onto me and cling to my cloak, and watch that you do not fall!

**Bon.** I shall watch myself well.

<summary>Bonifacio is forced to swear he has committed no other crimes and pays a "fine" to the rogues to secure his release. The scene ends with a parodic "holy union" between the husband, the wife, and the wife's lover, as they all exit together.</summary>

### SCENE XXIV.

->Sanguino. Ascanio.<-

**San.** Now, what do you think of your master and **Bonifacio**?
**Asc.** From what I see of him: good.
**San.** Is he not a gentleman, wise, shrewd, brave, and worthy of every esteem?
**Asc.** As much as any man of his kind.
**San.** And who do you think is his equal?
**Asc.** Anyone who knows and understands no more and no less than he does, and anyone who is worth no more and no less than he is.
**San.** Since there are many species of madness, in which one do you think this fellow labors?
**Asc.** We can categorize the types of madness by many headings; but taking it from this perspective—that among madmen some are indifferent, some are wicked, and others are good—he turns out to be a triple-distilled batch of all three. Asleep, he is indifferent; awake, he is wicked; dead, he would be good.
**San.** Why did **Lady Carubina** take him as a husband?
**Asc.** Because he is a fool.
**San.** Do you think she did well?
**Asc.** According to the advice of the mustache and the beard of that woolly old crone, **Lady Angela**, she did more than well—that is, excellently. That woman was her advisor; she is the shepherdess of all the beautiful daughters of Naples. If someone wants a Lamb of God <note>original: "Agnus dei" — a wax medallion blessed by the Pope</note>, or blessed grains, or the water of **St. Peter Martyr**, the seed of **St. John**, the manna of **St. Andrew**, the oil of fat, or the marrow from the reed-bones of the body of **St. Piantorio** <note>A fictional, satirical saint; the name implies "planting" or "fixing," often used in bawdy contexts</note>; if someone wants to hang a vow to find good fortune, let them go find **Lady Angela Spigna**. **Lady Carubina** went to this woman and said: "Mother, they want to give me a husband; **Bonifacio Trucco** presents himself, who has the means and the manner." The old woman replied: "Take him!" "Yes, but he is too aged," said **Carubina**. The old woman replied: "Daughter, do not take him!" "My relatives advise me to take him." She replied: "Take him!" "But I do not like him much," said **Carubina**. "Then do not take him!" she replied. **Carubina** added: "I know he is of good family." "Take him," said the old woman. "But I hear that he takes three bites out of a single bean <note>A metaphor for extreme stinginess or miserliness</note>." She replied: "Do not take him!" "I am informed," said **Carubina**, "that he has a good greyhound..."

### SCENE XXV.

->Barra. Marca. Corcovizzo. Manfurio. Sanguino.<-
->Ascanio.<-

**Bar.** That other fellow has been dispatched; what shall we do with this one, with the **Master Teacher** <note>original: "domino magister"</note>?

**San.** This one carries his guilt on his forehead. Do you not see that he is in disguise? Do you not see that that cloak was stolen from Tiburolo? Have you not seen him fleeing the court?

**Mar.** It is true; yet he offers certain plausible excuses.

**Bar.** Therefore, he should have no doubt about going to prison.

**Manf.** **True** <note>original: "Verum"</note>; but I shall fall into derision among my students and others because of the misfortunes that have been heaped upon my back.

**San.** Do you understand what this fellow is trying to say?

**Cor.** Even Samson could not understand him.

**San.** Come now, to make it short, see here, **Master**, what you wish to decide! Whether you want to come to prison, or instead give a gratuity to this company from those crowns <note>original: "scudi"</note> you have left inside your tunic—for as you say, the rogue only took those you had in hand to exchange—

**Manf.** **By no means** <note>original: "Minime"</note>, I have absolutely nothing else. Those I had were all taken from me. **So help me Hercules, by Jove, by the high-thunderer! You stars, I call you to witness!** <note>original: "Ita mehercle, per Jovem, per altitonantem! Vos, sidera, testor." — Manfurio uses grand, pedantic Latin even in a moment of distress.</note>

**San.** Understand what I am telling you! If you do not wish to experience the rigors of the <term>Vicaria</term> <note>The Vicaria was the main courthouse and prison in Naples, notorious for its harsh conditions.</note>, and you have no money, choose one of these two alternatives: either take ten lashes with this **whip** \*) of leather that you see, or else with your breeches down you shall have a "wooden horse" <note>A form of punishment where a person is hoisted up and whipped</note> of fifty lashes; for in any case, you shall not depart from us without penance for your faults.

**Manf.** **When two evils are proposed, the lesser is to be endured; just as when two goods are proposed, the better is to be chosen, as the Prince of the Peripatetics says.** <note>original: "Duobus propositis malis, minus est tolerandum: sicut duobus propositis bonis, melius est eligendum, dicit Peripateticorum princeps." The "Prince of the Peripatetics" refers to Aristotle.</note>

**Asc.** Master, speak so you are understood! For these people are suspicious types.

**Bar.** Is it possible that this fellow speaks well only when he does not wish to be understood?

**Manf.** *I pray for no evil to fall upon you* <note>original: "Nil mali vobis imprecor"</note>; I call down no ill upon you.

**San.** Pray for us as much as you like; for you will not be heard by us.

**Cor.** Choose quickly what pleases you, or we will tie you up tighter and lead you away.

**Manf.** *It will be less shameful to be struck on the palm than for them to heap lashes upon my old buttocks; for that is a childish thing* <note>original: "Minus pudendum erit palma feriri, quam quod congerant in veteres flagella nates; id enim puerile est." Manfurio finds the dignity of his age more important than the pain of his hands.</note>.

**San.** What are you saying? What are you saying to your own misfortune?

**Manf.** I offer you the palm of my hand.

**San.** Touch it, Corcovizzo; strike hard!

**Cor.** I strike. Take one.

**Manf.** Alas Jesus! Oh!

**Cor.** Open the other hand wide! Take that! That’s two.

**Manf.** Oh, oh! Jesus Mary!

**Cor.** Stretch out your hand well, I tell you. Keep it straight like this! Take that! That’s three.

**Manf.** Oy, oy, alas! Ugh, oh oh oh! For the love of the passion of our Lord Jesus, *rather* <note>original: "potius"</note> have me hoisted onto the horse <note>original: "alzar a cavallo" — a punishment where the victim is lifted onto someone's back or a frame to be flogged</note>, because I cannot suffer such pain in my hands.

**San.** Come then, Barra, take him on your shoulders! You, Marca, hold him firm by the feet so he cannot move! You, Corcovizzo, unfasten his **breeches** <note>original: "brache"</note> and keep them pulled well down, and let me do the currying! And you, Master, count the **lashes** <note>original: "staffilate"</note> one by one so that I can hear you, and watch closely; for if you make a mistake in the counting, we will need to start over. You, Ascanio, watch and judge!

**Mar.** Everything is ready. Start dusting him off <note>original: "spolverare" — a euphemism for a beating</note>, and take care not to damage his clothes, for they are blameless.

**San.** In the name of **Saint Scoppettella** <note>A mock saint; the name is derived from "scoppetta," a slap or a crack</note>, count! Whack!

**Manf.** Whack, one; Whack, oh—three. Whack—oh, oy, four. Whack. Alas, alas! Whack, ah, alas! Whack, oh for the love of God, seven.

**San.** Let us start from the beginning again; see if seven follows four. You should have said five.

**Manf.** Alas! What shall I do? There were, *in the truth of the matter* <note>original: "in rei veritate"</note>, seven.

**San.** You should have counted them one by one. Come now, once more—whack!

**Manf.** Whack, one; Whack, alas! Two; Whack, whack, whack, three, four, whack, whack, five, alas! Whack, whack, six. Oh, for the love of God, whack, no more! Whack, whack! No more! For we want—whack—to see in the **cloak** <note>original: "giornea" — a short, sleeveless gown or surcoat</note>—whack—if there are some **coins** <note>original: "scudi"</note> in there.

**San.** We must start from the beginning, for he has left out many that he did not count.

<summary>In this scene, the pedantic Master Manfurio is subjected to a beating by the rogues, choosing a flogging over hand-strikes for the sake of his "dignity," though his inability to count the lashes correctly leads to a repetitive ordeal. The dialogue highlights the physical comedy and the mocking of Manfurio’s Latinate, overly formal speech during his suffering.</summary>

**San.** He has nothing.

**Bar.** By what blood! There are more than seven scudi here.

**Manf.** Mercy! Take the scudi, the tunic, and everything else you want, *I yield them to you* <note>original: "dimittam vobis"</note>.

### SCENA XXVI.

->Manfurio. Ascanio.<-

**Manf.** *What manner of behavior is this?* <note>original: "Ecquis iste modus?"</note>

**Asc.** Hey there, Master Manfurio, Master Manfurio!

**Manf.** Who is it? Who knows me? Who distinguishes me in this attire and state of fortune? Who calls me by my own proper name?

**Asc.** Do not worry about that, for it matters little or nothing to you. Open your eyes and see where you are! Look at where you find yourself!

**Manf.** *So that I may see better* <note>original: "Quo melius videam"</note>, to strengthen my intuition and confirm the act of the visual faculty <term>potenza visiva</term> <note>Aristotelian term for the power of sight</note>, so that the edge of the pupil may more effectively, through the visual line, emitting the ray to the visible object, come to introduce its image into the internal sense—that is, by means of the common sense, place it in the cell of the imaginative faculty—I wish to apply my spectacles to my nose. — Oh, I see the circle of many spectators.

**Asc.** Does it not seem to you that you are within a comedy?

**Manf.** *Indeed it does* <note>original: "Ita sane"</note>.

**Asc.** Do you not believe you are on stage?

**Manf.** *Beyond all doubt* <note>original: "Omni procul dubio"</note>.

**Asc.** At what point would you like the comedy to be?

**Manf.** At the heel, at the end; *for I too do not stretch my sides with laughter* <note>original: "neque enim et ego risu ilia tendo" – a reference to Horace, indicating he is too tired or miserable to find it funny</note>.

**Asc.** Now then, do your part, and give the call for applause <term>plaudite</term> <note>original: "plaudite" – the traditional command for the audience to clap at the end of a Latin comedy</note>!

<summary>Manfurio is robbed of his money and clothes by the bandits before being confronted by Ascanio, who breaks the fourth wall to reveal they are in a play. The scene ends with Manfurio acknowledging the audience and preparing to conclude the comedy.</summary>
<keywords>Manfurio, Ascanio, robbery, metafiction, spectacles, visual faculty, comedy, applause</keywords>

**Manf.** *How poorly I am able to applaud,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Having been tested in patience!*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*For the applause made by me*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Has for a long time now been miserable;*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And with the sound of gold coins. Amen!*
<note>original: "Quam male possum plaudere... Et aureorum sonitu. Amen!" — Manfurio's Latin verses complain that his "applause" is actually the sound of his own beating and the loss of his money.</note>

**Asc.** I say, give the request for applause <term>plaudite</term> <note>the traditional call for applause at the end of a Roman comedy</note>, and force yourselves to do it again, and do everything well, like the master and man of letters that you are; otherwise, people will return to the stage, which will be bad for you.

**Manf.** *I shall do so with a cheerful mind, in the manner that follows.* <note>original: "Hilari efficiam animo, forma, quae sequitur"</note> Just as sailors, even though they have a broken mast, a lost sail, snapped rigging, and a lost rudder due to the turbulent storm, nevertheless, because they have reached the harbor, are accustomed to *applaud, and according to the Virgilian* <term>maroniana</term> <note>referring to Publius Vergilius Maro, the poet Virgil</note> *maxim,*

> *The saved sailors shall pay their vows on the shore*
> *To Glaucus, and Panopea, and Melicertes, son of Ino:*
<note>original: "Votaque servati solvent in littore nautae / Glauco, et Panopea, et Inoo Melicertae" — A quote from Virgil’s Georgics (I, 436-7) regarding sailors' gratitude for surviving the sea.</note>

*likewise I, Manfurio, professor of Greek, Latin, and vernacular literature—not, I say, of the king* <term>regius</term>, *nor of the herd* <term>gregius</term>, *but extraordinary* <term>egregius</term>, *which is by etymology 'one chosen from the flock'* <note>The pedantic Manfurio makes a pun on the Latin "e grege," meaning "out of the flock," which is the root of "egregious" or "extraordinary."</note> *—and also doctor of philosophy, medicine, both branches of law* <term>juris utriusque</term> <note>referring to expertise in both Civil Law and Canon (Church) Law</note>, *and of theology, had I wished it; because I have reached the port of my laborious and calamitous successes (hereafter about to pay my vows), I applaud. Therefore, I say to you, most noble spectators, whose faces and eyes I see are all turned toward me: just as I find myself at the end of my role as a tragic character, if not with my hands, tunic* <term>giornea</term> <note>a sleeveless over-garment</note>, *and clothes, yet with my heart and soul, I applaud. Thus—and even better for you who have been moved by better fortune than ours, and who have been joyful and happy spectators of our annoying and troublesome misfortunes—farewell, and applaud!* <note>original: "valete, et plaudite!" — the standard closing formula of Latin comedy.</note>

## TO THE DISCONTENTED.

---

If you are pierced by the <term>cynical tooth</term> <note>A reference to the "Cynic" philosophers, whose name derives from the Greek word for "dog-like." In this context, it refers to biting, snarling criticism.</note>,
Blame yourself, you barbaric <term>cur</term>! <note>original: "perro" — Bruno uses the Spanish word for dog here as a sharp insult.</note>
For you show me your staff and blade in vain,
If you do not refrain from showing me contempt.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because you approached me with wrong against my right,
Therefore I tear your skin and lay you open;
And if it happens thereafter that my own body is struck down,
Your disgrace is written in diamond. <note>Meaning the critic's shame is permanent and indestructible, like a diamond.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Do not go naked to steal honey from the bees!
Do not bite, if you do not know whether it be stone or bread!
Do not go barefoot to sow thorns!

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Do not despise, little fly, the <term>spider's webs</term>! <note>original: "aragne" — an archaic form of "ragni" (spiders).</note>
If you are a mouse, do not follow the frogs! <note>A reference to the *Batrachomyomachia* (The Battle of Frogs and Mice), an ancient Greek parody of epic poetry often attributed to Homer.</note>
Flee from the foxes, oh chicken-hearted one,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And believe the <term>Gospel</term>,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which says with righteous zeal:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From our field he reaps penance,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who sowed the seeds of error there.

---

<note>This poem serves as a defiant warning to the readers and critics who might find Bruno’s revolutionary cosmological ideas (such as the infinite universe) offensive or heretical. He portrays himself as a formidable opponent who will expose the "errors" of his detractors.</note>

<summary>A defiant sonnet addressing potential critics, warning them that their attacks will only result in their own disgrace and metaphorical injury. It uses a series of animal metaphors to mock the "malcontent" who challenges the author's work.</summary>
<keywords>sonnet, polemic, animal metaphors, cynicism, penance, Giordano Bruno, satire</keywords>

# PREFATORY EPISTLE
## WRITTEN
### TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND EXCELLENT
# LORD OF MAUVISSIÈRE,

-> KNIGHT OF THE ORDER OF THE KING, AND COUNSELOR <-
-> OF HIS PRIVATE COUNCIL, CAPTAIN OF <-
-> FIFTY MEN-AT-ARMS, GOVERNOR GENE- <-
-> RAL OF SAINT-DIZIER, AND AMBASSADOR OF <-
-> FRANCE TO ENGLAND. <-

---

**N**ow here is presented to you, my Lord, not a nectarous feast of the **High-Thunderer** <note>A poetic title for Jupiter (Zeus), the king of the gods</note>, for a majesty; not a **protoplastic** <note>Refers to the "first-formed" humans, Adam and Eve, and the eating of the forbidden fruit that led to the Fall of Man</note> one, for human desolation; not that of **Ahasuerus**, <margin>See Esther 1.</margin> for a mystery; not of **Lucullus** <note>A Roman general famous for his extravagant banquets</note>, for wealth; not of **Lycaon** <note>A mythical king who was turned into a wolf after serving human flesh to Zeus</note>, for a sacrilege; not of **Thyestes** <note>A mythological figure who was unknowingly served his own children at a feast</note>, for a tragedy; not of **Tantalus** <note>Punished in the underworld by being forever teased by food and water he could not reach</note>, for an ordeal; not of **Plato** <note>Referring to the *Symposium*, a philosophical dialogue set during a banquet</note>, for a philosophy; not of **Diogenes** <note>The famous "Cynic" philosopher who lived in a barrel and rejected all luxuries</note>, for a misery; not of the leeches, for a trifle; not of an **Archpriest of Pogliano** <note>A character appearing in the satirical poems of Francesco Berni</note>, for a <term>Bernesque poem</term> <note>A style of humorous, mocking poetry named after Francesco Berni</note>; <meta>This page continues the prefatory epistle to Michel de Castelnau. Having previously listed various types of famous or mythological banquets that this book is *not*, Bruno now begins to describe what this specific "supper" actually entails, blending philosophical seriousness with sharp, satirical humor.</meta>

a philosopher with **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who founded a school based on mathematics and reincarnation</note>, laughing with **Democritus** <note>Known as the "laughing philosopher" because he mocked the follies of mankind</note>, weeping with **Heraclitus** <note>Known as the "weeping philosopher" for his melancholy view of human life</note>. I mean to say, after you have caught the scent with the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about while teaching</note>, eaten with the **Pythagoreans**, and drunk with the **Stoics**, you will still find something to suck on with that man who, baring his teeth, had a laugh so kind that his mouth touched both ears. For, by breaking the bones and drawing out the marrow <note>A metaphor for finding deep meaning beneath a rough exterior, famously used by Rabelais</note>, you will find something to make even the dissolute **Saint Colombino** <note>Giovanni Colombini (1304–1367), the founder of the order of the **Jesuati** (not to be confused with the Jesuits)</note>, patriarch of the Jesuati, achieve any bargain, make monkeys drop their jaws, and break the silence of any cemetery.

You will ask me: what kind of symposium, what kind of banquet is this? It is a supper. What supper? **The Ash Wednesday Supper**. What does "Ash Wednesday Supper" mean? Was this meal perhaps placed before you previously? Might one say here: "I ate ashes like bread" <note>original: "*Cinerem tanquam panem manducabam*"—a quote from Psalm 102:9</note>? No; rather, it is a banquet held after sunset on the first day of the forty days of Lent, called by our priests the "Day of Ashes" <note>original: "*dies cinerum*"</note>, and sometimes the "day of remembrance" <note>original: "*memento*"—referring to the liturgical phrase "Remember, man, that thou art dust"</note>. What is the subject of this banquet, this supper? It is certainly not an examination of the spirit and the qualities of the very noble and well-bred **Sir Fulke Greville** <note>A prominent Elizabethan poet and statesman in whose London house the dialogue is set</note>, in whose honored chambers we met; nor is it about the honorable customs of those most civilized gentlemen who were present as spectators and listeners; rather, it is about wanting to see how much Nature can do in creating two fantastic hags <note>Bruno is satirizing two pedantic Oxford doctors who argue with him in the dialogue</note>, two dreams, two shadows, and two quartan fevers. While the historical sense of this is being sifted, and then tasted and chewed, there are drawn out relevant topographical, geographical, rational, and moral speculations, as well as others that are metaphysical, mathematical, and natural.

Thus you will see in the **FIRST DIALOGUE** two subjects proposed on the field, with the reasoning behind their names, if you wish to understand it; second, for their sake, the scale of the binary number is celebrated; third, the laudable conditions of the rediscovered and repaired philosophy are brought forward; fourth, it is shown how much praise **Copernicus** <note>The astronomer who proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun</note> is capable of receiving; fifth, the fruits of the **Nolan philosophy** <note>Bruno's own philosophy, named after his birthplace, Nola</note> are set before you, with the difference between this and other ways of philosophizing.

You will see in the **SECOND DIALOGUE**, first, the original cause of the supper; second, a description of paths and passages which will be judged by everyone to be perhaps more poetic and <term>tropological</term> <note>A method of interpretation that finds moral or spiritual meanings behind literal descriptions</note> than historical; second, how one falls confusedly into a moral topography, where it seems that with the eyes of **Lynceus** <note>An Argonaut from Greek mythology renowned for his superhumanly sharp eyesight</note> one looks here and there.

the vanity of two great persuasions, with which Aristotle and others have been so blinded that they did not see the truth and necessity of the motion of the earth, and have been so hindered that they could not believe such a thing to be possible; by doing so, many secrets of nature, hidden until the present, are discovered.

the moon, over the waters and other types of humors, as well as regarding other natural things, which seem to recognize the principle of their motion from an external agent. Fourth, he determines against those doubts that proceed from the most foolish reasoning concerning the **gravity** <note>weight</note> and **levity** <note>lightness; in Aristotelian physics, some objects were thought to have an inherent quality of "lightness" that made them rise</note> of bodies, and demonstrates that every natural motion approaches the **circular**, either around its own center or around some other middle point. <meta>This page continues the introductory epistle to Michel de Castelnau. Bruno has just discussed the serious philosophical and physical implications of his work and is now transitioning to defend its satirical and comedic tone, justifying the use of humor to expose the ignorance of his academic rivals.</meta>

Beyond what appears on the surface, those who have given us the occasion to create this dialogue—and perhaps a satire or a comedy—have a way to become more circumspect, especially when they measure men with the same rod used to measure velvet, and balance souls on scales meant for metals. Those who are spectators or readers, seeing the manner in which others are touched <note>In the sense of being criticized or poked</note>, will have the chance to become wise and learn at another’s expense. Those who are wounded or stung will perhaps open their eyes; seeing their own poverty, nakedness, and unworthiness, they might—if not for love, then at least for shame—correct or cover themselves, if they do not wish to confess.

If it seems to you that our **Teofilo** and **Frulla** <note>Characters in the dialogue: Teofilo usually represents Bruno’s own philosophical voice, while Frulla acts as a sharp-witted or mocking observer</note> touch the backs of certain subjects too heavily or rigidly, consider, my Lord, that these animals do not have such tender hides. For even if the blows were a hundred times greater, they would value them not at all, nor would they feel them any more than if they were being patted by a young girl. 

Nor would I wish you to judge me worthy of blame because, upon such trifles and so unworthy a field as these doctors have provided, we have chosen to elaborate such serious and worthy propositions. For I am certain you know that there is a difference between taking something as a **foundation** and taking it as an **occasion** <note>In Bruno’s rhetoric, an "occasion" is a catalyst—a specific event or person that triggers a broader philosophical discussion, even if the trigger itself is trivial</note>. Foundations must indeed be proportioned to the size, condition, and nobility of the building; but occasions can be of all sorts, for all effects. Small and sordid things are often the seeds of great and excellent things; foolishness and madness are accustomed to provoke great counsel, judgments, and inventions. It is clearly manifest that errors and crimes have many times provided the occasion for the greatest rules of justice and goodness.

If, in this portrait, it seems to you that the colors do not perfectly match the life, and the outlines do not seem entirely proper, know that the defect arises from this: the painter could not examine the portrait from those distances and spaces that the masters of the art are accustomed to take. For besides the fact that the canvas, or the field, was too close to the face and eyes, one could not withdraw even a tiny step backward, or move to one side or the other, without fear of taking that leap made by the son of the famous **defender of Troy** <note>original: "difensor di Troia"; this refers to Astyanax, the infant son of Hector, who was thrown from the walls of Troy during the city's destruction</note>. Nevertheless, take this portrait as it is, where those two, those hundred, those thousand, or all of them are depicted; considering that it is not sent to you to inform you of what...

<summary>Bruno justifies the satirical and harsh tone of his dialogue, arguing that the ignorance of "pedantic doctors" serves as a necessary catalyst (or "occasion") for revealing higher philosophical truths. He uses the metaphor of a painter working in cramped quarters to explain the stylistic imperfections of his work.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the dedicatory epistle to Michel de Castelnau, the French Ambassador to England. Having justified the satirical tone of the work on the previous page, Bruno now addresses his patron directly, praising his hospitality and his role as the representative of the French King.</meta>

...you know, nor is it intended to add water to the rapid river of your judgment and wit; but because I know that, as is common, even though we know things more perfectly in the flesh, we are not accustomed to despising the portrait and representation of them. Besides, I am certain that your noble spirit will direct the eye of consideration more toward the gratitude of the affection with which the gift is given, than to the present from the hand that offers it to you. 

This work is directed to you, who are closer and show yourself more propitious and more favorable to our **Nolan** <note>Giordano Bruno often referred to himself as "the Nolan" because he was born in Nola, near Naples</note>; and therefore you have rendered yourself a most worthy recipient of our respects in this climate—where merchants without conscience or faith easily become **Crœsuses** <note>Proverbially wealthy figures, named after the fabulously rich King Crœsus of Lydia</note>, and the virtuous without gold are easily made into **Diogenes** <note>A reference to Diogenes the Cynic, who famously lived in poverty and rejected material wealth</note>. It is dedicated to you, who with such magnificence and liberality have welcomed the Nolan under your roof and to the most eminent place in your house; where, if this land, instead of sending forth a thousand grim giants <note>Likely a jab at his English academic rivals or "pedants"</note>, produced as many **Alexander the Greats**, you would see more than five hundred coming to court this Diogenes—who, by the grace of the stars, has no one but you to stand in his sun <note>Original: "levar il sole." This refers to the famous meeting where Alexander the Great asked Diogenes if he needed anything, and the philosopher replied, "Yes, stand out of my sunlight." Bruno implies Castelnau is the only one who respects his light</note>. If indeed, so as not to make him poorer than that cynical rascal, some direct or reflected ray is sent into that "hole" <note>Probably referring to the specific rooms or the diplomatic "refuge" Bruno occupied at the French embassy</note> that you know of.

To you this is consecrated, for in this Britain you represent the highness of so magnanimous, so great, and so powerful a King <note>Henry III of France, whom Castelnau served as ambassador</note>, who from the most noble breast of Europe, with the voice of his fame, makes the extreme hinges of the earth resound. He who, when he growls in anger like a lion from a high cave, brings terror and mortal horror to the other powerful predators of these woods; and when he rests and is quiet, sends forth such a glow of liberal and courteous love that it inflames the nearby tropics, warms the frozen Bear, and dissolves the rigor of the **Arctic desert** that turns under the eternal guardianship of fierce **Boötes** <note>A constellation in the northern sky; Bruno uses this astronomical imagery to suggest the King’s (and by extension, the Ambassador’s) civilizing influence reaches even the coldest, most "barbaric" regions</note>.

->Farewell!<- <note>Original: "Vale!"</note>

# FIRST DIALOGUE.

->Interlocutors:<-
->**Smitho. Teofilo**, philosopher. **Prudenzio**, pedante.<-
->**Frulla.**<-

->**Smitho.**<-

**Did they speak Latin well?**
**Teo.** Yes.
**Smi.** Honorable men?
**Teo.** Yes.
**Smi.** Of good reputation?
**Teo.** Yes.
**Smi.** Learned?
**Teo.** Competently enough.
**Smi.** Well-bred, courteous, civil?
**Teo.** Only very moderately.
**Smi.** Doctors?
**Teo.** Yes, sir; yes, father; yes, my lady; yes, mother; from <term>Oxford</term> <note>Original: "Oxonia," the Latin name for Oxford University, where Bruno famously clashed with the faculty</note>, I believe.
**Smi.** Well-qualified?
**Teo.** Why not? Men of high standing, in long robes, dressed in velvet; one of whom had two chains of shining gold around his neck, and the other—by God—with that precious hand which bore twelve rings on two fingers, looked like a very wealthy jeweler who would pluck out your eyes and heart while he stood there admiring himself.
**Smi.** Did they show knowledge of Greek?
**Teo.** And of beer <term>moreover</term> <note>Original: "eziandio." Teofilo is mocking the English academics' habit of heavy drinking</note>.
**Pru.** Get rid of that "moreover"; it is an obsolete and antiquated expression. <note>Prudenzio, the caricature of a picky grammarian, is more interested in correcting Teofilo's vocabulary than listening to the story</note>
**Fru.** Be quiet, Master, for he is not speaking to you.
**Smi.** What did they look like?
**Teo.** One looked like the constable of the giantess and the ogre; the other like the high official of the goddess of reputation.
**Smi.** So there were two of them?
**Teo.** Yes; because this is a mysterious number.
**Pru.** >So that there might be two witnesses <note>Original Latin: "Ut essent duo testes." A biblical and legal reference implying that a truth must be confirmed by at least two people</note>.

<meta>This page continues the first dialogue of the "Cabala of the Pegasean Horse." Having just mocked the appearance and pedantry of the Oxford doctors, the characters now pivot to a philosophical discussion on the nature of the number two, transitioning from Teofilo's serious Pythagorean philosophy to Frulla's satirical and "asinine" examples.</meta>

->**Frulla**<-

**Fru.** What do you mean by those *witnesses*?
**Pru.** Witnesses, examiners of the Nolan's <note>The "Nolan" is Giordano Bruno himself, referring to his birth in Nola, Italy</note> competence. **But by Hercules!** <note>Original Latin: "At mehercle!"</note> why did you say, Teofilo, that the number two is mysterious?
**Teo.** Because there are two primary pairings, as Pythagoras says: the finite and the infinite, the curved and the straight, right and left, and so on. There are two types of numbers: even and odd, of which one is male and the other is female. There are two Cupids: the superior and divine, and the inferior and vulgar. There are two acts of life: cognition and affection. There are two objects of these: the true and the good. There are two types of motion: straight, by which bodies tend toward self-preservation, and circular, by which they are preserved. There are two essential principles of things: matter and form. Two specific differences of substance: the rare and the dense, the simple and the mixed. Two primary contrary and active principles: heat and cold. Two primary parents of natural things: the sun and the earth.
**Fru.** In keeping with the theme of those aforementioned "twos," I shall make another scale for the number two. The beasts entered the ark two by two; they came out again two by two. There are two leaders of the celestial signs: **the ram and the bull** <note>Original Latin: "aries et taurus"</note>. There are two types of those who **"must not become"** <note>Original Latin: "nolite fieri," a reference to Psalm 32:9: "Do not be like the horse or the mule, which have no understanding"</note>: the horse and the mule. There are two animals made in the image and likeness of man: the monkey on earth, and the owl <note>Specifically the "barbagianni" or barn owl, often used as a symbol of foolishness or mock-wisdom</note> in the heavens. There are two false and honored relics of Fierze <gloss>*</gloss> <note>The original text "Fierze" is likely a typo for Florence (Firenze)</note> in this homeland: the teeth of Sassetto and the beard of Pietruccia. There are two animals that the prophet said had more intellect than the people of Israel: the ox, because it knows its owner, and the ass, because it knows how to find its master’s manger. Two were the mysterious mounts of our Redeemer, which signify his ancient Hebrew believer and the new Gentile: the she-ass and the foal. Two are the names derived from these that formed the titles of Augustus's secretary: Asinius and Pollio <note>A pun on "Asinus" (ass) and "Pullus" (foal/colt)</note>. There are two kinds of asses: the domestic and the wild. Two are their most common colors: gray and dark brown. There are two pyramids upon which the names of these two and other similar doctors must be written and dedicated to eternity: the right ear of Silenus’s horse, and the left ear of the antagonist of the god of gardens <note>The "antagonist of the god of gardens" (Priapus) is the ass, whose braying famously interrupted Priapus's nocturnal schemes</note>.
**Pru.** **A genius of the finest character! An enumeration by no means to be despised!** <note>Original Latin: "Optimae indolis ingenium! enumeratio minime contemnenda!"</note>
**Fru.** I take pride, my Master Prudenzio, because you—who are more prudent than Prudence itself—approve of my discourse; for you are Prudence **of the masculine gender** <note>Original Latin: "masculini generis." Frulla is mocking Prudenzio's name and pedantic nature</note>.
**Pru.** **And that is not without wit and grace!** <note>Original Latin: "Neque id sine lepore et grazia!"</note> Come now, put those things aside—

<meta>This page transitions into the second dialogue of "The Ash Wednesday Supper" (La Cena de le Ceneri). ...us praises! *Let us sit, because, as the prince of the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticorum princeps" — a title for Aristotle, whose followers were called "Peripatetics" because they walked while teaching.</note> says, by sitting and resting we gain wisdom;* <note>original: "Sedeamus, quia... sedendo et quiescendo sapimus"</note> and so until the setting of the sun we will prolong our <term>tetralogue</term> <note>A conversation between four people, contrasting with a dialogue (two).</note> regarding the outcome of the **Nolan's** <note>Giordano Bruno, who was born in Nola.</note> colloquy with Doctor **Torquato** and Doctor **Nundinio**.

**Pru.** *Tetralogue* I said, *that is, a speech of four*, <note>original: "id est, quatuorum sermo"</note> just as *dialogue* means *a speech of two*, <note>original: "duorum sermo"</note> trilogue *a speech of three*, <note>original: "trium sermo"</note> and so on, with pentalogue, heptalogue, and others, which are incorrectly called dialogues—as some say, *as if they were the words of different people*; <note>original: "quasi diversorum loghi"</note> but it is not likely that the Greeks, the inventors of this name, took that first syllable *di-* as the head of that Latin word *diversum* <note>Prudenzio is arguing that "dialogue" comes from "di" (two) rather than "dia" (through), a common pedantic error of the time.</note>.

**Pru.** *O the times!* <note>original: "O saeclum!"</note> You seem to make little account of good letters.
