Now, to give a beginning and bring the matter back to the start: come and inspire me, O Muses! I do not speak to you who speak through bloated and proud verse on Mount Helicon; for I fear that perhaps you might complain about me in the end, when after having made such a long and tiresome pilgrimage, crossed such perilous seas, and tasted such fierce customs, it became necessary for you to return home quickly, barefoot and naked—because here there are no fish for Lombards. <note>A proverbial expression meaning there is nothing to be gained here for outsiders.</note> I shall leave aside that you are not only foreigners, but you are also of that race of which a poet said:

->*No Greek was ever clear of malice.*<-

Besides, I cannot fall in love with something I do not see; others, others are those who have enchained my soul. To you others, then, I speak: gracious, gentle, soft, tender, young, beautiful, delicate, with golden hair, white cheeks, vermilion faces, succulent lips, divine eyes, marble breasts, and hearts of diamond, for whom I build so many thoughts in my mind, gather so many affections in my spirit, conceive so many passions in my life, shed so many tears from my eyes, exhale so many sighs from my chest, and from my heart spark so many flames—to you, **Muses of England**, <note>A reference to the noblewomen of the Elizabethan court, whom Bruno admired during his stay in London.</note> I say: inspire me, breathe into me, warm me, ignite me, distill me, and dissolve me into liquid, give me your juice, and make me appear not with a small, delicate, narrow, short, and succinct epigram...

From these, we have reached a judgment that could only be born after many active ages. He added that these astronomers are, in effect, like those interpreters who translate words from one language to another; but it is others, then, who delve into the meanings, and not the translators themselves. They are like those rustics who report the events and the form of a battle to an absent captain; they themselves do not understand the business, the reasons, and the art by which the victory was won, but rather the captain does, who has experience and better judgment in the military art. ->*But where my country, where Phoebus calls me, I shall follow.*<- <note>original: "Sed quo vocat me patria, quo Phoebus, sequar"</note>
->*You, my daughter, guiding your father who lacks light,*<- <note>original: "Tu lucis inopem gnata genitorem regens"</note>
->*Report the clear signs of the sacred prophecy!*<- <note>original: "Manifesta sacri signa fatidici refer!" — These verses are from Seneca’s tragedy *Oedipus*.</note>

Similarly, what could we judge, if the many and diverse verifications of the appearances of the celestial or surrounding bodies had not been declared and placed before the eyes of reason? Certainly nothing. Nevertheless, after having given thanks to the gods, the distributors of gifts that proceed from the first and infinite almighty light, and having praised the study of these noble spirits, we know most clearly that we must open our eyes to what they have observed and seen, but not give our consent to what they have conceived, understood, and determined.

**Smi.** Please, let me understand: what opinion do you have of Copernicus?

**Teo.** He had a grave, elaborate, diligent, and mature genius; a man who is inferior to no astronomer who was before him, except by place of succession and time: a man who, as far as natural judgment is concerned, was far superior...

<meta>This page continues the speech by Teofilo, who is discussing the history of astronomy and the role of Nicolaus Copernicus. to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric (Earth-centered) model dominated Western thought for over a millennium.</note>, **Hipparchus** <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BC) famous for discovering the precession of the equinoxes.</note>, **Eudoxus** <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 390–337 BC) who designed an early model of planetary motion using nested spheres.</note>, and all the others who have walked in their footsteps. He reached this point by freeing himself from several false assumptions of common and vulgar philosophy—I will not go so far as to call it blindness, but he did not distance himself very far from it. Because he was more a student of **mathematics** <note>In Bruno’s time, "mathematics" often referred to the calculation of planetary positions, while "natural philosophy" dealt with the actual physical nature of the universe.</note> than of nature, he was not able to go deep enough or penetrate far enough to completely uproot the causes of inconvenient and empty principles. Thus, he could not perfectly resolve all opposing difficulties, nor succeed in freeing both himself and others from so many vain inquiries into things that are constant and certain.

Despite all this, who can fully praise the magnanimity of **this German** <note>Referring to Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), the Polish-German astronomer who proposed the Sun-centered system.</note>? Paying little heed to the foolish multitude, he stood firm against the torrent of opposing belief. And though he was almost unarmed with living reasons, by taking up those rejected and rusty fragments of antiquity that he could get his hands on, he polished, assembled, and welded them back together with his discourse—which was more mathematical than natural. In doing so, he took a cause that was once ridiculed, rejected, and despised, and made it honored, prized, and more plausible than its opposite, and most certainly more convenient and efficient for theory and the logic of calculation.

Thus this **German** <note>original: "Allemano," a variant of "German" used for Copernicus.</note>, although he lacked sufficient means to not only resist but also to sufficiently conquer, defeat, and suppress falsehood, nevertheless stood his ground. He determined in his own mind and most openly confessed that one must necessarily conclude in the end that it is more likely this globe moves in relation to the universe, than to think it possible that the vastness of so many innumerable bodies—many of which are known to be more magnificent and larger than ours—should, in defiance of nature and reason (which cry out the contrary with very evident motions), recognize this Earth as the center and base of their circuits and influences.

Who, then, will be so rude and discourteous toward this man’s study that they would forget all he has done? He was ordained by the gods as a **dawn** <note>Bruno views Copernicus as a transitional figure who brought the first light, but not the full clarity of the "Sun" (Bruno's own philosophy).</note> that was meant to precede the rising of this sun of the ancient true philosophy, which for so many centuries had been buried in the dark caverns of blind, malignant, stubborn, and envious ignorance. Who would wish—noting him only for what he was *not* able to do—to place him in the same rank as the common herd, who discourse, guide themselves, and rush headlong more by the sense of hearing a brutal and ignoble faith? Rather, should we not count him among those who, with happy genius, were able to stand tall and raise themselves up through the most faithful guidance of the eye of divine intelligence?

Now, what shall I say of the **Nolan** <note>Giordano Bruno himself, born in Nola.</note>? Perhaps because he is as close to me as I am to myself, it is not fitting for me to praise him? Certainly, no reasonable man will rebuke me for this, considering that sometimes it is not only appropriate but also necessary, as that clear and cultivated **Tansillo** <note>Luigi Tansillo (1510–1568), a famous Neapolitan poet and friend of Bruno's family, whom Bruno often uses as a literary authority.</note> well expressed:

<summary>Teofilo praises Copernicus for reviving the heliocentric theory against common prejudice, though he argues Copernicus was a mere mathematician who lacked the deeper physical insights of "the Nolan" (Bruno).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech by Teofilo, who is building a defense for the "Nolan" (Giordano Bruno himself). After praising Copernicus on the previous page as a precursor, Teofilo now prepares to justify why the Nolan might appear to praise his own discoveries, comparing them to the daring voyages of the Argonauts and Christopher Columbus.</meta>

*Although for a man who desires prize and honor,*
*To speak much of himself is quite unbecoming,*
*Because the tongue, where the heart fears and loves,*
*Is not worthy of trust in its own speech,*
*Yet to be the herald of one's own fame*
*Sometimes seems appropriate,*
*When one comes to speak for one of two reasons:*
*To avoid blame, or to help others.*

Even if someone is so arrogant that they will not, for any reason, tolerate self-praise (or what seems like it), let them know that such praise sometimes cannot be separated from the present and reported effects of one’s work. Who will rebuke <term>Apelles</term> <note>The most renowned painter of ancient Greece (4th century BC), known for his technical skill.</note> if, when presenting his work to someone who wants to know, he says it is his own handiwork? Who will blame <term>Phidias</term> <note>A famous Greek sculptor and architect (5th century BC), responsible for the statue of Zeus at Olympia.</note> if, to one who asks for the author of this magnificent <term>sculpture</term>, he responds that it was he? Now then, so that you may understand the present business and its importance, I propose a conclusion to you that will very soon be proven most easily and clearly: that if the ancient <term>Tiphys</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the pilot of the *Argo*, the ship of the Argonauts.</note> is praised for having invented the first ship and, with the <term>Argonauts</term> <note>The band of heroes who sailed with Jason to find the Golden Fleece.</note>, crossed the sea—

> *He was overbold who first broke the treacherous waves with such a fragile raft, and seeing his own lands behind his back, entrusted his life to the light breezes;* <note>original: "Audax nimium, qui freta primus / Rate tam fragili perfida rupit, / Terrasque suas post terga videns, / Animam levibus credidit auris;" — Seneca, Medea, lines 301–304.</note>

—and if in our own times <term>Columbus</term> <note>Christopher Columbus (1451–1506), the explorer whose voyages to the Americas were often seen by Renaissance thinkers as the fulfillment of ancient prophecies.</note> is magnified for being the one of whom it was so long ago prophesied:

> *There shall come a time in the later years when Ocean shall loosen the bonds of things, and a vast land shall open up; Tiphys shall discover new worlds, and Thule shall no longer be the furthest land —* <note>original: "Venient annis / Saecula seris, quibus Oceanus / Vincula rerum laxet, et ingens / Pateat tellus, Tiphysque novos / Detegat orbes, nec sit terris / Ultima Thule —" — Seneca, Medea, lines 375–379. This famous passage was widely interpreted in the Renaissance as a prophecy of the discovery of the Americas.</note>

—then what should be done for this man <note>Teofilo refers here to the Nolan (Giordano Bruno), the author of the text.</note>, who has found the way to ascend to heaven, to traverse the circumference of the stars, and to leave behind the convex surface of the firmament? The likes of Tiphys found the way to disturb the peace of others, to violate the local spirits of different regions, to confuse what provident nature kept distinct, and through trade to double the flaws and add the vices of one generation to those of another; to violently propagate new follies and plant unheard-of madness where it did not exist—concluding in the end that the strongest is the wisest. They showed new studies, instruments, and arts for tyrannizing and assassinating one another. By virtue of these deeds, a time will come when, having learned these lessons at their own cost through the force of the flux of things, those people will know how to, and be able to, return to us similar and even worse fruits of such pernicious inventions.

<summary>Teofilo justifies the Nolan's self-praise by comparing his intellectual "ascent to heaven" to the daring voyages of Tiphys and Columbus, while simultaneously offering a sharp critique of how physical exploration leads to colonization and the spread of vice.</summary>

**The Nolan** <note>Giordano Bruno's self-designated title, referring to his birthplace, Nola, near Naples.</note>, in order to cause entirely opposite effects, has set free the human spirit and knowledge, which was imprisoned in the narrowest dungeon of the turbulent air, from where it barely had the power to gaze at the most distant stars as if through certain small holes; its wings were clipped so that it might not fly to pull back the veil of these clouds and see what truly might be found up there, and to free itself from the chimeras of those who—having emerged from the mud and caves of the earth as if they were **Mercuries** and **Apollos** descended from heaven—have, with multiform imposture, filled the whole world with infinite follies, beastliness, and vices, as if they were so many virtues, divinities, and disciplines, extinguishing that light which made the souls of our ancient fathers divine and heroic, and instead approving and confirming the misty darkness of the <term>sofisti</term> <note>Sophists: here used as a derogatory term for academic philosophers who use clever but fallacious arguments.</note> and asses. > *Who will ascend for me, my lady, to heaven,*
> *To bring back my lost wits?*
<note>original: "Chi salirà per me, madonna, in cielo..." from Ludovico Ariosto's *Orlando Furioso*, Canto XXXIV. In the poem, Astolfo travels to the moon to recover the lost sanity (wits) of Orlando.</note>

Thus, in the presence of all sense and reason, with the key of most diligent inquiry, he has opened those cloisters of truth that we were able to open; stripping bare nature, which was covered and veiled, he has given eyes to the moles, illuminated the blind who could not fix their eyes and gaze at their own image in so many mirrors that faced them from every side; he has loosened the tongues of the mute who did not know how, or did not dare, to explain their intricate feelings; he has mended the lame who were not able to make that progress with their spirit which the lowly and dissolvable body cannot; he makes them no less present than if they were the very inhabitants of the sun, the moon, and other named stars; he demonstrates how similar or dissimilar they are,

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument for an infinite universe. Having previously critiqued the narrow view of the world held by the ancients, the speaker (Teofilo) now describes the liberation of the human mind through the realization that the Earth is a star among stars, and that divinity is found within all things rather than in a distant, localized heaven.</meta>

...greater or worse than those bodies we see far off compared to the one that is near to us and to which we are joined. It opens our eyes to see this deity <note>nume: Bruno often uses "deity" or "numen" to describe the divine nature of the Earth and other celestial bodies.</note>, this mother of ours, who feeds and nourishes us on her back after producing us from her womb—to which she always welcomes us back. It teaches us not to think any longer that she is a body without soul and life, or even the dregs among corporal substances.

In this way we know that if we were on the moon, or on other stars, we would not be in a place very different from this, and perhaps in a worse one, just as other bodies can be as good as this one, and even better in themselves and for the greater happiness of their own living beings <note>original: "animali." In Bruno’s cosmology, all stars and planets are inhabited by living beings.</note>. Thus we recognize so many stars, so many heavenly bodies, so many deities, which are those many hundreds of thousands that assist in the ministry and contemplation of the first, universal, infinite, and eternal efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the agency that brings something into being; here, Bruno refers to God as the source of the infinite universe.</note>.

Our reason is no longer imprisoned by the chains of those eight, nine, or ten imaginary movable spheres and their movers <note>A critique of the traditional Ptolemaic and Aristotelian cosmology, which envisioned the planets fixed to a series of physical, concentric crystal spheres.</note>. We know there is but one heaven, one immense ethereal region, where these magnificent lights keep their proper distances for the sake of participating in perpetual life. These flaming bodies are those ambassadors that announce the excellence of the glory and majesty of God. 

Thus we are promoted to discover the infinite effect of the infinite cause, the true and living vestige of infinite vigor; and we are taught not to seek divinity far removed from us, if we have it nearby—or rather within us, more than we are within ourselves. Just so, the inhabitants of other worlds should not seek divinity near us, having it near and within themselves, given that the moon is no more "heaven" to us than we are to the moon. 

Thus we can apply to a certain better purpose what **Tansillo** <note>Luigi Tansillo (1510–1568), a Neapolitan poet and friend of Bruno, whose verses Bruno often incorporates into his dialogues.</note> said as if in a game:

> *If you do not take the good that is near you,*
> *How will you take that which is far away?*
> *To despise your own seems to me an outright error,*
> *And to crave what is in another's hand.*
> *You are the one who abandoned himself,*
> *Desiring his own image in vain:*
> *You are the hound that falls into the stream,* <note>A reference to Aesop's fable of the dog who drops his meat in a river to snap at its larger-looking reflection.</note>
> *While desiring the shadow of what he holds in his mouth.*
>
> *Leave the shadows and embrace the truth!*
> *Do not exchange the present for the future!*
> *I do not despair of having better hereafter;*
> *But to live more joyful and secure,*
> *I enjoy the present and hope for the future:*
> *Thus I procure for myself a double sweetness.*

With this, one man alone—though he be alone—can and will be able to conquer, and in the end will have conquered and triumphed against the general ignorance; and it is not...

<summary>Bruno argues that the Earth is a living, divine entity and that the universe is an infinite ethereal space without fixed spheres, where every world acts as a "heaven" to others. He emphasizes that divinity is immanent (internal) rather than distant, urging the reader to embrace the truth of the present world over "shadows."</summary>
<keywords>cosmology, infinite universe, plurality of worlds, Tansillo, immanence, divinity, reason, ethereal region, corporal substances</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section, where Teofilo (speaking for Giordano Bruno) explains that the new infinite cosmology is not for the masses, but for those with the capacity for reason. The speakers are Prudenzio (a pedantic scholar), Teofilo (the philosopher), and Frulla (a more colloquial, humorous character).</meta>

...doubt—whether the matter is to be determined not by a multitude of blind and deaf witnesses, by insults and empty words, but by the power of disciplined reason, which must ultimately prevail. For in fact, all the blind people in the world are not worth a single one who sees, and all the fools cannot serve as a substitute for one wise man.

**Prudenzio.** *In things, and in sense, if what was before no longer remains,*
> *Live content with what the times provide!*
> *Never, as a lone man, despise the judgment of the people,*
> *Lest you please no one, while wishing to despise the many.*
<note>original: "Rebus, et in sensu, si non est quod fuit ante, / Fac vivas contentus eo, quod tempora praebent! / Judicium populi nunquam contempseris unus, / Ne nulli placeas, dum vis contemnere multos." These are Latin verses likely reflecting the common-sense, traditionalist view that one should not go against the majority opinion.</note>

**Teofilo.** This is most prudently said regarding social gatherings, the common rule of law, and the practice of civil conversation; but certainly not regarding the knowledge of truth and the rule of contemplation, for which the same wise man said:
> *Learn, but from the learned; teach the unlearned yourself!*
<note>original: "Disce, sed a doctis; indoctos ipse doceto!" This counters Prudenzio's quote by suggesting that while social conformity is good for peace, truth is a matter for the educated.</note>

What you say also applies to doctrine that is expedient for the many; it is therefore advice that concerns the multitude. For this burden <note>Bruno refers to the "burden" of understanding the true nature of the infinite universe.</note> is not for just anyone’s shoulders, but for those who can carry it—like the **Nolan** <term>The Nolan: Giordano Bruno’s nickname for himself, as he was born in Nola, Italy.</term>, or at least for those who can move it toward its goal without running into unseemly difficulty, as **Copernicus** was able to do. Furthermore, those who possess this truth should not communicate it to every sort of person, unless they wish to, as the saying goes, "wash the donkey’s head" <note>An old proverb meaning to waste one's labor on a hopeless task.</note>, or if they wish to see what pigs do with pearls. Otherwise, they will reap only those fruits of their study and labor that rash and foolish ignorance usually produces, along with presumption and incivility, which are ignorance's constant and faithful companions. 

We can, therefore, be teachers to those unlearned people and illuminators to those blind ones who are called "blind" not because of a natural inability or a lack of talent and discipline, but solely for failing to notice and consider. Their blindness comes from the lack of the act of seeing alone, and not from a lack of the faculty <note>Teofilo distinguishes between those who are naturally stupid and those who simply haven't been taught to use their reason.</note>. Among these, however, are some so malicious and wicked that, out of a certain lazy envy, they grow angry and proud against anyone who seems to want to teach them. Because they are believed to be—and, what is worse, believe themselves to be—learned doctors, they burn with rage and go mad if someone dares to show they know what these "doctors" do not.

**Frulla.** Just like what happened to those two "Barbary" doctors <note>barbareschi: A term implying they are uncivilized or foreign to true learning.</note> we were going to talk about. One of them, not knowing how to respond or what to argue anymore, stood up as if he wanted to finish the debate with a supply of Erasmus’s adages, or rather with his fists, and yelled:
> *What? Are you not sailing to Anticyra?* <note>original: "quid? nonne Anticyram navigas?" To "sail to Anticyra" was a classical idiom meaning someone was crazy and needed to go there to get hellebore, a plant used to treat madness.</note> *Are you that first-molder of philosophers, who grants nothing to Ptolemy, nor to the majesty of so many and such great philosophers and astronomers? Are you looking for a knot in a bulrush?* <note>original: "Tu ne nodum in scirpo quaerites?" An idiom meaning to look for a difficulty where there is none, or to find a problem in something perfectly smooth.</note>

...and other such remarks, which deserved to be "decided" upon his back with those double rods called sticks, with which porters take the measure to make jackets for donkeys <note>A humorous way of saying the doctor deserved a good beating for his arrogance.</note>.

<summary>Teofilo argues that scientific and philosophical truth is not determined by majority vote but by reason, warning that sharing deep truths with the ignorant or arrogant often leads to hostility. Frulla recounts an anecdote of a traditionalist doctor who, unable to win an argument against Bruno's theories, resorted to insults and appeals to the authority of Ptolemy.</summary>

**Teo.** Let us set aside these arguments for now! **Smi.** Now, what would you say if the majority of people in our times thought the exact opposite, especially regarding doctrine?

**Teo.** I am not surprised; because, as is common, those who understand the least believe they know *more*, and those who are completely mad think they know everything.

**Smi.** Tell me, in what way can these people be corrected?

**Fru.** By taking away that head of theirs and planting a new one there.

**Teo.** By taking away, through some form of argumentation, that self-estimation of knowledge, and with sharp persuasions stripping them, as much as possible, of that foolish opinion, so that they might become listeners; having first ensured that the one who teaches finds them to be capable and able minds. This is because, if the doctrine is perfect in itself and has been perfectly understood by them, it clears away all doubts and removes all contradictions. 

Furthermore, if it happens that one finds a more polished mind, then that person will be able to see how much can be added, taken away, corrected, or changed. Only then can they compare these principles and conclusions, and thus reasonably consent or dissent, question and answer; otherwise, it is not possible to know how to doubt or question appropriately regarding an art or science, or with the proper order, if one has not heard it first. Since I know nothing, how will I be able to recognize the difference between worthiness and unworthiness, between the poverty and the richness of those who consider themselves, and are considered by others, to be wise? 

I see clearly that we are all born ignorant and easily believe ourselves to be so; we grow up and are raised with the discipline and customs of our own household. We hear the laws, rituals, faith, and customs of our adversaries—those alien to us—blamed no less than our own are praised. The roots of zeal for our own ways are planted in us by the force of a certain "natural nourishment" just as firmly as they are planted in many other diverse peoples for their own ways. ...doctor, with no less satisfaction of my soul, I will consider myself to have gained more under the arrogant and fortunate ignorance of a horse, than anything else under someone less ignorant, or even a learned man. # SECOND DIALOGUE

## Teofilo.

Then Sir <term>Fulke Greville<note>Folco Grivello in the original Italian. He was an English poet, dramatist, and statesman at the court of Queen Elizabeth I.</note></term> said to him: "Pray, Sir Nolan, let me understand the reasons for which you believe the earth moves!" To which he replied that he would not be able to give him any reason, not knowing his capacity; and not knowing how he might be understood, he feared acting like those who speak their reasons to statues and talk to the dead. Therefore, he asked that Greville first make himself known by proposing those reasons that persuade him to the contrary, so that according to the light and strength of the intellect he demonstrates in bringing those forth, resolutions could be given to him. He added to this that, out of the desire he holds to show the weakness of opposing opinions using the very same principles with which they think they are confirmed, it would be no small pleasure to find people judged sufficient for this task, and he would always be ready and prepared to answer. In this way, the power of the foundations of his philosophy against the common one could be seen all the better, as a better opportunity would be presented to him to respond and clarify.

Sir Fulke was very pleased with this response and said: "You do me a most gracious service; I accept your proposal, and I wish to set a day on which people will oppose you, who perhaps will not fail to provide you material to bring your ideas into the field. Wednesday in eight days, which will be <term>Ash Wednesday<note>This specific date gives the book its title, "The Ash Wednesday Supper."</note></term>, you shall be a guest with many gentlemen and learned figures, so that after eating, there may be a discussion of beautiful and varied things." 

"I promise you," said the Nolan, "that I will not fail to be present then, and every time such an occasion presents itself; for there is little within my choice that would delay me from the study of wanting to understand and know. But I pray you, do not bring before me ignoble, ill-bred persons, with little understanding in such speculations." And certainly he had reason to doubt, because many doctors of this country, with whom he has discussed letters, he has found in their way of proceeding to have more of the <term>plowman<note>original Italian: "bifolco." Bruno used this term to describe the Oxford scholars he found to be crude, pedantic, and lacking in intellectual refinement.</note></term> than of anything else that could be desired. Sir Fulke replied that he should not doubt; for those he proposes are well-man-

From the other side, we were delayed by common boredom and by a certain spirit that spoke certain reasons more true than they are worthy to repeat.

**Fru.** It is lawful and within the power of princes to exalt lowly things; if the princes are of a certain character, those things will be judged worthy—and truly will be worthy. In this, their acts are more illustrious and notable than if they were to make the great even greater; for there is nothing the great do not believe they deserve because of their own size. Or, if superiors were merely maintained in their superiority, they would say such things were due to them not by the grace, courtesy, and magnanimity of a prince, but by justice and reason. Thus, princes do not ordinarily exalt the worthy and virtuous, because it seems to them that such men have no occasion to return as many thanks as a promoted loafer or the dregs of scoundrels. Furthermore, they have this wisdom: to make it known that fortune (to whose blind majesty they are much obliged) is superior to virtue. If they occasionally exalt a good and honored man among those others, they will rarely let him keep that rank without placing someone above him to make him realize how much authority weighs over merit, and that merit is worth nothing except what authority permits and dispenses. Speaking of Europe, I leave it to the whole world to judge what rank she holds among all other princes. Certainly, if the empire of Fortune corresponded and were equal to the empire of her most noble spirit and intellect, it would be necessary for this great **Amphitrite** <note>In Greek mythology, the goddess of the sea and wife of Poseidon; Bruno uses this as a poetic title for Queen Elizabeth I, the "Sea-Queen" of the British Isles.</note> to open her robes and widen her circumference so much that, just as she already encompasses one Britain and Ireland, Fortune would give her another entire globe to equal the size of the universe—so that with a fuller significance, her powerful hand might sustain the globe of a general and entire monarchy. 

You have no reason to speak of anything but the mature, discreet, and provident counsel with which that heroic soul, for twenty-five years and more, has made peace and quiet triumph with but a blink of her eyes in the center of the tempests of a sea of adversity. She has maintained herself firm amidst such vigorous floods and swelling waves of various storms, which this proud and mad ocean surrounding her on all sides has cast against her with all its might. 

In that place—although I do not know them personally, nor do I have any thought of knowing them—I hear the names of most illustrious and excellent knights: a great Treasurer of the kingdom, and **Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester**, the most noble humanity of whom is so well known to the world, mentioned alongside the fame of the Queen and the realm, and so highly praised in neighboring provinces as one who welcomes with particular favor every sort of foreigner who does not show himself entirely incapable of grace and respect. 

These men, together with the most excellent **Sir Francis Walsingham**, Great Secretary of the Royal Council—as those who sit near the sun of royal splendor—are sufficient with the light of their great civility to extinguish and annul all darkness, and with the heat of their loving courtesy to refine and purge whatever rudeness or rusticity might be found, not only among the Britons, but even among the Scythians, Arabs, Tartars, Cannibals, and **Anthropophagi** <term>Anthropophagi|A historical term for man-eaters or cannibals</term>. 

It is not appropriate for you to recount the honest conversation, civility, and good breeding of many knights and very noble personages of the kingdom, among whom is so well known—and to us most particularly, by reputation first when we were in Milan and in France, and then by experience now that we are in his homeland—the most illustrious and excellent knight, **Sir Philip Sidney**. His most polished intellect, in addition to his most praiseworthy customs, is so rare and singular that even among the most singular and rare men, both outside and inside Italy, you will hardly find his equal.

...a common people who, in being disrespectful, uncivilized, coarse, rustic, wild, and ill-bred, yield to no other that the earth might nourish in its bosom. **Pru.** *Every division ought to be two-membered, or reducible to two members.* <note>original Latin: "Omnis divisio debet esse bimembris, vel reducibilis ad bimembrem." Prudenzio, the pedantic scholar, is quoting a rule of formal logic.</note>

**Teo.** Of which one consists of artisans and shopkeepers who, recognizing you in some fashion as a foreigner, twist their noses at you, laugh, sneer, mock you with their mouths, and call you in their own language "dog," "traitor," or "stranger." This, to them, is a most insulting title, one that makes the person so named liable to receive every wrong in the world, whether he be a young man or old, a magistrate or a soldier, a nobleman or a gentleman. 

Now, if by ill luck it happens that you have cause to touch one of them, or lay hand on your weapon, behold: in a single moment you will find yourself—for as long as the street stretches—in the midst of an army of "thick-skinned" oafs. <note>original: "coticoni," literally those with thick rinds like pork; used here to mean coarse, insensitive ruffians.</note> More suddenly than those armed men who (as the poets imagine) rose from the dragon's teeth sown by **Jason**, they seem to spring from the earth—though they most certainly emerge from their shops. <note>In Greek myth, Jason sowed dragon teeth that instantly grew into a crop of fully armed warriors.</note> 

They create a most "honorable" and "gentle" spectacle of a forest of clubs, long poles, halberds, partisans, and rusty pitchforks—which, although granted to them by the Prince <note>Referring to the Crown or the State authority.</note> for excellent purposes, they always have ready and waiting for this and similar occasions. Thus, with a rustic fury, you will see them hurl themselves upon you, without regard for whom, why, where, or how, and without any of them consulting the other. Each one, venting that natural disdain he has against the foreigner, will come at you with his own hand (unless he is blocked by the crowd of others doing the same) and with his own rod will "take the measure" of your <term>tunic</term> <note>original: "sajo," a type of military tunic or short cloak.</note>—and if you are not careful to save yourself, even your hat on your head. 

And if by chance some worthy man or gentleman were present who might be displeased by such villainy—even if he were a Count or a Duke—he would be forced to seethe inwardly and wait, standing at a distance, for the end; for he would fear that by trying to help you, he would only become your companion in suffering without any benefit to you, as these people have no respect for anyone when they see themselves armed in this fashion. Now, at length, <note>original Latin: "tandem"</note> when you think you might finally be allowed to go find a barber and rest your tired and mistreated frame, behold: you will find that those very same people are so many <term>constables</term> and <term>guards</term> <note>original: "birri" and "zaffi"; derogatory terms for low-level law enforcement or "catchpoles" known for their corruption and brutality.</note> who, if they can pretend that you have...

**Teofilo.** Those of the **first rank** are the poor and needy gentlemen who, for the sake of wealth or favor, bring themselves under the wings of the great. Those of the **second rank** are petty merchants who have failed, or artisans, or those who have studied reading, writing, or some other art without profit; these are either taken or have fled from some school, warehouse, or shop. In Paris, you will find as many of them as you like at the palace gate; in Naples, at the steps of San Paolo; in Venice, at the Rialto; in Rome, at the Campo de' Fiori. Of these last three types are those who, to show how powerful they are in their own home, and being people of "good stomach" <term>good stomach: a contemporary idiom meaning having great courage or a strong constitution</term>, act like good soldiers and hold the whole world in contempt. To anyone who does not look like they intend to give them a wide berth, they will give a shove with their shoulder—like the prow of a galley—that will send him spinning all around, showing him how strong, robust, and powerful they are, and in a time of need, capable of breaking through an army. And if the one they encounter is a foreigner, no matter how much space he gives them, they want him to know by any means how well they can play the role of **Caesar**, **Hannibal**, **Hector**, or even a charging ox. They do not act only like the donkey, which—especially when loaded—is content to keep to its straight path, where if you do not move, it will not move either, and one of you must give way; but they act like these water-carriers who, if you are not careful, will make you feel the point of that iron nozzle at the mouth of the jar. <note>Commonly called a *gerla* [a conical back-basket].</note> Likewise, the same is done by those who carry beer and *ale* <note>original: "ala"</note>, who, going about their business, if they bump into you through their own carelessness, will make you feel the force of the load they carry—showing they are powerful enough not only to carry it on their shoulders but to knock down a house or even pull a wagon if needed. 

These individuals, because of the "authority" they hold while carrying a burden, deserve some excuse, for they have more in common with horses, mules, and donkeys than with men; but I accuse all the others, who have a small measure of reason and are more like the image and likeness of man than the aforementioned. Instead of wishing you a good day or good evening after putting on a pleasant face—as if they knew you and wanted to greet you—they will come and give you a brutish shove. I accuse, I say, those others who, sometimes pretending to flee, or wanting to pursue someone, or rushing to some necessary business, dash out from inside a shop and with that fury come at you from behind or from the side to give you such a shove as a provoked bull might give. This happened a few months ago to poor **Master Alessandro Citolino** <note>Alessandro Citolino (c. 1500–1582) was an Italian humanist and exile who lived in London; this passage documents a real assault he suffered.</note>, whose arm was broken and shattered in such a way, to the laughter and pleasure of the whole square; when the magistrate later wanted to take measures, he could not even find evidence that such a thing could have happened in that square.

...arm yourselves with a breastplate of patience, one that can withstand a shot from a **harquebus** <term>harquebus: an early type of portable gun supported on a tripod or a forked rest</term>, and always prepare yourself to bear the lesser evil willingly, if you do not wish to bear the worst by force! By which animals is the nobility of the human race represented on the dreaded Day of Judgment, if not by lambs and kids? Now, these are those virile, intrepid, and high-spirited ones, who shall not be divided from one another like **sheep from the goats** <note>original Latin: *oves ab hoedis*</note>, but like the more venerable, fierce, and "bumping" ones, they shall be distinguished as the fathers of the lambs from the fathers of the kids. **Pru.** **Aries first, then Taurus himself.** <note>original Latin: *Aries primo, post ipse taurus*</note>

**Teo.** Next to this great captain and first prince of the flocks, who else was worthy of being his neighbor and second-in-command, except for the great duke of the herds, to whom are joined—as if they were two pages, or two Ganymedes—those two beautiful twin boys? Consider, then, the nature and greatness of such a race of people, who hold primacy elsewhere than inside a rotting ark!

**Fru.** I certainly wouldn't know how to find any difference between these people and that genus of animals, except that those bump with their heads, while these bump with their shoulders as well. **Teo.** Now, after the Nolano had received about twenty of these **pikes** <term>pikes: *spuntonate*, literally blows from a pike-staff, here used to describe heavy shoves from the porters' shoulders</term>, particularly at the pyramid near the palace where three roads meet, we were met by six "gentlemen," one of whom gave him such a "gentle" and greedy <note>The original Italian *gorda* may be a misspelling of *ingorda* (greedy/heavy) or *corda* (cord/string).</note> shove that it alone could have counted for ten; and he caused him to be given another against the wall that could certainly have been worth another ten. **Teo.** This was the last storm; for shortly thereafter, by the grace of Saint Fortunio <note>Saint Fortunio: A play on "Fortune," personified here as a saint of luck.</note>, after having traversed such poorly trodden path—

...paths, having passed such doubtful turnings, crossed such rapid rivers, left behind such sandy shores, overcome such slimy mud, waded through such turbid marshes, explored such stony lava-flows, traversed such slippery roads, stumbled upon such rough stones, and bumped into such perilous rocks, we arrived by the grace of heaven alive at the port—that is, at the door—which was opened immediately upon our knocking. <meta>This page continues the Third Dialogue. The previous page introduced Dr. Nundinio, one of the Oxford scholars, as he prepared to speak at the Ash Wednesday supper. **Teo.** You would not imagine this of him! Even though he has been practicing in this country for nearly a year, he understands no more than two or three very common words, which he knows are greetings, but he does not know specifically what they mean; and if he wanted to utter one of them, he could not.

**Smi.** What does it mean that he has given so little thought to understanding our language?

**Teo.** There is nothing that compels him or inclines him toward it, because those honorable men and gentlemen with whom he is accustomed to converse all know how to speak either Latin, French, Spanish, or Italian. These men, knowing that the English language is not used outside this island, would consider themselves savages if they did not know any language other than their own natural tongue.

**Smi.** This is true everywhere; it is an unworthy thing, not only for a well-born Englishman but for any other nation, to know how to speak no more than one language. Yet in England—as I am certain is also true in Italy and France—there are many gentlemen of this condition, with whom someone who does not know the language of the country cannot converse without that distress felt by one who interprets and the one for whom the interpretation is made.

**Teo.** It is true that there are also many who are "gentlemen" by nothing more than lineage, whom it is better for their own sake and ours that they are neither understood nor even seen.

### Nundinio's second proposal.

**Smi.** What did Dr. Nundinio add?

**Teo.** "I, then," he said in Latin <note>Nundinio switches to Latin to ensure he is understood by the international guests, as discussed in the previous paragraph.</note>, "wish to interpret for you what we were saying: that it is to be believed that Copernicus did not hold the opinion that the earth moved, because this is an inconvenient and impossible thing; but that he attributed the motion to the earth rather than to the eighth sphere for the convenience of calculations." <term>eighth sphere: in the traditional Ptolemaic system, the outer shell containing the "fixed" stars</term> <term>supputations: mathematical calculations or astronomical tables used for predicting planetary positions</term>. The Nolano <note>The Nolano is the nickname for Giordano Bruno himself, referring to his birthplace in Nola, Italy.</note> said that if Copernicus said the earth moved for this reason alone, and not also for the other reason <note>i.e., because the earth physically and truly moves in reality</note>, he understood little of the matter and not enough. But it is certain that Copernicus understood it exactly as he said it, and proved it with all his effort.

**Smi.** Why did these men so vainly cast that judgment upon Copernicus’s opinion, if they cannot gather it from any of his propositions?

<meta>This page continues the Third Dialogue of 'The Ash Wednesday Supper.' The previous page ended with Teofilo describing Dr. Nundinio's arrival and the linguistic barriers at the dinner. Here, Teofilo begins to critique the reception of Copernicus's work, specifically focusing on the anonymous preface added to 'De Revolutionibus' by Andreas Osiander.</meta>

...lingering in grammar, he had heard of a certain <term>introductory epistle</term> <note>original: "epistola superliminare." This refers to the anonymous preface added to Copernicus's 'De revolutionibus' by Andreas Osiander without Copernicus's permission.</note> attached [to the book] by I know not what ignorant and presumptuous ass. This man, as if he wished to favor the author by excusing him, or perhaps so that other asses, finding their own lettuce and small fruits in this book, might have no reason to depart entirely hungry, warns them in this manner before they begin reading the book and considering its propositions:

„I do not doubt that some learned men“ — he rightly said *some*, of whom he might be one — „the fame of the new suppositions of this work having already been spread (which holds that the earth is mobile and the sun stays steady and fixed in the middle of the universe), feel strongly offended, thinking that this is a principle that will throw into confusion the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>The traditional university curriculum consisting of the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy).</note> which have been so well-ordered for so long a time. But if these men wish to consider the matter better, they will find that this author is not worthy of reproach; because it is the specific task of astronomers to gather, diligently and skillfully, the history of celestial motions; and since they cannot by any reason find the true causes of these motions, they are permitted to feign and fashion them according to their own will as principles of geometry, by means of which they can calculate the past as well as the future. Hence, it is not only unnecessary for these suppositions to be true, but they need not even be likely. Such must the hypotheses of this man be esteemed, unless there be someone so ignorant of optics and geometry as to believe that the distance of forty degrees or more, which <term>Venus</term> <note>The planet's maximum elongation from the sun.</note> acquires when moving away from the sun on one side or the other, is caused by its movement in an <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used to explain planetary variations.</note>. If this were true, who is so blind that he does not see what would follow, contrary to all experience: that the diameter of the star would appear four times larger, and the body of the star more than sixteen times larger, when it is nearest the opposite of the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "auge." The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion. If the planet moved on an epicycle, its distance from Earth—and thus its apparent size—would vary wildly, which was not observed.</note> than when it is furthest away, where it is said to be at its apogee? There are still other suppositions no less inconvenient than this one, which it is not necessary to relate.“

And he concludes at the end: „Let us, therefore, allow ourselves to take up the treasure of these suppositions, solely for the wonderful and skillful ease of calculation; for if anyone takes these fictional things as true, he will leave this discipline more foolish than when he entered it.“

Now see, what a fine gatekeeper! Consider how well he opens the door for you to enter into the participation of that most honored knowledge, without which knowing how to calculate, and measure, and do geometry and perspective is nothing other than a pastime for ingenious madmen! Consider how faithfully he serves the master of the house! For Copernicus, it was not enough merely to say that the earth moves, but he also protests and confirms it, writing to the Pope, and saying that the opinions of philosophers are very far from those...

<summary>Teofilo quotes and mocks the anonymous preface to Copernicus's 'De revolutionibus' (written by Osiander), which claimed heliocentrism was just a mathematical fiction rather than physical truth. Bruno argues that this "gatekeeper" betrays Copernicus, who truly believed in the physical reality of the Earth's motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Third Dialogue of 'The Ash Wednesday Supper.' Teofilo is mid-argument, transitioning from a defense of Copernicus's physical reality to a deeper discussion on the physics of light and how our senses perceive distant celestial bodies.</meta>

...so let us set this conclusion: from the appearance of the quantity of a luminous body, we cannot infer the truth of its size, nor of its distance; because, just as there is not the same rule for an opaque body and a luminous body, so there is not the same rule for a less luminous body, another more luminous, and another most luminous, by which we might judge their size or distance. The mass of a man's head at two miles cannot be seen; while the much smaller mass of a lamp, or another similar thing of flame, will be seen without much difference—or at least with little difference—at a distance of sixty miles; just as from Otranto in Apulia <note>Otranto is a coastal town in the "heel" of Italy.</note> one often sees the candles of Vlorë <note>original: "Avellona," a port city in modern-day Albania.</note>, between which countries lies a great stretch of the Ionian Sea. Everyone who possesses sense and reason knows that if those lamps were of a light twice as bright, they would be seen at a distance of one hundred and forty miles without changing their size, just as they are now seen at a distance of seventy miles; at three times the brightness, they would be seen at two hundred and ten; at four times, two hundred and eighty; likewise always judging by the other additions of proportions and degrees. This is because the rule of the diameter and mass of a body is usually maintained more by the quality and intense power of the light than by the quantity of the burning body. Do you then wish, O wise opticians <term>ottici</term> and clever perspective-artists <term>perspettivi</term> <note>In the 16th century, these terms referred to those who studied the science of vision and light.</note>, that if I see a light one hundred stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note> away having a diameter of four fingers, the rule should be that at a distance of fifty stadia it must have eight; at a distance of twenty-five, sixteen; at twelve and a half, thirty-two; and so on, until it becomes as large as you think when it is very close?

**Smi.** So much so that, according to what you say, although it may be false, the opinion of **Heraclitus of Ephesus** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his theory of constant change; he famously claimed the sun was about the width of a human foot.</note>—who said the sun was of the size that it offers to the eyes—cannot be proven wrong by geometric reasons. **Epicurus** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and founder of Epicureanism.</note> subscribed to this, as it appears in his letter to **Sophocles**; and in the eleventh book *On Nature* <note>original: "De natura"</note>, as **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> reports, he says that, as far as he can judge, the size of the sun, the moon, and the other stars is as great as it appears to our senses. For, he says, if they lost their size because of distance, they would even more likely lose their color; and certainly, he says, we ought not to judge those lights otherwise than those which are near us.

**Pru.** To this also the Epicurean **Lucretius** testifies in the fifth book *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "Illud quoque Epicureus Lucretius testatur quinto de Natura libro"</note>:

> The sun’s wheel cannot be much larger, nor its heat less,
> Than it appears to our senses to be.
> For from whatever distance fires can cast their light
> And breathe warm heat upon our limbs...
<note>original: "Nec nimio solis major rota, nec minor ardor / Esse potest, nostris quam sensibus esse videtur. / Nam quibus e spatiis cumque ignes lumina possunt / Adicere, et calidum membris adflare vaporem." This Latin verse is from Lucretius's 'De Rerum Natura,' arguing that the sun must be roughly the size it appears because its light and heat reach us with such intensity.</note>

extending the line **B 1**. If it is placed at the second, greater distance, it will come to illuminate according to the ratio of the larger arc **E F**, extending the line **B 2**. If it is at the third and even greater distance, it will terminate according to the ratio of the largest arc **G H**, bounded by the line **B 3**. From this, it is concluded that it can happen that the <term>luminous body</term> <note>A source of light, like the Sun.</note> **B**, maintaining the strength of such brightness that it can penetrate as much space as is required for such an effect, will be able, by moving very far away, to eventually encompass an arc larger than a semicircle. And the cause of this is that the obstruction arising from the diameter always decreases along with that diameter, the more the <term>angle</term> <note>The angle formed at the light source B by the lines of light touching the sphere.</note> **B** becomes more acute. And it is necessary in the end that the angle be made so acute—for in the physical division of a finite body, anyone who believes progress can be made to infinity (whether they mean it in act or in potential) is a fool—that it is no longer an angle, but a line. Along this line, two visible opposite bodies can be in sight of each other without the object in the middle being able to obstruct them at any point; this is because the intervening body has lost all proportionality and diametrical difference, while that difference persists in luminous bodies. 

Therefore, it is required that the intervening opaque body be at such a distance from both that it has lost the said proportion and difference of its diameter. This is seen and observed with the Earth, whose diameter does not prevent two diametrically opposite stars from seeing each other, just as the eye, without any difference, can see both from the <term>hemispheric center</term> <note>The observer's point of view on the surface of the Earth, looking out at the dome of the sky.</note> **N** and from the points of the circumference **A N O**. <meta>This page continues the geometric demonstration regarding optics and visibility. where, for that reason—since the line **A N** is the <term>diameter</term> <note>The straight line passing through the center of a circle.</note>—it forms a **right angle** at the <term>circumference</term> <note>The outer boundary or edge of the circle.</note>. At the second position, it forms an **acute angle**; at the third, one even more acute. It must eventually reach the point of being most acute, and finally reach that limit where it no longer appears as an angle at all, but as a line. Consequently, the relationship and difference of the <term>semidiameter</term> <note>The radius, or half the diameter.</note> is destroyed, and for the same reason, the difference of the entire diameter **A O** will be destroyed. 

From this, it is ultimately necessary that two very bright bodies—which do not lose their apparent diameter so quickly—will not be prevented from seeing each other reciprocally. This is because their diameter has not vanished, unlike that of a non-luminous or less bright body placed between them. 

It is concluded, therefore, that a larger body, which is more prone to losing its apparent diameter, even if it stands in a perfectly straight line in the middle, will not block the <term>perspective</term> <note>The line of sight or visual path.</note> of two other bodies, no matter how much smaller they are, provided they retain the diameter of their visibility, which in the larger body is lost.

<meta>This page continues the optical demonstration from the previous page, transitioning from the geometry of angles to a physical analogy of visibility involving a stick and a candle. It then moves into a cosmological discussion about the Earth appearing as a star from a distance and cites the views of Nicholas of Cusa regarding the composition of the Sun.</meta>

[placed] close to the eye, its view will be completely hindered from seeing the light of a candle placed at a certain distance. As the stick is moved closer to that light—and thus further from the eye—it will hinder the view less and less, until it is so close that it reaches the light itself. At that point, just as it was once close to the eye, it will perhaps not block any more than the actual width of the stick. Now, consider this: if the stick remains there and the light is moved even further away, the stick will come to hinder the view much less. Thus, by increasing the <term>equidistance</term> <note>The equal distance of two points from a central object.</note> of the eye and the light from the stick more and more, you will eventually see only the light, without any <term>sensibility</term> <note>The ability to be perceived by the senses; here, the stick becomes "invisible" to the eye.</note> of the stick at all. Having considered this, even a <note>original: "grosso intelletto"</note> simple mind, however much it desires, can be led to understand what was said shortly before.

**Smitho.** It seems to me that, regarding this point, I should be quite satisfied; but a certain confusion remains in my mind concerning what you said earlier: how we, by rising from the earth and losing sight of the <term>horizon</term> <note>The boundary where the sky and earth appear to meet.</note>—the <term>diameter</term> of which becomes increasingly thin—will see this body [the Earth] as a star. I would like you to add something to what you have said regarding this; since you estimate that there are many earths similar to this one, indeed innumerable ones. I also remember seeing <note>referring to reading the works of</note> <term>Nicholas of Cusa</term> <note>Original: "il Cusano." A 15th-century German philosopher and theologian who suggested the Earth was in motion and that stars were other worlds.</note>, whose judgment I know you do not reject; he maintains that even the sun has dissimilar parts, like the moon and the earth. For this reason, he says that if we fix our eyes attentively on its body, we will see a most notable <term>opacity</term> <note>The quality of being non-transparent or dark; not reflecting or emitting light.</note> in the midst of that brightness, which is more concentrated toward the outer edge.

**Teofilo.** It was divinely said and understood by him, and most laudably applied by you! If I remember correctly, I also said a short while ago that while an opaque body easily loses its visible diameter, a luminous one does not easily do so. Through distance, the appearance of the dark part is annulled and vanishes, while that of the illuminated <term>diaphanous</term> <note>Transparent or translucent; allowing light to pass through.</note> part—or light of another kind—tends to unite. From those dispersed luminous parts, a visible, continuous light is formed. Therefore, if the moon were further away, it would not <term>eclipse</term> <note>To obscure the light from one celestial body by passing in front of it.</note> the sun; and any man who is knowledgeable can easily consider in these matters that, being further away, it would even appear more luminous. If we were upon it, it would not be more luminous to our eyes: just as, being on this earth, we do not see that light of hers which she offers to those who are on the moon—a light which is perhaps greater than that which she reflects back to us by the sun's rays diffused in her <term>liquid crystal</term> <note>The fluid ether or atmosphere surrounding the planet, thought to be reflective like a crystal.</note>. Regarding the particular light of the sun, I do not know at present whether we should judge it according to this same manner or another. Now see how far we have strayed from that occasion; it seems to me time to return to the other parts of our proposition.

**Smitho.** It will be well to hear the other claims which he [the opponent] may have brought forward.

## Dr. Nundinio’s third proposal.

**Teo.** Next, Nundinio said that it cannot be likely that the earth moves, since it is the middle and center of the universe, which must be the fixed and constant foundation of all motion. The <term>Nolano</term> <note>Giordano Bruno himself, named after his birthplace, Nola.</note> replied: that this very same thing could be said by one who holds the sun to be in the middle of the universe, and therefore immobile and fixed, as understood by <term>Copernicus</term> <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), the astronomer who proposed the heliocentric model where the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note> and many others who have given a circumferential limit to the universe. Thus, his reasoning—if it is even reasoning—is useless against them, as it simply assumes its own premises. It is also useless against the Nolano, who claims that the world is infinite, and therefore there is no body within it to which it simply belongs to be in the middle, or at the edge, or between those two boundaries; rather, these positions exist only through certain relationships to other bodies and through <note>original: "termini intenzionalmente appresi"</note> boundaries conceived in the mind.

**Smi.** What do you think of this?

**Teo.** Loftily said! For just as no natural body has ever been proven to be perfectly round, and consequently to have a perfect center, so too among the motions we see sensibly and physically in natural bodies, there is not one that does not differ greatly from a perfectly circular and regular motion around some center. Let those who invent these <note>original: "borre et empiture"</note> paddings and fillings of unequal spheres, differing diameters, and other <term>plasters and prescriptions</term> <note>Bruno uses medical metaphors to describe how astronomers "patch up" their flawed theories to make nature fit their models.</note> to "heal" nature, exert themselves as much as they like until they force nature to serve Master <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose geocentric, finite model of the universe was the standard academic authority in the 16th century.</note> or someone else, concluding that every motion is continuous and regular around the center. 

But we, who look not at fantastic shadows but at the things themselves—we, who see an aerial, ethereal, spiritual, liquid space, a place capable of motion and rest, even one that is immense and infinite (which we must affirm, at least because we see no limit either through our senses or through reason)—we know for certain that, being the effect of an infinite cause and an infinite principle, the universe must be infinitely infinite according to its bodily capacity and its nature. And I am certain that not only for Nundinio, but for all who are professors of understanding, it is never possible to find even a semi-probable reason why there should be a margin to this bodily universe, and consequently why the stars contained within its space should be finite in number; or, furthermore, why there should be a naturally determined center and middle within it.

**Smi.** Now, did Nundinio add anything to this? Did he bring any argument or probability to imply, first, that the universe is finite; second, that it has the earth as its middle; and third, that this middle is entirely and in every way immobile in terms of local motion?

**Teo.** Nundinio, like one who says what he says...

<summary>Teo recounts the Nolano's argument that in an infinite universe, there is no absolute center or edge, debunking Nundinio's Aristotelian claim that the Earth must be the fixed center of the cosmos.</summary>

### *Nundinio’s fourth proposal.*

Because the <term>Nolano</term> <note>Giordano Bruno's self-reference, meaning "The man from Nola."</note> mentioned in passing that there are innumerable earths similar to this one, Doctor Nundinio—acting like a clever debater who, having nothing to add to the current topic, begins to ask questions out of turn—shifted from what we were saying about the mobility or immobility of this globe to ask about the quality of other globes. He wanted to know what material those bodies were made of, which are commonly thought to be composed of <term>quintessence</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, the "fifth essence" (aether), a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements, believed to be unchanging and eternal.</note>—an unalterable and incorruptible matter of which the stars are supposedly the densest parts.

**Fru.** This question seems out of place to me, though I understand nothing of logic.

**Teo.** Out of courtesy, the Nolano did not wish to reproach him for this. But after telling him that he would have preferred if Nundinio had followed the main subject or asked questions regarding it, he replied: that the other globes, which are "earths," are not in any way different in kind from this one; they differ only in being larger or smaller, just as inequality occurs among individuals of other animal species. However, those spheres that are made of fire, such as the sun, he believes *for the time being* differ in kind—just as hot differs from cold, or a body that is luminous in itself differs from one that is illuminated by another.

**Smi.** Why did he say he believed this *for the time being*, rather than asserting it absolutely?

**Teo.** Because he feared that Nundinio would again abandon the question he had just raised and would seize and cling to...

this one, he dropped the point that—since the earth is a living being <note>original: "animale." In Bruno's philosophy, the Earth and other celestial bodies are considered "animals" because they possess a vital principle or soul that governs their movement.</note> and consequently a <term>dissimilar body</term> <note>A heterogeneous body composed of different organs or parts, rather than a single uniform substance.</note>—it should not be considered a cold body in all its parts, especially those on the exterior aired out by the atmosphere; but in its other members, which are greater in number and size, it must be believed to be both hot and very hot. He further dropped the point that, by arguing partly using the principles of the opponent—who wishes to be esteemed and makes a profession of being a <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of Aristotle, whose students traditionally walked about the Lyceum in Athens while debating.</note>—and partly using his own principles (which are not merely granted, but proven), the earth would turn out to be as hot as the sun by some comparison.

**Smi.** How is that?

**Teo.** Because, based on what we have said, through the fading of the dark and opaque parts of the globe and the union of the crystalline and shiny parts, light comes to spread further and further into more distant regions. Now, if light is the cause of heat (as Aristotle and many others affirm, who believe that even the moon and other stars are more or less hot based on their greater or lesser share of light, so that when some planets are called "cold," they mean it only in a certain relative comparison), it follows that the earth, with the rays it sends to the distant parts of the <term>ethereal region</term> <note>The celestial space beyond the Earth's atmosphere.</note>, would communicate an equal power of heat according to the power of its light. But it is not clear to us that a thing is hot simply because it is shiny; for we see many shiny things near us that are not hot.

Now, to return to Nundinio: look at how he begins to show his teeth, widen his jaws, squint his eyes, wrinkle his brow, flare his nostrils, and send a croak like a capon through the passage of his lungs. He did this so that by this laughter those standing around would think that he understood well, that he was right, and that the other man was saying ridiculous things.

**Fru.** And is it truly to be seen how he laughed at him?

**Teo.** This is what happens to one who gives sweets to pigs. When asked why he laughed, he replied that this talk and imagining that there are other earths which have the same properties and accidents was taken from the "true stories" of Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist. His "A True Story" is a parody of travel tales that includes a voyage to the Moon; Nundinio is mocking Bruno by comparing his science to ancient satire.</note>. The Nolano replied that if Lucian, when he said the moon was another earth inhabited and cultivated like this one, said it to mock those philosophers who affirmed there were many earths (and particularly the moon, whose similarity to our own globe is so much more noticeable because it is closer to us), he was not right, but showed himself to be in the common state of ignorance and blindness. For if we consider carefully, we will find that the earth and so many other bodies called <term>stars</term> <note>original: "astri." In this context, it refers to any celestial body including planets.</note> are principal members of the universe; just as they give life and nourishment to the things that take matter from them and return it to them, so they—and much more so—have life within themselves, through which, with an orderly...

born of natural will from an internal principle, they move toward things and through the spaces appropriate to them. And there are no other external movers which, by moving imaginary spheres, come to transport these bodies as if they were nailed into them; if that were true, the motion would be violent and outside the nature of the moving body, the mover would be more imperfect, and both the motion and the mover would be anxious and laborious, and many other inconveniences would follow. Consider then, that just as the male moves toward the female and the female toward the male—every herb and animal, some more and some less explicitly—moves toward its vital principle, such as the sun and other stars; the magnet moves to the iron, the straw to the amber, and finally every thing goes to find its like and flees its contrary. 

Everything happens from a sufficient interior principle, by which it naturally comes to be stirred, and not from an exterior principle, as we see always happen to those things that are moved either against or outside their own nature. Therefore, the earth and the other stars move according to their own local differences from an internal principle, which is their own soul.

## *Nundinio's Fifth Proposal.*

Nundinio, being pressured by both the Nolano and the others to leave aside questions of "why," "how," and "what," and to finally make some actual argument—

**Pru.** *Through "how" and "why," any ass knows how to argue.* <note>original Latin: "Per quomodo et quare quilibet asinus novit disputare." Prudenzio is the pedantic character who often speaks in Latin tags.</note>

**Teo.** At last he did this, using an argument of which all the common textbooks are full: that if it were true that the earth moves toward the side we call the East, it would be necessary for the clouds in the air to always appear to run toward the West, by reason of the extremely fast and rapid motion of this globe, which in the space of twenty-four hours must have completed such a great circuit. 

To this, the Nolano replied that this air, through which the clouds and winds run, is part of the earth. Because under the name of "earth," he intends—and it must be so for this purpose—the whole machine and the entire living being, which consists of its diverse parts. Thus the rivers, the rocks, the seas, and all the vaporous and turbulent air which is enclosed within the highest mountains, belongs to the earth as a member of it, or even like the air that is in the lungs and other cavities of animals, through which they breathe, their arteries dilate, and other effects necessary for life are fulfilled. The clouds, therefore, are moved by the circumstances within the body of the earth and are as if in its entrails, just as the waters are. This was understood by Aristotle in the first book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteora." Bruno is citing Aristotle's work on natural phenomena to support his own atmospheric theory.</note>, where he says that...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from "The Ash Wednesday Supper," specifically addressing the physics of the atmosphere and how it relates to the Earth as a living entity. Teofilo is explaining that what we perceive as the "sky" is actually a dense layer of vaporous air, and our true position is within the Earth's "body" rather than on its outermost boundary.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>

This air, which is near the earth, humid and warm due to the earth's exhalations, has above it another air, which is warm and dry, and there no clouds are found. This air exists outside the circumference of the earth and the surface that defines it—allowing the earth to be perfectly round—and the generation of winds occurs only within the bowels <note>An archaic way of describing the internal parts or depths of a body.</note> and cavities of the earth. Therefore, above high mountains, neither clouds nor winds appear; there, the air moves regularly in a circle, like the universal body. This is perhaps what Plato <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedo*, where he suggests humans live in the "hollows" of the Earth, much like frogs or ants around a pond, unaware of the "true" surface above.</note> meant when he said that we inhabit the hollows and dark parts of the earth, and that we have the same relationship to the animals living above the earth as fish have to us, who live in a thicker moisture. 

He means that, in a certain sense, this vaporous air is water, and the pure air, which contains more blessed animals, is above the earth; just as this Amphitrite <note>Amphitrite was a Greek sea goddess and wife of Poseidon; here, the name is used poetically to represent the ocean.</note> is water to us, so our air is water to them. Here, then, is how one can respond to the argument mentioned by Nundinio: for just as the sea is not on the surface, but in the bowels of the earth—like the liver <term>epate: the liver, which in the medical tradition of the time was considered the source of the body's humors and blood</term> is the source of humors within us—this turbulent air is not outside, but is like being within the lungs of animals.

*Smitho.* Now, how does it happen that we see the entire hemisphere, given that we live in the bowels of the earth?

*Teofilo.* From the mass of the globose earth—not only on the outermost surface but also on those interior ones—it happens that at the sight of the horizon, one convexity gives way to another. Thus, that obstruction cannot occur which we see when a mountain is interposed between our eyes and a part of the sky; for a mountain, being close, can take away the perfect view of the circle of the horizon. The distance, then, of such mountains—which follow the convexity of the earth, which is not flat but orbicular <note>Spherical or circular.</note>—ensures that our being within the bowels of the earth is not sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible" or "noticeable" to our senses.</note> to us; as can be somewhat considered in the present figure,
