<meta>This page continues the dialogue from "The Ash Wednesday Supper," where Teofilo explains the physical structure of the Earth. He argues that the Earth's "true" surface includes the atmosphere we breathe, and that what we call mountains are often just small ridges within much larger geological features.</meta>

<page-num>169</page-num>

On the surface there are many details of the sea and other continents, such as point **M**, from which we see the entire hemisphere no less than from point **A** and other points on the outermost surface. There are two reasons for this: the immense size of the earth and its circumferential convexity <term>convessitudine: the outward curve of a sphere.</term>. Because of this, point **M** is not so obstructed that it cannot see the hemisphere. The highest mountains do not interpose themselves at point **M**, as the line **M B** would—which I believe would happen if the earth’s surface were flat—but rather like the line **M C** — **M D**. This does not cause such an obstruction, as can be seen by virtue of the circumferential arc. Furthermore, note that just as **M** relates to **C** and **M** to **D**, so also **K** relates to **M**; therefore, what Plato <note>A reference to the *Phaedo*, where Plato suggests humans live in the "hollows" of the Earth, unaware of the true, pure world on the surface above.</note> said about the great concavities and basins of the earth should not be considered a fable.

**Smi.** I would like to know if those who live near the highest mountains suffer from this obstruction of the view?

**Teo.** No, but those who are near smaller mountains do; for mountains are not truly "highest" unless they are likewise so vast that their greatness is imperceptible to our sight. In this way, they encompass many different local horizons, where the conditions of one do not affect the others. However, by "highest," we do not mean ranges like the Alps and the Pyrenees and such, but rather regions like the whole of France, which lies between two seas: the Northern Ocean and the Southern Mediterranean. From these seas toward Auvergne <note>A high volcanic plateau in central France.</note>, one is always ascending, as one also does from the Alps and Pyrenees. These ranges were once the peak of a single, exceedingly high mountain, which has been broken down over time. Time produces new mountains elsewhere through the cycle of renewal <term>vicissitudine de la rinovazione: the philosophical and geological idea that the Earth is a living body that constantly recycles its parts.</term> of the earth's parts, forming the many specific peaks we call mountains. 

Therefore, regarding a certain objection that Nundinio <note>One of the scholars challenging Bruno’s theories in the dialogue.</note> raised about the mountains of Scotland (where perhaps he has been), it shows that he cannot grasp what is meant by the "highest mountains." In truth, this entire island of Britain is a mountain that raises its head above the waves of the Ocean; the summit of this mountain is the most elevated place on the island. If this summit reaches the tranquil part of the air, it proves that this is one of those "highest mountains" where perhaps "happier animals" <note>Bruno suggests that the upper atmosphere might be home to more refined, spiritual beings or "daemons."</note> dwell. Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>An influential ancient Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> discusses Mount Olympus, where, through the evidence of sacrificial ashes <note>An ancient legend claimed that ashes left on the altar of Mt. Olympus remained undisturbed for years because the mountain reached above the wind-blown atmosphere into the still, "pure" air.</note>, he demonstrates the nature of a highest mountain and of the air above the borders and members of the earth.

**Smi.** You have satisfied me most sufficiently and have revealed many secrets of nature that were hidden under this key. Regarding what you reply to the argument concerning the winds...

<meta>This page continues the physical and cosmological arguments of Teofilo. In the previous page, they discussed the "highest" parts of the Earth and the atmosphere. Here, the dialogue moves to the "Ship Experiment," a famous argument used to explain why we do not feel the Earth's rotation.</meta>

->170<-

...and clouds, we also take the answer of that other thinker, which Aristotle brought forth in the second book of *On the Heavens* <note>original: "cielo e mondo", referring to Aristotle's *De Caelo*</note>, where he says it would be impossible for a stone thrown upward to return down in the same perpendicular line; rather, it would be necessary <note>Original text has three 'b's in "sarebbbe".</note> for the earth’s extremely fast motion to leave it far behind toward the West. For since this projection happens within the earth, it is necessary that with the earth’s motion, every relationship of straightness and obliquity changes. This is because there is a difference between the motion of the ship and the motion of those things that are *in* the ship. If this were not true, it would follow that when a ship races through the sea, no one could ever throw something in a straight line from one side to the other, nor would it be possible to jump and return with one's feet to the spot from which they were lifted. Therefore, all things that are on the earth move with the earth. If, however, something were thrown toward the earth from a place *outside* of it, it would lose its straightness because of the earth's motion. As is seen with the ship, *) which, passing along the river, if someone on the bank tries to throw a stone straight, their aim will fail by as much as the speed of the current carries the ship. But if someone is placed atop the <term>mast</term> <note>original: "arbore", literally tree, but used here for the mast of a ship</note> of said ship, no matter how fast it runs, they will not miss their mark at all; so that the stone or other heavy object thrown will fall in a straight line from the point at the top of the mast or the crow's nest to the point at the base of the mast, or any other part of the belly and body of said ship. Likewise, if someone inside the ship throws a stone straight from the base to the top of the mast or the crow's nest, it will return down along the same line, no matter how much the ship moves, provided it does not tilt.

**S m i.** <note>Smitho, one of the participants in the dialogue.</note> <note>The abbreviation "Smi." is also noted as potentially meaning "Similitudine" (Similitude or Analogy) in the margin of some editions.</note> From the consideration of this difference, the door opens to many and very important secrets of nature and profound philosophy, seeing as it is a very frequent and little-considered thing: how great the difference is between one who heals themselves and one who is healed by another. It is quite manifest that we take greater pleasure and satisfaction if we feed ourselves with our own hand than by the arms of another. Children, as soon as they can use their own instruments to take food, do not willingly use those of others; as if nature in a certain way makes them learn that, just as there is not so much plea—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of relative motion and the "Ship Experiment" started on page 170. Teofilo concludes the argument that an object shares the motion of the system it is part of (like the Earth or a ship), explaining why we do not notice the Earth's rotation in our daily lives.</meta>

...to fall, there is still not much profit. Little children who nurse, you see, how they cling with their hand to the breast? And I have never been so terrified by a robbery as by one committed by a domestic servant: for I do not know what shadow or portent a household member brings with them more than a stranger, for it reflects a kind of evil genius and a formidable omen.

**Teofilo.** Now, to return to the point: if there are two people, one of whom is inside a ship that is racing along, and the other is outside of it, and both the one and the other have their hand at nearly the same point in the air, and from that same place at the same time each lets a stone drop without giving them any push, the stone of the first man—without losing any time or deviating from its line—will reach the designated spot <note>Meaning it will fall straight down relative to the ship's mast</note>; and the stone of the second man will find itself left behind. This proceeds from nothing else except that the stone which leaves the hand of the man supported by the ship (and consequently moves according to the ship's motion) has such <term>impressed virtue</term> <note>original: "virtù impressa", a Renaissance physical concept similar to momentum or inertia, where a mover imparts a "power" of motion to an object</note> which the other stone does not have, as it comes from the hand of the man who is outside—even though the stones have the same weight, the same air between them, and depart (if possible) from the same point and endure the same push. Of this diversity, we can bring no other reason except that things that are fixed to or similar belongings of the ship move with it; and one stone carries with it the "virtue" of the mover which moves with the ship, while the other lacks that participation. From this, it is clearly seen that a thing does not take its power to travel straight from the starting point of the motion, nor from the end point where it goes, nor from the medium through which it moves, but from the efficacy of the "virtue" primarily impressed upon it, upon which the whole difference depends. And this seems to me sufficient to have considered regarding the proposals of Nundinio <note>Nundinio is one of the Aristotelian doctors Bruno is debating in the dialogue</note>.

**Smitho.** Now tomorrow we shall meet again to hear the points that Torquato added.

**Prudenzio.** Let it be so! <note>original: "Fiat!", Latin for "so be it" or "let it be done."</note>

# FOURTH DIALOGUE

->Smitho<-

**Smith.** Do you want me to tell you the reason why?
**Teofilo.** Go ahead and say it!
**Smith.** Because Divine Scripture—the meaning of which should be highly commended to us as something proceeding from higher intelligences that do not err—suggests and supposes the opposite in many places.
**Teofilo.** Now as for this, believe me: if the gods had deigned to teach us the theory of natural things, just as they have done us the favor of proposing the practice of moral things, I would sooner draw near to the faith of their revelations than move a single point from the certainty of my reasons and my own senses. But as everyone can see very clearly, in the divine books, for the service of our intellect, demonstrations and speculations concerning natural things are not treated as if it were philosophy; rather, for the sake of our mind and affection, the practice of moral actions is ordered through the laws. Therefore, the <term>divine legislator</term> <note>A reference to God or the inspired authors of the Bible</note> having this goal before his eyes, he does not care in other matters to speak according to that truth which would not profit the common people in withdrawing themselves from evil and clinging to good. Instead, he leaves the thinking on such matters to <term>contemplative men</term> <note>Philosophers and scientists</note>, and speaks to the common folk in such a manner that, according to their way of understanding and speaking, they come to understand that which is most important.
**Smith.** It is certainly a fitting thing, when one seeks to record history or give laws, to speak according to common understanding, and not to be anxious about indifferent things. A historian would be a fool if, while treating his subject, he wanted to ordain words considered new, or reform old ones, acting in such a way that the reader would be more delayed in observing and interpreting him as a grammarian than in understanding him as a historian. Even more so for one who wants to give the law and a way of living to the common world: if he used terms that only he and very few others understood, and made a point of considering matters indifferent to the purpose for which the laws are ordained, it would certainly seem that he is not directing his doctrine to the general public and the multitude—for whom those laws are ordained—but to the wise and noble spirits, and those who are truly men, who do what is right without the law. For this reason, <term>Al-Ghazali</term> <note>original: "Alcazele"; Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111) was a major Persian theologian and philosopher</note>, a philosopher, high priest, and <term>Muslim</term> <note>original: "macumetano"</note> theologian, said that the purpose of laws is not so much to seek the truth of things and speculations, as it is the goodness of customs...

...the benefit of civilization, the gathering of peoples, and practice for the convenience of human social interaction, the maintenance of peace, and the growth of <term>republics</term> <note>In this context, "republics" refers generally to organized states or commonwealths</note>. For instance, when the <term>wise man</term> <note>A reference to Solomon, specifically Ecclesiastes 1:5: "The sun rises and the sun sets..."</note> said, "the sun rises and sets, turns toward the south, and bends toward the north," had he instead said: "the earth rotates toward the east, leaving behind the sun which sets, and bends toward the two tropics—Cancer toward the <term>south</term> <note>original: "austro"</note>, and Capricorn toward the <term>north</term> <note>original: "aquilone"</note>," his listeners would have stopped to wonder: "How can this man say the earth moves? **Teofilo.** Do these reverend men perhaps want it to be understood that when Moses said God made two great lights among the other luminaries—the sun and the moon—this must be taken in an absolute sense, such that all other stars are smaller than the moon? Or rather according to the common sense and ordinary way of understanding and speaking? Are there not many stars larger than the moon? Might they not even be larger than the sun? What is the Earth lacking that it should not be a luminary more beautiful and larger than the moon? For the Earth, by receiving the great splendor of the sun upon the body of the Ocean and other Mediterranean seas, can appear as a most brilliant body to those other worlds called stars, just as they appear to us as so many flashing torches.

Certainly, the fact that he does not call the Earth a luminary, great or small, but says the sun and moon are such, was well and truly said for his purposes. This is because he had to make himself understood according to common words and sentiments, and not act like one who, like a fool and a simpleton, uses knowledge and wisdom inappropriately. To speak in terms of technical truth where it is not necessary is to wish that the common folk and the foolish multitude—from whom only practical action is required—should have specialized understanding. It would be like wanting the hand to have an eye; yet the hand was not made by nature for seeing, but for working and acting in agreement with sight.

Thus, even if he understood the nature of spiritual substances, to what end should he have discussed them, except insofar as some of them have dealings and ministry with men when they act as <term>messengers</term> <note>The word for "messengers" (ambasciatrici) refers to the Greek meaning of 'angelos' or angels</note>? Even if he had known that everything that pertains to our world—or at least something similar—also pertains to the moon and other worldly bodies (both those seen and those invisible to us), do you think it would have been the duty of a legislator to take up and give these burdens to the people? <meta>This page continues Teofilo’s explanation of how the Holy Scriptures should be interpreted. He is finishing a thought from the previous page regarding the social and moral purpose of the law, suggesting that the primary goal of divine writing is the regulation of human conduct and the "laws and exercise of our virtues" rather than the teaching of technical physics.</meta>

...laws and the exercise of our virtues with those others? Therefore, where divine men speak, presupposing the commonly received understanding of natural things, they should not be used as an authority; rather, [they should be consulted] where they speak indifferently, and where the common people have no established resolution. In such matters, I want regard to be given to the words of divine men, and even to the **enthusiasms** <note>original: "entusiasmi"; referring here to the divine inspiration or "poetic madness" believed to grant higher insights</note> of the poets who have spoken with a superior light. We must not take as a metaphor that which was not said as a metaphor, nor, on the contrary, take as the literal truth that which was said as a <term>similitude</term> <note>A comparison or symbolic likeness used to explain a difficult concept</note>. But it does not belong to everyone to wish to understand this distinction between the metaphorical and the true, just as it is not given to everyone to be able to grasp it.

Now, if we wish to turn our eye of consideration to a book that is contemplative, natural, moral, and divine, we will find this philosophy very much supported and favorable. I speak of the **Book of Job**, which is one of the most singular books that can be read, full of all good theology, natural science, and morality, and filled with the wisest discourses, which Moses, like a <term>sacrament</term> <note>Used here to mean a sacred mystery or a vehicle for hidden truth</note>, joined to the books of his Law. In that book, one of the characters, wishing to describe the provident power of God, said that He "makes peace in his heights" <note>A reference to Job 25:2: "He maketh peace in his high places"</note>—that is, among his sublime sons, which are the stars, the gods. Some of these are fires, others are waters, just as we say some are suns and others are earths; and these exist in concord because, although they are opposites, nevertheless one lives, is nourished, and grows by the other, while they do not merge together; instead, they move around one another at certain distances.

Thus, the universe is divided into **fire** and **water**, which are the subjects of the two primary formal and active principles: **cold** and **heat**. Those bodies that breathe out heat are the suns, which are bright and hot in themselves; those bodies that breathe out cold are the earths. These, being likewise heterogeneous bodies, are called "waters" instead, because it is through the water [on them] that such bodies become visible; hence we rightly name them for that reason by which they are sensible to us—sensible, I say, not by themselves, but by the light of the suns scattered across their faces. 

Moses conforms to this doctrine when he calls the air the **firmament**, in which all these bodies have their persistence and location, and through the spaces of which the "lower waters" (which are those on our globe) are distinguished and divided from the "upper waters" (which are those of the other globes), where it is also said that "water was divided from water" <note>A reference to the creation story in Genesis 1:6–7</note>. And if you consider well many passages of the divine Scripture, the gods and ministers of the Most High are called waters, abysses, earths, and burning flames. What was stopping him from calling them neutral, inalterable, and immutable bodies, <term>quintessences</term> <note>The "fifth element" of Aristotelian physics, which Bruno rejected in favor of a universe made of the same elements as Earth</note>, denser parts of the spheres, beryls, carbuncles, and other fantasies, with which—being equally indifferent—the common people could just as easily have been fed?

<summary>Teofilo argues that the Bible uses metaphorical language for the masses but reveals a "true" cosmology in books like Job, where stars are described as suns (fire) and earths (water) moving through the air.</summary>

**Smith.** I am certainly moved a great deal by the authority of the Book of **Job** and of **Moses**, and I can easily rest in these literal meanings rather than in metaphorical and abstract ones—were it not for certain "parrots" of **Aristotle**, **Plato**, and **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle were central to university life but often conflicted with literal scripture</note>. These men, having been promoted to theologians from that very philosophy, claim that these meanings are metaphorical; and so, by virtue of their metaphors, they make the texts signify whatever they please, out of jealousy for the philosophy in which they were raised.

**Teofilo.** Now, you can judge how consistent these metaphors are by this: the same Scripture is in the hands of Jews, Christians, and Muslims—sects so different and contrary that they give birth to countless other opposing factions. All of them are able to find in the text whatever purpose pleases them and suits them best. They find not only different purposes, but the complete opposite, turning "yes" into "no" and "no" into "yes," as for example in certain passages where they claim that God speaks with <term>irony</term> <note>The rhetorical device of saying the opposite of what is meant; here used to explain away biblical passages that contradict a speaker's specific doctrine</note>.

**Smith.** Let us stop judging these people! I am certain it does not matter to them whether this is or is not a metaphor; therefore, they can easily let us rest in peace with our philosophy.

**Teofilo.** One should not fear the censure of honorable spirits, the truly religious, and also those who are naturally good men—friends of civilized conversation and sound doctrine. For when they have considered it well, they will find that this philosophy not only contains the truth but also favors religion more than any other kind of philosophy. Contrast this with those philosophies that posit that the world is finite; that the effect and efficacy of divine power are finite; that the **intelligences** <note>Spiritual or divine beings thought to be responsible for moving the celestial spheres</note> and intellectual natures are only eight or ten; that the substance of things is corruptible; and that the soul is mortal—as if it consisted of an accidental disposition, the effect of a physical composition, and a dissolvable temperament and harmony. Consequently, they make the execution of divine justice over human actions worth nothing, and they claim the knowledge of particular things is completely removed from the first and universal causes. There are many other such inconveniences which, being false, not only blind the light of the intellect, but also, being lazy and impious, extinguish the fervor of good affections.

**Smith.** I am very glad to have this information about the philosophy of **the Nolano** <note>A nickname for the author, Giordano Bruno, who was born in Nola, Italy</note>. **Frulla.** Ignorance and arrogance are two inseparable sisters in one body and one soul.

**Teofilo.** This man, with an emphatic look—just as the **Father of the gods** <note>original: "divúm pater"; a title for Jupiter</note> is described in the ***Metamorphoses*** <note>original: "metamorfosi"; the famous narrative poem by Ovid</note> as sitting in the middle of the assembly...

**Teo.** On the contrary, he <note>the Nolan</note> replied that he had not come there to read a lecture, nor to teach, but to respond; and that the symmetry, order, and measurement of celestial motions is presupposed to be exactly as it is, and as it has been known by both ancients and moderns. <meta>This page continues the debate between the Nolan (Giordano Bruno) and the pedantic Dr. Torquato. Having just explained that he agrees with the mathematical observations of the astronomers but disagrees on the physical nature of the universe, the Nolan begins to describe his vision of a living, moving Earth among other "worlds."</meta>

<page-num>178</page-num>

...to one another, and to share the vital principle with each other. At certain spaces and at certain distances, some complete their circuits around others, as is evident in these seven <note>The "seven" refers to the traditional celestial bodies of the solar system known at the time: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon—though here Bruno is specifically discussing those orbiting the sun, including Earth.</note> that revolve around the sun. The Earth is one of these, which, by moving for the space of 24 hours from the side called the West toward the East, causes the appearance of this motion of the universe around her, which is called the mundane and diurnal <note>daily</note> motion. This imagination is utterly false, contrary to nature, and impossible; for it is possible, convenient, true, and necessary that the Earth moves around its own center to participate in light and darkness, day and night, heat and cold; and around the sun for the participation in spring, summer, autumn, and winter; and toward the so-called poles and opposite hemispheric points for the renewal of the ages and the changing of its face, so that where there was sea, there shall be dry land; where it was scorching, it shall be cold; where the tropic was, the equinox shall be; and finally, that there be a vicissitude <note>a natural change or succession</note> of all things, in this star as in the others, which were not without reason called **worlds** by the true ancient philosophers. Now, while the Nolan was saying this, Doctor Torquato was shouting: *To the point, to the point, to the point!* <note>original Latin: "Ad rem, ad rem, ad rem!"</note> At last, the Nolan began to laugh and told him that he was not arguing against him, nor answering him, but was merely proposing his views; and therefore, *these are the points, the points, the points,* <note>original Latin: "ista sunt res, res, res"</note> and that it was now Torquato's turn to bring forward something *to the point*.

**Smi.** Because this ass thought he was among the clumsy and the dull-witted, he believed they would accept his "to the point" as an actual argument and a determination; he thought a simple shout and the sight of his golden chain would satisfy the crowd.

**Teo.** Listen to what happened next! While everyone was waiting for that long-desired argument, Doctor Torquato, turning to the fellow guests from the depths of his own self-sufficiency, unsheathed an Erasmian adage <note>A reference to the famous collection of proverbs and adages compiled by Desiderius Erasmus.</note> and slapped it right across the Nolan's face: *He is sailing to Anticyra.* <note>original Latin: "Anticyram navigat." This was a common classical proverb meaning someone is insane. Anticyra was a Greek city famous for producing hellebore, a plant used to treat madness.</note>

**Smi.** An ass could not have spoken better, and one should expect to hear no other voice when dealing with asses.

Therefore, I can only hate you for this reason as much as I hate myself, when I was younger, more boyish, less wise, and less discerning."

<page-num>184</page-num>

# FIFTH DIALOGUE

->Teofilo<-

**Because** the other stars are no more fixed to the sky, nor fixed in any different way, than this star—which is the Earth—is fixed in the same <term>firmament</term> <note>While traditional astronomy saw the "firmament" as a solid dome, Bruno here redefines it as the "air" or the vast, fluid space in which all celestial bodies move.</note>, which is the air; and the place where the tail of the <note>original: "l'orsa"</note> Great Bear is located is no more worthy of being called the **eighth sphere** <note>In the older Ptolemaic system, the eighth sphere was the outermost shell of the universe containing all the "fixed" stars.</note> than the place where the Earth is, upon which we reside; for in one and the same ethereal region, as if in the same great space and field, these bodies are distinct and separated from one another by certain appropriate intervals. Consider the reason why there were judged to be seven heavens for the **wanderers** <note>The "erranti" or "planets," from the Greek *planētēs* meaning "wanderer." These included the Sun, Moon, and the five known planets.</note>, and only one for all the others. The varied motion observed in the seven, and the single uniform motion in all the other stars—which perpetually maintain the same distance from each other and the same order—makes it seem as though they all share one motion, one fixation, and one orbit, and that there are no more than eight sensible spheres for the heavenly bodies, which are as if nailed into them. 

Now, if we come to such light and such a disciplined sense that we recognize this appearance of cosmic motion proceeds from the rotation of the Earth; if, from the similarity of the consistency of this body in the midst of the air, we judge the consistency of all the other bodies, we can first believe, and then demonstratively conclude, the opposite of that dream and that fantasy—which was that first error which generated, and is bound to generate, so many other countless ones. From this arises the error, just as it happens to us when, from the center of the horizon, turning our eyes in every direction, we can judge the greater or lesser distance from, between, and within those things that are closer; but beyond a certain limit, they all appear equally distant. 

Thus, looking at the stars of the firmament, we perceive the difference in the motions and distances of some closer stars, but the more distant and furthest ones appear to us as immobile, and equally distant and far away in terms of <term>longitude</term> <note>In this context, Teofilo refers to the angular distance along the celestial sphere.</note>; just as a tree will sometimes appear closer to another because it approaches the same <term>line of sight</term> <note>original: "semidiametro." Literally "semi-diameter," used here to mean the radial line stretching from the observer's eye to the object.</note>, and because the difference is negligible, they will seem as one; and yet, for all that, there will be a greater distance between these than between those that are judged much further apart due to the difference in their lines of sight. So it happens that a certain star is estimated to be much larger when it is much smaller, or much further away when it is much closer. As in the following figure:

<summary>Teofilo argues that the Earth is a celestial body like any other, moving through an infinite ethereal space. He explains that the "fixed" appearance of stars is a perspective illusion caused by their immense distance from the observer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of Dialogue Five, moving from the theoretical placement of stars to the mathematics of perspective. Teofilo is explaining why the stars appear "fixed" despite the infinite nature of the universe and the inherent motion of all celestial bodies.</meta>

<page-num>185</page-num>

**O** is the sight, or the eye; **O A B**, **O C**, **O D** are the lengths, <term>longitudes</term>, and visual lines; **A C**, **A B**, **C D** are the widths and <term>latitudes</term> <note>In this context, Bruno uses "longitude" and "latitude" to refer to the depth and width of the visual field in a geometric diagram.</note>. Where to eye **O**, star **A** appears to be the same as star **B**, and even if it shows itself to be distinct, it will appear very close; and star **C**, being on a very different <term>semidiameter</term> <note>A radius or line of sight extending from the observer.</note>, will appear much farther away, even though in fact it is much closer. Therefore, the fact that we do not see many motions in those stars, and they do not appear to move away from or approach one another, is not because they do not perform their circuits just as these [planets] do. For there is no reason why the same <term>accidents</term> <note>A philosophical term meaning the properties or characteristics of a thing.</note> should not occur in those stars as in these, by which a body—in order to receive vital power from another—must move around that other. 

They should not, however, be called **fixed** because they truly maintain the same equal distance from us and from each other, but because their motion is not sensible to us. This can be seen in the example of a ship very far away; if it makes a turn of thirty or forty paces, it will nonetheless appear to stand still, as if it were not moving at all. Thus, one must consider proportionally the case of greater distances, in massive and most luminous bodies, of which it is possible that many others and innumerable ones are as large and as bright as the sun, or even more so, whose much larger circles and motions are not seen. 

Hence, if any variation in proximity occurs in some of those stars, it cannot be known except through very long observations, which have neither been begun nor pursued because no one has believed in, sought, or presupposed such motion. And we know that the beginning of all <term>inquiry</term> <note>original: "inquisizione"</note> is knowing and recognizing that a thing is, or is possible and appropriate, and that profit may be drawn from it.

**Pru.** *You hit the nail on the head.* <note>original: "Rem acu tangis." A Latin idiom literally meaning "you touch it with a needle," used to praise someone for getting to the exact heart of a matter.</note>

**Teo.** Now, this distinction of bodies in the ethereal region was known by Heraclitus, Democritus, Epicurus, Pythagoras, Par[menides]...

<summary>Teofilo explains that stars only appear "fixed" due to their immense distance from Earth, using a geometric diagram and a ship analogy to argue that all celestial bodies are actually in motion. He attributes this understanding of an infinite, moving universe to ancient pre-Socratic philosophers.</summary>

--- Page 228 ---
<meta>This page continues the Dialogue from Giordano Bruno's "On the Infinite, the Universe, and the Worlds" (1584). In the previous page, Teofilo explained that the stars are not actually "fixed" but appear so due to their immense distance. He now moves on to discuss the ancient philosophical roots of these ideas and the internal nature of celestial motion.</meta>

<page-num>186</page-num>

...Parmenides and Melissus <note>Two Pre-Socratic philosophers; Bruno often looked to them for support of his ideas regarding the unity and infinity of the universe.</note>, as those fragments we have of them clearly show. From these, one can see that they knew of an infinite space, an infinite region, an infinite **forest** <note>Bruno uses the word "selva" (forest) to represent the vast, unformed expanse of matter or the cosmic wilderness.</note>, and an infinite capacity for innumerable worlds similar to this one. These worlds complete their circuits just as the Earth completes its own, and for this reason, they were called in ancient times <term>etria</term> <note>Derived from the Greek 'aither,' but Bruno creatively etymologizes it here to mean "runners" or "couriers" to emphasize their motion.</note>—that is, runners, couriers, ambassadors, and heralds of the constitution of nature, the living mirror of the infinite deity. 

That name of <term>etria</term> was taken away from them by blind ignorance and attributed to certain <term>quinte essenze</term> <note>The "quintessence" or fifth element, which Aristotelian physics claimed made up the celestial spheres.</note>, in which these fireflies and lanterns [the stars] are supposed to be nailed like so many nails. These "runners" possess the principle of their motion within themselves: their own nature, their own soul, and their own intelligence. The liquid and subtle air is not sufficient to move such massive and great machines; for the air to do this, it would need a pulling or pushing power, or other similar forces, which cannot occur without the contact of at least two bodies, one of which pushes with its extremity while the other is pushed. 

And certainly, all things moved in this manner acknowledge the principle of their motion as being either against or outside their own nature—meaning it is either a "violent" motion or, at the very least, not a natural one. It is, therefore, a thing suited to the convenience of existing things and to the effect of the most perfect cause, that this motion be natural, arising from an internal principle and its own impulse without resistance. This applies to all bodies that move without the sensible contact of any other thing pushing or pulling them. 

Therefore, those who say that the <term>calamita</term> <note>The Italian word for a magnet or lodestone.</note> pulls the iron, the amber pulls the straw, the jet pulls the feather, or the sun pulls the <term>elitropia</term> <note>The heliotrope, a plant known for turning its face toward the sun.</note>, understand things backwards. Rather, in the iron, there is a kind of sense which is awakened by a spiritual power that spreads from the magnet; by this sense, the iron moves toward it. The straw moves toward the amber, and generally, everything that desires and has a need moves toward the thing it desires, transforming itself into it as much as possible, beginning with the wish to be in that same location. 

From this consideration—that nothing moves locally by an external principle without a contact stronger than the resistance of the object—one can see what a profound foolishness and impossible thing it is to persuade a well-ordered mind that the moon moves the waters of the sea. It is often said that the moon causes the tides, makes the humors [bodily fluids] grow, fertilizes fish, fills oysters, and produces other effects. In truth, however, the moon is merely a **sign** of all these things, and not the cause. It is a sign and a marker, I say, because seeing these things happen alongside certain positions of the moon (and seeing different things happen in contrary positions) proceeds from the inherent order and correspondence of things. The laws of one change are simply conformed and corresponding to the laws of the other.

**Smitho:** From the ignorance of this distinction, it follows that many scrapbooks are full of similar errors, which teach us so many...

<summary>Teofilo argues that celestial bodies move via an internal, intelligent principle rather than being pushed by external forces or fixed in spheres. He uses magnetism and the tides as examples to show that what we perceive as external "pulling" is actually an internal response or a cosmic correspondence between different parts of a unified universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue of Giordano Bruno's "On the Infinite, the Universe, and the Worlds" (1584). Having established that celestial bodies move by their own internal souls rather than being fixed to physical spheres, the character Teofilo now critiques the tendency of contemporary "schoolmen" to mistake mathematical descriptions for physical causes.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>

...strange philosophies, where things that are merely signs, circumstances, and accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that can change without the thing itself changing—like the color of a shirt. Bruno argues that geometry is an "accident" of nature, not its driving force.</note> are called causes. Among these follies, one is the "queen": the claim that perpendicular and straight rays are the cause of greater heat, while acute and oblique angles cause greater cold. This, however, is merely an accident of the sun—the true cause—depending on whether it stays for a longer or shorter time above the earth. Reflected and direct rays, acute and obtuse angles, perpendicular, incident, and flat lines, larger and smaller arcs, this or that aspect—these are mathematical circumstances and not natural causes. It is one thing to play with **geometry**, it is another to verify with **nature**. It is not lines and angles that make the fire heat more or less, but rather the nearby or distant placement, and the long or brief duration of its stay.

**Teofilo.** You understand this very well; see how one truth clarifies another. Now, to conclude the point: if these great bodies were moved from the outside—in any way other than toward a desired end or good—they would be moved violently. Even if they possessed that power called "non-repugnant" <note>A technical Scholastic term referring to a potentiality that does not resist an external force.</note>, the only truly non-repugnant state is the natural one; and the natural state, whether one wills it or not, is an intrinsic principle that carries the thing where it belongs by its own power. Otherwise, the external mover would not move the body without effort, or else it would not be necessary, but superfluous. If you insist that an external mover is necessary, you accuse the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being or initiates motion—in this context, God or a Prime Mover.</note> of being deficient in its effect, and of occupying the most noble movers with much more unworthy mobile objects. This is what those people do who claim the actions of ants and spiders come not from their own foresight and skill, but from "unerring divine intelligences" that give them, for example, those pushes called "natural instincts" and other things signified by words without meaning. For if you ask these "wise men" what that instinct is, they can say nothing but "instinct," or some other word just as vague and foolish. This "instinct" merely means an "instigating principle"—a very common name used to avoid saying "a sixth sense," or "reason," or even "intellect."

**Prudenzio.** These questions are too difficult! <note>original: "Nimis arduae quaestiones!"</note>

**Smith.** Only to those who do not wish to understand them, but who want to obstinately believe what is false. But let us return to our topic! I would know well enough how to answer those who find it difficult to believe the earth moves because it is such a large, thick, and heavy body. Yet, I would like to hear your way of responding, for I see you are so resolute in your reasoning.

**Prudenzio.** I am not of such a mind. <note>original: "Non talis mihi." Prudenzio is being dismissive of Smith's curiosity.</note>

**Smith.** That is because you are a mole <note>Bruno frequently mocks his opponents as being "blind" like moles to the light of new philosophical truths.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Teofilo's discourse in the third dialogue of Giordano Bruno’s "On the Infinite, the Universe, and the Worlds" (1584). Having just argued that geometry is not a physical cause, Teofilo now dismantles the Aristotelian concepts of gravity and levity, proposing instead that "weight" is merely a relational force of parts seeking their whole.</meta>

<page-num>188</page-num>

---

...the same could be said of the moon, the sun, and other massive bodies—so many and so countless—which the adversaries claim circle the earth so swiftly with such immense revolutions. Yet they consider it a great feat that the earth should rotate around its own center in 24 hours, and around the sun in a year. Know that neither the earth nor any other body is absolutely **heavy** or **light**. No body is heavy or light in its own place; but these differences and qualities do not belong to the primary bodies and perfect individual parts of the universe, but rather apply to the parts that are divided from the whole and find themselves outside their own container, like foreigners. These parts strive toward the place of their <term>conservation</term> <note>Bruno uses "conservazione" to describe the natural tendency of an object to maintain its integrity by returning to the "whole" it belongs to.</note> no less naturally than iron toward a **magnet**, which seeks it out not specifically downward, upward, or to the right, but in every local direction, wherever it may be.

Parts of the earth come toward us through the air because their sphere is here; however, if that sphere were on the opposite side, they would move away from us, directing their course there. So it is with water, and so with fire. Water in its own place is not heavy, and it does not weigh down those things that are in the depths of the sea. The arms, the head, and other limbs are not heavy to their own torso, and nothing naturally constituted causes an act of violence in its natural place. 

**Gravity** and **levity** are not actually seen in a thing that possesses its natural place and arrangement; but they are found in things that have a certain <term>impetus</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance physics, "impetus" was the force or "shove" that kept an object moving.</note>, with which they force themselves toward the place suitable for them. Therefore, it is an absurd thing to call any body naturally heavy or light, given that these qualities do not belong to a thing that is in its natural constitution, but to one outside of it. This never happens to the sphere <note>Meaning the planet as a whole.</note> itself, but sometimes to its parts. These parts, however, are not determined toward a certain local direction according to our perspective <note>Bruno is rejecting the Aristotelian idea that "up" and "down" are absolute directions in the universe.</note>, but are always determined toward the place where their own sphere and the center of their conservation reside. 

Hence, if another kind of body were found within the earth, parts of the earth would naturally rise from that place; and if a spark of fire were found—to speak according to common parlance—above the concave of the moon, it would come downward with the same speed with which it ascends upward from the surface of the earth. Thus water descends to the center of the earth (if space is given) no less than it ascends from the center of the earth to its surface. Likewise, air moves with equal ease in every local direction. What then does "heavy" and "light" mean? Do we not sometimes see a flame go downward and to other sides to ignite a body disposed toward its nourishment and conservation? Everything that is natural, therefore, is most easy; every natural place and motion is most fitting. With that same ease with which things that do not move naturally persist fixed in the...

<summary>Teofilo argues that gravity and levity are not inherent properties of matter but are forces of "attraction" that occur only when a part is separated from its whole. He compares this to a magnet, suggesting that motion is always a natural striving toward self-preservation rather than a fixed movement toward an absolute "up" or "down."</summary>

...in its own place, the other things, which naturally move, march through their own spaces. In this context, Bruno uses the term to mean the state of being stationary or fixed in place, rather than the modern nuclear sense.</note> violently and against nature. Only common ignorance, the lack of sensory evidence, and the lack of reason.

**Smith.** I have understood this very well: that the earth in its own place is no heavier than the sun is in its own, and the members of the principal bodies—such as the waters in their spheres—would move toward those spheres if they were separated from them from any place, site, or direction. Thus, from our perspective, we could call them no less heavy than light, both heavy and light, or even indifferent. We see this in comets and other celestial fires which, depending on the bodies they burn, sometimes send their flames to opposite places, which is why they call them <term>hairy</term> <note>original: "comate." These are comets where the "hair" or coma surrounds the head.</note>; sometimes toward us, which is why they call them <term>bearded</term> <note>original: "barbate." These are comets with a distinct tail pointing away.</note>. The air, which is the most general container and is the <term>firmament</term> <note>original: "firmamento." Bruno uses this in the sense of a foundational or stabilizing medium that supports the spherical bodies, rather than just the sky.</note> of spherical bodies, exits from all parts, enters into all parts, penetrates through everything, and spreads to everything. Therefore, the argument these people bring forward regarding the reason for the <term>fixedness</term> of the earth—claiming it must be so because it is a heavy, dense, and cold body—is vain.

**Teofilo.** I praise God that I see you so capable, and that you relieve me of such effort. You have well understood that principle by which you can respond to the more robust persuasions of common philosophers, and you have gained access to many profound contemplations of nature.

**Smith.** Before you come to other questions, I would currently like to know how we should say that the sun is the true element of fire and the primary heat, and that it is fixed in the middle of these wandering bodies, among which we include the earth? Because it occurs to me that it is more likely that this body moves rather than the others, based on what we can see through the experience of the senses.

**Teofilo.** Tell me your reasoning!

**Smith.** The parts of the earth, wherever they are held—whether naturally or by force—do not move. Likewise, parts of water outside the sea, in rivers and other living containers, stay still. But the parts of fire, when they do not have the ability to climb high—as when they are held within the hollows of furnaces—swirl and rotate in circles, and there is no way to restrain them. If, therefore, we want to take some argument and evidence from the parts, motion is more appropriate for the sun and the element of fire than for the earth.

**Teo.** To this I first respond that, because of what has been said, one could concede that the sun moves around its own center, but not around another midpoint; it is sufficient that all the surrounding bodies move around it, as much as they have need of it, and also for that which it might perhaps desire from them. **Teo.** The reason is that fire exerts more force to flee from this region, which is more natural to a body of the opposite quality. **Smi.** You have said "vaporous air": what would you say of pure and simple air?

**Teo.** That is no more subject to heat than to cold; it is no more capable or receptive of moisture when it is thickened by cold, than of vapor and exhalation when water is thinned by heat.

**Teo.** The cause of such motion is the renewal and rebirth of this body, which cannot be perpetual according to the same disposition; just as things that cannot be perpetual in number (to speak in common terms) are made perpetual according to their **species**. Those substances that cannot...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 190. Teofilo is explaining the philosophical necessity of motion and change in the universe, arguing that while the underlying "matter" of the world is eternal, its outward forms must constantly shift to experience all possible states of being.</meta>

<page-num>191</page-num>

...perpetuate themselves under the same face, they are nonetheless constantly changing their appearance. Because the matter and substance of things is incorruptible, and because it must—in all its parts—be the subject of all forms, so that in all its parts (as far as it is capable) it may be everything. It must be everything, if not in the same time and instant of eternity, at least in different times and various instances of eternity, successively and through **vicissitudes**. For although all matter is capable of all forms together, every individual part of matter cannot be capable of all those forms at the same time. 

Therefore, since death and dissolution are not appropriate for this entire mass—of which this globe, this star, consists—and since annihilation is impossible for all of nature, it comes to renew itself from time to time in a certain order, altering, changing, and transforming all its parts. This must happen with a certain succession, each part taking the place of all the others; otherwise, these bodies, which are dissoluble, would actually dissolve at once, as happens to us particular and lesser animals. But to these great bodies, as Plato believes in the *Timaeus*, and as we also believe, it has been said by the First Principle:

> *You are dissoluble, but you shall not be dissolved.* <note>original: "Voi siete dissolubili, ma non vi dissolverete." This is a famous reference to Plato's *Timaeus* 41a-b, where the Creator tells the stars and lesser gods that although they are not immortal by nature, his will shall keep them from ever being destroyed.</note>

It happens, then, that there is no part in the center and middle of the star that does not eventually move to the circumference and beyond it; there is no portion on that outermost and external edge that must not at some time become innermost and internal. Our daily experience demonstrates this to us: for in the womb and bowels of the earth, some things are gathered in, and other things are sent out from them. 

And we ourselves, and our possessions, come and go, pass away and return; there is nothing of ours that does not become foreign, and nothing foreign that does not become ours. There is nothing of which we are made that must not eventually be ours, just as there is nothing which is ours of which we must not eventually be made—if the matter of things is one, in one <term>genus</term> <note>In this context, "genus" refers to a fundamental category or kind of substance.</note>; or if there are two matters, in two genera. For I do not yet determine whether the substance and matter we call "spiritual" changes into that which we call "corporal," and vice versa, or truly not. 

Thus, all things in their kind have all vicissitudes of dominion and servitude, happiness and unhappiness, of that state called life and that called death, of light and darkness, of good and evil. And there is nothing to which it is naturally appropriate to be eternal, except for the **substance**, which is the matter, to which it is no less appropriate to be in continual mutation. Of the **supersubstantial** <note>A term often used in Renaissance Neoplatonism to refer to God or the Divine Essence, which exists above the level of physical or even metaphysical substance.</note> substance I do not speak at present, but return to reason particularly about this great individual, who is our perpetual nurse and mother, regarding whom you asked for what reason there was <term>local motion</term> <note>A technical term in Aristotelian physics for "change of place"—literally, moving from one location to another.</note>. ...the parts, it is the end of the **vicissitude** <term>vicissitude: the constant, cyclical change or "turning" of things from one state to another</term>, not only so that everything may be found in all places, but also so that through this means everything may possess all dispositions and forms. For this reason, **local motion** <term>local motion: the physical movement of a body from one place to another</term> has been most worthily esteemed as the principle of every other transformation and form; and once this is removed, no other can exist. 

Aristotle was able to perceive change according to dispositions and qualities in all parts of the earth, but he did not understand the local motion that serves as their root principle. Yet, at the end of the first book of his *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorology* (Meteorologica) Book I, Chapter 14, where he argues that the earth changes "like the bodies of plants and animals," causing seas to become land and vice versa.</note>, he spoke like one who prophesies and divines. For, although he himself sometimes does not understand his own meaning—limping along, as it were, and always mixing something of his own error with divine inspiration—he speaks the truth in the main and for the most part. Now let us present what he says, which is both true and worthy of consideration, and then we shall add the causes of these things, which he was unable to know. 

"The same places on earth," he says, "are not always moist or dry, but they change according to the birth and failure of rivers. Therefore, that which was and is the sea has not always been and will not always be the sea; that which will be and has been land is not, nor was it always, land. Instead, through a certain **vicissitude**, a determined circle and order, we must believe that where there is one, the other shall be, and where there is the other, the first shall be." 

And if you ask Aristotle for the principle and cause of this, he replies that the interior parts of the earth, like the bodies of plants and animals, have their period of perfection and then grow old. But there is a difference between the earth and those other bodies. For the latter, as whole entities, undergo progress, perfection, and decline—what he calls maturity and old age—in all their parts at the same time. In the earth, however, this happens successively, part by part, with the alternation of cold and heat causing growth and decay. This follows the sun and its circuit, through which the parts of the earth acquire different constitutions and powers. 

Because of this, watery places remain so for a time, then dry up and grow old once more, while others are revived and become watery in certain parts. Thus we see springs vanish, and rivers that were once small become large, while others that were large become small and finally dry up. And from this decline of rivers, it follows by necessary consequence that pools are removed and the seas are shifted. 

However, since this happens successively across the earth over vast and slow periods of time, our own life and that of our fathers can hardly judge it. This is because the lifespan and memory of entire nations fail sooner; great destructions and changes occur through desolation and wilderness, through wars, through plagues, and through deluges—along with alterations of languages and scripts, the migration of peoples, and the barrenness of lands—long before we can remember these things from beginning to end through such long, varied, and most turbulent centuries. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Aristotle's *Meteorology*, specifically expanding on the observation that the Earth’s surface is in a constant state of flux, with seas and lands exchanging places over vast periods of time. The speaker, Teofilo, provides historical and contemporary evidence to support the idea that the world’s climate and geography are shifting northward.</meta>

<page-num>193</page-num>

These changes are shown in the antiquity of Egypt, in the mouths of the Nile, all of which—except for the **Canopic outlet** <note>The westernmost branch of the Nile Delta in antiquity.</note>—were made by human hand; and in the dwellings of the city of **Memphis**, where the lower areas were inhabited only after the higher ones. The same is seen in **Argos and Mycenae**; at the time of the **Trojans**, the former region was swampy and very few lived there, while Mycenae, being more fertile, was much more honored. In our own times, the opposite is true: Mycenae has become completely dry, and Argos has become temperate and quite fertile. 

Now, just as this happens in these small places, we must think the same regarding great regions and entire lands. Therefore, just as we see that many places which were once watery are now dry land, so too has the sea overtaken many others. We see these mutations happening little by little, like those already mentioned, and as we are shown by the **erosions of very high mountains** far distant from the sea, which—as if they were fresh—still show the traces of the impetuous waves. 

This is confirmed by the histories of **Felix the Martyr of Nola** <note>Saint Felix of Nola (3rd century AD). This reference is a personal touch, as Giordano Bruno was himself from Nola.</note>, which declare that in his time (which was a little more or less than a thousand years ago), the sea was near the walls of the city, where there is a temple that still keeps the name of **Porto** <note>original: "Porto" (meaning Harbor or Port).</note>, whereas at present it is twelve thousand paces away. Do we not see the same in all of **Provence**? Do not all the stones scattered through the fields show that they were once agitated by the waves? 

Does it seem to you that the climate of **France** has changed but little from the time of **Caesar** to our own? In those days, no place there was fit for vines; yet now it sends forth wines as delicious as any other part of the world, and even from its northernmost lands the fruits of the vineyards are harvested. And this year I have even eaten grapes from the gardens of **London**—not quite as perfect as those from the worst parts of France, to be sure, but nonetheless such as they claim have never been produced before in English soil. 

From this, therefore—seeing that the Mediterranean Sea is leaving France and parts of **Italy** (which I have seen with my own eyes) drier and warmer, and is tilting toward the **scales** <term>the scales: a reference to the celestial Libra, signifying a shift in the Earth's equilibrium or seasonal balance</term>—it follows that as Italy and France become warmer and warmer, and **Britain** becomes more temperate, we must judge that the character of these regions is generally changing, and that the cold disposition is gradually diminishing toward the **Arctic pole**. 

Ask **Aristotle**: why does this happen? He answers: from the **sun** and from **circular motion**. How confusedly and obscurely, yet also how divinely, loftily, and truly he has spoken! But how? Perhaps as a philosopher? No: but rather as a diviner, or as one who understood but did not dare to speak; perhaps like one who sees, but does not believe what he sees, and even if he believes it, hesitates to affirm it, fearing that someone might come to force him to provide a reason which he does not have. He reports it, but in such a way...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the Earth’s geological and climatic changes. Teofilo is now moving from empirical observations of landscape changes to the underlying astronomical causes, critiquing Aristotle’s failure to recognize the Earth’s motion as the true driver of these cycles.</meta>

<page-num>194</page-num>

...with which he shuts the mouth of anyone who would wish to know more; or perhaps it is a manner of speaking taken from the ancient philosophers. He says, therefore, that heat, cold, dryness, and moisture increase and decrease over all parts of the earth, in which everything undergoes renewal; and wishing to provide the cause of this, he says: *on account of the sun and the circulation* <note>original: "propter solem et circumlationem." Teofilo is quoting Aristotle's *Meteorology*.</note>. Now, why does he not say: *on account of the sun’s circulation* <note>original: "propter solis circulationem"</note>? Because it was determined by him, and granted among all philosophers of his time and disposition, that the sun with its motion could not cause this diversity; for insofar as the ecliptic deviates from the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note>, the sun eternally turned between the two tropical points; and therefore it would be impossible for any other part of the earth to be heated, but the zones and climates would eternally remain in the same disposition. 

Why did he not say: by the circulation of other planets? Because it was already determined that all of those—even if some do not overstep by a little—move only within the latitude of the <term>zodiaco</term> <note>The Zodiac, described here as the "worn path of the wanderers" (the planets).</note> called the "well-trodden path of the wanderers." Why did he not say: by the circulation of the <term>primo mobile</term> <note>The "First Mover," the outermost sphere in ancient astronomy which was thought to move all others.</note>? Because he knew no other motion than the diurnal <note>The daily rotation of the sky.</note>, and in his time there was only a slight suspicion of a motion of retardation, similar to that of the planets. Why did he not say: by the circulation of the heavens? Because he could not say how or of what kind it might be. Why did he not say: by the circulation of the earth? Because he held as a supposed principle that the earth is immobile. Why, then, did he say it? Forced by the truth, which makes itself heard through natural effects. 

It remains, then, that it is from the sun and from motion. From the sun, I say, because it is that unity which diffuses and communicates the vital virtue; and from motion as well, because, if either it did not move toward other bodies, or other bodies toward it, how could a body receive that which it does not have, or give that which it has? It is therefore necessary that there be motion, and this of such a sort that it is not partial; rather, by the same logic with which it causes the renewal of certain parts, it comes to bring it to those others which, being of the same condition and nature, have the same passive power—to which, if nature is not unjust, the active power must correspond. 

But with all this, we find much less reason why the sun and the entire university of stars should have to move around this globe, than that the globe, on the contrary, should turn itself toward the aspect of the universe, making its annual circle around the sun, and shifting and inclining toward it from all sides with certain regulated successions, as toward the living element of fire. There is no reason that, without a certain end and urgent occasion, the innumerable stars—which are so many worlds, even greater than this one—should have such a violent relationship to this single one. There is no reason that should make us say rather that the pole trembles, the axis of the world changes, the hinges of the universe stumble, and so many innumerable, larger, and more magni- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "magnificent" or "magnificent things."</note>

<summary>Teofilo argues that Aristotle was forced to admit a "circulation" caused geological change, but his geocentric bias prevented him from realizing it was the Earth's own motion. He posits that it is far more logical for the small Earth to move around the sun and stars than for the entire infinite universe to revolve around the Earth.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, geocentrism vs heliocentrism, Aristotle, planetary motion, vital virtue, Primum Mobile, Zodiac, Earth's rotation</keywords>

...spheres can shake, turn, twist, be patched up, and—in defiance of nature—be "quartered" <note>Bruno is likely critiquing the complex mathematical "fixes" like epicycles used in the old Ptolemaic system to explain planetary movement.</note> to such an extent that the earth (as subtle <term>opticians</term> <note>Scientists specializing in the study of light and vision.</note> and <term>geometers</term> can show) comes to occupy the center as a body that is uniquely heavy and cold. However, it cannot be proven that the earth is any different from any other body that shines in the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the stars; the heavens.</note>, neither in its substance and matter, nor in the nature of its location. For if this body can be embraced <note>original: "vagheggiato." Literally "wooed" or "caressed," Bruno uses this poetic term to describe how the air or ether surrounds and interacts with a planet.</note> by this air in which it is fixed, and those other bodies can likewise be embraced by that which surrounds them—and if those others, by their own soul and nature, can divide the air and circle around a center, then this one [the Earth] can do no less.

**Smi.** I beg you, let us take this point as granted for the moment. For my part, I consider it a most certain thing that the earth must necessarily move, rather than believing that "planking and nailing of lamps" <note>original: "intavolatura, et inchiodatura di lampe." A sarcastic description of the Ptolemaic system where stars were thought to be fixed onto a physical, crystalline sphere like lanterns hung on a ceiling.</note> could be possible. **Teo.** Very willingly; for this digression would have made us wait too long to conclude what I intended regarding the necessity and the state of all parts of the earth. All these parts must successively participate in all the aspects and relations of the sun, becoming the subject of all temperaments and conditions. Now, for this purpose, it is convenient and necessary that the motion of the earth be such that, with a certain alternation, where the sea is, the continent shall be; and conversely, where there is heat, there shall be cold; and conversely, where it is habitable and more temperate, it shall become less habitable and temperate; and conversely, in conclusion, each part comes to have every relation that all other parts have to the sun: so that every part may come to participate in every life, every generation, and every happiness. 

First, therefore, for its own life and that of the things contained within it, and to provide a kind of respiration and inspiration through diurnal heat and cold, light and darkness, the earth moves around its own center in a space of twenty-four equal hours, exposing its entire surface to the sun as much as possible. 

Second, for the regeneration of the things that live and dissolve upon its surface, it circles the shining body of the sun with its center in approximately three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter; where, from four points of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky; the points Bruno mentions represent the four seasons.</note>, it makes the proclamation of the generation, the youth, the maturity, and the decline of its things. 

Third, for the renewal of ages, it participates in another motion, by which that relationship which this upper <term>hemisphere</term> of the earth has to the universe...

<summary>Teofilo argues that the Earth is a celestial body similar to the stars and planets, possessing its own "soul" that allows it to move through the ether. He then outlines the three primary motions of the Earth: its daily rotation, its annual orbit around the sun, and a third motion related to long-term geological and cosmic cycles.</summary>

...comes to occupy the lower <term>hemisphere</term> <note>One half of the Earth, usually divided by the equator or the horizon.</note>, and that the latter succeeds the position of the upper one. Fourthly, because of the change in the appearances and conditions of the Earth, another motion is necessarily required of it. By this motion, the orientation that this pole of the Earth has toward the point near the <term>arctic</term> <note>The North Pole.</note> changes with the orientation that the other pole has toward the opposite point of the <term>antarctic</term> pole. 

The first motion is measured from a point on the Earth’s <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The Earth's equator; the line where day and night are of equal length.</note> line, such that it returns either to the same point or nearly the same point. 

The second motion is measured from an imaginary point on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky, which in this model represents the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note>, which is the path of the Earth around the sun, until it returns to the same point, or nearly so. 

The third motion is measured by the orientation of a hemispheric line of the Earth—which serves as the <term>horizon</term> <note>The boundary between the Earth and the sky as seen by an observer.</note>—relative to the universe, until that same line, or one proportional to it, returns to the same orientation. 

The fourth motion is measured by the progress of one of the Earth's poles which, passing through the other pole along the line of some <term>meridian</term> <note>A great circle passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a given location.</note>, returns to the same, or nearly the same, aspect where it was before. 

Regarding this, it must be considered that although we say there are four motions, nonetheless, they all concur in a single composite motion. Note that of these four motions:
* The first is derived from the fact that in a natural day, everything appears to move around the Earth above the "poles of the world," as they say. 
* The second is derived from the appearance that the sun circles the entire <term>zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note> in one year. Every day, according to **Ptolemy** in the third book of the <term>Almagest</term> <note>The influential 2nd-century mathematical and astronomical treatise on the motions of stars and planets.</note>, it travels fifty-nine minutes, eight seconds, seventeen thirds, thirteen fourths, twelve fifths, thirty-one sixths <note>These "thirds," "fourths," etc., are sexagesimal subdivisions of a degree, each being 1/60th of the previous unit.</note>; according to **Alfonso** <note>Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the "Alphonsine Tables" in the 13th century.</note>, fifty-nine minutes, eight seconds, eleven thirds, thirty-seven fourths, nineteen fifths, thirteen sixths, fifty-six sevenths; according to **Copernicus**, fifty-nine minutes, eight seconds, and eleven thirds. 
* The third motion is derived from the appearance that the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars in ancient astronomy.</note> moves according to the order of the signs, contrary to the daily motion, above the poles of the zodiac. It moves so slowly that in two hundred years it moves no more than one degree and twenty-eight minutes; thus, it completes its circle in forty-nine thousand years. They attribute the beginning of this motion to a <term>ninth sphere</term> <note>A theoretical sphere added by later astronomers to explain the slow wobble or precession of the stars.</note>. 
* The fourth motion is derived from the "trepidation," "access," and "recess" <note>Historical astronomical theories used to explain variations in the precession of the equinoxes.</note> that they say the <term>eighth sphere</term> performs upon two equal circles, which they imagine to exist within the concavity of the ninth sphere, above the points of <term>Aries</term> and <term>Libra</term> of its zodiac. This is derived from what they see as necessary: that the ecliptic of the eighth sphere is not always understood to intersect the <term>equinoctial</term> at the same points, but is sometimes at the start of Aries, and sometimes beyond it on either side of the ecliptic. From this, they see that the greatest declinations of the zodiac are not always the same; from which it necessarily follows that the <term>equinoxes</term> and <term>solstices</term> <note>The two days of the year when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon.</note> vary continuously, as effectively—

<meta>Teofilo continues his explanation of the Earth’s complex physical movements using the analogy of a ball or globe, moving from the visual diagram to the specific types of planetary motion.</meta>

<page-num>198</page-num>
<meta>catchword: emi-</meta>

The momentum of gravity does not remain fixed, but shifts obliquely because it belongs to a globe, which can easily tilt in all directions. Therefore, points **I** and **K** <note>Referring to the diagram on the previous page.</note> do not always rotate along the same straight path. Thus, it is necessary that—whether through a long, short, interrupted, or continuous journey—the motion eventually reaches the point where point **O** moves to where point **V** is, and vice versa. Among these motions, if even one is not regulated, it is enough to ensure that none of the others are regulated; if one is unknown, it makes all the others unknown. Nevertheless, they possess a certain order, by which they approach or move away from regularity to varying degrees. Thus, among these differences of motion, the most regulated—being closest to the perfectly regular—is that of the center. Next to this is the motion around the center’s diameter, which is faster. Third is the motion which, through the irregularity of the second (consisting of fluctuating speed and slowness), gradually changes the entire appearance of the hemisphere. The last, the most irregular and uncertain, is that which changes the sides; for sometimes, instead of moving forward, it turns backward, and with great inconsistency finally changes the position of one opposite point with the position of another. The earth moves similarly. First, it has the motion of its center, which is the annual motion, more regular than all others and most consistent with itself; second, the less regular diurnal <term>diurnal</term> <note>Daily rotation on its axis.</note> motion; third, the irregular motion we call the hemispheric; fourth, the most irregular, is the polar or <term>colural</term> <note>Related to the colures, the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere.</note> motion.

**Smith:** I would like to know in what order and by what rule the <term>Nolano</term> <note>Giordano Bruno himself, who was born in Nola.</note> will make us understand these motions?

**Prudenzio:** What limit shall there be? Shall we always and forever stand in need of new theories? <note>original Latin: "Ecquis erit modus? Novis usque, et usque semper indigebimus theoriis?"</note>

You, Master Prudenzio, provide the conclusion and a moral epilogue only for our <term>tetralogue</term> <note>A dialogue between four speakers.</note>; for the scientific inquiry, drawn from the *Ash Wednesday Supper*, is now concluded.

->Most illustrious and unique Knight!<-

**I**f I turn the eyes of my consideration to behold your patience, perseverance, and solicitude, with which—adding service to service and benefit to benefit—you have won me over, bound me, and held me fast; and seeing how you wish to overcome every difficulty, escape from whatever peril, and bring all your most honorable designs to fulfillment: I come to see how properly that noble device <term>device: a heraldic emblem or motto used by a nobleman to represent his character or goals</term> suits you, with which you adorn your formidable crest. There, that liquid humor <note>referring to water</note> which gently wounds, while it drips continuously and frequently, by force of perseverance softens, carves, tames, breaks, and levels a certain dense, harsh, hard, and rough stone. <note>Bruno is likely referring to the Latin proverb *Gutta cavat lapidem*—"the drop hollows the stone"—praising Castelnau's persistence in the face of political and personal obstacles.</note>
