Although, according to certain **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential qualities, like color or shape, that can change while the underlying substance remains</term>, everything "changes its face" and is transmuted now under one composition, now under another, leaving and taking up now this, now that mode of being.

Eleventh, that the **Aristotelians**, **Platonists**, and other sophists <note>Bruno uses "sophists" to criticize traditional university scholars who prioritized rhetoric over physical truth</note> have not known the substance of things. It is clearly shown that in natural things, whatever they call "substance" besides matter is actually pure accident. Furthermore, from the knowledge of the true form, one infers the true understanding of what life is and what death is. Once the vain and childish terror of death is completely extinguished, one recognizes a portion of the happiness that our contemplation brings, according to the foundations of our philosophy; for it removes the dark veil of foolish sentiment regarding **Orcus** <note>a Roman name for the Underworld or the god of the dead</note> and greedy **Charon** <note>the mythological ferryman who carries souls across the river Styx</note>, through which the sweetest part of our life is snatched away and poisoned.

Twelfth, form is distinguished, not according to the reason...

Thirteenth, it concludes with the true definitive reasoning of the **formal principle** <term>formal principle: the active, shaping force or "soul" that gives matter its specific identity</term>, showing how the form is a perfect species, distinct within matter according to accidental dispositions. These dispositions depend on the material form—that is, the form which consists of different degrees and arrangements of active and passive qualities. It is shown how this principle is both variable and invariable, how it defines and limits matter, and how it is, in turn, defined and limited by matter. Finally, it is shown with a certain analogy suited to common understanding how this form, this soul, can be "whole in the whole" and in any part of the whole one might wish <note>original: "tutta in tutto"; a classic philosophical phrase meaning the soul is fully present in the entire body and simultaneously fully present in every individual part</note>.

### In the **THIRD DIALOGUE**

After the first dialogue discussed form—which has more the character of a "cause" than a "principle"—we proceed to the consideration of **matter**, which is considered to have more the character of a "principle" and "element" than a "cause." Leaving aside the introductory remarks at the start of the dialogue:

First, it is shown that David of Dinant <margin>A pantheist and follower of Amalric of Bène near Chartres. His books were burned in the year 1210. See *Albertus Magnus, Summa Theologica*, Vol. 1, treatise IV, question 20, section 2.</margin> was not foolish in his own way for treating matter as something most excellent and divine.

Second, it shows how different ways of philosophizing can lead to different understandings of matter, even though it is truly one primary and absolute thing. Because matter manifests in different degrees and is hidden under various outward forms, different thinkers may grasp it differently according to the logic that suits them. This is no different than how a number is taken purely and simply by the arithmetician, harmonically by the musician, symbolically by the Kabbalist <note>The Kabbalah is a tradition of Jewish mysticism; Bruno refers here to the practice of finding hidden meanings in numbers</note>, and by other fools or wise men as other subjects.

Third, the meaning of the name (*matter*) is declared through the difference and similarity between natural and artificial subjects <note>An "artificial subject" refers to raw materials used by humans, like wood for a table, used as an analogy for how nature uses "matter"</note>.

Fourth, it proposes how stubborn people should be dealt with, and to what extent we are obligated to respond and debate.

Fifth, from the true reasoning of matter, it is inferred that no **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the essential nature of a thing that makes it what it is (e.g., the "soul" of a tree)</term> ever loses its being. It strongly argues that the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle used to walk around while teaching</note> and other common philosophers, although they use the term "substantial form," have never known any substance other than matter.

<meta>This page continues Bruno's summary of the Third Dialogue, transitioning from the nature of the material principle to the unity of the universe. It follows the previous page's discussion on the material principle as defined by thinkers like David of Dinant.</meta>

<page-num>208</page-num>

Sixth, a constant **formal principle** is established, just as a constant material principle is recognized. Through the diversity of arrangements found in matter, this formal principle transitions into the multiform shapes of different species and individuals. It is also shown how it came to be that some raised in the **Peripatetic school** <term>Peripatetic school: the followers of Aristotle, known for walking in the Lyceum while they taught; Bruno often critiques their rigid logic</term> refused to recognize anything as "substance" other than matter.

Seventh, why it is necessary for reason to distinguish **matter** from **form**, and **potency** from **act** <term>potency and act: a classic philosophical distinction; potency is the capacity to be or do something, while act is the actual realization of that capacity</term>. It repeats what was said secondarily: that the subject and principle of natural things can be understood in different ways according to different philosophical methods without being wrong. However, it is more useful to consider them according to "natural and magical" methods <note>Bruno refers to "magical" in the Renaissance sense: the practical application of natural philosophy to effect change in the world</note>, and more varied according to mathematical and rational methods—especially if these latter are so focused on the rules and exercise of logic that they fail to produce anything of value in action or yield any practical fruit, without which all contemplation would be deemed vain.

Eighth, two ways are proposed in which matter is usually considered: as a **potency** and as a **subject**. Beginning with the first, it is distinguished into active and passive, and in a certain way, these are brought back into a unity.

Ninth, it is inferred from the eighth proposition how the supreme and divine is everything that *can* be, and how the universe is everything that *can* be, whereas other individual things are not everything that they have the potential to be.

Tenth, as a consequence of what was said in the ninth, it is demonstrated in a profound, brief, and open manner why there are vices, monsters, corruption, and death in nature.

Eleventh, in what way the universe is in no single part, yet is in all parts, which provides an opening for an excellent contemplation of the divinity.

Twelfth, why it happens that the human intellect cannot grasp this most absolute act and this most absolute potency.

Thirteenth, the excellence of matter is concluded, which coincides with form just as potency coincides with act.

Finally, both from the fact that potency coincides with act and that the universe is everything that it can be, as well as from other reasons, it is concluded that the **Whole is One**.

<meta>This page continues the summary of arguments from the Third Dialogue of Giordano Bruno’s "Concerning the Cause, Principle, and One," transitioning into the outline of the Fifth Dialogue. It focuses on the ontological unity of substance versus the superficiality of accidental changes.</meta>

...not according to accidental existence: because everything that is seen and made manifest through accidents <term>accidents: non-essential properties of a thing, such as its color, size, or location, which can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</term> based on dimensions is pure accident, while the individual substance remains ever constant and coincides with individual matter.

Hence, it is clearly seen that from the unfolding <note>original: "esplicazione"</note> of things we can grasp nothing but accidents; so much so that **substantial differences** are hidden, as **Aristotle** said when forced by the truth. In such a way that, if we consider carefully, we can infer from this that there is one uniform substance, one true being <term>ente: a philosophical term for "that which exists" or "being"</term>, which appears according to innumerable circumstances and individuals, manifesting itself in so many and such diverse subjects <note>original: "suppositi" (individual manifestations of a substance)</note>. Sixthly, it is stated how far from all reason is that which **Aristotle** and others like him intend regarding matter "being in potency" <term>potency: the capacity to become something, as opposed to "act," which is the state of being it currently</term>. This is surely nothing, given that, according to these very thinkers, matter is so fundamentally permanent that it never changes or varies its being; rather, all variety and mutation happen around it. That which follows—the state of being that "could be"—always refers, even according to them, to the **composite** <note>the "composite" is the physical object made of both matter and form</note>. Seventhly, the "appetite" <term>appetite: a philosophical term for a natural tendency or "desire" of matter to take on new forms</term> of matter is determined, showing how vainly it is defined. This is argued using the very principles and suppositions of those who proclaim it to be the "daughter of privation" and liken it to the "insatiable greed of a woman" <note>Bruno is critiquing a common Aristotelian metaphor of his time that compared matter's "desire" for form to a woman’s supposed desire for a man.</note>.

In the **FIFTH DIALOGUE**, which deals specifically with **the One**, the foundation of the edifice of all natural and divine knowledge is completed. First, the proposition of the **coincidence of matter and form**, and of **potency and act**, is brought forward. Thus, that being which is logically divided into "what is" and "what can be" is, physically, undivided, indistinct, and one. This unity is simultaneously infinite, immobile, and impartible, without difference between the whole and the part, or the principle and the thing proceeded from it. Second, it is shown that in this Unity, a century is not different from a year, a year from a moment, a palm from a stadium, or a stadium from a parasang <note>The "palm," "stadium," and "parasang" are ancient units of measurement for length, ranging from the width of a hand to several miles.</note>. In its essence, this or that specific being is not "one thing and another"; and therefore, in the universe, there is no number, and thus the universe is **one**. Third, that in the infinite, the point is not different from the body, because potency is not one thing and act another. There, if the point can flow into a length, the line into a width, and the surface into a depth, then the one is long, the other is wide, the other is deep; and everything is long...

wide and deep, and consequently the same and one; and the universe is all center and all circumference. Fourthly, how from the fact that **Jupiter** <note>original: "Giove"; Bruno frequently uses the names of Roman gods to refer to the Divine Mind or the Universal Intellect that governs nature</note>—as they call him—is more intimately within the whole than one can imagine the form of the whole to be (because he is the **essence** <term>essence: the fundamental nature or core reality of a thing</term> through which everything that exists has its being, and since he is in everything, every thing possesses the "whole" more intimately than its own individual form), it is inferred that all things are in each thing, and consequently, all is one. Eighthly, with a new contemplation, it is repeated to you that the one, the infinite, the being, and that which is in everything, is through everything—rather, it is the very same **everywhere** <note>original: "ubique"</note>; and thus infinite dimension, not being a physical magnitude, coincides with the individual point, just as the infinite multitude, not being a number, coincides with unity. Ninthly, how in the infinite there is no "part and part" <note>meaning there are no distinct, separable portions in the infinite whole</note>, whatever may be explicitly seen in the universe, where everything we see of diversity and difference is nothing other than a different and diverse face of the same substance. Tenthly, how in the two extremes—which are said to be at the far ends of the scale of nature—one should no longer contemplate two principles instead of one, two beings instead of one, or two contraries and diverse things instead of one concordant and identical thing. Eleventhly, how certain geometric names, such as "point" and "one," are used to promote the contemplation of **Being** and the **One**, and are not sufficient in themselves to signify it. Wherefore **Pythagoras**, **Parmenides**, and **Plato** must not be so foolishly interpreted according to the pedantic...

## TO ONE’S OWN SPIRIT.

*Mountain, although the earth captures you, held fast*
*by deep roots, you are able to stretch your peak toward the stars.*
*A kindred mind calls from the highest summit of things*

## TO TIME.

*Slow old man, and yet swift; both closing and releasing,*
*would anyone call you good, or would they call you evil?*
*You are generous, and you are stingy; the gifts you offer, you take away,*
*and what is brought out from your own depths, you hide again within those depths.*
*You, who are permitted to snatch away with your throat what is ready in your lap,*
*since you make all things, and since you destroy all things; for this reason,*
*could I not call you good, could I not call you evil?*
*Furthermore, when you, raving, shall be frustrated in your dreadful blow,*
*cease to stretch out your hands, threatening with that scythe,* <note>original: "Falce"; the traditional tool of Father Time, used to "reap" or end life.</note>
*in that place where no footprints of dark Chaos* <term>Chaos: the void or formless state preceding the creation of the universe</term> *remain pressed,*
*lest you appear good, lest you appear evil!*

## ON LOVE.

> Love, through whom I discern the truth from such a height,
> Who opens the gates of diamond and of darkness,
> Through the eyes enters my deity; and to see
> He is born, lives, is nourished, and holds eternal reign.
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He makes visible all that heaven, earth, and hell contain,
> He makes present the true images of those who are absent,
> He regathers his strength, and striking with a steady aim,
> He always wounds the heart and reveals every internal secret.
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Oh then, you vile commoners, attend to the truth!
> Lend your ear to my speech, which is not deceptive;
> Open, open your eyes, if you can, you who are insane and squinting!
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You believe him a child <note>original: "Fanciullo"; a reference to the traditional depiction of Cupid as a winged boy.</note> because you understand so little;
> Because you change so quickly, he seems fleeting to you;
> Because you yourselves are sightless, you call him blind! <note>Bruno is arguing against the common trope of "Blind Love," suggesting that true, heroic love is actually a form of supreme intellectual vision.</note>

> <term>Cause, Principle, and One</term> <note>original: "Causa, Principio et Uno"; these are the three primary designations Bruno uses for the divine source of the universe. <meta>The previous page concluded the introductory poems of Giordano Bruno’s work, shifting from a poetic exploration of "Heroic Frenzies" and intellectual love to the start of a structured philosophical debate. # FIRST DIALOGUE.

---

### Interlocutors:

->Elitropio. Filoteo. Armesso.<-
<note>Filoteo (meaning "Lover of God") serves as the spokesperson for Bruno himself; Elitropio ("Heliotrope" or "Sun-turner") is a supportive seeker of truth; Armesso (related to "Hermes") acts as a skeptical but curious mediator.</note>

---

### Elitropio.

Like criminals accustomed to the darkness, who, once freed from the depths of some dark tower, emerge into the light, many of those practiced in common philosophy <note>original: "volgar filosofia"; referring to the traditional Scholastic and Aristotelian teachings dominant in the universities of the time</note> and others will be terrified, will be amazed, and, being unable to endure the new sun of your clear concepts, will be troubled.

**Fil.** The defect is not in the light, but in the eyes; the more beautiful and excellent the sun is in itself, the more hateful and unwelcome it will be to the eyes of nocturnal owls <note>original: "notturne strige"; literally "screech-owls," a metaphor for those who are blinded by the brilliance of new truths</note>.

**Elit.** The undertaking you have accepted, O Filoteo, is difficult, rare, and singular, as you seek to cast us out from the blind abyss and lead us to the open, tranquil, and serene sight of the stars, which we see scattered with such beautiful variety across the cerulean mantle of heaven. Although the helping hand of your merciful zeal assists men alone, the effects of the ungrateful toward you will be no less varied than the various animals that the kind earth generates and nourishes in her maternal and capacious womb. This is especially true if it is a fact that the human species, particularly in its individual members, displays a greater variety than all others, because in each individual, the whole <note>Bruno refers to the idea of the human as a microcosm, containing the essence of the entire universe</note> is more expressly present than in other species. 

Thus, we shall see some who, like dim-sighted moles, as soon as they feel the open air, will immediately burrow into the earth again, returning to their native, dark, inner chambers. Others, like nocturnal birds, as soon as they see the crimson messenger of the sun rising from the shining east, will be invited by the weakness of their eyes to retreat into the gloom. All those creatures banished from the sight of the celestial lamps, and destined for the eternal cages, pits, and caves of Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld; here representing the "hell" of ignorance or physical limitation</note>, summoned by the terrifying and Fury-like <note>original: "erinnico"; referring to the Erinyes or Furies of Greek myth</note> choir of Aletto <note>Alecto, one of the three Furies, responsible for vengeance and anger</note>, will spread their wings and direct their swift course back to their dwellings. But those creatures born to see the sun, having reached the end of the hateful night, giving thanks for the kindness of heaven, and...

<summary>This opening dialogue introduces the theme of intellectual enlightenment, comparing those who resist Bruno's new cosmology to nocturnal animals terrified by the rising sun. It establishes the characters and the metaphorical conflict between the "darkness" of old philosophy and the "light" of the infinite universe.</summary>

<keywords>Giordano Bruno, cosmology, enlightenment, Aristotelianism, allegory, infinite universe, Filoteo, Elitropio, metaphors of light and darkness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the opening dialogue of the work. Elitropio is concluding a lengthy metaphorical description of how various "beings"—from men to beasts—will react to the "sunrise" of Filoteo’s (Bruno's) new infinite cosmology. The previous page established that while the truth is bright, it can be blinding or irritating to those used to the darkness of traditional philosophy.</meta>

...preparing themselves to receive into the center of the globular crystal of their eyes the so greatly longed for and awaited rays, with unusual applause of heart, voice, and hand, they will adore the rising east. From its gilded balcony, having driven forth his fiery steeds, the fair **Titan** <note>The sun god, Helios or Apollo.</note> having broken the drowsy silence of the humid night, men will converse; the gentle, harmless, and simple fleecy flocks will bleat; the horned herds under the care of the rough plowmen will low; the horses of **Silenus** <note>Silenus was the tutor of Bacchus, often depicted riding a donkey; his donkey's braying was said to have once terrified the Giants during their battle with the gods.</note>—so that once again, in favor of the bewildered gods, they may strike terror into the most stupid of those huge giants—will bray. 

Wallowing in his muddy bed, the tusked boars will deafen us with persistent grunting; the tigers, bears, lions, wolves, and deceitful foxes, thrusting their heads from their dens and contemplating the open hunting grounds from the desert heights, will send forth from their wild breasts their grunts, snarls <note>original: "ricti", from the Latin *rictus*, meaning an open-mouthed snarl or grin.</note>, bellows, growls, and howls. In the air and upon the branches of leafy plants, the roosters, eagles, peacocks, cranes, turtledoves, blackbirds, sparrows, nightingales, crows, magpies, ravens, cuckoos, and cicadas will not be negligent in repeating and redoubling their noisy chatter. From the liquid and unstable field, even the white swans, the multicolored ducks, the industrious divers, the marshy bitterns <note>original: "brutii"; likely a reference to a type of marsh bird.</note>, the hoarse geese, and the complaining frogs will strike our ears with their noise. Thus, the warm light of this sun, spread through the air of this more fortunate hemisphere, will be accompanied, saluted, and perhaps annoyed by as many and such various voices as there are spirits who drive them out from the depths of their own breasts.

**Fil.** It is not only ordinary, but also natural and necessary, that every animal makes its own sound; and it is impossible for beasts to form regular accents and articulate sounds like men, as their temperaments are contrary, their tastes diverse, and their nourishments various.

**Arm.** Pray, grant me the liberty to speak my part as well—not concerning the light, but concerning certain circumstances by which the senses are usually not so much consoled as the feelings of whoever sees and considers them are troubled. For the sake of your peace and quiet, which I desire for you with brotherly charity, I would not want these discourses of yours to result in comedies, tragedies, laments, dialogues, or whatever we wish to call them, similar to those which, a short time ago, having come out into the open for a stroll, forced you to remain shut up and retired in your house. <note>Armesso refers to the hostile reception Giordano Bruno received in London after publishing his earlier dialogues, particularly "The Ash Wednesday Supper," which offended many English academics.</note>

**Fil.** Speak freely!

**Arm.** I shall not speak like a holy prophet, like an abstract divine, like one caught up in an apocalypse, nor as the angelicized ass of **Balaam** <note>A biblical reference to the donkey that was given the power of speech to warn the prophet Balaam.</note>; I shall not reason as one inspired by **Bacchus**, nor inflated with wind by the whore Muses of **Parnassus**, or like a Sibyl im— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely heading toward "impazzita" (crazed) or "immortale" (immortal).</note>

<summary>Elitropio uses a vivid metaphor of nature awakening at sunrise to describe how different levels of society will noisily react to Filoteo's philosophy, while Armesso warns Filoteo about the potential for further social persecution.</summary>

**Elitropio.** And that might be enough for a prologue.

**Armesso.** Come then, to get to the rest, I would like to understand from you—leaving aside for a moment the voices and languages regarding the light and splendor that your philosophy might bring—with what words you wish us to specifically salute that "luster of doctrine" which emerges from the book of *The Ash Wednesday Supper*? *Fil.* Do not be surprised, brother, for this was nothing other than a supper, where brains are governed by the passions, which are presented to them by the potency of flavors and the fumes of drinks and foods. Just as the physical and bodily supper may be, so consequently follows the verbal and spiritual one. Thus, this dialogical supper has its various and diverse parts, just as that other kind usually has its own; in the same way, this one has its own conditions, circumstances, and means, which that other could have as its own.

*Arm.* Pray, let me understand you!

*Fil.* There, as is ordinary and proper, one usually finds things for salads, for the main course, for fruit, for everyday use, from the kitchen, from the apothecary <note>original: "speciaria," referring to a spice shop or pharmacy where medicinal ingredients were kept</note>, for the healthy, for the sick, things cold, hot, raw, cooked, from the water, from the land, domestic, wild, roasted, boiled, ripe, and unripe; and things for nourishment alone, and for taste—substantial and light, salty and bland, bitter and sweet, harsh and mild. *Arm.* That is true; but what will you say if, besides this, in your banquet, in your supper, things appear that are good for neither salad, nor meal, nor fruit, nor the usual fare? Things neither cold nor hot, neither raw nor cooked, nor of value for appetite or hunger, nor good for the healthy or the sick? And it is fitting that they do not come from the hands of a cook or an apothecary?

*Fil.* You will see that even in this, our supper is no different from any other that could be. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Filoteo (representing the author) and Armesso. ...our first parent **Adam**, through whom perverse human nature is condemned to always have distastes joined to tastes.

**Arm.** Piously and holily said! Now, what do you answer to those who say that you are a rabid **Cynic**? <note>The Cynics were a school of ancient Greek philosophers known for their rejection of social conventions and their biting, often "dog-like" criticism of others’ follies.</note>

**Fil.** I will easily grant part of this, if not all.

**Arm.** But do you not know that it is not so much a disgrace for a man to receive outrages as it is to commit them?

**Fil.** It is enough for me that my actions are called revenges, and those of others are called offenses.

**Arm.** Even the gods are subject to receiving injuries, suffering infamies, and bearing blame; but to blame, defame, and injure is the mark of the vile, the ignoble, the worthless, and the wicked.

**Fil.** This is true; however, we do not injure, but rather we repel the injuries that are done—not so much to us as to the despised philosophy—acting in such a way that other displeasures are not added to those already received.

**Arm.** Do you wish, then, to appear like a biting dog, so that no one dares to molest you?

**Fil.** It is so; because I desire peace, and I dislike being displeased.

**Arm.** Yes, but they judge that you proceed too rigorously.

**Fil.** So that they do not return a second time, and so that others learn not to come and dispute with me and others by treating these conclusions with such halfway measures <note>original: "mezzi termini," here meaning shallow or evasive arguments</note>.

**Arm.** The offense was private, but the revenge is public.

**Fil.** It is not for this reason unjust; for many errors are committed in private that are justly punished in public.

**Arm.** But by doing this you come to spoil your reputation, and you make yourself more blameworthy than they; because it will be said publicly that you are impatient, whimsical, bizarre, and a scatterbrain.

**Fil.** I do not care, as long as they or others are not bothersome to me anymore. For this reason I show the <term>Cynic's staff</term> <note>The staff was a traditional symbol of the Cynic philosopher, used both for travel and to symbolically beat back ignorance or harassment.</note>, so that they leave me to my own business in peace; and if they do not wish to show me kindness, let them at least not come to exercise their incivility upon me.

**Arm.** Now, does it seem to you that it is the role of a philosopher to dwell on revenge?

**Fil.** If these people who molest me were a **Xantippe**, I would be a **Socrates**. <note>Xantippe was the wife of the philosopher Socrates, famous in history for her supposed argumentative and difficult temperament.</note>

**Arm.** Do you not know that long-suffering or patience becomes everyone? Through it, men come to be like the heroes and eminent gods, who, according to some, are slow to take revenge, and according to others, neither take revenge nor become angry.

**Fil.** You deceive yourself, thinking that I have been dwelling on revenge.

**Arm.** And what then?

**Fil.** I have been dwelling on correction, in the exercise of which we are also like the gods. You know that poor **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire and the forge, often depicted as a hardworking but physically scarred or "lowly" deity among the Olympians.</note>

<summary>Filoteo defends his aggressive and "Cynic" style of argument, claiming it is a defensive "correction" of those who insult philosophy rather than petty personal revenge. ...he was granted a dispensation by **Jupiter** <note>The king of the gods in Roman mythology.</note> to work even on feast days, and that cursed anvil never tires or grows weary of bearing the shocks of so many and such fierce hammers; for no sooner is one raised than another is struck down, to ensure that the righteous lightning bolts, with which the delinquent and guilty are punished, do not fail.

**Arm.** But what if they do not accept you as a philosopher, nor as a doctor, nor as a countryman?

**Fil.** That will not prevent me from being so.

**Arm.** Who vouches for you?

**Fil.** The gods who placed me here; I, who find myself here; and those who have eyes to see me here.

**Arm.** You have very few and little-known witnesses.

**Fil.** Very few and little-known are the true doctors; almost everyone is a true patient. I repeat: they do not have the liberty—some to act, others to allow—that such treatment be given to those who offer honorable wares, whether they be foreigners or not.

**Arm.** Few recognize these wares.

**Fil.** Yet gems are no less precious for that, and we must defend them with all our strength—and cause them to be defended, liberated, and avenged from being trampled by **swinish feet** <note>original: "piè porcini." <summary>Filoteo argues that the true philosopher is a universal citizen and a "doctor" of the mind, whose duty is to protect the dignity of Philosophy from being degraded by ignorant pretenders and pedants.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue regarding the dignity of the philosopher. On the previous page, Filoteo argued that a true philosopher is a "citizen of the world" and should be judged by the truth of his science rather than his origin.</meta>

...to serve as a pastime at home, and as a scarecrow for birds in the countryside.

**Elitropio.** To tell the truth, the company of philosophers is considered more lowly by most of the world than the company of priests; for just as the priesthood has been brought into contempt by all sorts of riff-raff who have been admitted into it, so too has philosophy been held in disdain by all kinds of beastly men who have been given the name.

**Filoteo.** Let us then praise antiquity in its own kind, for in those days philosophers were such that they were promoted to be lawmakers, counselors, and kings; and those who were counselors and kings were such that from that status they rose to become priests. In these times, the majority of priests are such that they are themselves despised, and through them, the divine laws are despised. Almost all those whom we see acting as philosophers are such that they are held in contempt, and through them, the sciences are brought into disdain. Furthermore, among these, the multitude of scoundrels—like stinging nettles—customarily use their contrary dreams to oppress that rare virtue and truth which reveals itself only to the few.

**Armesso.** I have never found a philosopher who grows so angry over the contempt shown to philosophy, nor, Elitropio, do I see anyone as deeply affected by his science as this Teofilo <note>Teofilo, meaning "lover of God," is the primary speaker in Bruno's "Ash Wednesday Supper." Here, the characters are discussing him as both a person and a literary figure.</note>. What would happen if all other philosophers were of the same condition—that is to say, so lacking in patience?

**Elitropio.** These other philosophers have not discovered as much; they do not have as much to watch over, nor as much to defend. They too can easily hold in low esteem a philosophy that is worth nothing, or another that is worth little, or one they do not even know. But the man who has found the truth—which is a hidden treasure—and is inflamed by the beauty of that divine face, becomes no less jealous to ensure she is not defrauded, neglected, or contaminated, than another might be with a sordid passion for gold, rubies <term>carbuncle: a deep-red gemstone, often a garnet or ruby, believed in the Renaissance to glow with its own light</term>, or diamonds, or even for a beautiful female form.

**Armesso.** But let us return to our subject, and come to the point! <note>original: "veniamo al quia," a Latinism meaning "to get to the 'why' or the reason for a thing."</note> They say of you, Teofilo, that in that Supper of yours, you tax and insult an entire city, an entire province, an entire kingdom.

**Filoteo.** Such a thing I never thought, never intended, and never did; and if I had thought, intended, or done it, I would condemn myself as the worst of men, and I would be prepared to offer a thousand retractions, a thousand revocations, a thousand palinodes <term>palinode: a poem or song in which the author retracts a view expressed in a former poem</term>. I would feel this not only if I had insulted a noble and ancient kingdom such as this one <note>Bruno is referring to England, where he lived while writing this dialogue.</note>, but any other, however much it might be considered "barbaric." I say not only any city, however much it might be defamed as uncivil, but any lineage, however much it might be rumored to be savage, or any family, however much it might be called inhospitable. For there can be no kingdom, city, race, or entire house that is, or should be presumed to be, of one single character <note>original: "unore," referring to the medical theory of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which were thought to dictate temperament.</note>, and where there might not be opposites and contraries.

<summary>Filoteo defends the dignity of true philosophy against modern "beastly" philosophers and priests who bring their professions into disrepute. He also denies accusations that he intended to insult the entire kingdom of England in his previous writings.</summary>

**Filoteo.** Now, what are these named customs? Can similar, worse, and much stranger ones in kind, species, and number not be found in the most excellent parts and provinces of the world? This remains true even if one were to further exaggerate what our own poets have sung of her, who no less make her the teacher of all vices, deceits, avarice, and cruelties.

**Elitropio.** This is certain according to the principles of your philosophy, by which you maintain that <term>opposites coincide in their principles</term> <note>This refers to "Coincidentia Oppositorum," a core concept in Bruno’s philosophy where extreme opposites (like greatest and smallest, or vice and virtue) meet at their source.</note> and proximate subjects; because those same minds which are most fit for high, virtuous, and noble undertakings, if they be perverted, fall headlong into extreme vices. Thus, in different ways, it seems the same measure of perfections and imperfections is given to many nations.

**Filoteo.** You speak the truth.

<meta>This page continues the critique of the University of Oxford. Filoteo and his companions are now mocking the requirements for obtaining a degree there.</meta>

...sity, to which they are bound by oath, entail that **no one may be promoted to the mastership or doctorate of philosophy and theology, unless he has drunk from the fountain of Aristotle.** <note>original: "nullus ad philosophiae et theologiae magisterium et doctoratum promoveatur, nisi epotaverit e fonte Aristotelis." This refers to the strict academic statutes of the time that mandated Aristotelianism as the only path to a degree.</note>

Since water is drawn from these three fountains to make beer and ale <note>In the 16th century, beer and ale were the primary drinks at universities because water was often unsafe; Bruno is joking that the students "drink" the ancient philosophers only because their names were put on the wells used for brewing.</note>—water which even the oxen and horses do not fail to drink—it follows that there is no person who, having stayed less than three or four days in those studies and colleges, does not come to be soaked not only by the fountain of **Aristotle**, but also those of **Pythagoras** and **Plato**.

Now then, such being the common crowd of doctors among us in this age—excepting, however, the reputation of certain celebrated men for their eloquence, learning, and civil courtesy, such as a **Tobie Matthew**, a **Culpepper** <note>Tobie Matthew was the Dean of Christ Church and later Archbishop of York; Martin Culpepper was the Warden of New College, Oxford. Therefore, those who are noble by lineage or other circumstances, even though the principal part of nobility—learning—is added to them, are ashamed to take degrees and be called doctors, for being learned is enough for them; and you will find a greater number of these in the courts than there are pedants <note>A person who is excessively concerned with minor details or rules, or with displaying academic learning.</note> to be found in the university.

Fil. Do not complain, **Armesso**! Because in all places where there are doctors and priests, one finds both types of seeds. Arm. Now let us leave these subjects! What book is this you hold in your hand?

Fil. They are certain dialogues.

**Filoteo:** What then?

**Armesso:** Others [dialogues], in which the cause, the principle, and the one are treated, according to our way of thinking.

**Filoteo:** Which interlocutors? Perhaps we have some other devil like Frulla or Prudenzio <note>Characters from Bruno’s earlier work, *The Ash Wednesday Supper*, known for being troublesome or foolish.</note>, who will put us in some fresh trouble?

**Armesso:** Here, for one, you will find that learned, honest, loving, well-bred, and so faithful friend, **Alexander Dickson**, whom the Nolan <note>Bruno refers to himself as "the Nolan," as he was born in Nola, Italy.</note> loves as his own eyes; he is the reason this matter has been brought into the field. For the second, you have **Theophilus**, who is I; according to the occasion, I come to distinguish, define, and demonstrate regarding the subject matter. A derogatory term for those who "cook up" their style by copying the Roman orator Cicero without original thought.</note>, thinks that here **Demosthenes** is resurrected, here **Tullius** [Cicero] flourishes, here **Sallust** lives! He is an **Argus** <note>A hundred-eyed giant from Greek myth; meaning he watches every tiny detail.</note> who sees every letter, every syllable, every word. Here **he calls the shadows of the silent** <note>original: "Radamanto umbras vocat ille silentum." Another underworld judge who decides fates; the pedant is judging words as if they were souls.</note>. 

They call orations to examination and discuss phrases, saying: "These taste of the poet, these of the comedian, this of the orator! This is heavy, this is light, that is sublime, that other is a **humble style of speaking** <note>original: "humile dicendi genus." A technical term in rhetoric for the simplest level of style.</note>." This oration is rough—it would be smooth if it were formed thus. This writer is an infant, little studious of antiquity; **he does not smell of the man from Arpinum, he lacks the taste of Latium** <note>original: "non redolet Arpinatem, desipit Latium." A snobbish way of saying the writer doesn't sound like Cicero (who was from Arpinum) and lacks true Roman/Latin character.</note>. This word is not Tuscan; it is not used by **Boccaccio**, **Petrarch**, or other approved authors. One should not write *homo* [man], but *omo*; not *honore* [honor], but *onore*; not *Polyhymnio*, but *Poliinnio*. With this he triumphs, he is content with himself, and these things please him more than any other...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Bruno’s *Cabala del cavallo pegaseo* (The Cabala of the Pegasean Horse), shifting from the description of the pedantic grammarian's self-importance to Elitropio’s defense of "sweet madness" and subjective happiness. ...his own affairs; he is a Jupiter, who from his high watchtower gazes upon and considers the life of other men subject to so many errors, calamities, miseries, and useless labors; he alone is happy, he alone lives a celestial life, when he contemplates his own divinity in the mirror of a collection of passages, a dictionary, a Calepino <note>Ambrogio Calepino was the author of a famous 15th-century Latin dictionary; his name became a synonym for "dictionary."</note>, a lexicon, a cornucopia, a Nizolio <note>Marius Nizolius was a 16th-century scholar famous for his Ciceronian lexicon; Bruno uses these names to mock those who rely on reference books rather than original thought.</note>. Endowed with this self-sufficiency, while everyone else is just one person, he alone is everything. If he happens to laugh, he is called Democritus; if he happens to grieve, he is called Heraclitus; if he disputes, he is called Chrysippus; if he discourses, he is called Aristotle; if he creates chimeras, he is named Plato; if he bellows out a little sermon, he is titled Demosthenes; if he constructs Virgil, he is Maro <note>Publius Vergilius Maro is the full name of the poet Virgil.</note>. Following the introductory matter and the praise of Queen Elizabeth I on the previous page, the scene shifts to a formal philosophical discussion. # SECOND DIALOGUE.

->Interlocutors:<-

->**Alexander Dickson. Teofilo. Gervasio. Polyhymnius.**<-

---

->**Dickson.**<-

**By** your leave, Master Polyhymnius, and you, Gervasio, do not interrupt our discourse any further!
**Pol.** Let it be so! <note>original: "Fiat!"</note>
**Ger.** If this man, who is the master <note>original: "magister"</note>, speaks, I certainly cannot remain silent.
**Dic.** So you say, Teofilo, that everything which is not the first principle and first cause has a principle and a cause?
**Teo.** Undoubtedly, and without any controversy.
**Dic.** Do you believe, for this reason, that he who knows caused and originated things also knows the cause and principle?
**Teo.** Not easily the proximate cause and proximate principle; and with the greatest difficulty—even as a trace <note>original: "vestigio." In Renaissance thought, a "trace" or "vestige" is a faint sign or footprint left by God in the physical world.</note>—the first cause and principle.
**Dic.** Now, how do you intend for things—which have a first and proximate cause and principle—to be truly known, if according to the nature of the <term>efficient cause|The agent or force that brings something into being; for example, a carpenter is the efficient cause of a table.</term>, which is one of those factors that contribute to the real knowledge of things, they are hidden?
**Teo.** I grant that it is an easy thing to organize a demonstrative doctrine, but the demonstration itself is difficult. It is a very easy thing to arrange the causes, circumstances, and methods of doctrines; but then our methodologists and analysts perform poorly when they put into execution their instruments, the principles of their methods, and the "art of arts."
**Ger.** Like those who know how to make such beautiful swords, but do not know how to use them?
**Pol.** Precisely! <note>original: "Ferme!"—a Latin adverb meaning 'firmly' or 'exactly,' often used by pedants to show agreement.</note>
**Ger.** May your eyes be fixed <note>Gervasio makes a pun on Polyhymnius’s Latin word "ferme" and the Italian "fermati" (stopped or fixed), essentially telling the pedant to keep his eyes shut.</note>, so that you may never open them!
**Teo.** I say, however, that it is not required of the <term>natural philosopher|A historical term for a scientist who studies the physical world and its laws.</term> to bring forth all causes and principles, but only the physical ones, and among these, the principal and proper ones. Thus, although things are said to have that [first] cause and that [first] principle because they depend upon the first principle and cause, nevertheless, there is no such necessary relationship that from the knowledge of the one, the knowledge of the other is inferred; and therefore, it is not required that they be organized within the same discipline.

<meta>This page continues the Second Dialogue from page 232. Teofilo is explaining why the first cause (God) cannot be fully understood through its effects (the physical universe), building on the previous discussion regarding the difficulty of philosophical demonstration.</meta>

**Dic.** How is this so?

**Teo.** Because from the knowledge of all dependent things, we cannot infer any other information about the first principle and cause, except in a way less effective than a **trace** <note>original: "vestigio." In Renaissance philosophy, a vestige is a faint footprint or mark left by God in the physical world.</note>, given that everything derives from his will or goodness, which is the principle of his operation, from which the universal effect proceeds. This same thing can be considered in artificial things: so much so that he who sees the statue does not see the sculptor; he who sees the portrait of Helen does not see **Apelles** <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece, often cited as the pinnacle of artistic skill.</note>, but sees the effect of the operation, which comes from the goodness of the genius of Apelles. All of this is an effect of the **accidents** and circumstances of the **substance** of that man, who, as for his absolute being, is not known at all.

**Dic.** So much so that knowing the universe is like knowing nothing of the being and substance of the first principle, because it is like knowing the <term>accidents of accidents|In Aristotelian logic, an 'accident' is a non-essential quality (like color or size). Knowing an 'accident of an accident' implies being two levels of reality removed from the actual essence or substance.</term>.

**Teo.** That is how it is; but I would not want you to imagine that I mean there are accidents in God, or that he can be known through his accidents.

**Dic.** I do not attribute such a dull wit to you, and I know that it is one thing to say there are accidents, another to say they are *his* accidents, and yet another to say that everything which is foreign to the divine nature is *like* his accidents. In this last way, I believe you mean that they are the effects of the divine operation; these, although they are the substance of things—indeed, even the natural substances themselves—are nonetheless like the most remote accidents for us, in terms of letting us reach an apprehensive knowledge of the divine supernatural essence.

**Teo.** You say it well.

**Dic.** Here, then, it follows that we can know nothing of the divine substance, both because it is infinite and because it is most distant from those effects which are the final limit of the path of our <term>discursive faculty|The human ability to reason step-by-step from one premise to another, as opposed to direct intuitive understanding.</term>. We can know it only by way of a trace, as the <term>Platonists</term> say; by a remote effect, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> say; by "garments," as the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Jewish mystics who studied the Kabbalah.</note> say; by "shoulders or back parts," as the <term>Talmudists</term> say; and by "mirror, shadow, and enigma," as the <term>Apocalytics</term> say.

**Teo.** Moreover, because we do not see this universe perfectly—whose substance and principal part is so difficult to comprehend—it happens that with far less reason do we know the first principle and cause through its effect than Apelles might be known through his fashioned statues. For we can see all of these statues and examine them part by part, but we cannot see the great and infinite effect of the divine power. Therefore, that comparison must be understood without proportional equivalence.

**Dic.** That is so, and that is how I understand it.

<summary>Teofilo explains that God's essence is unknowable through the physical world, which acts only as a remote "trace" or "shadow" of the divine. He uses the analogy of an artist and his work to show that while we see the effect, the creator's true nature remains hidden.</summary>

**Teo.** It would be best, then, to refrain from speaking of such a high matter.

**Dic.** I agree, because it is morally and theologically sufficient to know the first principle only insofar as the higher deities have revealed it and divine men have declared it. Furthermore, not only every law and theology, but even all reformed philosophies <note>In Bruno’s time, this referred to the "new" philosophies emerging during the Renaissance that challenged traditional medieval Scholasticism.</note> conclude that it is the mark of a profane and turbulent spirit to want to rush headlong into demanding reasons for, and wanting to define, those things which are above the sphere of our intelligence.

**Teo.** Well said. But those who are worthy of rebuke are not so much those who refrain, as those who are most worthy of praise: those who strive toward the knowledge of this principle and cause to learn of its greatness as much as possible. They do this by observing with the eyes of regulated senses these magnificent stars and flashing bodies, which are so many inhabited worlds, and great animals <note>Bruno famously proposed that planets and stars were "celestial animals"—living, ensouled beings moving through an infinite cosmos.</note>, and most excellent deities. These seem to be, and indeed are, innumerable worlds not much different from this one which contains us. Since it is impossible for these to have their being from themselves—seeing as they are composite and dissoluble, though they are not for that reason destined to be dissolved, as was well said in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato which discusses the nature of the physical world and the "Demiurge" or creator.</note>—it is necessary that they know a principle and a cause. Consequently, through the greatness of their being, living, and operating, they show and preach in an infinite space with innumerable voices the infinite excellence and majesty of their first principle and cause. Leaving aside then, as you say, that consideration insofar as it is superior to every sense and intellect, let us consider the principle and cause insofar as it is either nature itself as a **trace** <note>original: "vestigio." A philosophical term for the "footprint" or mark left by God in the physical world.</note>, or as it shines forth within the scope and lap of nature. Ask me, then, in order, if you want me to respond in order!

**Dic.** I shall do so. But first, since you are accustomed to saying "cause" and "principle," I would like to know if these are taken by you as synonymous names?

**Teo.** No.

**Dic.** Well then, what is the difference between one term and the other?

**Teo.** I reply that when we call God the "first principle" and "first cause," we mean the same thing under different aspects; but when we speak of "principles" and "causes" within nature, we are speaking of different things with their own different aspects. We call God the **first principle** insofar as all things come after him according to a certain order of priority and posteriority—whether according to nature, duration, or dignity. We call God the **first cause** insofar as all things are distinct from him, as the effect is from the efficient producer, or the thing produced from the one producing it. These two aspects are different because not every thing that is prior and more worthy is the "cause" of that which is posterior and less worthy; and not every

thing, which is a cause, is prior and more worthy than that which is caused, as is quite clear to anyone who reasons well.
**Dic.** Now tell me, in terms of natural philosophy <note>The study of nature and the physical universe that was the precursor to modern science.</note>, what is the difference between a cause and a principle?
**Teo.** Although the terms are sometimes used interchangeably, nonetheless, speaking strictly, not everything that is a principle is a cause. For example: a point is the principle of a line, but is not its cause; the instant is the principle of an operation; the starting point is the principle of motion, but not its cause; premises are the principle of an argument, but are not its cause. Therefore, "principle" is a more general term than "cause."
**Dic.** Therefore, by narrowing these two terms to certain specific meanings—following the custom of those who speak more precisely—I believe you mean that a *principle* is that which intrinsically contributes to the constitution of a thing and remains in the effect. For example, matter and form, which remain in the composite whole, or even the elements from which a thing is composed and into which it eventually resolves. By *cause*, do you mean that which contributes to the production of things from the outside, and has its being external to the composition, such as the efficient cause <term>the agent or force that brings something into being</term> and the final cause <term>the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists</term> toward which the produced thing is directed?
**Teo.** Very well put.
**Dic.** Now, since we have resolved the difference between these things, I first desire that you present your view regarding the causes, and then regarding the principles. As for the causes, I would first like to know about the primary efficient cause, and the formal cause, which you say is joined to the efficient; in addition to the final cause, which is understood as the motive force of the latter.
**Teo.** Your proposed order of inquiry pleases me greatly. Now, regarding the effective cause, I say that the universal efficient cause is the **universal intellect**, which is the primary and principal faculty of the **soul of the world**, which itself is the world's universal form.
**Dic.** You seem to me not only to agree with the opinion of Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who proposed that the universe was composed of four elements moved by the forces of Love and Strife.</note>, but to be more certain, more distinct, and more explicit; furthermore, as far as I can see, more profound. Therefore, you would do us a great favor by coming to a detailed declaration of the whole matter, beginning by saying what this universal intellect is.
**Teo.** The universal intellect is the innermost, most real, and proper faculty, and the potential part of the soul of the world. This is one and the same thing that fills the whole, illuminates the universe, and directs nature to produce its species as is fitting. Thus, it relates to the production of natural things in the same way our own intellect relates to the proper production of rational ideas. This is called by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that numbers and harmony were the principles of all things.</note> the motor and agitator of the universe, as the poet explained when he said:
> *A mind infused through all the limbs* <note>Original Latin: "Totamque infusa per artus mens." A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the spirit that sustains the universe from within.</note>

*...moves the mass, and mingles with the whole body.* <note>original: "agitat molem, et toto se corpore miscet." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 6, lines 726–727, describing the world-soul.</note> \*) This is named by the Platonists the world-builder. This craftsman, they say, proceeds from the superior world <note>The realm of pure ideas or divine intellect.</note>, which is entirely one, to this sensible world <note>The physical world we perceive through our senses.</note>, which is divided into many, where not only friendship but also discord reigns due to the distance between the parts. This intellect, by infusing and extending something of itself into matter, while itself remaining quiet and immobile, produces everything. It is called by the Magi <term>Magi: ancient practitioners of secret wisdom or natural magic</term> most fertile in seeds, or even the sower, because it is that which impregnates matter with all forms, and according to their logic and condition, proceeds to figure, form, and weave them into so many wonderful orders, which cannot be attributed to chance, nor to any other principle that cannot distinguish and order.

Orpheus calls it the eye of the world, because it sees all natural things within and without, so that everything, not only intrinsically but also extrinsically, comes to be produced and maintained in its proper symmetry. By Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who theorized that the world was composed of four elements moved by Love and Strife.</note> it is called the "distinguisher," as it never tires of unfolding the forms confused within the womb of matter, and of sparking the generation of one thing from the corruption of another. Plotinus calls it father and progenitor, because it distributes the seeds in the field of nature, and is the immediate dispenser of forms.

By us, it is called the internal artificer, because it forms matter and figures it from within—just as from within the seed or root it sends forth and unfolds the stem; from within the stem it pushes out the branches; from within the branches it forms the twigs; from within these it unfolds the buds; from within it forms, figures, and weaves the leaves, flowers, and fruits, as if from nerves; and from within, at certain times, it recalls its juices from the leaves and fruits to the twigs, from the twigs to the branches, from the branches to the stem, and from the stem to the root. Similarly, in animals, unfolding its work from the first seed and from the center of the heart to the external members, and from those at the end folding the unfolded faculties back toward the heart, it acts as if it were re-gathering the already extended threads. 

Now, if we believe that a work we know how to craft with a certain order and imitation upon the surface of matter is not produced without thought and intellect—such as when, by carving and sculpting wood, we make the image of a horse appear—how much greater must we believe that intellect-artificer to be, which from the interior of the seminal matter strengthens the bones, extends the cartilages, carves out the arteries, breathes into the pores, weaves the fibers, branches out the nerves, and with such admirable mastery disposes the whole? How much greater, I say, is this artificer, who is not attached to a single part of the matter, but works continuously, "all in all"? There are three sorts of intellect: the divine, which is all; this mundane intellect, which makes all; <note>The text likely continues to the third type, the human or particular intellect, on the following page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the Second Dialogue of "On the Cause, Principle, and Unity." Teofilo has just identified the Universal Intellect as the "world-builder" or "efficient cause." He is now explaining how this intellect operates both from within and outside of physical matter.</meta>

<page-num>237</page-num>

...all other particulars, which comprise the whole; for it is necessary that between the extremes one finds this middle ground, which is the true **efficient cause** <term>Efficient cause: the agent or force that brings something into being, like a carpenter making a chair</term>, being not only extrinsic but also intrinsic to all natural things.

**Dic.** I would like to see you distinguish how you understand it to be an extrinsic cause, and how it is intrinsic?

**Teo.** I call it an **extrinsic cause** because, as the efficient agent, it is not a part of the composite things and products it creates. It is an **intrinsic cause** in the sense that it does not operate *upon* matter from the outside, but rather from within, as was said just a moment ago. Thus, it is an extrinsic cause insofar as its being is distinct from the substance and essence of its effects, and because its existence is not like that of things that are born and die <note>original: "generabili e corrottibili"</note>, even though it concerns itself with them. It is an intrinsic cause in regard to the act of its operation.

**Dic.** It seems to me that you have spoken enough about the efficient cause; now I would like to understand what you mean by the **formal cause** <term>Formal cause: the "blueprint" or essential pattern that makes a thing what it is</term> joined to the efficient one. Is it perhaps the **ideal reason** <note>The "ideal reason" refers to the Platonic idea that there is a perfect mental concept for every object before it is made.</note>? For every agent that operates according to an intellectual rule only seeks to bring something into effect according to some intention, and this intention requires the mental grasp of something; and this is nothing other than the form of the thing to be produced. Therefore, this intellect—which has the faculty to produce every species and to draw them out with such beautiful architecture from the potential of matter into actual existence—must already possess them all according to a certain formal reason. Without this, the agent could not proceed with its manufacture, just as it is impossible for a sculptor to execute various statues without having first thought out their different forms.

**Teo.** You understand it excellently. For I want two kinds of forms to be considered: one, which is the cause—not the efficient agent itself, but the means through which the agent effects change; the other is the **principle**, which is raised up from matter by the efficient agent.

**Dic.** The goal and the **final cause** <term>Final cause: the ultimate purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists</term> proposed by the efficient agent is the perfection of the universe. This perfection consists in all forms having actual existence in different parts of matter. In this goal, the intellect takes such delight and pleasure that it never tires of raising all sorts of forms from matter, as it seems **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who believed the universe was driven by the forces of Love (unifying) and Strife (dividing).</note> also intended.

**Teo.** Very well said. And I add to this that, just as this efficient agent is universal in the universe, and is special and particular in the parts and members of it, so too are its form and its goal.

**Dic.** Now enough has been said of causes; let us proceed to reason about **principles**!

**Teo.** To come to the constitutive principles of things, I will first speak of **form**, as it is in a certain way the same as the efficient cause already mentioned: because the intellect, which is a...

The dialogue shifts from discussing the "causes" of things (why they are made) to their "principles" (what they are made of), starting with the concept of Form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 237 regarding the nature of the Universal Intellect and the World Soul. Teofilo is further defining how the World Soul acts as both an internal "principle" (shaping things from within) and an external "cause" (governing from above).</meta>

<page-num>238</page-num>

...power of the **world soul** <term>World Soul (Anima Mundi): An intrinsic force believed by many ancient and Renaissance philosophers to animate the entire universe, just as a human soul animates a body.</term>, it has been called the proximate efficient cause of all natural things.

**Dic.** But how can the same subject be both a **principle** and a **cause** of natural things? How can it have the nature of an extrinsic <note>extrinsic: acting from the outside</note> part, and not an intrinsic <note>intrinsic: acting from within</note> part?

**Teo.** I say that this is not an inconsistency, considering that the soul is in the body like a **pilot in a ship**; which pilot, insofar as he is moved together with the ship, is a part of it; but considered insofar as he governs and moves it, he is not understood as a part, but as a distinct efficient cause. So the soul of the universe, insofar as it animates and informs, comes to be an intrinsic and formal part of it; but as it directs and governs, it is not a part, and does not have the nature of a principle, but of a cause. This is even granted to us by **Aristotle** himself <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), the Greek philosopher whose views on the soul and nature were the standard for centuries, though Bruno often challenges them.</note>, who, although he denies that the soul has the same relationship to the body as the pilot to the ship, nevertheless, considering it according to that power with which it understands and knows, he does not dare to call it the "act" and "form" of the body. Instead, seeing it as an efficient cause separated from matter according to its being, he says that it is something that **"comes from outside"** <note>original: "viene di fuora". This refers to Aristotle's concept of the 'active intellect' which enters the human from elsewhere.</note>, according to its subsistence being divided from the composite thing.

**Dic.** I approve of what you say; for if being separate from the body is appropriate for the intellectual power of our soul, and having the nature of an efficient cause, much more should it be affirmed of the world soul. For **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), the founder of Neoplatonism, whose mystical philosophy heavily influenced Bruno.</note> says, writing against the **Gnostics**, that the world soul rules the universe with greater ease than our soul rules our body. Furthermore, there is a great difference in the way that the former and the latter govern. The former [the world soul], not being bound, rules the world in such a way that it does not itself bind what it takes; it does not suffer from other things, nor with other things; without impediment it rises to higher things. In giving life and perfection to the body, it does not receive any imperfection from it, and therefore it is eternally conjoined to the same subject. This other one [the human soul] is clearly of the opposite condition. Now if, according to your principle, the perfections found in lower natures must be attributed and known more highly in superior natures, we must without any doubt affirm the distinction you have brought forward. This is affirmed not only of the soul of the world, but also of **each star**, being—as the said philosopher holds—that they all have the power to contemplate God, the principles of all things, and the distribution of the orders of the universe. And he maintains that this does not happen by way of memory, discourse, or consideration, because every one of their works is an eternal work, and it is not an act that can be new to them. Therefore they do nothing that is not entirely fitting, perfect, with a certain and prefixed order, without the act of cogitation <note>cogitation: the process of thinking or pondering. Plotinus argues that higher beings act by their very nature without needing to "stop and think."</note>; just as, for example, a perfect writer or lute- <note>The text ends mid-word: "cita-", likely referring to a *citaredo* or lute-player who plays perfectly by instinct without needing to think about each finger movement.</note>

<summary>Teofilo explains that the World Soul is both a part of the universe (as its formal principle) and a separate governor (as its efficient cause), using the analogy of a pilot in a ship. He cites Aristotle and Plotinus to argue that superior beings like the World Soul or the stars operate through eternal, effortless contemplation rather than laborious thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Teofilo’s explanation of how the Universal Intellect and the World Soul operate within nature. It picks up from the discussion on page 238 regarding Aristotle's view of the soul as an efficient cause that governs matter without being a mere physical part of it.</meta>

->239<-

...[Aristo]tle <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing the reference to the Greek philosopher Aristotle from the previous page.</note> also shows this when he argues that just because nature does not deliberate or rethink its actions, one cannot conclude that she works without intellect or a final purpose. He notes that exquisite musicians and writers are less consciously attentive to what they are doing and yet they do not make mistakes, unlike the clumsy and unskilled who, by overthinking and straining, produce less perfect work, and not without error.

**Teo.** You understand it. Now let us come to the specifics. It seems to me that those who refuse to understand or affirm that the world and its members are **animated** <term>animated: Endowed with a soul or life-force (from the Latin 'anima').</term> detract from the divine goodness and the excellence of this "great animal" and image of the **First Principle** <term>First Principle: A philosophical term for the ultimate source or cause of all existence, often identified with God.</term>. It is as if God were envious of His own image, or as if an architect did not love his own singular work—of which **Plato** <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BCE) famously described the universe as a "living creature" in his dialogue *Timaeus*.</note> says that the Creator took delight in His handiwork because of the resemblance to Himself that He saw reflected in it. And truly, what more beautiful thing than this universe could present itself to the eyes of divinity? And since the universe consists of various parts, to which of them should beauty be more attributed than to the **formal principle** <term>formal principle: The internal "blueprint" or soul that gives a thing its specific shape and nature, as opposed to its raw material.</term>? I leave aside a thousand natural reasons for a better and more detailed discussion, beyond this topical or logical one.

**Dic.** I do not mind that you exert yourself in this, given that there is no philosopher of any reputation—even among the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they held their lessons in ancient Athens.</term>—who does not maintain that the world and its celestial spheres are in some way animated. I would now like to understand: in what way do you propose this **form** enters into the **matter** of the universe?

**Teo.** It joins with it in such a way that the nature of the body—which, in itself, is not beautiful—becomes a participant in beauty to the extent that it is capable. For there is no beauty that does not consist in some **species** <note>original: "specie." In this context, it refers to the outward appearance or "type" that defines a thing's identity.</note> or form; and there is no form that is not produced by the soul.

**Dic.** I seem to hear something very new. Do you mean perhaps that not only the form of the universe, but every single form of natural things is a soul?

**Teo.** Yes.

**Dic.** Are all things then animated?

**Teo.** Yes.

**Dic.** Now, who will agree with you on this?

**Teo.** And who can disprove it with reason?

**Dic.** It is common sense that not all things are alive.

**Teo.** The most common sense is not the truest.

**Dic.** I can easily believe that this position can be defended. But it is not enough for a thing to be "defensible" to make it true; it must also be possible to prove it.

**Teo.** That is not difficult. Are there not philosophers who say the world is animated?

**Dic.** There are indeed many, and the most eminent ones.

<summary>Teofilo argues that the entire universe and every individual thing within it is "animated" or possesses a soul, suggesting that beauty and form can only originate from a spiritual principle. This challenges the common-sense view that some matter is inanimate, asserting instead that life is a fundamental property of all existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Teofilo, Dicsono, Polinnio, and Gervasio regarding the animation of the universe. Having established that the World Soul acts as an internal formal principle, the speakers now debate whether this life-force extends to every individual part of the world, no matter how small or seemingly inanimate.</meta>

**Teo.** Now, why will these same people not say that all the parts of the world are **animated** <term>animated: Possessing a soul or vital principle.</term>?

**Dic.** They certainly say it, but only regarding the principal parts—those that are true parts of the world. They argue, with no less reason, that the soul is "all in the whole world" and "all in whatever part of it," just as the soul of animals perceptible to us is entirely present throughout their whole bodies.

**Teo.** Now, which parts do you think they consider *not* to be true parts of the world?

**Dic.** Those which are not "first bodies," as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who walked about (peripateo) while teaching.</note> call them—such as the earth with its waters and other components which, according to your view, constitute the whole animal: the moon, the sun, and other bodies. Besides these principal animals, there are those things that are not primary parts of the universe, of which some are said to have a vegetative soul, others a sensitive soul, and others an intellectual soul.

**Teo.** Now, if the soul—because it is in the whole—is also in the parts, why do you not want it to be in the parts of the parts?

**Dic.** I do want that; but only in the parts of the parts of **animated things**.

**Teo.** Now, which are these things that are not animated, or are not parts of animated things?

**Dic.** Does it seem to you that we have few of them before our eyes? All things that have no life.

**Teo.** And which are the things that have no life, or at least no vital principle?

**Dic.** Do you mean to say, then, that in general there is no thing that does not have a soul, or at least does not have a principle and germ of life?

**Teo.** That is exactly what I mean in the end.

**Pol.** So a dead body has a soul? Then my <term>wooden clogs</term> <note>original: *calopodj*</note>, my slippers, my boots, my spurs, and my ring and <term>gloves</term> <note>original: *chiroteche*</note> are all animated? My gown and my cloak are animated?

**Ger.** Yes, sir; yes, Master Polinnio. Why not? I certainly believe that your gown and your cloak are quite "animated" when they contain an animal like you inside them; boots and spurs are animated when they contain feet; the hat is animated when it contains the head, which is not without a soul; and the stable is also animated when it contains the horse, the mule, or your lordship. Do you not understand it this way, Teofilo? Does it not seem to you that I have understood it better than the **Lord Master** <note>original Latin: *dominus magister*</note>?

<margin>*) Virgil, Eclogues 3, 1.</margin>
<margin>**) A Greek word, meaning inept.</margin>
**Pol.** **Whose flock [is this]?** <note>original Latin: *Cujum pecus?*</note> *) How is it that one finds asses who are **again and again** <note>original Latin: *etiam atque etiam*</note> subtle? Do you have the audacity, you **unrefined clod** <term>unrefined clod: One lacking a sense of beauty or education.</term> <note>original Greek: *apirocalo*</note> **), you beginner of the alphabet, to wish to equate yourself to a **headmaster** <term>headmaster: A chief teacher.</term> <note>original Greek: *archididascalo*</note> and a moderator of a **school of learning** <term>school of learning: Literally a "Minervan game," referring to an academy of arts and wisdom.</term> <note>original: *ludo minervale*</note> such as I?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Teofilo, Dicsono, Polinnio, and Gervasio. Having previously discussed whether the World Soul is present in all parts of the universe, the characters now debate the specific nature of "animation" in seemingly inanimate objects like wood, stone, or glass.</meta>
