**Ger.** Peace be with you, master; I am the servant of servants, and the footstool of your feet! <note>original: "Pax vobis, domine magister, servus sum servorum, et scabellnm pedum tuorum!" Gervasio uses a mock-humble Latin greeting.</note>
**Pol.** May God curse you for ages and ages! <note>original: "Maledicat te deus in saecula saeculorum!" Polinnio responds with a traditional liturgical curse formula, highlighting the tension between the characters.</note>
**Dic.** Without anger! Let us be the ones to determine these matters.
**Pol.** Let Theophilus, then, pursue his dogmas! <note>original: "Prosequatur ergo sua dogmata Theophilus!"</note>
**Teo.** I shall do so. I say, then, that the table as a table is not **animated**, nor the garment, nor the leather as leather, nor the glass as glass; but, as natural and composite things, they possess within themselves matter and form. No matter how small and minute a thing may be, it has within itself a portion of **spiritual substance**, which, if it finds the subject disposed, extends itself to become a plant, to become an animal, and receives the members of whatever body is commonly called **animated**; for spirit is found in all things, and there is no tiny corpuscle that does not contain within itself such a portion that it does not animate it.
**Pol.** Therefore, whatever exists is an animal. <note>original: "Ergo quidquid est, animal est."</note>
**Teo.** Not all things that have a soul are called "animals."
**Dic.** So, at the very least, all things have life?
**Teo.** I concede that all things have a soul within them, they have life according to their substance, though not according to the act and operation recognizable by all the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, whom Bruno often critiques for their rigid definitions.</note>, and those who define life and soul according to certain criteria that are far too coarse.
**Dic.** You reveal to me a plausible way in which one might maintain the opinion of <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who famously claimed that "everything is in everything."</note>, who held that "everything is in everything"; because, if the spirit, or soul, or universal form is in all things, then everything can be produced from everything.
**Teo.** I do not say "plausible," but "true"; for that spirit is found in all things, which, if they are not animals, are at least **animated**. If they are not sensitive of their animality and life in an active sense, they are nonetheless so according to the principle and a certain primary act of animality and life. I will say even more, for I wish to pause and consider the properties of many small stones and gems which, when broken and cut and placed in disordered pieces, have certain powers to alter the spirit and engender new affections and passions in the soul, not just in the body. And we know that such effects do not proceed, nor can they originate, from purely material qualities, but necessarily refer to a symbolic, vital, and animal principle. Furthermore, we see the same thing visibly in dead stalks and roots which, by purging and gathering humors and altering the spirits, necessarily show the effects of life.
I will also mention that it is not without reason that <term>necromancers</term> <note>Those who practice magic involving the dead; Bruno suggests here that even dead matter retains a "spark" of life.</note> hope to effect many things through the bones of the dead, believing that those bones retain, if not the very same life, then at least a certain kind of act of life that serves their purpose for extraordinary effects. Other occasions will allow me to discourse at greater length concerning the mind, the spirit, the soul, and the life that penetrates all, is in all, and moves...

<summary>Teofilo argues that all matter, no matter how small or seemingly inanimate, contains a spiritual substance and is "animated," even if it is not a biological "animal." He connects this to Anaxagoras's idea that everything exists in everything and uses the medicinal powers of gems and the practices of necromancy as evidence of residual life in all things.</summary>

**Dic.** This seems to me in conformity not only with the thought of *Pythagoras*, whose opinion the poet recites *) when he says:

> *In the beginning, the heaven, the earth, and the watery plains,*
> *and the glowing orb of the moon, and the Titan stars,*

but also with the thought of the theologian, who says: **) The spirit fills and occupies the earth, and that which contains all things. <note>The "theologian" refers to the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Bible. **Teo.** If then the spirit, the soul, and life are found in all things and, according to certain degrees, fill all matter, they certainly become the true <term>act</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" is the state of being fully realized, as opposed to "potency" or potential.</note> and the true <term>form</term> <note>The "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> of all things. The **Soul of the World** is therefore the constitutive <term>formal principle</term> of the universe and of all that it contains. I say that, if life is found in all things, the soul becomes the form of all things; it presides over matter everywhere and rules in composite things, effecting the composition and consistency of their parts. Therefore, it appears that persistence belongs no less to such a form than it does to matter. I understand this form to be one in all things; however, according to the diversity of the dispositions of matter, and according to the faculty of the active and passive material principles, it comes to produce different configurations and effect different powers. At times it shows the effect of life without sense, sometimes the effect of life and sense without intellect, and at times it seems that all its powers are suppressed and restrained, either by the weakness or by some other condition of the matter. Thus, though this form changes its seat and its circumstances, it is impossible for it to be annihilated, because **spiritual substance** is no less subsistent than **material substance**. Therefore, only external forms change and are even annulled, because they are not "things," but *belong* to things; they are not substances, but are the <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities, like color or weight, that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note> and circumstances of substances.

**Pol.** Not beings, but of beings. <note>original: "Non entia, sed entium." A Latin philosophical maxim suggesting that accidents do not have an independent existence but only exist through the substances they inhabit.</note>

**Dic.** Certainly; if any part of the substances were annihilated, the world would be emptied.

**Teo.** Thus we have an intrinsic formal principle, eternal and subsistent, incomparably better than that which the sophists have feigned, who concern themselves with accidents; they are ignorant of the substance of things and end up positing corruptible substances...

<summary>Teofilo argues that the World Soul is the eternal, formal principle that animates all matter, drawing on Virgil and scripture to suggest that spirit contains matter rather than the reverse. He distinguishes between eternal spiritual substance and transitory "accidents" or external forms.</summary>

corruptible; for this reason they give the name <term>substance</term> <note>In philosophy, "substance" refers to that which exists in itself, rather than as a quality of something else.</note>—most of all, primarily, and principally—to that which results from the composition of parts. However, such a composition is nothing more than an <term>accident</term> <note>An "accident" is a property that can change or disappear without the thing itself ceasing to exist (like the color of a car or, in Bruno’s view, the specific shape of a body).</note>, which contains no stability or truth within itself, and dissolves into nothing. **They say** that the "true man" is that which results from this composition; that the "true" <term>soul</term> is either the perfection and act of a living body, or simply something resulting from a certain symmetry of temperament and limbs. > *All things change, nothing perishes* <margin>*) Ovid, Metamorphoses 15, 153—159; 165.</margin> <note>original: "O genus attonitum gelidae formidine mortis, / Quid Styga, quid tenebras et nomina vana timetis, / Materiam vatum, falsique pericula mundi? / Corpora, sive rogus flamma, seu tabe vetustas / Abstulerit, mala posse pati non ulla putetis: / Morte carent animae, semperque priore relicta / Sede, novis habitant domibus vivuntque receptae. / Omnia mutantur, nihil interit." This quote comes from the speech of Pythagoras in Ovid's poem, used here to support the idea of the transmigration of souls and the conservation of matter.</note>

**Dic.** In accordance with this, it seems to me that Solomon, esteemed as the wisest among the Hebrews, says: <margin>**) Ecclesiastes 1:9–10.</margin> *What is that which is? The same that was. What is that which was? The same that shall be. There is nothing new under the sun.* <note>original: "Quid est, quod est? Ipsum quod fuit. Quid est, quod fuit? Ipsum, quod futurum est. Nihil sub sole novum."</note>

**Pol.** So, then, this <term>form</term> that you propose—is it not something that exists only within and clings to <term>matter</term> for its being? Does it not depend on the body and on <term>matter</term> in order to subsist?

**Teo.** That is correct. Furthermore, I do not yet determine if all <term>form</term> is accompanied by <term>matter</term>. Just as I say with certainty regarding <term>matter</term> that there is no part of it entirely destitute of form, except when considered logically—as is done by Aristotle, who never tires of using reason to divide that which is undivided according to nature and truth. <note>Bruno is critiquing Aristotle for separating matter and form in theory (logic), whereas in reality (nature), they are always joined.</note>

**Dic.** Do you mean to say there is no other <term>form</term> than this eternal companion of <term>matter</term>?

**Teo.** There is a more natural one still, which is the "material form," of which we shall speak later. For now, note this distinction of <term>form</term>: there is a kind of <term>first form</term> <note>The "first form" or "World Soul" is the universal principle that gives life and structure to the entire cosmos.</note>, which informs, extends, and depends; and because this form informs the whole, it is in everything; and because it extends itself, it communicates the perfection of the whole to its parts; and because it depends [on the whole] and has no operation of its own, it communicates the operation of the whole to the parts in a similar way...

<summary>Teofilo argues that death is merely the dissolution of a temporary "accidental" composition, while the underlying matter and form are eternal and indestructible. He uses quotes from Ovid and Solomon to support his claim that nothing truly perishes, only changes form.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, substance vs accident, World Soul, Ovid, Solomon, Aristotle, Giordano Bruno, metaphysics, transmigration</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 243, where Teofilo is explaining that "form"—the organizing principle of life—and "matter" are both eternal. Here, he begins to classify the different ways form manifests in the world, distinguishing between purely physical properties and the higher spiritual soul.</meta>

the name and the being. Such is the **material form**, like that of fire; because every part of fire that heats is called "fire" and is indeed fire. Second is another kind of form, which gives shape to and depends on the body, but does not extend through it; and such a form, because it makes the whole perfect and brings it into action, is in the whole and in every part of it. Because it does not extend <note>By "not extending," Bruno means the soul is not a physical substance that can be stretched or cut into pieces like dough; it is a spiritual presence that exists entirely within every part of the body at once.</note>, it happens that the action of the whole is not attributed to the parts; however, because it depends on the body, the operation of the whole is communicated to the parts. Such is the **vegetative soul** <note>The power of growth and nutrition shared by plants and animals.</note> and the **sensitive soul** <note>The power of perception and feeling shared by animals and humans.</note>, because no single part of an animal is itself "the animal," and yet every part lives and feels. 

Third is another kind of form, which activates and makes the whole perfect, but does not extend through it nor depend upon it regarding its operation. This form, because it activates and perfects, is in the whole, and throughout the whole, and in every part. Because it does not extend, the perfection of the whole is not attributed to the parts; because it does not depend on the body, it does not communicate its operation to the parts. Such is the **soul**, insofar as it can exercise the **intellective power**, and it is called "intellective." This power does not make any specific part of a man something that could be named "a man," nor is that part a man, nor can it be said that the part understands. Of these three species, the first is material, which cannot be understood by itself, nor can it exist without matter. The other two species—which ultimately coincide as one according to their substance and being, but are distinguished by the manner we described above—we call the <term>formal principle</term>, which is distinct from the <term>material principle</term>.

**Dicsono.** I understand.

**Teofilo.** Beyond this, I want it to be noticed that, speaking in the common way, we say there are five degrees of forms: that of the <term>element</term> <note>The simplest physical building blocks, like earth or water.</note>, the <term>mixture</term> <note>Compounds made of multiple elements.</note>, the <term>vegetal</term>, the <term>sensitive</term>, and the <term>intellective</term>. However, we do not mean this according to the common understanding; for this distinction is based on the operations that appear and proceed from the subjects, not according to the logic of the primary and fundamental being of that spiritual life, which fills everything in the same way, though not in the same manner.

**Dicsono.** I understand. So this form, which you propose as a principle, is a <term>subsistent form</term> <note>A form that has its own independent existence and does not disappear when the physical body dies.</note>; it constitutes a perfect species, exists in its own right, and is not merely a "part" of a species, like the <term>peripatetic</term> <note>Referring to the followers of Aristotle, who believed the soul was merely the "function" of the body and could not exist without it.</note> form.

**Teofilo.** That is so.

**Dicsono.** The distinction of forms within matter does not come from accidental arrangements, which depend on the material form.

**Teofilo.** True.

**Dicsono.** Therefore, even this separate form is not multiplied by number, because all numerical multiplication depends on matter. <note>In this philosophy, there is only one "Humanity" or "Life" in essence; there are only "many humans" because the one form is reflected in many different pieces of matter.</note>

**Teofilo.** Yes.

**Dicsono.** Furthermore, it is invariable in itself, though it appears variable because of the subjects and the diversity of the materials. And such a form, although within the subject it creates—

<summary>Teofilo distinguishes between material forms (which are divisible) and the soul (which is indivisible and present in every part of a body). He argues that the soul is a "subsistent form" that does not depend on matter for its existence and remains one and unchanging, despite appearing diverse in different physical bodies.</summary>

**Teo.** Very well.
**Dic.** So, in a certain way, you approve of the view of **Anaxagoras**, who calls the particular forms of nature "latent"; somewhat that of **Plato**, who derives them from the **Ideas**; somewhat that of **Empedocles**, who makes them proceed from the intelligence; and in a way that of **Aristotle**, who makes them as if emerging from the potency of matter?
**Teo.** Yes; because, as we have said, where the form is, in a certain way everything is; where the soul, the spirit, the life is, everything is. The shaper is the <term>intellect</term> <note>The "Universal Intellect" is the inner craftsman that shapes matter from within.</note> through the ideal species and forms; if it does not raise them out of matter, it does not go begging for them from outside of it, because this spirit fills the whole.
**Pol.** **I would like to know how form is the soul of the world, everywhere whole, if it is individual?** <note>original Latin: "Velim scire, quomodo forma est anima mundi ubique tota, se la è individua?"</note> It must then be very large—indeed, of infinite dimension—if you say the world is infinite.
**Ger.** It is for good reason that it should be large, as a preacher in **Grandazzo** in **Sicily** also said of our Lord. To show that He is present in all the world, he ordered a crucifix as large as the church itself, in the likeness of God the Father, who has the empyrean heaven for a canopy, the starry heaven for a seat, and has legs so long they reach down to the earth, which serves as His footstool. A certain local man came to ask him, saying: "My reverend Father, now how many ells of cloth will be needed to make Him stockings?" And another said that all the chickpeas, kidney beans, and broad beans of **Melazzo** and **Nicosia** would not be enough to fill His belly. See then, that this <term>soul of the world</term> is not made in this same fashion.
**Teo.** I would not know how to respond to your doubt, Gervasio, but...

...well to that of Master Poliinnio; nevertheless I will speak with a simile, to satisfy the request of both; because I want you as well to reap some fruit from our reasonings and discourses. You must therefore know briefly, that the <term>soul of the world</term> <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, this is the vital principle that animates the entire universe, similar to how a human soul animates a body.</note> and the divinity are not all present everywhere and in every part in the way that something material might be there; for this is impossible for any body or any spirit; but in a way that is not easy to explain to you otherwise than by this. You must note that if the soul of the world and the **universal form** are said to be everywhere, it is not meant corporally or dimensionally; for they are not such, and thus cannot be in any part in that way; but they are all in everything spiritually, as for example—though a crude one—you could imagine a voice, which is entirely in an entire room, and in every part of it, because it is heard in its entirety everywhere: just as these words that I speak are heard in their entirety by everyone, even if there were a thousand present, and my voice, if it could reach the whole world, would be everywhere in its entirety. I say to you, therefore, Master Poliinnio, that the soul is not indivisible like a point, but in a certain way like a voice; and I respond to you, Gervasio, that the divinity is not everywhere in the way that the God of Grandazzo <note>A reference to a large, well-known devotional statue in the Sicilian town of Grandazzo. Bruno uses it to contrast physical presence (parts in different places) with spiritual presence (the whole in every place).</note> is in his whole chapel; for that statue, although it is in the whole church, is not however entirely in every part of it, but has the head in one part, the feet in another, the arms and the torso in other different parts: but divinity is entirely in any part whatsoever, just as my voice is heard from all parts of this hall.

**Pol.** I understood perfectly. <note>original Latin: "Percepi optime."</note>

**Ger.** I certainly understood your voice.

**Dic.** I believe you regarding the voice, but regarding the subject, I think it entered through one ear and went out the other.

**Ger.** I think it didn't even enter, because it is late and the clock I keep inside my stomach has struck the hour for supper.

**Pol.** This is what it means to have one's **mind in the frying pans.** <note>original: "Hoc est, id est aver il cervello in patinis." A Latin-derived idiom for being distracted by hunger or thinking only of food.</note>

**Dic.** Enough, then! Tomorrow we shall meet to discuss, perhaps, the **material principle**. <note>The discussion shifts from "Form" (soul/spirit) to "Matter," the other half of the philosophical duo used to explain existence.</note>

**Teo.** Either I will wait for you, or you will wait for me here.

# THIRD DIALOGUE

->Gervasio.<-

The hour has finally arrived, and those men haven't come yet! Since I have no other thoughts pulling at me, I want to take some pleasure in hearing these people talk; from them, besides being able to learn some move in this <term>chess of philosophy</term> <note>original: "scacco di filosofia". A metaphor for intellectual sparring or tactical maneuvers in a debate.</note>, I can have a fine pastime with those whims that dance in that irregular brain of <term>Poliinnio the pedant</term> <note>A "pedant" in this context is a schoolmaster obsessed with minor rules and showing off his learning, often used as a comic figure in Renaissance literature.</note>. He is someone who, while saying he wants to judge who speaks well, who discourses better, and who makes incongruities and errors in philosophy, when it is time to say his part and he doesn't know what to offer, starts to pull out from the handle of his hollow pedantry a little salad of trite proverbs and phrases in Latin or Greek that never have anything to do with what others are saying. Thus, without much difficulty, even a blind man can see how he is a fool by the letter, while others are wise in the vernacular. Oh, here he is, by my faith! Look how he comes; it seems that even in the way he moves his feet, he knows how to walk according to the letter. Welcome, *Lord Master!* <note>original: "dominus magister"</note>

Pol. That "Master" does not please me, since in this deviant and enormous age it is attributed no more to my peers than to any barber, cobbler, or pig-gelder; therefore it is advised: *Do not be called Rabbi!* <note>original: "Nolite vocari Rabbi!" A reference to Matthew 23:8. Poliinnio uses a biblical prohibition against pride to ironically show off his own status.</note>

Ger. How then do you wish me to address you? Does "Most Reverend" please you?

Pol. *That is for priests and the clergy.* <note>original: "Illud est presbyterale et clericum."</note>

Ger. Do you have a longing for "Most Illustrious"?

Pol. *Let arms yield to the toga!* <note>original: "Cedant arma togae!" A famous line from Cicero, suggesting that civil/academic authority (the toga) is superior to military power (arms).</note> This is for the knightly class as well as for the <term>men in purple</term> <note>original: "purpurati". High-ranking officials or cardinals who wore purple or scarlet robes.</note>.

Ger. Imperial Majesty, then?

Pol. *Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's!* <note>original: "Quae Caesaris, Caesari!" Polinnio quotes the famous gospel phrase to reject a title he deems too high even for himself.</note>

Ger. Take then the title of "Lord"; come, take upon yourself the name of the <term>heavy-thundering</term> <note>original: "gravitonante". A classical epithet for Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note> one, the *father of the gods!* <note>original: "divúm pater"</note> Let’s get to us; why are you all so late?

Pol. I believe the others are entangled in some other business, just as I—in order not to let this day pass without a line—have been occupied with the contemplation of the model of the globe, commonly called the <term>world map</term> <note>original: "mappamondo". In Bruno's time, this referred to a map or a globe representing the known earth.</note>.

Ger. What do you have to do with the world map?

Pol. I contemplate the parts of the earth, the climates, provinces, and regions, all of which I have traveled through with my ideal reason, and many with my actual steps as well.

Ger. I wish you would travel a bit inside your own self.

<summary>Gervasio mocks the pedantic Poliinnio, who refuses common titles in favor of pompous Latin phrases. Poliinnio claims he was late because he was busy studying a world map.</summary>

**Ger.** And how will you persuade me of that?

**Ger.** As the soul is to the body.

**Pol.** These words, being well understood, cause the meaning to be well considered too; therefore from the knowledge of languages—in which I am more practiced than anyone else in this city, and I do not consider myself less learned than anyone who keeps an open <term>school of Minerva</term> <note>original: "ludo di Minerva"; Minerva was the goddess of wisdom, here referring to a grammar school or academy.</note>—proceeds the knowledge of whatever science you please.

<meta>This page continues the satirical dialogue between Poliinnio, a pedantic schoolmaster, and Gervasio. Having previously discussed the relationship between the microcosm (man) and the macrocosm (universe), the conversation now shifts to the value of linguistic mastery versus the actual understanding of nature and philosophy. Gervasio is currently launching a critique of those who value the "shell" of words over the "kernel" of meaning.</meta>

...the sense of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) was the dominant philosophical authority of the Middle Ages and Renaissance; Bruno frequently challenged his views on physics and cosmology.</note>, and to recognize many errors in it. As is clearly seen, this idolatry, which revolved around the authority of that philosopher—principally regarding natural things—is now entirely abolished among all those who understand the ideas brought forth by this other sect. One who knows neither Greek, nor Arabic, and perhaps not even Latin, like <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who rejected traditional medical authorities in favor of direct observation and chemical cures.</note>, may have better understood the nature of medicines and healing than <term>Galen</term> <note>Aelius Galenus (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in European universities.</note>, and all those who make themselves heard in the Roman tongue <note>original: "lingua romana"; referring to Latin, the language of the academic elite.</note>. Philosophies and laws do not go to ruin for a lack of interpreters of words, but for a lack of those who dive deep into the meanings.

**Pol.** So, then, do you come to count a man of my standing among the number of the foolish multitude?

**Ger.** Heaven forbid! For I know that with your knowledge and study of languages—which is a rare and singular thing—not only you, but all your peers are most valiant in making judgments on doctrines, after having sifted through the sentiments of those who take the field.

**Pol.** Because you speak the absolute truth, I can easily persuade myself that you do not say it without reason; therefore, as it is not difficult for you, let it not be a burden to provide that reason.

**Ger.** I shall speak, always submitting myself to the censorship of your prudence and literacy. It is a common proverb that those who are outside the game understand it more than those who are inside it; just as those who are in the audience can better judge the performance than those characters who are on the stage, and a better assessment of music can be made by one who is not part of the chapel choir or the concert. The same appears in games of cards, chess, fencing, and other such things. Thus, you gentlemen <term>pedants</term> <note>In the Renaissance, a "pedant" specifically referred to a schoolteacher who was often mocked for being obsessed with grammatical rules while lacking real-world wisdom.</note>, by being excluded and outside of every act of science and philosophy, and by never having had any participation with Aristotle, <term>Plato</term>, and others like them, can better judge them and condemn them—with your grammatical sufficiency and the presumption of your natural character—than the <term>Nolan</term> <note>Giordano Bruno himself, born in Nola, Italy. He often refers to himself in the third person as "the Nolan."</note>, who finds himself in that very same theater, in the same familiarity and intimacy, so much so that he easily contends with them after having known their innermost and deepest sentiments. You, I say, by being outside every profession of gentlemen and wandering geniuses, can better judge them.

**Pol.** I would not know how to respond so suddenly to such impudence. My voice stuck in my throat! <note>original: "Vox faucibus haesit!"; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, used here to show the pedant's reliance on classical tags even when speechless.</note>

**Ger.** Yet your peers are so presumptuous, unlike others who have their feet inside the matter; and therefore I assure you, that you worthily claim for yourselves the office of approving this, rejecting that, glossing the other, making a concordance and collation here, and an appendix there.

**Pol.** This most ignorant man—based on the fact that I am an expert in good human letters—wants to infer that I am ignorant in philosophy!

<summary>Gervasio uses biting irony to mock the pedant Poliinnio, arguing that linguists who focus only on grammar and translation are "outside the game" of true philosophy compared to thinkers like the Nolan and Paracelsus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Gervasio was critiquing the obsession with linguistic mastery over philosophical depth. He now directs his wit toward Poliinnio, the embodiment of the pedantic academic, and contrasts true philosophers with those who merely "sew and unsew" the words of the ancients.</meta>

**Ger.** Most learned Master Poliinnio, I mean to say that if you possessed all the languages that exist—which our preachers say are seventy-two...

**Pol.** *And a half.* <note>original: "Cum dimidia." A pedantic correction reflecting the medieval tradition that there were exactly seventy-two languages created at the Tower of Babel.</note>

**Ger.** For that reason, it does not only follow that you would be unfit to judge philosophers, but furthermore, you could not prevent yourself from being the greatest, most awkward beast that ever lived with a human face. Moreover, there is nothing to stop one who knows barely one language—and a "bastard" one at that—from being the most wise and learned man in the whole world. Now, consider the "progress" made by two such men: one a French arch-pedant <note>Pietro Ramo (Peter Ramus), died 1572. A famous humanist who attempted to restructure the <term>Liberal Arts</term>—the traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, and rhetoric—and wrote "Animadversions against Aristotle," a series of critical remarks.</note>, who established schools on the liberal arts and criticisms against Aristotle; and another piece of Italian pedantic filth <note>Francesco Patrizzi, died 1597. He wrote "Peripatetic Discussions" (Basel, 1581) and "The New Philosophy of the Universe" (Venice, 1591). Bruno views him as a mere compiler of others' ideas.</note>, who has stained so many notebooks with his <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Refers to the followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about.</note> discussions. Everyone can easily see that the first one shows himself to be very eloquent but hardly wise; the second, simply speaking, shows himself to have much of the beast and the ass about him. 

Of the first, we can at least say that he understood Aristotle, though he understood him poorly; and if he had understood him well, he might have had the wit to wage an honorable war against him, as the most judicious <term>Telesio of Cosenza</term> <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), an Italian philosopher who rejected Aristotelian metaphysics in favor of a physics based on sensory experience. Bruno held him in high regard.</note> has done. Of the second, we cannot say that he understood him either poorly or well, but only that he read and re-read him, stitched him together and unstitched him, and compared him with a thousand other Greek authors, both friends and enemies of his. In the end, he put in a massive amount of effort, not only without any profit but even with a massive blunder. Thus, anyone who wants to see into what madness and presumptive vanity a pedantic habit can plunge and sink a man, let him look at that one book, before the seed of it is lost. But look, here are Teofilo and Dickson!

**Pol.** *Welcome, happy sirs!* <note>original: "Adeste felices, domini!"</note> Your presence is the reason why my boiling temper does not break out into thunderous sentences against the vain talk of this babbling <term>frugiperda</term> <note>A Latin term meaning "fruit-destroyer," often used as a literary insult for someone who consumes resources without producing anything of value.</note>.

**Ger.** And it takes away my opportunity to play around with the majesty of this most reverend owl <note>In the Renaissance, the owl was sometimes used to symbolize the pedant who stays in the dark of his study, unable to see the light of true nature.</note>.

**Dic.** All is well, as long as you do not grow angry.

**Ger.** Whatever I say, I say in jest, for I love the master.

**Pol.** *I also, though I am angry, am not seriously angry, because I do not hate Gervasio.* <note>original: "Ego quoque, quod irascor, non serio irascor, quia Gervasium non odi."</note>

**Dic.** Good! Then let me talk with Teofilo!

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue where Teofilo (the voice of Bruno) is explaining his metaphysical system. Having previously discussed the limitations of pedantic academic study, the conversation now shifts to the core of Bruno’s philosophy: the relationship between matter and form, and how his views differ from the ancient Atomists and the contemporary alchemists.</meta>

<page-num>251</page-num>

**Teo.** Democritus, then, and the Epicureans, who say that whatever is not a body is nothing, consequently maintain that matter alone is the substance of things, and even that it is the divine nature; as a certain Arab said, called Avicebron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021–1058), a Sephardic Jewish philosopher and poet known in the Latin world as Avicebron.</note>, as he shows in a book titled: *The Source of Life* <note>original: "Fonte di vita." This influential work argued that all things, including spiritual substances, are composed of matter and form.</note>; these same men, along with the Cyrenaics, Cynics, and Stoics, maintain that forms are nothing other than certain accidental arrangements of matter. And for a long time I was a firm adherent of this opinion, solely because it has foundations more in harmony with nature than those of Aristotle. But after having considered more maturely, taking many things into account, we find that it is necessary to recognize two kinds of substance in nature: one, which is form; and the other, which is matter. For it is necessary that there be a most substantial act, in which is the active power of everything, and also a power and a subject, in which there is no less passive power of everything: in the former is the power to make, in the latter is the power to be made.

**Dic.** It is manifest to anyone who measures well that it is impossible for the one to always be able to make everything, without there always being that which can be made into everything. How could the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>The "Anima Mundi," a concept suggesting that the universe itself is a living being with a spiritual component that organizes and animates matter.</note>—I mean every form, which is indivisible—be a shaper, without the subject of dimensions or quantity, which is matter? And matter, how can it be shaped? Perhaps by itself? It seems we could say that matter is shaped by itself, if we wish to consider the whole formed body of the universe to be matter, and call it matter, just as we would call an animal with all its faculties "matter," distinguishing it not from the form, but only from the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The agent or force that brings something into being, as opposed to the material it is made of or the "form" it takes.</note>.

**Teo.** No one can prevent you from using the name "matter" in your own way, just as many sects have similarly given it many meanings. But this way of considering things, of which you speak, I know could only suit a mechanic or a practical physician, such as one who divides the body of the universe into Mercury, Salt, and Sulfur <note>The "Tria Prima" or Three Primes. In Renaissance alchemy, these were considered the fundamental spiritual-material components of all matter: Sulfur (the soul/flammability), Mercury (the spirit/volatility), and Salt (the body/solidity).</note>. To say such a thing does not so much demonstrate the divine wit of a physician as it might show a most foolish man who wished to be called a philosopher. The philosopher’s goal is not only to reach that distinction of principles which is made physically through the separation proceeding from the power of fire <note>Referring to chemical distillation or laboratory experiments.</note>, but also to 그that distinction of principles which no material agent can reach. For the soul, inseparable from Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, is the <term>formal principle</term>; it is not subject to material qualities, but is entirely the master of matter. It is not touched by the work of chemists, whose division ends at those three aforementioned things, and who recognize a different kind of soul than this one of the world, which we must define.

<summary>Teofilo argues that while early materialist philosophers and alchemists correctly identified the importance of matter, a true philosopher must recognize "Form" (the Soul of the World) as a distinct, active substance that shapes matter. He rejects the purely chemical view of the world, asserting that the formal principle is a "master of matter" beyond physical separation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Teofilo (speaking for Bruno) established the necessity of two substances: matter and form. Here, the participants distinguish between how different disciplines (medicine vs. philosophy) view these causes, before diving into a foundational definition of matter using the "analogy of art," a classic pedagogical tool in Renaissance philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>

**Dic.** You speak excellently, and this consideration pleases me greatly; for I see some so little discerning that they do not distinguish the causes of nature viewed absolutely according to the whole scope of their being (which are considered by philosophers), from those taken in a limited and specific way. The former way is excessive and useless to physicians, insofar as they are physicians; the latter is truncated and diminished for philosophers, insofar as they are philosophers.

**Teo.** You have touched upon that point for which Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who famously challenged traditional medical authorities.</note> is praised, having treated medicinal philosophy, and Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries; Bruno suggests Galen over-theorized medicine until it became ineffective.</note> is blamed, insofar as he introduced a "philosophical medicine" to create a tedious mixture and a web so tangled that, in the end, it produces a somewhat refined physician but a very confused philosopher. But let this be said with some respect, for I have not had the leisure to examine all the parts of that man's work.

**Ger.** Please, Teofilo, first do me this favor, since I am not so experienced in philosophy: explain to me what you mean by this term "matter," and what is it that constitutes matter in natural things?

**Teo.** All those who wish to distinguish matter and consider it by itself without form, resort to the analogy of art. So do the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who saw numbers and geometry as the basis of reality.</note>, the Platonists, and the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note>. Consider a type of art, like that of the woodworker, which for all its forms and all its works has wood as its subject, just as the blacksmith has iron and the tailor has cloth. All these arts, within their own matter, create various likenesses, arrangements, and figures, none of which is inherent or natural to that matter. Thus nature, to which art is similar, must have a matter for its operations; for it is impossible that there be any agent who, if he wishes to make something, does not have something from which to make it, or, if he wishes to work, has nothing to work upon. There is, therefore, a kind of subject from which, with which, and in which nature effects its operation and its work, and which is formed by her into so many forms that present such a variety of species to the eyes of our consideration. 

And just as wood of itself has no artificial form, but can have them all through the work of the woodworker, so the matter of which we speak, of itself and in its own nature, has no natural form, but can have them all through the operation of the <term>active agent</term> <note>original: "agente attivo." In Bruno's system, this is the universal intellect or the Soul of the World that gives shape to matter.</note>, the principle of nature. This natural matter is not as sensible <note>Meaning perceptible by the physical senses.</note> as artificial matter; for the matter of nature has absolutely no form, but the matter of art is something already formed by nature, since art cannot operate except on the surface of things formed by nature, such as wood, iron, stone, wool, and similar things; but nature works from the center, so to speak, of its subject or matter, which is altogether formless.

<summary>Teofilo explains that while craftsmen work with matter that already has a natural form (like wood or iron), Nature works with a primordial, formless matter from the inside out. He also critiques the over-intellectualization of medicine by Galen, preferring the more practical philosophical approach of Paracelsus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous section where Teofilo (representing Giordano Bruno’s own views) began explaining the concept of "matter" to Gervasio. Having previously distinguished between how physicians and philosophers view natural causes, Teofilo now uses the "analogy of art"—comparing nature to a craftsman—to explain how one underlying substance can take on many different forms.</meta>

<page-num>253</page-num>

Therefore, the <term>subjects</term><note>Here, "subject" (Italian: *soggetto*) refers to the "substrate" or underlying material—the "stuff" that remains the same even when its appearance changes.</note> of the arts are many, but the subject of nature is one. This is because the subjects of art, having been diversely formed by nature, are different and varied; but the subject of nature, not being formed in any way at all, is entirely indifferent, seeing as every difference and diversity proceeds from the **form**.

**Ger.** So much so that things formed by nature are the "matter" of art, and one single formless thing is the "matter" of nature.

**Teo.** That is so.

**Ger.** Is it possible that, just as we see and clearly know the subjects of the arts, we can similarly know the subject of nature?

**Teo.** Quite well; but by different principles of cognition. For just as we do not know colors and sounds through the same sense, so we do not see the subject of the arts and the subject of nature with the same eye.

**Ger.** You mean to say that we see the former with our physical eyes, and the latter with the **eye of reason**.

**Teo.** Precisely.

**Ger.** Now, please formulate this reasoning!

**Teo.** Willingly. That relationship and regard which the form of art has toward its own matter, according to due proportion, is the same as the relationship the form of nature has toward its matter. Just as, therefore, in <term>art</term><note>In the Renaissance, "art" (*arte*) referred to any human craft, skill, or technology, such as carpentry or smithing, rather than just the "fine arts."</note>—if it were possible to vary the forms into infinity—it is always one and the same matter that persists beneath them. For example, beneath the form of a tree is the form of a trunk, then a beam, then a board, then a bench, then a stool, then a chest, then a comb, and so on; yet the "being of wood" always persists. It is no different in nature: though forms vary and succeed one another into infinity, the **matter** remains always the same.

**Ger.** How can this comparison be made firm?

**Teo.** Do you not see that what was seed becomes grass? And from what was grass, an ear of grain is made; from the ear, bread; from bread, <term>chyle</term><note>original: "chilo." A milky fluid produced in the intestines during digestion; in Bruno's time, it was seen as an intermediate stage in the transformation of food into blood.</note>; from chyle, blood; from this, seed; from this, an embryo; from this, a man; from this, a corpse; from this, earth; from this, stone or another thing—and so on, reaching all natural forms?

**Ger.** I see it easily.

**Teo.** It must be, then, that there is one and the same thing which in itself is not stone, nor earth, nor corpse, nor man, nor embryo, nor blood, nor anything else; but which, after it was blood, becomes an embryo, receiving the "being of an embryo"; and after it was an embryo, receives the "being of a man," becoming a man. This is just like the material formed by nature which becomes the subject of art: from that which was a tree and a board, it receives the "being of a board"; from that which was a board, it receives the "being of a door," and so it is a door.

<summary>Teofilo explains that while human crafts use various materials already "formed" by nature (like wood), nature itself operates on a single, formless underlying matter. He uses the transformation of food into blood and eventually into a human being to illustrate how one substance persists through endless changes in form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Teofilo explains that "matter" is a single, underlying substance. Gervasio has just accepted that while we see the "matter" of human crafts (like wood or stone) with our eyes, the "matter" of nature can only be perceived through the "eye of reason."</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>

**Ger.** Now I have understood it very well; but this <term>subject</term><note>Here, "subject" refers to the underlying substrate or "stuff" that makes up the natural world.</note> of nature seems to me that it cannot be a body, nor possess any certain quality; for this thing, which keeps shifting and escaping now under one form and natural state, and now under another form and state, does not show itself corporally, like wood or stone. These materials always show themselves for what they are materially or subjectively, no matter what form they are given.

**Teo.** You speak well.

**Ger.** Now what shall I do when I happen to discuss this thought with some stubborn person who does not want to believe that there is one single **matter** under all the formations of nature, just as there is one under all the formations of every craft? Because the latter, which is seen with the eyes, cannot be denied; but the former, which is seen by **reason** alone, can be denied.

**Teo.** Send him away, or do not answer him!

**Ger.** But what if he is persistent in demanding evidence, and he is some person of rank—one whom I cannot simply send away, or who might rather send *me* away—and who would take it as an insult if I did not answer him?

**Teo.** What would you do if a blind "demigod," worthy of every honor and respect, were arrogant, persistent, and stubborn in wanting to understand and demanding evidence of colors, or the external shapes of natural things? For instance: what is the shape of a tree? What is the shape of the mountains, or a star? Or even: what is the shape of a statue or a garment—things that are so manifest to those who can see?

**Ger.** I would answer him that if he had eyes, he would not ask for evidence, but could see them for himself; but being blind, it is impossible for anyone else to show them to him.

**Teo.** Similarly, you can say to those people that if they had **intellect**, they would not ask for other evidence, but could see it for themselves.

**Ger.** They would be ashamed of such an answer, and others would consider it too <term>cynical</term><note>In this context, "cynical" refers to the biting, blunt, and often socially dismissive style of the ancient Cynic philosophers.</note>.

**Teo.** Then you shall say it to him more subtly, like this: "My most illustrious Lord," or "Sacred Majesty, just as some things cannot be evident except through the hands and touch, others only through hearing, and others only through taste or the eyes—so this **matter** of natural things cannot be evident except through the **intellect**."

**Ger.** That person, perhaps catching the underlying meaning, and because he is not entirely dim-witted, might say to me: "You are the one who lacks intellect; I have more of it than any of your peers."

**Teo.** You should believe him no more than if a blind man told you that *you* are the blind one, and that he sees more than all those who—like you—think they can see.

<summary>Teofilo argues that the fundamental "matter" of the universe is an invisible substrate that can only be perceived by the intellect, not the senses. He uses the analogy of a blind man to explain that those who demand physical proof for metaphysical truths simply lack the necessary "organ" of reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue on the nature of matter. Following the previous discussion on the "eye of reason," Dixon now introduces the Pythagorean concept of analogy to explain how matter persists through the transformation of elements. Teofilo uses this to argue for the immortality of both matter and the soul, while mocking the complex terminology of Scholastic Aristotelians.</meta>

<page-num>255</page-num>

**Dic.** Enough has been said to demonstrate more clearly than I have ever heard what the name **matter** signifies, and what should be understood as matter in natural things. Thus spoke the Pythagorean Timaeus <note>Timaeus of Locri, a character in Plato’s dialogues whom Bruno treats as a historical Pythagorean philosopher.</note>, who teaches us to find that matter which is hidden—and which cannot be known except by a certain analogy—through the transmutation of one element into another. Where the form of earth was, he says, soon after appears the form of water; and here one cannot say that one form "receives" the other, because a contrary does not accept or receive its opposite. That is, the dry does not receive the moist, nor does dryness receive moisture; rather, from a "third thing," dryness is driven out and moisture is introduced. That third thing is the <term>subject</term><note>The underlying substrate or "stuff" that remains constant while qualities change.</note> of both one contrary and the other, and is not itself contrary to anything. Therefore, if we are not to think that the earth has vanished into nothingness, we must conclude that something which was in the earth has remained and is now in the water. For the same reason, when water is changed into air—because the power of heat happens to thin it into smoke or vapor—that same thing will remain and will be in the air.

**Teo.** From this one can conclude, even to their chagrin, that nothing is annihilated or loses its being, except for the external and material accidental form. Therefore, both matter and the <term>substantial form</term><note>The essential nature or "soul" that gives a thing its specific identity.</note> of any natural thing—which is the soul—are indissoluble and incapable of being annihilated <note>The original Italian "annichilabili" is paired with "indissolubili" (indissoluble), implying they cannot be reduced to nothing.</note>, never losing their being entirely. 

Certainly, this cannot be said for all the "substantial forms" of the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> and others like them. Their forms consist of nothing more than a certain combination and order of accidents; everything they are able to name, except for their "prime matter," is nothing but accident, combination, a habit of quality, a principle of definition, or <term>quiddity</term><note>From the Latin "quidditas," meaning the "what-ness" or essence of a thing.</note>. 

Regarding this, certain "hooded" <note>original: "cucullati". A derogatory reference to the monks and friars of the Scholastic tradition.</note> subtle metaphysicians among them, wishing rather to excuse the insufficiency of their deity, Aristotle, have invented "humanity," "bovinity," and "olivinity" as "specific substantial forms." They claim this "humanity" is the same as "Socrates-ness" <note>original: "socrateità"</note>, and that this "bovinity" or "horse-ness" is the numerical substance. They have done all this just to grant us a substantial form that might deserve the name of "substance" in the same way that matter has the name and being of substance. Yet they have never gained anything by it; for if you ask them in order: "In what does the substantial being of Socrates consist?" they will answer: "In Socrates-ness." If you then ask: "What do you mean by Socrates-ness?" they will answer: "His own substantial form and his own matter." 

Now, let us leave aside that substance which is matter, and tell me: what is the substance as form? Some answer: "His soul." You then ask: "What is this soul?" If they say: "An <term>entelechy</term><note>Aristotle's term for the "actuality" or "perfection" of a body. Bruno argues this definition makes the soul a mere property (accident) of the body rather than a true substance.</note> and a perfection of a body that can live," consider that this is merely an accident. If they say it is a principle of life, sense, vegetation, and intellect, consider...

...that, although that principle is some substance—when considered fundamentally as we are considering it—nevertheless, this man <note>Referring to Aristotle or a typical Aristotelian philosopher.</note> does not present it as anything but an **accident**. For to be the "principle" of this or that thing does not express a substantial and absolute reason, but rather an accidental reason relative to that which is "principiate" <note>The "principiate" is the thing that results from a principle; here, the finished object or being.</note>. See then how they treat this **substantial form**, which is the soul; for even if by chance they have recognized it as a substance, they have never named it or considered it as such. You can see this confusion much more clearly if you ask these people what the substantial form of an inanimate thing consists of—for example, the substantial form of wood. Those who are more subtle will imagine it lies in "woodiness." Now, take away that matter which is common to iron, wood, and stone, and tell me: what substantial form of iron remains? They will never tell you anything but **accidents**, and these are among the <term>principles of individuation</term><note>The specific qualities (like shape, weight, or color) that make one specific object different from another of the same kind.</note> and provide particularity. For matter cannot be narrowed down to particularity except by some form; and because this form is the constitutive principle of a substance, they want it to be "substantial." But then they cannot demonstrate it physically, only as something accidental. In the end, when they have done all they can, they have a substantial form, yes—but it is a **logical** one, not a **natural** one. And so, in the end, some logical intention comes to be placed as the principle of natural things.

**Dic.** Did Aristotle not realize this?

**Teo.** I believe he certainly did realize it, but he could not find a remedy for it; therefore, he said that the "ultimate differences" are unnamable and unknown.

**Dic.** It seems to me that he thus openly confesses his ignorance. Therefore, I too would judge it better to embrace those principles of philosophy which do not plead ignorance in this important question—such as **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, and your **Nolan** <note>The "Nolan" is Giordano Bruno himself, born in Nola.</note>, whose opinions you touched upon yesterday.

**Dic.** This doctrine pleases me greatly, because it seems to lack nothing. And truly, it is a necessary thing that, just as we can posit a constant and eternal material principle, we should similarly posit a formal principle. We see that all natural forms cease from matter, and anew...

...come and go in matter; thus it truly seems that nothing is constant, firm, eternal, and worthy of being regarded as a principle, except for matter. Therefore matter, which always remains the same and fertile, must have the primary prerogative of being known as the only substantial principle—the thing that *is* and which always remains. **T e o.** Those people were led into this error by not knowing any form other than the accidental. **T e o.** Not easily; because absolutely nothing acts upon itself, and there is always some distinction between that which is the agent and that which is made, or that upon which the action and operation take place. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Teofilo and Dicuono regarding the nature of the cosmos. <page-num>258</page-num>

...the species. Thus, within this body, we speak of three things: first, the **universal intellect** <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, the Universal Intellect is the "inner craftsman" that shapes matter from within.</note> inherent in all things; second, the **vivifying soul** of the whole; and third, the **subject** <note>Here, "subject" refers to the underlying matter or substrate that receives forms.</note>. But we shall not, for this reason, deny that he is a philosopher who takes as the genus of his philosophizing this formed body—or, as we might say, this **rational animal**—and begins to take as first principles the members of this body: such as air, earth, and fire; or the ethereal region and the stars; or spirit and body; or even the **vacuum and the plenum** <note>The "void" and "fullness," a central debate in ancient physics regarding whether empty space can exist.</note>, though understanding the vacuum not as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) famously argued that "nature abhors a vacuum," claiming it was physically impossible.</note> understood it, but in some other fitting way.

It does not seem to me that such a philosophy deserves to be rejected, especially when—upon whatever foundation it presupposes or whatever structure it proposes—it succeeds in achieving the perfection of speculative science and the knowledge of natural things, as has indeed been done by many of the most ancient philosophers. For it is the mark of an ambitious, presumptuous, vain, and envious mind to wish to persuade others that there is only one way to investigate and come to the knowledge of nature; and it is the mark of a madman and a man without reason to convince himself of such a thing.

Therefore, although the most constant and firm way, the most contemplative and distinct, and the highest method of consideration must always be preferred, honored, and sought after, we should not so heavily blame that other method, which is not without good fruit, even if it does not grow from the same tree.

*Dic.* Then you approve of the study of diverse philosophies?

*Teo.* Very much so, for those who have an abundance of time and talent; for others, I approve the study of the best, provided the gods grant that they find it.

*Dic.* I am certain, however, that you do not approve of all philosophies, but only the good and the best.

*Teo.* That is so. Just as in the various branches of medicine, I do not condemn that which is done **magically** through the application of roots, the hanging of stones, and the murmuring of incantations—if the rigor of theologians permits me to speak as a pure naturalist. I approve of that which is done **physically**, proceeding by apothecary recipes, with which one pursues or drives away <term>choler, blood, phlegm, and melancholy</term> <note>The "Four Humors" of traditional Galenic medicine, which were believed to determine a person's health and temperament.</note>. I also accept that which is done **chemically** <note>Referring to "Iatrochemistry" or alchemical medicine, popularized by figures like Paracelsus.</note>, which extracts **quintessences** and, through the work of fire, makes **Mercury** fly from all those compounds, makes **Salt** subside, and makes **Sulfur** flash or *dissolve* \*) <note>original: "discioglier"</note>.

But in the matter of medicine, I do not wish to determine which of these many good ways is the best; for the epileptic, upon whom the physician and the chemist have wasted their time, if he is cured by the magician, will approve—not without reason—[that method...]

---

\*) The text had *Disoglar*; I do not know if it was a mistake. Could it perhaps be *dissalar* [to de-salt], *disvolar* [to fly away], *divolare* [to vanish], or *distuonar* [to go out of tune]? <margin>Translator's note on a suspected typo in the original manuscript.</margin>

<summary>Teofilo argues against philosophical dogmatism, asserting that various systems (elements, atoms, or humors) can lead to truth. He uses an analogy with medicine—comparing magical, physical (Galenic), and chemical (alchemical) treatments—to show that the value of a method is often proven by its results.</summary>

<keywords>pluralism, universal intellect, rational animal, Aristotle, vacuum, four humors, alchemy, Mercury-Salt-Sulfur, Giordano Bruno, philosophy of science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Teofilo, Gervasio, and Dicuono. Following the discussion on the principles of the cosmos, the speakers now address the nature of professional rivalry, the qualities of a true philosopher-physician, and a critique of Aristotle’s intellectual legacy.</meta>

...reason more for this physician than for that one or another. You may reason similarly for other species, none of which will be less good than the others, provided that both the one and the others succeed in achieving the goal they propose. In specific cases, the best physician is the one who heals me, rather than the others who might kill or torment me.

**Gervasio:** Why is it that these sects of physicians are such enemies to one another?

**Teofilo:** Because of avarice, envy, ambition, and ignorance. Commonly, they hardly understand their own method of healing; thus they are even less capable of understanding the methods of others. Furthermore, the majority—being unable to rise to honor and profit through their own virtues—strive to advance themselves by putting down others, showing contempt for what they cannot acquire. But among these, the best and true physician is he who is not so much a <term>physicist</term> <note>In the 16th century, a "physicist" or "physician" was a natural philosopher who studied the "physics" (laws) of nature, not just a medical doctor in the modern sense.</note> that he is not also a chemist and a mathematician. 

Now, to come to the point: among the various types of philosophy, the best is that which most conveniently and profoundly perfects the human intellect, is most in harmony with the truth of nature, and is, as much as possible, a **cooperator** <margin>The context requires "cooperator" instead of "co-operators" as found in the original text.</margin> with nature. This is achieved by "divining"—by which I mean through the natural order and the law of <term>vicissitude</term> <note>Bruno uses "vicissitude" to describe the constant, cyclical change and transformation inherent in the universe.</note>, not by animal instinct like beasts and those like them; not by the inspiration of good or evil spirits as prophets do; nor by a <term>melancholy enthusiasm</term> <note>A reference to the "divine madness" or poetic inspiration that Renaissance thinkers often associated with a melancholic temperament.</note> as poets and other contemplatives do. Rather, it is achieved by establishing laws, reforming customs, healing, or even by knowing and living a more blessed and divine life. 

Thus you see how there is no kind of philosophy, ordered by a regulated sentiment, which does not contain within itself some good property not found in others. I mean the same for medicine, which derives from those principles that presuppose a complete mastery of philosophy—just as the operation of the foot or the hand presupposes the guidance of the eye. Therefore, it is said that one cannot have a good beginning in medicine who does not have a good foundation in philosophy.

**Dicuono:** I like what you say very much, and I praise you greatly; for, just as you are not as common <note>The original term "plebeio" (plebeian) suggests a lack of intellectual refinement or a "herd" mentality.</note> as Aristotle, you are also not as insulting and ambitious as he was—he who wished for the opinions of all other philosophers and their ways of philosophizing to be utterly despised.

**Teofilo:** Although, among all the philosophers that exist, I know of none more grounded in mere imagination and further removed from nature than he. And if he occasionally says excellent things, it is recognized that they do not depend on his own principles; they are always propositions taken from other philosophers, as we see many divine ones in his books on *Generation*, *Meteorology*, and on *Animals* and *Plants*.

**Dicuono:** Returning, then, to our point, do you wish that...

<summary>Teofilo argues that a true physician must also be a philosopher, chemist, and mathematician, while critiquing the sectarianism of his peers and the intellectual arrogance of Aristotle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Teofilo and Dicuono regarding the nature of the "matter" that constitutes the universe. Teofilo is beginning to expand on the idea that matter is not merely a passive substance but a fundamental principle that can be viewed from multiple philosophical perspectives.</meta>

...can matter be defined differently without error and without running into contradiction?

**Teofilo:** True, just as different senses can be judges of the same object, and the same thing can be introduced in different ways. Furthermore, as has been mentioned, the consideration of a thing can be approached from different starting points. The **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was composed of atoms and void; Bruno appreciates their focus on the material, even if he finds it limited.</note> said many good things, even though they did not rise above material quality. **Heraclitus** made many excellent things known, even though he did not ascend above the soul. **Anaxagoras** does not fail to make progress in nature because he wants to recognize an intellect—not only within nature, but perhaps outside and above it; this same intellect is called **God** by **Socrates**, **Plato**, **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed.</note>, and our own theologians. 

Thus, one who begins from the <term>experimental reason</term> <note>Empirical observation and practical experimentation.</note> of what they call "simples" can succeed just as well in discovering the secrets of nature as those who begin from rational theory. Among the latter, those who start from temperaments are no less successful than those who start from humors; nor are these more successful than one who descends from sensible elements, or even higher, from those absolute principles, or from the single matter—the highest and most distinct principle of all. For sometimes, he who takes a longer path does not necessarily make a better journey, especially if his goal is not so much contemplation as it is **operation** <note>In 16th-century philosophy, "operation" refers to practical application, alchemy, or the manipulation of natural forces.</note>. 

Regarding the method of philosophizing, it will be no less convenient to explain forms as if unfolding from an "enfolded" state, than to distinguish them as if from a chaos, or to distribute them as if from an ideal source, or to drive them into act as if from a possibility, or to bring them back as if from a womb, or to unearth them into the light as if from a blind and dark abyss. For every foundation is good if it is approved by the building; every seed is suitable if the trees and fruits are desirable.

**Dicuono:** Now, to come to our purpose, please provide the distinct doctrine of this principle!

**Teofilo:** Certainly. This principle, which is called matter, can be considered in two ways: first as a **potency**, and second as a **subject**. Insofar as it is taken in the same sense as <term>potency</term> <note>From the Latin *potentia*, meaning power or potentiality—the capacity of something to become something else.</note>, there is nothing in which it cannot be found in a certain way according to its own logic. The **Pythagoreans**, **Platonists**, **Stoics**, and others have placed it in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of ideas and spiritual truths, distinct from the physical world we perceive with our senses.</note> no less than in the sensible world. While we do not understand it exactly as they did, but with a higher and more explained reasoning, we reason about potency—or rather, "possibility"—in this way. 

Potency is commonly distinguished into **active potency**, by which the subject can operate, and **passive potency**, by which it can either be, or receive, or have, or be the subject of an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The agent or force that brings something into being.</note> in some manner. Not discussing active potency at the moment, I say that potency—which signifies in a passive way, even if it is not always passive—can be...

<summary>Teofilo argues that various philosophical schools (Epicureans, Platonists, etc.) offer valid perspectives on nature and introduces a dual definition of matter as both "potency" and "subject." He begins to distinguish between active and passive potency, setting the stage for a deeper metaphysical analysis of how possibility becomes reality.</summary>

<keywords>matter, potency, active potency, passive potency, Anaxagoras, Epicureans, Heraclitus, Trismegistus, intelligible world, sensible world, natural philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sentence from the previous page, where Teofilo was describing the different ways to consider the fundamental principles of nature. The word "considerare" (to consider) began on the previous page with "con-" and concludes here with "-siderare."</meta>

...sider <meta>completing the word "consider" from the previous page</meta> or rather absolutely, and thus there is no thing of which one can say "it is" without also saying "it can be." This responds so closely to **<term>active power</term>** <note>original: "potenza attiva"; the capacity of a cause to produce an effect.</note> that the one is never without the other in any way. Hence, if there has always been the power to make, to produce, and to create, there has always been the power to be made, produced, and created; for the one power implies the other. I mean to say, by positing the one, you necessarily posit the other.

This power—which does not imply weakness in the one it is attributed to, but rather confirms their virtue and efficacy, and is ultimately found to be entirely one and the same thing as active power—is something that no philosopher or theologian doubts attributing to the supernatural **<term>first principle</term>** <note>The ultimate source or divine origin of all existence.</note>. For **absolute possibility**, through which things that exist in act are able to be, does not come before actuality; nor does it come after it. Beyond the "ability to be," it exists with "being in act" and does not precede it; for if that which can be were to make itself, it would exist before it was made.

Now contemplate the first and best principle, which is everything that it can be; it would not be a whole if it could not be everything. In it, therefore, **<term>act</term>** <note>original: "atto"; the state of being fully realized or "actual" rather than just potential.</note> and power are the same thing. It is not so in other things which, although they are what they can be, could perhaps not be, or could certainly be something else, or in a different way than what they are. This is because no other thing is everything that it can be. Man is what he can be, but he is not everything that he can be. A stone is not everything it can be; for it is not lime, it is not a vase, it is not dust, it is not grass.

That which is everything it can be is one, which in its being encompasses all being. It is all that exists, and it can be any other thing that exists or can exist. Every other thing is not like this; therefore, in them, power is not equal to act, because it is not absolute act, but limited. Furthermore, power is always limited to a single act, because it never has more than one specified and particular way of being. Even if it looks toward every form and act, this happens by means of certain arrangements and through a certain succession of one state of being after another. Every power and act, then, which in the principle is folded together, united, and one, is in other things unfolded, dispersed, and multiplied. 

The universe—which is the great simulacrum, the great image, and the **<term>unigenita natura</term>** <note>original: "unigenita natura"; literally "only-begotten nature," a term Bruno uses to describe the universe as the singular, direct reflection of God's infinite power.</note>—is also itself everything that it can be in terms of the same species, the principal members, and the containment of all matter (to which nothing is added, and from which nothing of the total and unique form is missing). But it is not everything it can be in terms of the same differences, modes, properties, and individuals; thus, it is nothing other than a shadow of the first act and first power. Therefore, within the universe, power and act are not absolutely the same thing, because no part of it is everything that it can be. Beyond...

<summary>Teofilo argues that in God, the power to create and the potential for things to exist are identical and simultaneous, whereas in the physical universe, potential is limited and realized only through change and succession.</summary>
<keywords>active power, first principle, act and potency, absolute possibility, only-begotten nature, divinity, cosmology, potentiality</keywords>
