<meta>This page continues the discussion on the identity of "act" and "power" (potentiality) in the first principle, concluding a sentence about how things are considered either in parts or as an absolute whole.</meta>

...in that specific way, as we have said, that the universe is everything that it can be, according to an **<term>explicated</term>** <note>original: "esplicato"; refers to the "unfolding" or "manifesting" of the divine unity into the many diverse things of the physical world.</note> mode, dispersed and distinct. Its principle is unitary and indifferent, because everything is everything and the same thing most simply, without difference or distinction.

**Dic.** What will you say of death, corruption, vices, defects, and monsters? Do you wish for these also to have a place in that which is the whole—that which can be, and is in **act**, everything that it can be in **power**?

**Teo.** These things are not **act** and **power**, but are defect and impotence, which are found in explicated things because they are not everything that they can be, and they strive toward what they can be. Because of this, as they cannot be many things together and all at once, they lose one state of being to gain another; sometimes they confuse one state of being with another, and at times they are diminished, lacking, and crippled, due to the incompatibility of this being and that, and the preoccupation of **matter** with one form or the other. 

Now, returning to the subject: the first absolute principle is greatness and magnitude, and it is such magnitude and greatness that it is everything it can be. It is not "great" with the kind of greatness that could be larger, nor could it be smaller, nor could it be divided, like any other magnitude that is not everything it can be. Therefore, it is greatness at its maximum, its minimum, infinite, indivisible, and encompassing every measure. It is not larger, because it is the minimum; it is not smaller, because it is that same maximum; it is beyond all equality because it is everything it can be. 

What I say regarding greatness, understand to apply to everything that can be said; for it is similarly goodness, which is every goodness that can be; it is beauty, which is all the beautiful that can be; and there is no other beauty that is everything it can be, except for this **One**. The **One** is that which is all and can be all absolutely. In natural things, furthermore, we do not see anything that is other than what it is in **act**—according to which it is what it can be, having a certain kind of actuality. Yet, even in this unique specific being, any particular thing is never everything it can be. 

Consider the sun: it is not everything that the sun can be; it is not everywhere the sun can be. For when it is at the eastern horizon for the earth, it is not at the western, nor at the meridian, nor in any other position. Now, if we wish to show the way in which God is the sun, we will say—because He is everything that can be—that He is simultaneously east, west, meridian, **<term>midnight</term>** <note>original: "medinoziale"; the point or time directly opposite the noon meridian.</note>, and any point you like on the **<term>curvature</term>** <note>original: "convessitudine"; the rounded surface or arc of the earth or the heavens.</note> of the earth. Thus, if we wish to understand that this sun moves and changes location—either through its own revolution or that of the earth—we would say it moves because it is not actually in one point without the **power** to be in all others, and therefore it has the aptitude to be there. If, therefore, it is everything that...

<summary>Teofilo explains that while individual objects in the universe are limited by time and space, the divine First Principle exists as a coincidence of all possibilities simultaneously—being at once the maximum and the minimum.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue on the metaphysical identity of act and power in the first principle (God/the Universe). It concludes the thought from the previous page regarding the first principle's absolute magnitude and then uses the metaphor of a perfectly swift sun to illustrate how absolute movement and absolute rest coincide.</meta>

...can be, and possesses all that it is capable of possessing, it will be simultaneously everywhere and in everything. It is so utterly mobile and swift that it is also most stable and immobile. Thus, among the divine discourses, we find it said that He is stable in eternity and yet most swift, running from one end to the other. <note>The speaker refers to the Wisdom of Solomon 8:1: "She reaches mightily from one end of the earth to the other."</note> For by "immobile" we understand that which, in the very same instant, departs from the point of the East and has returned to that same point. Furthermore, it is seen no less in the East than in the West, or any other point of its circuit. For this reason, there is no more cause to say it departs and returns, or has departed and returned, from one point to another, than from any of the infinite other points to that same one. 

<margin>Exodus 3:14.</margin>

From this, it follows that it is entirely and always in the whole circle, and in every part of it; and consequently, every **<term>indivisible point</term>** <note>original: "punto individuo"; refers to a point that cannot be further divided, such as a geometric point or an atom.</note> of the **<term>ecliptic</term>** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere as seen from Earth.</note> contains the entire diameter of the sun. And thus the indivisible comes to contain the **<term>divisible</term>**; <note>original: "dividuo"; that which can be partitioned or measured in parts.</note> this does not happen through natural possibility, but supernatural—that is to say, when one supposes the sun to be that which is, in **act**, everything that it can be. This absolute power is not only what the sun can be, but what every thing is, and what every thing can be: the power of all powers, the act of all acts, the life of all lives, the soul of all souls, the being of all being. Hence it was loftily said by the **<term>Revealer</term>**; <note>A term Bruno often uses for Moses or the divine voice in Scripture.</note> *He who is, sends me; He who is, says this.* <note>original: "Quel, ch' è, me invia"; a translation of the Latin "Ego sum qui sum" from Exodus 3:14.</note> Therefore, that which elsewhere is contrary and opposite is, in Him, one and the same, and everything in Him is identical. This applies to the differences of times and durations, as well as to the differences of **actuality** and **possibility**; therefore, He is not a thing that is old, and He is not a thing that is new—which is why the Revealer rightly called Him the **First and the Last**.

**Dic.** This most absolute act, which is the same as the most absolute power, cannot be grasped by the intellect except by way of negation: it cannot, I say, be understood either in how it *can be* everything, or in how it *is* everything. For when the intellect wishes to understand, it must necessarily form an **<term>intelligible species</term>** <note>A Scholastic term for the mental representation or "image" of an object that allows the mind to know it.</note>—to liken itself to, measure itself against, and equalize itself with that thing. But this is impossible here; for the intellect is never so great that it could not be greater, whereas that principle, being immense in every direction and manner, cannot be larger. There is, therefore, no eye that can approach, or that has access to, such a supreme light and such a profound abyss.

**Teo.** The coincidence of this act with absolute power has been very clearly described by the divine spirit, where it says: *Darkness shall not be dark to you. Night shall be enlightened as the day. As is its darkness, so too is its light.* <note>original: "Tenebrae non obscurabuntur a te. Nox sicut dies illuminabitur. Sicut tenebrae ejus, ita et lumen ejus." A translation of Psalm 139:12.</note> Concluding then, you see how great is the excellence of this power, which...

<summary>Teofilo explains how the first principle's absolute nature resolves all opposites, such as motion and rest or darkness and light, using the metaphor of a sun that is simultaneously everywhere. Dixon notes that human intellect can only understand this absolute through negation because the infinite cannot be captured by finite mental images.</summary>

<keywords>absolute act, absolute power, coincidence of opposites, apophatic theology, Exodus 3:14, Psalm 139, ecliptic, intelligible species, infinity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue on the metaphysical identity of act and power in the first principle. On the previous page, the speakers used the metaphor of a perfectly swift sun to show how absolute movement and absolute rest are the same in the infinite. Now, they apply this logic to the concept of "matter" to show that at the highest level of reality, the material and the formal—the potential and the actual—merge into a single unity.</meta>

<page-num>264</page-num>

If you like to call it the **<term>principle of matter</term>** <note>original: "ragione di materia"; in this context, the underlying logic or essential nature of what constitutes "matter."</note>, which common philosophers have not grasped, you may—without detracting from divinity—treat it more deeply than Plato did in his **<term>Republic</term>** <note>original: "Politica"; though Bruno writes "Politics," he refers to Plato’s Republic, which explores the ideal state and its metaphysical underpinnings.</note> and the *Timaeus*. These men, by having raised the principle of matter too high, were scandalous to some theologians. This happened either because the former did not express themselves clearly, or because the latter did not understand them well; for theologians always take the meaning of "matter" only as the subject of natural things—being raised solely on the opinions of Aristotle—and they do not consider that for others, matter is something common to both the **<term>intelligible and sensible worlds</term>** <note>The "sensible" world is the physical world we perceive with our senses, while the "intelligible" world is the realm of pure thought or divine ideas.</note>, as they say, using the term in an analogous sense. Therefore, before they are condemned, these opinions must be very carefully examined, and languages must be distinguished <note>The original text contains a grammatical slip (anacoluthon) here; it suggests "distinguishing" the languages just as the "sentiments" (meanings) are distinguished.</note> just as meanings are. For although everyone may at times agree on a common principle of matter, they differ in its specific application.

And regarding our purpose: once the name "matter" is removed—and let the critic be as captious and malicious as they wish—it is impossible to find a theologian who could charge me with impiety for what I say and mean regarding the **<term>coincidence of potency and act</term>** <note>A central theme in Bruno’s thought: in God or the Universe as a whole, what *can* be (potency) and what *is* (act) are the same thing.</note>, taking both terms in their absolute sense. From this I would infer that, according to this proportion (which is lawful to say in this image of that act and that potency), because everything that is in "specific potency" is also in "specific act"—insofar as the universe in this way is everything that it can be, regardless of individual acts and potencies—it comes to have a power that is not separate from its action, and a soul not separate from the thing it animates; I do not mean the composite thing, but the simple essence. Thus, for the universe, there will be a single first principle, which itself is understood to be no more distinctly material than it is formal; this can be inferred from the similarity of the aforementioned absolute potency and act. Thus, it will not be difficult or burdensome to finally accept that the whole, according to its **<term>substance</term>** <note>The underlying reality that remains constant beneath changing appearances.</note>, is one—as Parmenides perhaps understood, who was treated ignobly by Aristotle.

**Dicsono.** Do you mean then that, although descending this ladder of nature there appears to be a double substance—one spiritual, the other corporeal—in the end, both are reduced to one being and one root?

**Teofilo.** If you think this can be tolerated by those who do not look deeper than the surface.

**Dicsono.** Very easily, provided you do not rise above the limits of nature.

**Teofilo.** That is already done. If we do not share that common sense and way of defining divinity, we have a particular one; it is not, however, contrary or alien to the common one, but...

<summary>Teofilo argues that "matter" and "form" (or act and potency) are ultimately the same at the highest level of reality, suggesting the universe is a single, unified substance—a view he attributes to Parmenides.</summary>

# FOURTH DIALOGUE

->Poliinnio<-

*And the mouth of the womb never says: "it is enough," that is to say, clearly, namely, as it were—which is to say, matter,* <note>original: "Et os vulvae nunquam dicit: sufficit... materia"</note> which is signified by these things, *is never filled up by the forms it receives.* <note>original: "recipiendis formis nunquam expletur"</note> Now, since there is no one else in this **<term>Lyceum</term>** <note>The name of the school founded by Aristotle; Poliinnio uses it to refer to their meeting place.</note>, *or rather Anti-Lyceum, I shall walk alone—so alone, I say, that I am the least alone of all—and I will converse with myself.* <note>original: "vel potius Antiliceo, solus, ita inquam solus, ut minime omnium solus, deambulabo, et ipse mecum confabulabor"</note> Matter, therefore, by the prince of the **<term>Peripatetics</term>** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note>, and the high-minded genius of the great Macedonian leader <note>Referring to Aristotle, who was from Macedonia and tutor to Alexander the Great.</note>, *no less* than by the divine Plato, is called *now chaos, now **<term>hyle</term>** <note>The Greek word for "matter" or "wood."</note>, now forest, now mass, now power, now aptitude, now mixed with deprivation, now the cause of sin, now ordained toward evil, now non-being in itself, now unknowable in itself, now knowable by analogy to form, now a blank slate, now unpainted, now a subject, now a substratum, now a foundation, now a field, now infinite, now indeterminate, now almost nothing, now neither a 'what,' nor a 'of what kind,' nor 'how much'* <note>original: "or caos, or hyle... or neque quid, neque quale, neque quantum"</note>—finally, after having aimed at defining this nature with various and diverse nomenclatures, *by those who hit the mark, she* is called "woman"; *finally, I say, so that one word might embrace all names, she is called "woman" by those who better weigh the matter. And by Hercules!* <note>original: "Et mehercle!"</note> It is not without a significant reason that it pleased these senators of the kingdom of **<term>Pallas</term>** <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom; Poliinnio is mockingly referring to philosophers.</note> to place these two things in the same balance: matter and woman. For after the experience they had of the rigor of the latter, they were driven to such rage and frenzy—and here a rhetorical flourish comes to me—these are a chaos of irrationality, a *hyle* of wickedness, a forest of roguery, a mass of filth, an aptitude for every perdition—another rhetorical flourish called by some a "complexion"!—Where there was potentiality, *not only remote, but even near* <note>original: "non solum remota, ma etiam propinqua"</note>...

<summary>The Third Dialogue concludes with an agreement to discuss matter as a "subject," and the Fourth Dialogue begins with a satirical monologue by the pedant Poliinnio. Poliinnio uses a string of Aristotelian and Platonic terms to mockingly equate the philosophical concept of "matter" with "woman," reflecting common academic prejudices of the era.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Plato, matter, hyle, potentiality, Peripatetics, Poliinnio, satire, scholasticism</keywords>

...the destruction of Troy? In a woman. Who was the instrument of the destruction of Samson’s strength? <note>original: "sansonica fortezza"</note> Of that hero, I say, who with that jawbone of an ass that he found, became the undefeated victor over the Philistines? A woman. Who tamed at Capua the impulse and force of the great captain and perpetual enemy of the Roman republic, Hannibal? A woman! Tell me, oh cithara-playing prophet, <note>A reference to King David, traditionally credited with the Psalms.</note> the cause of your fragility! *For my mother conceived me in sin.* <note>original: "Quia in peccatis concepit me mater mea." A quote from Psalm 51:5.</note> How, oh our ancient **<term>protoplast</term>** <note>From the Greek "first-formed," referring to Adam.</note>, being a gardener of paradise and a cultivator of the tree of life, were you so bewitched that you pushed yourself and the whole human seed into the deep pit of perdition? *The woman whom he gave to me, she, she deceived me.* <note>original: "Mulier, quam dedit mihi, ipsa, ipsa me decepit." Referring to Adam’s excuse in Genesis 3:12.</note> Without a doubt, form does not sin, and no error comes from any form, except by being joined to matter. Thus the form, signified by the male, being placed in familiarity with matter, and having come into composition or copulation with it, responds to **<term>Nature Naturing</term>** <note>A philosophical term (Latin: *natura naturans*) referring to the creative power of the universe or God as the source of all being.</note> with these words, or rather with this sentence: *The woman whom you gave to me* <note>original: "Mulier, quam dedisti mihi"</note>, i.e., matter, whom you have given me as a consort, *she deceived me* <note>original: "ipsa me decepit"</note>, that is, she is the cause of all my sin. 

Contemplate, contemplate, divine intellect, how the excellent philosophers and the discerning **<term>anatomists</term>** <note>original: "notomisti"; here referring to those who investigate the internal structure of nature.</note> of nature's vitals, to place fully before our eyes the nature of matter, have found no more fitting way than to warn us with this comparison: that the state of natural things regarding matter is like the economic, political, and civil state regarding the female sex. Open, open your eyes, and.... Oh, I see that colossus of idleness, Gervasio, who interrupts the thread of my vigorous oration. I suspect I have been heard by him; but what does it matter?

**Ger.** *Greetings, best master of doctors!* <note>original: "Salve, magister doctorum optime!"</note>
**Pol.** Unless, in your usual way, you wish to mock me, *greetings to you too!* <note>original: "tu quoque salve!"</note>
**Ger.** I would like to know what you were walking along ruminating about?
**Pol.** While studying in my little library, *I happened upon that passage which is in Aristotle* <note>original: "in eum, qui apud Aristotelem est, locum incidi"</note>, at the end of the first book of the *Physics*, where, wishing to clarify what primary matter was, he uses the female sex as a mirror—a sex, I say, stubborn, fragile, inconstant, soft, petty, infamous, ignoble, vile, abject, neglected, unworthy, reprobate, sinister, shameful, cold, deformed, void, vain, indiscreet, insane, treacherous, shiftless, putrid, filthy, ungrateful, truncated, mutilated, imperfect, incomplete, insufficient, cut off, amputated, wasted, rust, caterpillar, weed, plague, disease, death,

->Placed among us by nature and God<-
->As a burden and a heavy penalty.<-

**Ger.** I know that you say this more to exercise yourself in...

...the art of oratory, and to demonstrate how copious and eloquent you are, that you possess such a sentiment as you display through your words. For it is an ordinary thing for you **gentlemen humanists**, who call yourselves **<term>professors of fine letters</term>** <note>A term for scholars of the "humanities" (literae humaniores) who specialized in classical rhetoric and literature.</note>, that when you find yourselves full of those concepts that you cannot contain, you go to unload them nowhere else but upon poor women; just as when some other anger pressures you, you come to vent it upon the first offending student among your pupils. But beware, **gentlemen Orpheuses**, of the furious indignation of the Thracian women! <note>According to myth, the poet Orpheus was torn apart by the women of Thrace after he rejected them.</note>

**Pol.** I am Poliinnio, I am not Orpheus.
**Dic.** So then, you do not truly blame women?
**Pol.** **Not at all, not at all indeed.** <note>original: "Minime, minime quidem."</note> I speak in earnest, and I intend nothing other than what I say; for I do not make it my profession, **in the manner of the sophists**, <note>original: "sophistarum more." Sophists were ancient Greek teachers known for their ability to argue any side of an issue, regardless of the truth.</note> to demonstrate to you that white is black.
**Ger.** Why then do you dye your beard?
**Pol.** **But I speak candidly**, <note>original: "Ma ingenue loquor."</note> and I say that a man without a woman is like one of the **<term>Intelligences</term>** <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, these were the celestial, non-material beings that moved the heavenly spheres.</note>; he is, I say, a hero, a semi-god, **who has not taken a wife**. <note>original: "qui non duxit uxorem."</note>
**Ger.** And he is also like an oyster, and a mushroom too, and he is a truffle.
**Pol.** Whence the lyric poet divinely said:
->**Believe me, Pisonians, nothing is better than a celibate life.**<- <note>original: "Credite, Pisones, melius nil caelibe vita." A variation on a classical theme often attributed to Horace or pseudo-classical sources.</note>

And if you wish to know the reason, hear **Secundus the philosopher**: <note>Secundus the Silent, a 2nd-century philosopher known for his harsh, pithy definitions of women.</note> "Woman," he says, "is an obstacle to peace, a constant harm, a daily war, a prison of life, a storm in the house, a shipwreck of man." This was well confirmed by that **Biscayan**, <note>A person from the Basque region of Spain.</note> who, having become impatient and angry due to a horrible stroke of fortune and the fury of the sea, with a grim and angry face, turned to the waves and said: "Oh sea, sea, if only I could marry you off!" meaning to imply that a woman is the storm of storms. Therefore **Protagoras**, <note>A famous Greek Sophist.</note> when asked why he had given his daughter to an enemy, replied that he could do nothing worse to him than give him a wife. Furthermore, a good Frenchman will not make a liar of me; he, like all the others who were suffering a most dangerous storm at sea, was commanded by Cicala, <note>Possibly a reference to Scipione Cicala, a famous naval commander.</note> the master of the ship, to throw the heaviest things into the sea—and he, first of all, threw in his wife.

**Ger.** You do not, on the contrary, report so many other examples of those who have considered themselves most fortunate because of their women; among whom, not to send you too far away, look right here under this very roof at the **Lord of Mauvissière**, <note>Michel de Castelnau, Sieur de Mauvissière, the French ambassador to England and Bruno's patron.</note> who has encountered one who is not only endowed with no mediocre bodily beauty—which <insert>for her</insert> <note>Correction to the pronoun "him" (gli) in the preceding paragraph.</note> veils and cloaks his soul—but who also, with a **<term>triumvirate</term>** <note>A grouping of three. Here, Gervasio uses political terminology to describe her virtues.</note> of very discreet judgment, wise modesty, and most noble courtesy, holds the soul of her spouse bound with an indissoluble knot, and is powerful...

...winning over anyone who knows her. What will you say of that noble daughter, who has seen the sun for barely a **<term>lustrum</term>** <note>A period of five years; thus, the girl is six years old.</note> and a year, and from her speech you could not judge whether she is from Italy, or France, or England? From her hand upon musical instruments, you could not understand if she is a bodily or bodiless substance. From her mature goodness of character, you would doubt whether she descended from heaven or came forth from the earth. Everyone sees that in her, no less through the formation of such a beautiful body, there has flowed the blood of both parents, than to the construction of her singular spirit, the virtues of the heroic souls of those same ones. <note>It almost seems as if a fault is hidden here, unless the flattery should be called exorbitant.</note>

**Pol.** **A rare bird** <note>original: "Rara avis"</note>, like Maria from Boshtel! **A rare bird**, like Maria from Castelnovo!

**Ger.** The same rarity you speak of in women can also be said of men.

**Pol.** In the end, to return to the point, a woman is nothing other than **matter**. If you do not know what a woman is because you do not know what matter is, study the **<term>Peripatetics</term>** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who traditionally viewed "matter" as a passive, feminine principle and "form" as an active, masculine one.</note> for a while; by teaching you what matter is, they will teach you what a woman is.

**Ger.** I see clearly that, because you have a Peripatetic brain, you learned little or nothing of what Teofilo said yesterday regarding the essence and power of matter.

**Pol.** Be that as it may, I stand firm on the point of blaming the **<term>appetite</term>** <note>In traditional physics, "appetite" refers to the inherent tendency of matter to seek out and join with a "form" or specific identity.</note> of both, which is the cause of every evil, passion, defect, ruin, and corruption. Do you not believe that if matter were content with its present form, no alteration or passion would have dominion over us, we would not die, and we would be incorruptible and eternal?

**Ger.** And if it had been content with that form which it had fifty years ago, what would you say? Would you, Poliinnio—if it had remained under that of forty years past—be so **adulterous**—I mean, so **adult**, so perfect, and so learned? <note>Gervasio makes a pun on the similarity between the words "adultero" (adulterous) and "adulto" (adult) to mock Poliinnio's pedantry.</note> Just as it pleases you that other forms have yielded to this one, so it is the will of Nature, which orders the universe, that all forms yield to all others. I will add that it is a greater dignity for this substance of ours to become everything, receiving all forms, than by retaining only one, to be a partial thing. Thus, within its capacity, it possesses the likeness of Him who is all in all. <note>Gervasio argues that matter’s ability to change is what makes it divine, as it mimics the infinite nature of God.</note>

**Pol.** You are beginning to appear learned to me, stepping outside your natural character. Now, if you can, apply this to similar things, bringing forth the dignity that is found in the female.

**Ger.** I shall do so very easily. Oh, here is Teofilo!

<summary>Gervasio defends the potential of women and the philosophical dignity of matter, arguing that the ability to change and take on new forms is a divine quality rather than a defect. The pedantic Poliinnio remains skeptical as the philosopher Teofilo enters the scene.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Dialogue of "On the Cause, Principle, and One." After a brief digression on the virtues of women, the character Teofilo returns to the central metaphysical argument: the unity of matter across both the physical and spiritual realms.</meta>

<page-num>269</page-num>

**Pol.** And Dickson <note>Alexander Dickson, a Scottish follower of Bruno’s mnemonic arts and a character in these dialogues.</note>. Another time then. **Enough of these things!** <note>original: "De iis hactenus!"</note>

**Teo.** Do we not see that the **<term>Peripatetics</term>** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, as well as the **<term>Platonists</term>** <note>Followers of Plato.</note>, divide substance by the difference between the corporal and the incorporal? Just as these differences are reduced to the **potential** <note>The capacity to become something; "potenza."</note> of the same **genus** <note>A logical category; "geno."</note>, it must follow that forms are of two sorts. Some are transcendent—that is, superior to any specific category—which are called principles, such as entity, unity, the "one," "thing," "something," and other similar terms. Others belong to a specific genus and are distinct from other genera, such as substantiality or accidentality. Those of the first kind do not distinguish matter into different types, nor do they create different potentials within it; rather, as most universal terms that encompass both corporal and incorporal substances, they signify that most universal, most common unity of both. 

Furthermore, as **Avicebron** <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021–1058), a Jewish philosopher whose work "The Fountain of Life" argued that a "universal matter" underlies both physical and spiritual beings. Bruno championed this then-controversial view.</note> said, what prevents us from recognizing this? Before we recognize the matter of accidental forms (which is the composite object), we recognize the matter of the substantial form (which is a part of it). In the same way, before we know matter as it is restricted to being under corporal forms, can we not come to know a potentiality that is capable of receiving either a corporeal or an incorporeal nature, whether dissoluble or indissoluble?

Again, if everything that exists—starting from the highest and supreme being—possesses a certain order and forms a dependency, a scale, upon which one climbs from composite things to simple ones, and from these to the simplest and most absolute via proportional, joining, and participating means of the nature of both extremes, and which are by their own nature neutral: there is no order where there is no certain participation; there is no participation where there is no certain connection; there is no connection without some participation. It is therefore necessary that for all things that are subsisting, there be one principle of subsistence. 

Add to this that reason itself cannot help but presuppose an indistinct thing before any distinguishable thing—I speak here of those things that exist; for between "being" and "non-being" I do not intend a real distinction, but only a vocal and nominal one. This indistinct thing is a common ground to which difference and distinctive form are added. And certainly it cannot be denied that, just as every sensible thing <note>Something that can be perceived by the senses.</note> presupposes the subject of sensibility, so every intelligible thing <note>Something that can be understood by the mind but not seen.</note> presupposes the subject of intelligibility. 

There must be, then, a thing that corresponds to the common ground of both subjects. This is because every essence is necessarily founded upon some "being," except for that first Essence, which is one and the same as its own being: for its potential is its act, because it is everything that it can be, as was said yesterday. Furthermore, if matter—according to these same adversaries—is not a body, and precedes by its nature "corporal being," what then can make it so alien from...

<summary>Teofilo argues for a "universal matter" that exists beneath both the physical and spiritual worlds, using the "Scale of Being" and the philosophy of Avicebron to show that all things share a common ground of existence.</summary>

...the substances called incorporeal? **And** there are some among the **<term>Peripatetics</term>** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> who say: just as in corporeal substances one finds a certain element that is formal and divine, so in divine things it is fitting that there be something material, so that lower things may be harmonized with the higher, and the order of the one depends on the order of the others. **And** the theologians, although some of them are raised in the **<term>Aristotelian doctrine</term>** <note>The philosophical system of Aristotle, which dominated medieval Christian theology.</note>, should not be troubled by me in this, if they admit they are more indebted to their Scripture than to philosophy and natural reason. "Do not worship me," said one of their angels to the patriarch **Jacob** <note>Bruno likely refers here to the biblical tradition where angels identify as "fellow servants" or "brothers" to humans (e.g., Revelation 22:9), though he attributes the specific sentiment to the context of Jacob's struggle or angelic encounters.</note>, "because I am your brother!" Now, if this speaker—as they understand it—is an intellectual substance, and affirms by his speech that that man and he agree in the reality of a single subject, regardless of any formal difference, it remains that the philosophers have an oracle from these theologians as testimony.

**Dic.** I know that this is said by you with reverence; for you know that it is not fitting for you to beg for arguments from such places, which are outside of our harvest. <note>Dickson suggests that philosophical proof should rely on reason rather than religious scripture.</note>

**Teo.** You speak well and truly; but I do not allege that as a reason or confirmation, but rather to avoid causing offense as much as I can; for I fear appearing to be contrary to theology no less than I fear actually being so.

**Dic.** Natural reasons will always be admitted by discreet theologians, however much they may wander, provided they do not determine anything against divine authority, but submit themselves to it.

**Teo.** Such are my reasons, and such they shall always be.

**Dic.** Good! Then proceed!

**Teo.** **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who wrote the *Enneads*.</note> also says in his book on matter, *) that if in the **<term>intelligible world</term>** <note>The realm of pure thought or spirit, as opposed to the physical world of the senses.</note> there is a multitude and plurality of species, it is necessary that there be something common, beyond the property and difference of each one of them: that which is common holds the place of matter; that which is specific, and creates distinction, holds the place of form. He adds that if this physical world is an imitation of that spiritual world, the composition of this one is an imitation of the composition of that one. Furthermore, if that world has no diversity, it has no order; if it has no order, it has no beauty or ornament; and all of this concerns matter. For this reason, the higher world must not only be esteemed as entirely indivisible, but also, through some of its conditions, as divisible and distinct; its division and distinction cannot be understood without some underlying matter. **And** although he says that all that multitude fits into a single impartible being, and is outside of any dimension, I will call that "matter" in which so many forms are united; that which, before it is conceived...

---

*) <note>original: "Ennead. 2, 4."</note> *Enneads*, Book 2, Tractate 4.

<summary>Teofilo argues that "matter" exists in the spiritual realm as a common substrate for diverse forms, citing both biblical references to angelic brotherhood and Plotinus's Neoplatonic philosophy to bridge the gap between the divine and physical worlds.</summary>

...varied and multiform, it was uniform in concept; and before it was a formed concept, it was an unformed one.

**Dic.** Although in what you have said with brevity, you have brought many strong reasons to conclude that matter is one, and <term>potency</term> <note>The capacity or potential to exist or act.</note> is one, by which everything that is exists in <term>act</term> <note>The actualized state of being, as opposed to mere potential.</note>; and that with no less reason this applies to incorporeal substances than to corporeal ones—since the former possess being through the "power to be" no differently than the latter possess being through the "power to be"—and since you have demonstrated this through other powerful reasons to anyone who considers and understands them deeply: nevertheless, if not for the perfection of the doctrine then for its clarity, I would like you to specify in some other way how in most excellent things, such as the incorporeal, there can be found something unformed and indefinite. How can there be the same logic of matter [in both], and yet by the occurrence of form and act they are not similarly called "bodies"? How, where there is no change, generation, or corruption whatsoever, do you claim there is matter, which has never been posited for any other purpose? How can we say the intelligible nature is simple, and yet say that within it there is matter and act? I do not ask this for myself, to whom the truth is manifest, but perhaps for others who might be more slow-witted and difficult, such as, for example, Master Polinnio and Gervasio.

**Pol.** I yield!

**Ger.** I accept, and I thank you, **Dickson**, for considering the necessity of those who do not have the courage to ask, as is the custom at <term>ultramontane</term> <note>Literally "beyond the mountains"; here referring to Northern European social customs from an Italian perspective.</note> tables, where those who sit in the second seats are not permitted to stretch their fingers outside their own square or round plate, but must wait for food to be placed in their hands, so that they do not take a mouthful that has not been paid for with a "great mercy" <note>A polite thank-you.</note>.

**Teo. I shall say**, as a resolution to the whole matter, that just as man, according to the proper nature of man, is different from a lion according to the proper nature of a lion, but according to the common nature of "animal," "corporeal substance," and other such categories they are indifferent and the same thing; similarly, according to its own logic, the matter of corporeal things is different from the <margin>*) That is, from that. "Da la" or "dalla" is "de illa" <note>Latin: "from that".</note>.</margin> matter of incorporeal things. Therefore, everything you bring up regarding being the constitutive cause of corporeal nature, being the subject of all sorts of transmutations, and being a part of compounds, applies to this [physical] matter because of its specific logic; because the same matter—I wish to speak more clearly—the same thing that *can be made*, or *can be*, or *is made*, exists by means of the dimensions and extension of the subject, and those qualities which have their being in the...

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Dialogue of "On the Cause, Principle, and One." Teofilo is refining the argument that "matter" is a universal substrate. He explains that while matter in the physical world changes forms over time, in the divine or "intelligible" world, matter possesses all its potential forms simultaneously.</meta>

<page-num>272</page-num>

...how much; and this is called **corporeal substance**, and it presupposes corporeal matter; or it is made—if indeed it has being anew—and it is without those dimensions, extension, and quality; and this is called **incorporeal substance**, and it similarly presupposes said matter. Thus to an **active power** <term>active power</term> <note>The capacity of a cause to produce an effect or give form.</note>, as much of corporeal things as of incorporeal things, or rather to a being as much corporeal as incorporeal, there corresponds a **passive power** <term>passive power</term> <note>The capacity of a thing to receive a form or be acted upon; the "potential" of matter.</note>, as much corporeal as incorporeal, and a "possibility of being" as much corporeal as incorporeal. If then we wish to speak of composition in the one nature as much as the other, we must understand it in different ways, and consider that in eternal things one says **matter** is always under one **act** <term>act</term> <note>The state of being fully realized or actualized, as opposed to mere potential.</note>, and that in variable things it always contains now one [act], now another. In those eternal things, matter has all at once, always and together, everything that it can be; but in these variable things, it has it at various times, through different periods and certain successions.

**Dic.** Some, although they concede that there is matter in incorporeal things, understand it, however, according to a very different logic.

**Teo.** Let there be as much diversity as you wish according to their own specific logic—by which one descends to corporeal being and the other does not, one receives sensible qualities and the other does not. It might not seem that there could be a common logic to that matter which is "repugnant" to quantity and to being a subject of qualities (which have their being in dimensions), and that nature to which neither is repugnant. Rather, both are one and the same, and as has been said many times, the whole difference depends on the **contraction** <note>A philosophical term referring to the narrowing or limiting of a universal essence into a specific, finite form.</note> to being corporeal or not being corporeal. Just as in being an animal, every sensitive being is one, but by "contracting" that **genus** <note>original: "geno"</note> to certain species, it is repugnant to a man to be a lion, and to this animal to be that other. 

And I add to this, if it pleases you—because you might tell me that what never is should be judged impossible and **against nature** <note>original: "contra natura"</note> rather than natural, and therefore, since that [incorporeal] matter is never found with dimensions, it should be judged that corporeality is against nature to it: and if this is so, it is not likely that there is a common nature to both before one is understood to be contracted to corporeal being—I add, I say, that we can no less attribute to that matter the necessity of all dimensional acts than, as you would have it, the impossibility. That matter, because it is actually everything that it can be, has all measures, has all kinds of figures and dimensions; and because it has them all, it has none of them [individually]; for that which is so many different things must necessarily not be any one of those particular things. It befits that which is everything to exclude every particular being.

**Dic.** Do you want, then, for matter to be **act**? Do you want, further, that in incorporeal things matter coincides with **act**?

<summary>Teofilo argues that matter in the spiritual realm contains all possible forms simultaneously, making it "actuality" itself, whereas physical matter only takes on forms one at a time. He uses the analogy of a genus containing various species to explain how one substance can manifest in seemingly contradictory ways.</summary>

<keywords>corporeal substance, incorporeal substance, active power, passive power, potentiality, actuality, contraction, genus and species, coincidence of opposites</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Dialogue where Teofilo explains that in the divine or absolute realm, matter (potentiality) and form (actuality) are not distinct but are a single, unified principle. He is now moving to explain how this "possibility of being" relates to the "act of being."</meta>

## Teo. How the **possibility of being** coincides with **being**.

**Dic.** Does it not differ, then, from form?

**Teo.** Not at all in **absolute power** <term>absolute power</term> <note>The total potential for everything to exist.</note> and **absolute act** <term>absolute act</term> <note>The complete realization of all existence; in Bruno's thought, these meet in God.</note>, which is at the furthest extreme of purity, simplicity, indivisibility, and unity; for it is absolutely everything. If it had certain dimensions, a certain way of being, a certain figure, a certain property, or a certain difference, it would not be absolute, and it would not be everything.

**Dic.** Is everything, then, that contains any kind of **genus** <term>genus</term> <note>A general category or class of things.</note> also **indivisible** <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "individua." In this context, it means something that cannot be further divided because it represents a totality or a fundamental unit.</note>?

**Teo.** So it is; because the form that contains all qualities is not any one of them; that which has all figures has none of them; that which has all sensible being is not itself sensed. More highly indivisible is that which has all natural being; more highly still is that which has all intellectual being; and most highly of all is that which has all the being that is possible.

**Dic.** In the likeness of this scale of being, do you intend there to be a scale of the **possibility of being**, and do you intend that as the formal logic ascends, so the material logic ascends also?

**Teo.** That is true.

**Dic.** You take this definition of matter and power very profoundly and highly.

**Teo.** True.

**Dic.** But this truth cannot be understood by everyone, for it is indeed difficult to grasp the way in which a thing can possess every kind of dimension, and yet not have any one of them; to have all formal being, and yet have no specific form.

**Teo.** Do you understand how this can be?

**Dic.** I believe I do; for I understand well that for the **act** to be everything, it must not be any one specific thing.

**Pol.** The same thing cannot be both the whole and a specific part; I understand that too. <note>original: "Non potest esse idem totum et aliquid; ego quoque illud capio."</note>

**Teo.** Therefore, you will be able to understand correctly that, if we wished to establish **dimensionability** <term>dimensionability</term> <note>The capacity to occupy space or have measurements.</note> as the logic of matter, such logic would not be repugnant to any sort of matter. However, one type of matter differs from another only by being either absolute from dimensions or contracted to dimensions. By being absolute, it is above all things and encompasses them all; by being **contracted** <term>contracted</term> <note>Limited, restricted, or condensed into a specific physical form.</note>, it is encompassed by some things and is subject to some.

**Dic.** You say well that matter, in itself, has no specific dimensions, and is therefore understood as indivisible; it receives dimensions according to the logic of the form it receives. It has certain dimensions under the human form, others under the horse form, others under olive oil, others under the myrtle tree. Thus, before it is under any of these forms, it has all those dimensions in its faculty, just as it has the power to receive all those forms.

<summary>Teofilo argues that in its absolute state, matter (potentiality) and form (actuality) are the same, as the "whole" cannot be limited to any specific "part." Matter is presented as an indivisible substrate that possesses the potential for all dimensions and forms before it is "contracted" into specific physical objects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Dialogue where Teofilo and Dicson are discussing the nature of matter. They have just established that absolute matter must be indivisible and contain all possible forms. **Pol.** They say, however, that it is for this reason—because it has no dimensions.

**Dic.** And we say that *it has none, in order that it may have all* <note>original: "ideo habet nullas, ut omnes habeat"</note>.

**Ger.** Why would you rather say that it includes them all, rather than excludes them all?

**Dic.** Because it does not receive these dimensions from the outside, but sends them forth and drives them out, as if from its own womb <term>womb</term> <note>original: "seno," literally bosom or lap; used here to denote the internal, fertile source of all things.</note>.

**Teo.** You speak very well. Moreover, it is a common way of speaking even for the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> who all say that the dimensional act and all forms emerge and come forth from the potentiality of matter. This is understood in part by **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly influential and controversial in the Renaissance.</note>, who, although he was an Arab and ignorant of the Greek language, nevertheless understood more of the peripatetic doctrine than any Greek we have read; and he would have understood even more had he not been so devoted to his deity, **Aristotle**. He says that matter, in its essence, encompasses indeterminate dimensions; wanting to suggest that these come to be limited now with this shape and dimension, now with that one or another, according to the changing of natural forms. By this sense, one sees that matter sends them forth from itself, and does not receive them from the outside. 

This was also understood in part by **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, the prince of the **Platonic** sect. He, making a distinction between the matter of higher things <note>Intelligible or divine matter.</note> and lower things <note>Physical or sensible matter.</note>, says that the former is everything at once, and since it possesses everything, it has nothing into which it may change; but this [lower matter], with a certain rotation through its parts, becomes everything, and from time to time becomes one thing and then another; however, it is always subject to diversity, alteration, and motion. Thus, that higher matter is never formless, nor is this lower matter, though they differ: the former in the instant of eternity, the latter in the instants of time; the former all at once, the latter successively; the former explicitly, the latter implicitly <note>original: "complicatamente," meaning "enfolded" or "infolded," a key concept in Bruno’s thought where many things exist as one potential.</note>; the former as many, the latter as one; the former through each thing and for each thing, the latter as a whole and every thing.

**Dic.** So much so that, not only according to your principles, but also according to the principles of other ways of philosophizing, you wish to infer that matter is not that *nearly nothing* <note>original: "prope nihil"</note>, that pure potentiality—naked, without act, without power and perfection.

**Teo.** That is it. I call it deprived of forms and "without" them, not as ice is without heat or the deep is deprived of light, but as a pregnant woman is without her offspring, whom she sends forth and releases from herself; and as the earth in this hemisphere during the night is without light, which it is capable of regaining by its own rotation.

**Dic.** See then, how even in these lower things, actuality coincides greatly—if not entirely—with potentiality.

**Teo.** I leave that to your judgment.

<summary>Teofilo argues that matter is not a passive void but a fertile source (like a womb) that contains all potential forms and dimensions. He draws on Averroes and Plotinus to show that matter and form (actuality and potentiality) are more closely linked than traditional Aristotelians admit.</summary>

**Dic.** And if this power from below were finally to become one with that from above, what would that be?

**Teo.** You judge for yourself! From this you can rise to the concept—I do not say of the highest and best principle <note>original: "summo et ottimo principio," a reference to God as the ultimate source</note>, which is excluded from our consideration—but of the **soul of the world** <term>soul of the world</term> <note>The "anima mundi," a concept where a vital spirit animates all matter in the universe, making the world a living being.</note>, as it is the act of all and the power of all, and is completely in all. Thus, in the end, even if there are innumerable individuals, everything is one; and to know this unity is the goal and limit of all natural philosophies and contemplations, leaving within its own boundaries that higher contemplation which ascends above nature—which, for one who does not believe, is impossible and nothing.

**Dic.** It is true; because one ascends to that through supernatural light, not natural light.

**Teo.** This light is not possessed by those who judge everything to be a body—either simple, like the ether, or composite, like the stars and astral things—and who do not seek divinity outside of the infinite world and infinite things, but within the world and in those very things.

**Dic.** In this alone does the faithful theologian seem to differ from the true philosopher.

**Teo.** So I also believe. I believe you have understood what I mean.

**Dic.** Very well, I think. So much so that from your words I infer that, although we do not let matter rise above natural things and we keep our footing on its common definition provided by the most vulgar philosophy, we will still find that it retains a better prerogative than that philosophy acknowledges. For that philosophy, in the end, grants it nothing else but the status of being a subject of forms and a receptive power for natural forms—without a name, without a definition, without any boundary, because it is without any actuality. This seemed difficult to certain **hooded ones** <term>hooded ones</term> <note>original: "cucullati"; a mocking or critical term for Scholastic monks or friars who strictly followed traditional Church teachings.</note> who, wishing not to accuse but to excuse this doctrine, say that matter has only an **entitative act** <term>entitative act</term> <note>A technical Scholastic term meaning the most basic level of existence—simply the fact that something *is*, even if it has no specific qualities yet.</note>—that is, something different from that which simply does not exist and has no being in nature, like some chimera or fictitious thing. For this matter, in the end, has being, and this is enough for it, even without the mode and dignity that depends on actuality, which they claim is nothing.

Why do you wish, O prince of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>, that matter should rather be nothing because it has no act, than be everything because it possesses all acts? Are you not the one who, always speaking of the "new being" of forms in matter, or of the generation of things, says that forms proceed and emerge from the interior of matter? And you were never heard to say that they come from the outside by the work of an efficient cause, but rather that the cause rouses them from within? Furthermore, you make the efficient cause of these things—which you call by the common name of **Nature**—an internal principle, and not...

**Dic.** And I say that being expressed, sensible, and unfolded is not the primary reason for actuality, but is a consequence and an effect of it. Just as the primary being of wood and the reason for its actuality does not consist in being a bed, but in being of such substance and consistency that it *can* be a bed, a bench, a beam, an idol, or anything else formed of wood. I will set aside the fact that, according to a higher reasoning, all natural things are made from natural matter just as artificial things are made from artificial matter; for art arouses forms from matter either by <term>subtraction</term> <note>original: "suttrazione." To these Moses also subscribed, who, in describing the generation of things commanded by the universal efficient cause, uses this way of speaking:

> Let the earth produce its animals; let the waters produce living souls;

it is as if he said: Let matter produce them. For, according to him, the material principle of things is water; hence he says that the efficient intellect, which he calls the "spirit," brooded over the waters—that is, he gave them procreative power, and from them produced the natural species, all of which are then said by him to be, in substance, water. Thus, speaking of the separation of the lower and upper bodies, he says that the Mind separated the waters from the waters, from the midst of which he suggests the dry land appeared. All these thinkers, therefore, believe things come from matter by way of separation, and not by way of addition and reception. Thus, one ought rather to say that matter contains the forms and includes them, than to think it is empty of them and excludes them. That matter, therefore, which unfolds what it holds enfolded, must be called a divine thing and the best parent, generator, and mother of natural things—

**Teo.** Certainly.

**Dic.** Indeed, I wonder greatly why our <term>Peripatetics</term> (followers of Aristotle’s philosophy) have not continued the analogy of art. In art, when one knows and handles many materials, one judges that material to be better and more worthy which is less subject to decay and more constant in its duration, and from which more things can be produced. Therefore, one judges gold to be more noble than wood, stone, or iron, because it is less subject to corruption; and whatever can be made of wood or stone can also be made of gold—and many other things besides, greater and better, because of its beauty, constancy, malleability, and nobility. And I certainly believe the particular form exists on the surface of matter just as an <term>accident</term> (a non-essential quality, like color) exists on the surface of a composite substance. Hence, the expressed form must have a lesser claim to actuality in respect to matter, just as an accidental form has a lesser claim to actuality in respect to the whole.

**Teo.** In truth, Aristotle resolves this poorly. He says, along with all the ancient philosophers, that principles must always be permanent; and then, when we search his doctrine for where the natural form has its perpetual permanence—this form which goes fluctuating on the back of matter—we will not find it in the fixed stars, for these particular things we see do not descend from on high; nor will we find it in the "ideal seals" <note>This refers to Plato's Theory of Forms, where "ideals" act as stamps or seals on reality.</note> separated from matter; for those certainly, if they are not monsters, are worse than monsters—I mean <term>chimeras</term> (impossible fancies) and vain fantasies. <meta>This page continues the Fourth Dialogue of "On the Cause, Principle, and One." are in the womb of matter? What then? She is the source of <term>actuality</term> (the state of being real and active). Do you want me to tell you more, and show you how great an absurdity Aristotle has fallen into? He says that matter is in <term>potentiality</term> (the capacity to become something). Now ask him: when will it be "in act" (actually real)? He and a great multitude will answer: "When it has form." Now follow up and ask: What is that thing which possesses this new being? They will answer, despite themselves: "The <term>composite</term> (the combination of matter and form), and not the matter; because matter is always the same, it is not renewed, it does not change." 

It is just as in artificial things: when a statue is made from wood, we do not say the wood has gained a new being, because it is no more or less wood now than it was before. Rather, that which receives being and actuality, and that which is newly produced, is the composite—I mean, the statue. How then can you say that "potentiality" belongs to that which will never be "in act," or never possess the "act"? Therefore, matter is not "in potentiality of being," or "that which can be," because she is always the same and immutable; she is that *around* which and *in* which change occurs, rather than that which changes. 

That which alters, increases, decreases, moves from place to place, or decays is always—according to you <term>Peripatetics</term> (followers of Aristotle) yourselves—the composite, never the matter. Why then do you say matter is sometimes "in potentiality" and sometimes "in act"? Certainly, there should be no doubt that whether matter is receiving forms or sending them out from herself, she does not receive any greater or lesser actuality in her essence and substance. Therefore, there is no reason for her to be called "in potentiality," a term which fits that which is in constant motion around her, but not her, who is in an eternal state—or rather, is the cause of that state. 

For if form, according to its fundamental and specific being, is of a simple and invariable essence—not only logically in concept and reason, but also physically in nature—it must reside in the perpetual faculty of matter. This matter is a potentiality indistinguishable from act, as I have explained in many ways when I have discussed potentiality so many times before.

<meta>This page concludes the Fourth Dialogue of "On the Cause, Principle, and One." Teofilo is finishing his argument against the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) view of matter, specifically addressing the idea that matter "desires" form like a female desires a male. He argues that matter is the eternal, divine source that precedes all transitory forms.</meta>

<page-num>279</page-num>

...an imperfect thing—such as the form of sensible things, which is always in motion—to an eternal thing? Or to another thing so perfect that, if one contemplates it well, it is a divine being within things? This is perhaps what David of Dinant <note>A 13th-century philosopher who was condemned for teaching that God, mind, and matter were the same primary substance</note> meant to say, though he was misunderstood by those who report his opinion. Matter does not desire form in order to be preserved by it; for a corruptible thing <note>Something that can decay or change</note> does not preserve an eternal thing. Furthermore, it is manifest that matter preserves the form; therefore, the form should rather desire matter in order to perpetuate itself. Because when the form separates from matter, the form loses its being, not the matter—for matter retains all that it had before that form existed, and can possess other forms. I will also point out that when the cause of <term>corruption</term> (the process of a thing breaking down or changing state) is given, one does not say that the form flees from the matter, or leaves the matter, but rather that the matter rejects that form in order to take another.

I add, moreover, that we have no more reason to say that matter <term>desires</term> (the philosophical concept of "appetite" or natural inclination) forms than to say, on the contrary, that she hates them—I speak of those forms which are generated and decay. This is because the source of forms, which is within matter itself, cannot desire them, considering that one does not desire what one already possesses. For the same reason that one might say she "desires" what she occasionally receives or produces, one can likewise say she "abhors" it when she rejects and casts it away. Indeed, she abhors more powerfully than she desires, considering that she eternally rejects that specific, individual form which she held for only a short time. If, then, you remember this—that she rejects as much as she takes—you must allow me to say that she feels disgust, just as I will allow you to say she feels desire.

**Gervasio**: Now behold, not only are the castles of Polyinnio <note>A pedantic character in the dialogue who represents traditional, rigid scholarship</note> cast to the ground, but those of others besides Polyinnio!

**Polyinnio**: Remember, however, to hurl such reproaches more sparingly at men! <note>original: "Parcius ista viris tamen obiicienda memento!" — a quote from Virgil's Eclogues III, used here by the pedant Polyinnio to demand more respect</note>

**Dicono**: We have understood enough for today. Until we meet again tomorrow!

**Teofilo**: Then, farewell!

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Fifth Dialogue of "On the Cause, Principle, and One." Having concluded the discussion on the nature of matter and its relationship to form in the previous dialogue, Teofilo now begins his famous synthesis: the description of the Universe as a singular, infinite, and divine unity that encompasses all contradictions.</meta>

<page-num>280</page-num>

## FIFTH DIALOGUE.

->Teofilo <note>The name means "Lover of God"; he serves as the primary spokesperson for Bruno’s own philosophical views.</note><-

**The** universe is, therefore, one, infinite, and immobile. One, I say, is the absolute possibility, one the act, one the form or soul, one the matter or body, one the thing, one the being, one the greatest and best. This "One" should not be capable of being <term>comprehended</term> (fully enclosed or understood by a finite mind), and is therefore indefinable and interminable, and thus infinite and indeterminate, and consequently immobile. It does not move locally, because it has nothing outside of itself to which it might be transported, given that it is the "all." It is not generated, because there is no other being that it could desire or expect, given that it possesses all being. It does not decay, because there is no other thing into which it could change, given that it is every thing. It cannot diminish or grow, given that it is infinite; just as nothing can be added to it, so nothing can be subtracted from it, because the infinite has no proportional parts. It cannot be altered into any other state, because it has no external force to suffer from, or by which it might be affected. Furthermore, because it contains all contradictions within its own being, in unity and harmony, and because it can have no inclination toward another or new being—or even toward another or different way of being—it cannot be subject to change according to any quality, nor can it have an opposite or something different that might alter it, because in it every thing is in agreement. It is not matter, because it is neither shaped nor shapeable, neither limited nor limitable. It is not form, because it does not give form or shape to anything else, given that it is everything, it is the greatest, it is one, it is the universe. It is not measurable, nor is it a measure. It does not contain itself, because it is not larger than itself. It is not contained, because it is not smaller than itself. It does not equal itself, because it is not "this" and "that," but one and the same. Being the same and one, it does not have "being" and "being" <note>Bruno means it does not have multiple distinct types of existence</note>, and because it does not have multiple types of being, it does not have part upon part; and because it does not have part upon part, it is not a composite. This "One" is a limit of such a kind that it is not a limit; it is form in such a way that it is not form; it is matter in such a way that it is not matter; it is soul in such a way that it is not soul; because it is the "all" without distinction, and therefore it is one; the universe is one. Within this unity, height is certainly no greater than length or depth; hence, by a certain analogy, it is called a sphere—though it is not a sphere <note>Bruno is referencing a famous medieval idea that "God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and circumference is nowhere."</note>. In a physical sphere, length, width, and depth are the same because they share the same boundary; but in the universe, width, length, and depth are the same thing because they likewise have no boundary and are infinite. If they have no center, no quadrant, and no other measures—if there is no measure, there is no proportional part, nor, strictly speaking, any part at all.

<summary>Teofilo begins the final dialogue by defining the universe as an infinite, singular, and immobile unity that transcends all physical categories like form, matter, and motion. He argues that because the universe is everything, it cannot change, move, or be divided into parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Teofilo's monologue from the beginning of the Fifth Dialogue. He is elaborating on the metaphysical identity of the "One," arguing that in an infinite universe, all distinctions—such as size, time, and geometric dimension—collapse into a single, unified reality.</meta>

...that differs from the whole. For if you wish to speak of a part of the infinite, you must call it infinite; if it is infinite, it coincides in one being with the whole: therefore the universe is one, infinite, and indivisible. And if no difference is found within the infinite, such as between whole and part, or between one thing and another, then certainly the infinite is one. Within the comprehension of the infinite, there is no greater part and no smaller part; for a part, however large it may be, does not approach the proportion of the infinite any more than another part, however small it may be.

And therefore, in infinite duration, the hour does not differ from the day, the day from the year, the year from the century, or the century from the moment; for moments and hours are no more numerous than centuries, and the former have no smaller proportion to eternity than the latter. Similarly, in the immense, a palm <note>original: "palmo"; an ancient unit of length based on the width of the hand.</note> is no different from a <term>stade</term> <note>original: "stadio"; an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note>, nor a stade from a <term>parasang</term> <note>original: "parasanga"; an ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 5 to 6 kilometers.</note>; for one does not approach the proportion of immensity any more through parasangs than through palms. Therefore, infinite hours are no more than infinite centuries, and infinite palms are no greater in number than infinite parasangs.

To the proportion, likeness, union, and identity of the infinite, you do not approach any closer by being a man than by being an ant, or by being a star than by being a man; for to that Being you draw no nearer by being a sun or a moon than by being a man or an ant; and therefore, in the infinite, these things are indifferent <note>In this context, "indifferent" means "not different" or having no distinct essence that separates them from the whole.</note>. And what I say of these, I mean for all other things of particular existence. Now, if all these particular things in the infinite are not "one thing and another," are not different, and are not distinct species, then by necessary consequence they are not a "number"; thus, the universe is also one and immobile. 

This universe, because it comprises everything and does not suffer from having one being or another, and allows for no change within or upon itself, is consequently all that it can be; and in it, as I said the other day, <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "atto"; the state of being fully realized or "in act."</note> is not different from <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potenza"; the capacity or power to become something.</note>. If actuality is not different from potentiality, it is necessary that within it the point, the line, the surface, and the body do not differ: for that line is a surface in the same way that a line, by moving, can become a surface; and that surface is moved and made into a body in the same way that a surface can move and, through its flow, can become a body. 

It is necessary, then, that the point in the infinite does not differ from the body; for the point, by flowing from its state as a point, becomes a line; by flowing from its state as a line, it becomes a surface; by flowing from its state as a surface, it becomes a body. The point, therefore, because it has the potentiality to be a body, does not differ from being a body in a state where potentiality and actuality are one and the same thing. Thus, that which is <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "individuo"; literally "the individual," but here referring to the geometric point or atom which cannot be divided.</note> is not different from that which is <term>divisible</term> <note>original: "dividuo"; things that can be partitioned.</note>, the simplest is not different from the infinite, and the center is not different from the circumference. 

Therefore, because the infinite is all that it can be, it is immobile; because in it all is indifferent, it is one; and because it possesses all the magnitude and perfection that can be had beyond and further beyond, it is the greatest, the best, and the immense. If the point does not...

And thus it was not said in vain that Jupiter fills all things <note>original: "Giove empie tutte le cose"; a reference to the Latin phrase *Iovis omnia plena*, often used by Bruno to represent the World Soul or the divine presence permeating the cosmos.</note>, inhabits all parts of the universe, and is the center of that which has its being as one in all, and through which "one" is "all." But you might ask me: "Why then do things change? Why does particular matter strive for other forms?" I reply to you that there is no mutation that seeks another *being*, but only another *way* of being. And this is the difference between the universe and the things within the universe: for the universe comprises all being and all ways of being; whereas of the things within it, each has all being, but not all ways of being. 

A particular thing cannot actually possess all circumstances and <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change (like color or size) without changing the essential nature of the thing itself.</note>, because many forms are incompatible within the same subject, either because they are opposites or because they belong to different species. For example, the same individual subject cannot exist under the <term>accidents</term> of both a horse and a man, or under the dimensions of both a plant and an animal. Furthermore, the universe comprises all being totally, because outside and beyond infinite being there is nothing that exists, having no "outside" nor "beyond." Of these particular things, however, each comprises all being, but not totally, because beyond each one there are infinite others. 

Therefore, understand that "all is in all," but not totally and in every possible way in each one. Therefore, understand how every thing is one, but not in a single way. Thus, he does not err who says that <term>Being</term> <note>original: "l'ente"; a technical term for that which exists.</note>, Substance, and Essence are one. Within the one, infinite, and immobile thing—which is the substance, which is the Being—one finds the "multitude," or number. But number, being merely a "mode" or a "multi-formity" of Being (which serves to name one thing after another), does not make Being more than one; rather, it makes it multi-modal, multi-formed, and multi-figured. Therefore, considering deeply with the natural philosophers <note>The "natural philosophers" were the scientists of Bruno's day, though he often contrasts them with "logicians" who deal only in words.</note> and leaving the logicians to their fantasies, we find that everything that creates difference and number is pure <term>accident</term>, pure figure, or pure complexion. <meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the "One."
